### 188th finding (Round 148, real DeliverEvent call site for CDROM class 0xF0000003 + live root-cause of why it didn't move the trace)

Per the user's explicit instruction ("find all subsystems, modules or drivers which are missing and implement them even if you have to reverse engineer the 0xF03 or DeliverEvent to figure out whats calling or needed... just do it"), directly following up on the 182nd/183rd/184th/187th findings' open question: what real IOP kernel event class/spec is the traced `ev=3,spec=5` (handle `0x0503`) and `ev=3,spec=15` (handle `0x0F03`) actually waiting on, and does anything in this project's own hardware models ever call `DeliverEvent` for it.

**Research (directly fetched, not guessed)**: pulled psx-spx's `kernelbios.md` raw source directly (`raw.githubusercontent.com/psx-spx/psx-spx.github.io/master/docs/kernelbios.md`, 1776 lines). Confirmed, quoted verbatim: the real PS1/PS2 kernel event class table lists `F0000003h IRQ2 (CDROM Decoder)`, and the per-completion-type spec table for that class lists `20h`/`8000h` (paired, general async completion - used by `CdAsyncSeekL`/`CdAsyncGetStatus`/`CdAsyncReadSector`) and `80h` (`CdAsyncReadSector`'s "reached end of disk", i.e. real hardware INT4). Under this project's own already-implemented `GetEv()`/`GetSpec()` hash (cited from emumaster, Round 142), class `0xF0000003` hashes to `ev=3` and spec `0x20`/`0x8000` hash to indices `5`/`15` - an exact, doubly-confirmed match to the traced handles `0x0503`/`0x0F03`, resolving what the 184th finding had explicitly flagged as an unconfirmed, AI-summary-sourced guess into a real, citable fact.

**Implemented**: `iop_hle_event_deliver_raw(class_code, spec_mask)` (`iop_hle_events.h`/`.c`) - a direct hardware-model entry point into the existing real `OpenEvent`/`EnableEvent`/`DeliverEvent`/`TestEvent` EvCB lifecycle (Round 142), documented as this project's clean-room stand-in for the real, cited "`DefaultInterruptHandlers`... does randomly trigger Events" always-on kernel mechanism (also directly quoted from the same psx-spx page) - since this project has no real BIOS-resident interrupt-handler-chain execution, hardware models call the delivery function directly instead. Wired into `iop_cdrom_legacy.c`'s `raise_int()`: `INT1`/`INT2` deliver spec `0x0020`+`0x8000`; `INT4` delivers spec `0x0080`. New test coverage in `tests/test_iop_cdrom_legacy.c` (four new assertions, 21->25 total): opens+enables real EvCB handles for both specs, issues a real Pause command sequence, confirms both specs are delivered on the resulting `INT2`. All 25 pass. (One self-caught bug during test-writing: forgot to call `EnableEvent` after `OpenEvent` before expecting delivery to take effect - `deliver_ev_spec()`'s pre-existing, correct `status != ACTIVE` guard silently no-ops otherwise, exactly as designed since Round 142. Fixed in the test, not the production code - the guard was correct.)

**Live re-verification found the real answer, not the one first assumed**: instrumented (diagnostic-only, not committed) `iop_cdrom_legacy.c`/`iop_hle_events.c` with call counters and ran the same 45M-instruction diskless boot trace used since Round 140. Findings:
- `dispatch_command()` fires **exactly once** in the entire 45M-instruction run, with `cmd=0x02` (Setloc).
- `raise_int()` fires **only** `INT3` (the synchronous command-acknowledge interrupt) - `INT1`/`INT2`/`INT4` never fire, because no second (actual seek/read) command is ever issued after Setloc.
- The driver **does** call `OpenEvent`+`EnableEvent` six times for class `0xF0000003` (confirmed: `last_open_class=0xF0000003`, `last_open_mode=0x2000`=NOINTR) - so the kernel-event registration side is real and does execute live.
- `iop_hle_event_deliver_raw()` is correctly wired and reachable (unit-tested), but is called **zero times** live, because `INT3` (the only interrupt that ever fires) is deliberately not mapped to any spec - `INT3` is the real hardware's synchronous stat-ack, not one of the three documented async-completion types (`20h`/`8000h`/`80h`), so this is correct behavior, not a gap.
- HCLRCTL (bank1 offset3, the real interrupt-acknowledge register) is written twice, confirming the driver did read the Setloc ack and moved on cleanly - not stuck spinning on it.
- The apparent "135K writes / 180K reads" from the CD-ROM MMIO handler functions turned out to be call-count noise from a shared bus-dispatch pattern (the handler is invoked for every IOP MMIO access project-wide and self-filters by address range) - only 1 real command write and 1 real status read ever actually land inside the CD-ROM's own address range.

**Honest conclusion**: this round's DeliverEvent implementation is real, correct, and now verified reachable in principle - but the CD-ROM subsystem is conclusively a **one-time early boot-time probe** (Setloc, ack, done) in this project's current boot trace, not an active polling loop, and it is **not** the cause of the persistent `IOP pc=0x0003ECA0` stall (unchanged across Rounds 142/145/146/147/148). The 184th/187th findings' working hypothesis - that the CD-ROM/memory-card event-delivery gap was *the* blocker - is now conclusively ruled out by direct live measurement, not just re-asserted. This is real negative-result progress: the DeliverEvent mechanism itself is done and no longer a suspect; the actual cause of the `0x0003ECA0` stall is unrelated and still open (tracked as a fresh lead, not a continuation of the CD-ROM thread).

**Verified**: `iop_cdrom_legacy.c`/`iop_hle_events.c`/`iop_hle_events.h` compile clean (`-Wall -Wextra`, no warnings). Full regression suite: **108/108 files, 0 failures** (re-verified in full this round, including files affected by the prior round's false-positive-prone ad hoc pass/fail text heuristics - all confirmed real passes). Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: exit 0, same single pre-existing unrelated `strncpy` warning as every prior round.

**Next**: root-cause what `IOP pc=0x0003ECA0` is actually doing/waiting on - a fresh investigation thread, unrelated to CD-ROM/memory-card/event-delivery (all three of which are now real, tested, and ruled out as the cause). Tracked as Round 149.

### 189th finding (Round 149, live-debugger + self-read confirmation of the real B0h/TestEvent polling loop; disc-mount experiment rules out "no disc" hypothesis; no source change)

Connected directly to a live PCSX2 DebugServer session (already available this session, no manual relay needed) and cross-checked against a self-read disassembly of this project's own IOP RAM (the established Round 133/141/154/162 technique) to precisely characterize the address cluster (`0x00031020-0x00031044`, `0x0003EC80-0x0003ECD0`) the IOP repeatedly revisits.

**Confirmed, via direct self-read of real BIOS instruction words**: `0x0003ECA0` is the real B0h kernel syscall trampoline for function `0x0B` (`li $t2,0xB0; jr $t2` / delay slot `li $t1,0x0B`) - i.e. `TestEvent`, exactly matching Round 141's original citation-based finding, now visually verified rather than inferred. The neighboring stubs at `0x0003EC90`/`0x0003ECB0`/`0x0003ECC0` are the same real trampoline pattern for other B0h functions (`0xA0`, `0xC0`, `0x02`, `0x08` in the delay-slot function-number registers) - confirms this is a real, dense cluster of kernel syscall stubs, not something specific to this project.

**Confirmed the exact polling loop body**: `0x00031020-0x00031044` is `lui a0,0x8005; lw a0,0x6C64(a0); jal 0x0003ECA0` (TestEvent on handle at RAM `0x80056C64`, i.e. `0x0503` = spec 5/class 3) `; beq/bne <check> ; lui a0,0x8005; lw a0,0x6C70(a0); jal 0x0003ECA0` (TestEvent on handle at `0x80056C70`, i.e. `0x0F03` = spec 15/class 3) `; bne ... -> loop`. This is precisely the loop Round 141/142/148 already reasoned about from citations and RAM contents - now confirmed byte-for-byte via direct self-read, closing any remaining doubt about what this loop actually is.

**Disc-mount experiment (new this round)**: built a synthetic ISO9660 disc image (same public/non-proprietary technique as `test_iop_cdrom_legacy.c`/`test_iso_loader.c`) and called the already-existing, opt-in `iop_cdrom_legacy_mount_iso()` before running the same 45M-instruction boot trace. **Result: byte-for-byte identical to the diskless case** - `dispatch_command()` still fires exactly once (`Setloc`), IOP still rests at `0x0003ECA0`. This rules out "the driver is correctly waiting because no disc is present" as an explanation - the boot flow never even attempts to check for a disc via a second CD-ROM command, mounted or not, so disc presence is not the variable that matters here.

**Extended-budget check (new this round)**: re-ran with 90M instructions (double the standard budget) - `dispatch_command()` call count still exactly 1, confirming this is a genuine steady-state loop, not a slow real-time retry that simply needs a bigger instruction budget.

**Refined conclusion**: the 188th finding's DeliverEvent implementation is correct and this round's investigation now shows precisely why it doesn't help: the polling loop is real, is genuinely testing the exact CD-ROM class-3/spec-5/15 handles this project implemented delivery for, and never resolves because nothing ever calls `DeliverEvent` for them - not because CD-ROM lacks the capability (Round 148 built it), but because the boot flow never issues the async CD-ROM command (`SeekL`/`GetStatus`/`ReadN`) that would trigger it, regardless of whether a disc is mounted. The remaining open question, scoped for a future round: trace the real caller of the observed `Setloc` (cmd `0x02`) to find why it never follows up with the actual async command - this needs a live backtrace/call-site trace at the moment `Setloc` executes (not yet captured; the live PCSX2 session used this round was mid-game, past this boot phase, so it could only confirm the trampoline architecture, not the live call site).

No source change this round - live-debugger + self-read diagnostic investigation only.

### 190th finding (Round 150, precise real caller of our own diskless boot's Setloc; two distinct CD-ROM code paths identified; no source change)

The user supplied a live-trace report (`pcsx2_setloc_real_caller_report.md`) giving a real backtrace for `Setloc` captured mid-game in a live GT3 session: resolved `Setloc` address `0x00004b3c`, caller `0x0000d7c4`. Followed up by self-reading that exact region from our own emulator's IOP RAM.

**Finding #1**: the address `0x0000d7c4` (the user's live-trace caller) is unloaded (all zero) in our own diskless boot at 45M instructions - it belongs to a dynamically-loaded module context that only exists once real game/disc loading has progressed far past where our diskless boot ever reaches. Not directly usable for our scenario as-is.

**Finding #2**: the real, resident kernel code at `0x00004b3c` (matching the user's resolved address, present in our own memory too since it's part of the always-resident BIOS-embedded kernel image) turned out to be a "full" Setloc wrapper: it installs two callback function pointers into fixed globals (meant to be invoked on CD-ROM interrupt completion), sets a busy flag, caches the loc parameters, and returns - it does not itself touch CD-ROM hardware registers. This is architecturally consistent with a real async driver pattern (register a completion callback, let the interrupt path invoke it later).

**Finding #3 (decisive)**: after our own diskless boot's real `Setloc` command dispatch fires, the callback-pointer globals this "full" wrapper would have set are still all zero. This proves our own boot's `Setloc` does **not** go through that wrapper at all - it's a separate, more primitive code path.

**Finding #4**: added a precise hook (captures the IOP `$ra` at the exact instant the real command dispatch fires, not sampled after the fact) and traced our own boot's actual caller: a generic-looking dispatch routine (distinct from the "full" driver) that conditionally stores its argument into a global near the already-known TestEvent-handle addresses, then calls a further function to actually issue the command. This confirms two genuinely separate, real code paths exist for issuing CD-ROM commands in the real kernel - our diskless boot only ever reaches the simpler one, consistent with no CDVDMAN-class module ever being loaded (expected for a diskless boot).

**Net result**: this refines but does not yet close the 189th finding's open question. The real caller chain for our own boot's Setloc is now precisely known down to the instruction level (self-read confirmed, not guessed), narrowing the search - the next step is to trace forward from this caller (specifically the function it jumps into to perform the actual dispatch) to see whether it, or something downstream of it, is what's supposed to issue the follow-up async command and/or drive the TestEvent-satisfying DeliverEvent call this project built in Round 148.

No source change this round - self-read + live-debugger investigation only, using the user-supplied live-trace report as a cross-reference (which turned out to describe a different, later-stage code path than our diskless boot exercises, itself a useful negative result).

### 191th finding (Round 151, traced the jal-target dispatcher; table contents inconclusive; scope note; no source change)

Followed up on the user's `pcsx2_address_analysis_0x00235aac.md` (which analyzed the wrong address space - `0x00235AAC` is an EE/game-ELF address from `pcsx2_full_disassembly.txt`, while the actual address in question, `0x00035AAC`, is IOP RAM - a different processor and address space entirely; noted and corrected for the user).

Self-read the real jal target (`0x00035AAC`) directly from our own emulator (the live PCSX2 session's IOP RAM was empty there too, same "not loaded yet in this mid-game context" situation as the prior round's caller address). Confirmed it is real, executable code: a small dispatcher that reads a one-byte "device type" selector from a fixed global, uses it to index a small table (`t6<<3` stride), and loads a 16-bit value from the indexed slot - a classic compiled switch-statement/jump-table pattern, architecturally consistent with a generic device-request router rather than CD-ROM-specific code.

**Read the actual table contents**: the device-type selector currently reads `0`, and the table slot it indexes (and, notably, every neighboring slot checked) holds an identical, uniform `0x007F007F`-repeating pattern rather than distinct per-device values. This is inconclusive - it may be a real sentinel/default pattern, or it may indicate this project's manual, by-hand MIPS decoding has drifted off the true table base (register reconstruction across several instructions is easy to get subtly wrong without a proper disassembler). Not confident enough to draw a conclusion from it.

**Scope note**: continued manual, by-hand decoding of raw MIPS instruction words (this round's technique) is reaching diminishing returns - it's slow and error-prone once the trail moves through table lookups and computed addresses, versus a proper disassembler. The live PCSX2 DebugServer connection (already established this session) has this natively (`pcsx2_disassemble`), but the *live* session is mid-game and no longer has the diskless-boot-equivalent code paths resident in memory to inspect directly. A more productive Round 152 approach: use the live session's conditional-breakpoint capability at the CD-ROM COMMAND register address during an actual disc-based boot (not mid-game) to catch a *real* second command dispatch in the act, with clean native disassembly and a real backtrace - rather than continuing to reconstruct control flow by hand from an already-diskless, already-terminal trace.

No source change this round - investigation only.

### 192nd finding (Round 152, live conditional-trace of real CD/DVD streaming during active FMV playback; no source change)

Controlled the user's live PCSX2 reference session directly (desktop access, granted by user) to advance a real disc-based GT3 boot from the language-select menu into an actual FMV intro - genuine ongoing CD/DVD streaming, not the one-time boot probe examined in Rounds 148-151.

**Watchpoint attempt inconclusive**: set write watchpoints on both the real PS2 CDVD register block (`0x1F402000`-`0x1F402020`, base address confirmed via the open-source ps2sdk `cdvdman.c` reimplementation - `GetBaseAddress(5)`/`SetBaseAddress(5, 0x1F402000)`) and the legacy PS1-style CD-ROM block (`0x1F801800`-`0x1F801804`, the block targeted in Rounds 145-151). Neither fired during active FMV streaming, despite confirmed real disc reads occurring (the FMV played correctly). The MCP watchpoint tool's schema has no CPU selector (unlike disassemble/backtrace, which do) - most likely it only scopes to EE-side memory access and cannot see IOP-local hardware register writes, which would fully explain the non-fire. Logged as a tooling limitation, not a game/hardware finding.

**Direct IOP register sampling (decisive)**: paused/read/resumed the live IOP CPU repeatedly during continuous FMV playback.
- Multiple samples over an initial ~9-second window landed on the exact same PC (`0x0000B694`) with byte-identical register state each time. Disassembly confirmed this is a literal `j` (jump) to its own address - a genuine infinite spin loop, not a polling read of any hardware register. This is real evidence that the retail IOP kernel's true idle state is a bare "jump to self," and that it can sit there, doing nothing, for multiple seconds at a time even while the console is actively streaming video off the disc.
- A later sample (after ~13 total seconds of continuous playback) caught the IOP away from that idle point, mid-burst, at `pc=0x0000BC64`, `ra=0x00004EB0`. Backtrace: frame #0 at entry `0x0000BB70` (current), frame #1 at entry `0x00004BC4` (immediately adjacent to the "full driver" Setloc wrapper's resident code region identified in Round 150, `0x00004AE8`-`0x4B80`).

**What the burst is doing** (self-read/disassembled live, architectural description only, no literal bytes transcribed here): the function at `0x0000BB70` is a driver-queue append/service routine - it takes a request-block pointer, checks a mode field, logs via a shared string-table print helper (`0x00011504`) for two distinct states, appends the request into a queue structure anchored at a fixed global (`0x00011A60`), and then - the exact branch our live pause landed on - checks a "busy count" global (`0x00011A64`): if zero, calls a queue-kick function at `0x0000B8EC`; otherwise walks the queue and calls a rate/throughput helper (`0x000110A4`) using two fields that look like elapsed-time and byte-count accumulators. Following `0x0000B8EC` further: it dequeues the head request, allocates a channel/slot index bounded to 128 (`0x0000B888`, `< 0x80`), indexes an 8-byte-stride per-channel table anchored at the same `0x00011A60` global, and dispatches to `0x0000B778` (not yet examined further this round) - architecturally, this is exactly where a real hardware register write to issue the next disc transfer would live.

**Conclusion**: real PS2 CD/DVD streaming during active gameplay/FMV is driven by a genuine async, queue-based I/O scheduler with per-channel dispatch (up to 128 channels - almost certainly a generic kernel I/O subsystem shared across drivers, not CD-ROM-specific code), serviced in occasional bursts, not a continuous CPU polling loop. This is structurally different from the one-time Setloc/TestEvent boot-time probe examined in Rounds 148-151, and confirms (independently, via live trace of real hardware) that Round 149's conclusion - "nothing ever calls DeliverEvent's CD-ROM class because the boot flow never issues a follow-up async CD command" - was about the *boot probe* specifically, not a general statement about how real CD/DVD I/O works. The real runtime mechanism (queue + channel table + rate limiter) is a materially bigger subsystem than anything implemented in this project's current CD-ROM driver.

No source change this round. This queue/channel architecture is a candidate direction for a future round if/when the project needs real in-game (not just boot-time) disc streaming, but implementing it is out of scope for this investigation round.

### 193rd finding (Round 153, task #307): real async I/O queue + labeled boot-unblock kick - confirmed real forward progress

Root-caused precisely why Round 149's TestEvent wait never resolves: `iop_cdrom_legacy.c`'s `raise_int()` already correctly calls `iop_hle_event_deliver_raw()` for class 0xF0000003 spec 0x0020/0x8000 on real INT1/INT2 completion (task #301, Round 148) - but Setloc (opcode 0x02, the only CD-ROM command this project's diskless boot ever issues) only produces INT3 (immediate ack), never INT1/INT2 (per psx-spx's real, cited command table, correctly modeled - see this file's earlier citation trail). With no other CD-ROM command ever issued, DeliverEvent for this class was structurally unreachable in the diskless boot, regardless of any device-dispatch table details (Rounds 150-152's investigation).

**Built two things this round, unified into one mechanism:**

1. `include/core/hw/iop_asyncio.h` / `source/hw/iop_asyncio.c` - a real, clean-room async I/O request queue with a 128-channel dispatch table and a busy-count/burst-servicing gate (services exactly one request per tick), architecturally modeled on Round 152's live trace of the real reference session's CD/DVD driver (queue-append, busy-count check, bounded channel allocator) - not a transcription of any real address, struct layout, or byte value. Wired into `iop_core_step()` (ticked unconditionally every scheduler slice, same rationale as the existing timer/VBLANK ticks) and `iop_core_init()`.

2. A clearly-labeled, explicitly NON-cited boot-unblock: Setloc's handler now also enqueues a completion request (`cdrom_boot_kick_complete()`) into the real async queue above. Its code comment states plainly that this is NOT a claim about real Setloc behavior (psx-spx does not document Setloc producing INT1/INT2/INT4) - it exists solely so this project's own diskless boot's real, cited B0h/TestEvent wait can resolve and boot can keep progressing, routed through genuine queue infrastructure rather than an unconditional bare call.

**Empirically verified the fix works** (host-native diagnostic, real `scph10000.bin`, `system_init`+`system_run_interleaved`, 45,000,000-slice budget): built and ran the exact same diagnostic against both the pre-fix code (via `git stash`, isolating just this round's changes) and the post-fix code.
- Before: IOP parked at `pc=0x0003ECA0` (the real B0h/TestEvent trampoline, confirmed stuck - exactly Round 149's finding).
- After: IOP has moved on to `pc=0x00032C84` - genuinely different code, real forward progress past the TestEvent wall.
- EE side is unchanged at `pc=0x80005E98` in both runs (the separate SBUS_SMFLG spin-wait from Round 131/task #172) - expected, since that's a distinct, later blocker this round doesn't address.

**Tests**: new `tests/test_iop_asyncio.c` (20 assertions: enqueue/service round-trip, one-request-per-service() burst semantics, round-robin channel reuse, 128-channel exhaustion/rejection). `tests/test_iop_cdrom_legacy.c` updated to link the new dependency; all its existing assertions (including the task #301 DeliverEvent checks) still pass unmodified. Full regression: **109/109 test files pass, 0 failures**. Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild succeeds (only one pre-existing, unrelated warning in `iop_module_loader.c`).

### 195th finding (Round 155, task #309): loop-blocking field identified as part of a large, non-CD-ROM-specific kernel subsystem; inconclusive on exact semantics; no source change

Systematically searched (self-read, whole-2MB-IOP-RAM scan for any LW/SW instruction with immediate offset exactly 0x6C94, taken after a 45M-slice real-BIOS boot run so the relevant module code is actually resident) rather than continuing manual guesswork from a single call site. ### 197th finding (Round 157, task #311): real reference session is doubly deadlocked - EE self-loop at 0x00081fc0 AND both EE/IOP interrupt controllers fully masked, ~4.2 billion real EE cycles with zero progress

Followed up on Round 156's discovery that the live reference session (real PCSX2 + real BIOS + real GT3, freshly reset) parks at EE `pc=0x00081fc0` rather than reaching the task #181 syscall(-5) trampoline. Disassembled a wider window (`0x00081f60`-`0x00081ffc`) on the live session to understand the surrounding structure precisely, instead of continuing to treat the earlier narrow dump as self-explanatory.

**Structure clarified:**
- `0x00081f90`-`0x00081fb4`: not code. Linear disassembly misdecodes this as garbage instructions (`?????`, a spurious `mult`, etc.), but the raw words at `0x00081fb0`/`0x00081fb4` are exactly `0x00081fec` and `0x00081ff4` - the addresses of the trampoline's `li v1,-5` and its post-syscall return point. This is a small literal/pointer table (data), not executed code - a classic pattern for a relocatable interrupt-dispatch stub that patches/reads its own continuation addresses.
- `0x00081fc0`-`0x00081fd8`: real code, a tight loop - six `nop`s followed by `b ->0x00081fc0` at `0x00081fd8`. Decoded at the opcode level: `0x1000fff9` = `BEQ $zero,$zero,-7` - an unconditional branch (MIPS's standard `b` pseudo-op encoding). There is no conditional exit; the only way out is an asynchronous interrupt that redirects PC elsewhere before/instead of returning here.
- `0x00081fe0`-`0x00081ff0`: the task #181 trampoline (`lui sp,8` / `jalr v1` / `addiu sp,sp,0x1fc0` / `li v1,-5` / `syscall`), confirmed at the exact addresses matching that earlier finding's quoted disassembly. `0x00081ff4` (task #181's originally-named halt PC) is the instruction immediately after the `syscall`.

**Confirmed genuinely stuck, not just under-sampled**: re-checked `pcsx2_status` after the Round 156 wait sequence - `Cycles` had advanced from ~11.8 million (immediately post-reset) to **4,214,751,232** (after ~90 real seconds of continued execution), yet EE `pc` was still exactly `0x00081fc0` both times. Over roughly 4.2 billion real EE cycles of continued execution, the CPU never advanced past the unconditional loop into the trampoline at `0x00081fe0`+.

**Interrupt state checked directly (real, live memory reads, not inferred):**
- EE INTC `I_STAT` (`0x1000f000`) = `0x00000000` - nothing pending.
- EE INTC `I_MASK` (`0x1000f010`) = `0x00000000` - every interrupt source individually masked off at the controller, regardless of COP0 `Status.IE`.
- COP0 `Status` = `0x70030c11` (IE=1, i.e. globally enabled) - but with `I_MASK=0` this is moot; no source can reach the CPU.
- IOP INTC `I_STAT` (`0x1f801070`) = `0x00000000`, `I_MASK` (`0x1f801074`) = `0x00000000` - the IOP side is in the identical fully-masked, nothing-pending state.

**Conclusion**: this is not a timing issue that more waiting would resolve. The real reference session has both CPUs simultaneously idling in unconditional/self-jump loops (EE at `0x00081fc0`, IOP at `0x0000b694`, per Round 156) with *every* interrupt source on *both* interrupt controllers masked off and nothing pending. Nothing in this state can ever wake either CPU, since the EE loop has no polling/comparison logic of its own (it is bare `nop`s + unconditional branch) and depends entirely on an interrupt that the current mask configuration forbids. This refines task #181's original framing: the real, immediate blocker at this boot stage is not "syscall v1=-5 is unimplemented" (this project's own emulator reaches and needs to handle that trampoline via a different path/timing) - it is this upstream self-loop, and getaway from it depends on whatever real kernel code path is supposed to call `EnableIntr`/unmask the relevant IRQ (VBLANK is the most likely real-hardware candidate for a kernel idle loop of this shape, though this was not confirmed with a citation this round) before this loop is ever entered, or on an interrupt handler that deliberately does not return to the interrupted PC.

No source change this round - investigation only, performed entirely via live reads against the real reference session.

### 198th finding (Round 158, task #312): real EE interrupt dispatcher is alive and populated - the gap is narrower than "nothing is set up," it's specifically that INTC_MASK (0x1000f010) itself was never written

Per explicit user direction to pursue the real kernel-code-path angle and to check whether PCSX2's own open-source repository has anything helpful for understanding real EE kernel behavior, cross-referenced two citable sources before returning to the live session:

1. **PCSX2's own source** (`Hw.cpp`, `https://github.com/PCSX2/pcsx2/blob/master/pcsx2/Hw.cpp`): `intcInterrupt()` requires `psHu32(INTC_STAT) & psHu32(INTC_MASK)` to be nonzero before it ever raises the EE's interrupt exception (cause code `0x400`); `hwIntcIrq(int n)` only calls `cpuTestINTCInts()` (which can lead to that exception) `if (psHu32(INTC_MASK) & (1<<n))`. PCSX2 does not reimplement the real BIOS kernel (it runs the real ROM), so this doesn't tell us who *should* write `INTC_MASK` - but it confirms, from the actual emulator's own hardware model, that nothing auto-enables it; it is purely software-controlled, matching this project's own existing INTC model.
2. **"Writing a PlayStation 2 BIOS in Rust"** (`https://rust-console.github.io/ps2-bios-book/md/3_exceptions.html`), a citable, openly-licensed (CC-BY-SA 4.0 text / GPLv3 code) community reference: documents the real EE exception vector addresses. With `Status.BEV=0` (confirmed from our Round 157 read of the live session's `Status=0x70030c11` - bit 22 clear), the EE's real Interrupt exception vector is `0000'0200` (i.e. `0x80000200` in the KSEG0-mapped form this project's traces consistently use).

**Live-disassembled the real handler at `0x80000200`** on the reference session: it's a real, fully generic, functioning priority-based interrupt dispatcher, not stub/dead code - `mfc0 Cause` / `mfc0 Status`, ANDs them, isolates the IP/IM byte, uses `plzcw` (parallel leading-zero count, a real EE MMI opcode) to find the highest-priority pending+enabled line, computes a table index, and `lw`+`jr`s through a 32-entry function-pointer jump table based at `0x800123c0`.

**Read that jump table directly** (`0x800123c0`, 32 words): it is **not** all-zero/uninitialized - several distinct real addresses are present (`0x80000380`, `0x800004c0`, `0x80000600`, `0x80001d58`, a repeated default-looking `0x80001630`, and a notably distant `0x80076488`, `0x800014d8`). This proves real kernel initialization ran far enough to populate specific interrupt handlers before the boot reached the Round 157 self-loop - the dispatch *infrastructure* is alive and real, not merely absent.

**Conclusion**: this narrows the gap identified in Round 157 considerably. It is not that "interrupt handling was never set up" - it demonstrably was, per this live, direct evidence. It is specifically that the raw hardware `INTC_MASK` register (`0x1000f010`) itself was never written to a nonzero value by whatever real kernel/game code path is supposed to do so (the standard homebrew-visible mechanism for this, per ps2sdk's public API surface already cited elsewhere in this project, is `EnableIntc()`/the kernel's internal equivalent) - so even though the dispatcher and its table are ready and real handlers exist, no source can ever actually reach `cpuTestINTCInts()`/the `0x400` exception per PCSX2's own confirmed model, and the CPU is left spinning in Round 157's self-loop indefinitely.

No source change this round - investigation only, via live reads against the real reference session plus two independently citable external sources.

### 199th finding (Round 159, task #313): Fast Boot ruled out - fresh reset with Fast Boot disabled reproduces the identical 0x00081fc0/INTC_MASK=0 stall

Per the user's own action (disabling PCSX2's "Fast Boot" setting) plus the still-outstanding Round 158 loose end, forced a genuinely fresh reset of the live reference session and re-checked. GUI interaction was unreliable this round (System > Reset clicks had no effect at all while the DebugServer held the CPU paused - `Cycles` and `pc` were bit-for-bit identical across two separate Reset attempts made while paused); the fix was to `pcsx2_continue()` first so the emulation thread was actually running, then issue the Reset click, then re-pause. This produced a real state change: `Cycles` dropped from `4,237,295,616` to `3,238,395,904` - a decrease that can only happen if the core genuinely reinitialized (cycle counters cannot go backwards during continued execution), confirming this was a real, fresh boot rather than a continuation of the old session.

**Result with Fast Boot disabled**: EE `pc` settled at exactly `0x00081fc0` again - the identical self-loop from Round 157. Re-read the EE INTC registers directly: `I_STAT` (`0x1000f000`) = `0`, `I_MASK` (`0x1000f010`) = `0` - the identical all-masked, nothing-pending state from Round 157/158.

**Conclusion**: this rules out Fast Boot as a confounding factor for the Round 157/158 findings. The real reference session reaches the same self-loop with the same fully-masked interrupt controller state whether Fast Boot is on or off, so the earlier findings describe a genuine property of this real BIOS+game combination's boot sequence at this stage, not an artifact of that setting. The open question from Round 158 (what real kernel/game code path is supposed to write `INTC_MASK` nonzero, and why it hasn't by this point) remains the live, correct next target - not session configuration.

**GUI note for future rounds**: PCSX2's System menu actions (Reset, Start Disc, Shut Down) appear to silently no-op while the DebugServer has the CPU paused; the emulation must be resumed (`pcsx2_continue()`) before issuing menu-driven System actions, then re-paused afterward once confirmed via `pcsx2_status`'s `Cycles` value (not via screenshot alone, which this session's window has repeatedly rendered unreliably).

### 200th finding (Round 160, task #313 continuation): extended watchpoint window on INTC_MASK stays at zero hits; partially mapped a candidate real registration-list dispatcher; found and documented a live-tooling reliability gap

Per the user's explicit "both" direction, pursued the Round 159 (a)/(b) options simultaneously against the live reference session.

**(a) Watchpoint on INTC_MASK.** Armed a real `write`-type watchpoint on `0x1000f010`-`0x1000f014` (`pcsx2_set_watchpoint`, confirmed via `pcsx2_list_watchpoints`) and let the reference session run continuously for a 180-second real-time window (three sequential 60s waits), the longest observation window used in this investigation so far. Result: **0 hits** throughout. A direct memory read of `0x1000f000`-`0x1000f0ff` at the end of the window confirms both `I_STAT` and `I_MASK` are still all-zero. A full `pcsx2_read_registers` snapshot at the same point shows EE `pc`/`EPC` both still exactly `0x00081fc0` (Round 157's self-loop) and `Status`/`Cause` unchanged in substance from Round 157-159. This is the strongest evidence yet that, within any practically-observable live window, this specific real BIOS+GT3 boot sequence simply does not write `INTC_MASK` nonzero at this stage - not a sampling-rate artifact.

**Live-tooling reliability gap found and worth flagging for future rounds**: mid-window, `pcsx2_status()` (called while the CPU was still running, `Paused: false`) reported `EE PC: 0x00264430`, and the immediately following `pcsx2_pause()` call reported `Paused at PC=0x0027ec60` - both wildly different from, and inconsistent with each other and with, the authoritative `pcsx2_read_registers()` snapshot taken immediately after pausing, which showed `pc=0x00081fc0` (matching every prior round, and matching the watchpoint's own `last_PC=0x00000000`/0-hits state). This means **`pcsx2_status`'s and `pcsx2_pause`'s reported PC fields are unreliable while the CPU is actively running at speed** (likely a read-tearing/sampling race against the live JIT), and must not be trusted for conclusions on their own - only `pcsx2_read_registers()`, called after a confirmed pause, is authoritative. This cost real time this round (a plausible-looking "the loop finally broke!" signal that turned out to be spurious) and is recorded here so future rounds don't repeat the mistake.

**(b) Backward-trace from Round 158's jump-table handlers.** Continued the `pcsx2_find_pattern`-driven search (using the corrected KSEG0 address range and little-endian byte-pattern construction established earlier this round) for `lui`/`ori`-style loads of the `0xB000`/`0xF000` hardware-register bases, manually disassembling candidate hits. Confirmed two more real, functional routines beyond the ones already logged mid-round: a direct `I_STAT`-bit1 (SBUS) check-and-dispatch stub at `0x8000cfc0`-`0x8000cfe4`, and - the most structurally significant find - a real VBLANK-wait routine at `0x8000af70`-`0x8000afbc` that **polls `I_STAT` bit2 directly** (ack-write 4, spin-read until set, ack again, `jal 0x8000AA60`), never touching `I_MASK` at all. This proves the real kernel has (at least) two coexisting, architecturally distinct waiting conventions: direct `I_STAT` polling (mask-independent, since PCSX2's own `hwIntcIrq()` sets `INTC_STAT` unconditionally on the hardware event per Round 158's citation) versus true exception-driven waiting via the Round 157 self-loop (which strictly requires `I_MASK`). Went on to disassemble a third candidate, a linked-list/table-walking dispatcher spanning roughly `0x8000fdd8`-`0x8000feb4`: it loads a value and compares it against several sentinel constants (`0xFFF0`, `0xFFF1`, `0xFFF2`, `0xFFFF`), calling `0x8000EF78` (apparent lookup-by-key, keyed off a saved register `s1`) and `0x80002840` (apparent invoke/callback, called with up to four arguments) depending on which sentinel matches. This has the shape of a real kernel registration/dispatch-table walker (plausibly `iAddIntcHandler`/`iEnableIntc`-equivalent internals, or a related class/spec-keyed event table matching this project's own already-cited PS1/PS2 kernel event-class conventions), but **no direct store instruction to `0x1000f010` was found within the portion of this function disassembled so far**, so it is not yet confirmed as the actual mask-writer - only as a plausible, not-yet-conclusively-linked candidate.

**Conclusion**: both tracks converge on the same refined picture rather than a resolution. Track (a) makes it very unlikely that a longer passive observation window alone will ever catch the write - if it hasn't happened in ~180s/billions of cycles across four separate fresh-reset attempts (Rounds 157-160), it is not merely "hasn't happened yet." Track (b) shows the real kernel has a mask-independent polling path that could plausibly explain how real hardware (and real games) get past this exact loop shape without ever needing `INTC_MASK` touched at this point - i.e., the self-loop at `0x00081fc0` may not, in fact, be a "wait for `EnableIntc`" idiom at all, but could be a fundamentally different kind of wait (e.g. waiting on a semaphore/flag set by a *polling* handler elsewhere, not on an interrupt of its own) that this investigation has been mis-modeling since Round 157. This reframing - rather than "which routine writes `INTC_MASK`" - is the most useful output of this round and the natural next target.

No source change this round - investigation only.

### 201st finding (Round 161, task #313 continuation): implemented and verified a pragmatic, explicitly-non-authentic clean-room unblock for the INTC_MASK self-loop deadlock

Per the user's explicit direction to stop chasing the exact real INTC_MASK trigger (five investigation-only rounds, 157-160, had exhausted the practical live-archaeology options without finding it) and instead implement a pragmatic HLE shortcut, added `ee_check_boot_unblock_selfloop()` to `source/core/ee/ee_core.c`: if the EE is ever seen at exactly `pc=0x00081fc0` (the real, live-confirmed self-loop address) with `INTC_MASK` still fully zero, force-enable only the `VBLANK_START`/`VBLANK_END` mask bits already raised as real `INTC_STAT` signals by the existing `ee_check_vblank()` (itself unchanged, real, and previously verified). This is explicitly documented in-source as unverified/pragmatic - not a claim about the real trigger, only the most defensible, most narrowly-targeted nudge available, chosen because three separate prior rounds' documented reasoning had already independently named VBLANK as the leading real-hardware candidate for this exact loop shape, and because Round 160 additionally found the real kernel has a mask-independent VBLANK-polling convention elsewhere, reinforcing that VBLANK activity is the relevant signal here. The hook only fires once (a static latch) and only when the mask is still genuinely zero, so it never overrides a real write if one ever occurs first.

**Verified end-to-end via a scoped, throwaway host-native unit test** (not committed, per this project's standing `/tmp`-diagnostics policy): rather than replaying the full real-BIOS boot from power-on (which, per this project's own precedent, can take billions of instructions to reach this exact point), the test directly constructed the known real-observed state (`pc=0x00081fc0`, `Status=0x70030c11` matching the live reference session's own register dump from Round 160, a synthetic generic-MIPS-ISA "branch to self" instruction - NOT copied real BIOS bytes - at the target address so the loop is genuinely self-sustaining, and a minimal, test-only identity TLB mapping so the CPU can legally fetch there at all) and single-stepped the real EE core. Result: the new hook fired on the very first step (`INTC_MASK` became `0x0000000C`), and a real MIPS Interrupt exception was genuinely taken 410,123 steps later - at exactly the next `VBLANK_END` phase boundary (`EE_CYCLES_VBLANK_DURATION`) - with `EPC=0x00081fc0` (the interrupted self-loop address), `Cause` correctly reflecting the Interrupt exception code, `Status.EXL` set, and `pc` landing exactly on `0x80000200`, the real BIOS interrupt vector this project's own Round 158 finding already confirmed is populated with a genuine, functional dispatcher. This confirms the fix's mechanism works exactly as designed - the CPU is genuinely no longer permanently deadlocked by this specific condition; what happens next is up to whatever real BIOS interrupt-handler code is actually resident at that point in a genuine, full boot run, which this narrow test does not (and does not need to) exercise.

**Also worth noting for future rounds**: while building this round's host-native diagnostic tooling (a fresh, full-boot replay harness, used before narrowing to the scoped unit test above), confirmed this project's own boot, run from a completely fresh `system_init()`, spends its first ~160M+ EE instructions in the already-documented `0x80005e58`-range SBUS_SMFLG poll (Round 131/286th finding) - i.e. a full fresh replay reaching all the way to the `0x00081fc0` self-loop from a cold start would require a very large instruction budget, consistent with this project's own historical precedent (Round 158's own 100M/2B-instruction budgets for earlier, shallower walls). The scoped unit test above was chosen specifically to avoid needing that full replay for this round's verification.

Full regression suite: 109/109 pass (added no new test file this round, since the fix's verification uses a throwaway `/tmp` harness per the project's own established convention for host-native diagnostics - see the many prior "no source change, throwaway diagnostic" findings for the same policy). Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: 0 errors, same pre-existing unrelated `strncpy` truncation warning as every prior round.

### 202nd finding (Round 162, task #313/#172 continuation): built a reusable checkpoint/resume diagnostic harness; confirmed this project's own diskless boot is still blocked at the pre-existing IOP PRMEMPT-bit poll wall (Rounds 131-140) for at least 3.39 billion EE instructions, never naturally reaching the Round 161 self-loop fix's target

Per the Round 161 ROADMAP plan (run the new pragmatic INTC_MASK unblock against a full, real boot to see what actually happens), attempted a fresh, complete diskless boot with the Round 161 fix in place.

**Tooling constraint found and worked around**: this session's `bash` tool caps any single command at ~40 real seconds with no cross-call process persistence (backgrounded/`nohup`'d processes are killed once the call returns) - a materially more restrictive environment than whatever ran this project's own historical multi-hundred-million/multi-billion-instruction diagnostics in earlier sessions. Rather than accept a ~35-second/~500-600M-instruction ceiling per round, built a throwaway (`/tmp`, not committed) checkpoint/resume harness: a header audit confirmed every `*_get_state()` struct in this project (`ee_state_t`, `iop_state_t`, and the 15 other hardware-module states) contains no pointers except `ee_state_t`/`iop_state_t`'s own `ram`/`bios` fields, so a flat `fwrite`/`fread` of each struct (with `ram`/`bios` specially preserved across the fresh allocation each run performs via `system_init()`) is a complete, faithful snapshot. Verified this works correctly by resuming mid-run and confirming `instructions_executed` and `pc` picked up exactly where the prior invocation left off, not from zero.

**Result across four chained ~35-second segments (3.39 billion cumulative EE instructions, ~424 million IOP instructions)**: the EE never leaves the narrow `0x80005e5c`-`0x80006278` range (the same SBUS_SMFLG-adjacent region already characterized in Round 131/171st finding), and the IOP never leaves its own narrow `0x00031008`-`0x00032D50` range (the same PRMEMPT-bit poll already root-caused in the 176th-181st findings, gated on `(byte read through a pointer resolved to 0x1F801800) & 0x08`). `INTC_MASK` stayed at `0x1002` (SBUS + Timer3, already-known real sources, set by prior rounds' fixes) throughout - **the EE never reached `pc=0x00081fc0`** even once, so Round 161's fix (which only activates at that exact address) never had an opportunity to fire in this run.

**Interpretation**: this does not contradict Round 161 - the scoped unit test from that round already proved the fix's mechanism works correctly in isolation. It does mean that, in this project's own current diskless-boot model, the wall Round 161 targets sits well downstream of an earlier, already-known, still-unresolved wall (the PRMEMPT-bit poll), and this round's 3.39-billion-instruction budget - itself larger than any single previously-recorded budget in this project's history - was not enough to get past it. Given this project's own precedent that some earlier walls (e.g. task #181's original discovery) were eventually reached only after several further fixes in subsequent rounds (not merely by waiting longer), the more productive next step is very likely resuming the PRMEMPT-bit poll investigation itself (already scoped in the 176th-181st findings) rather than continuing to extend this same budget indefinitely.

No source change this round - investigation only, plus the reusable (throwaway, uncommitted) checkpoint/resume harness, which should meaningfully help any future round that needs a longer effective diagnostic window than this sandbox's per-call time limit otherwise allows.


### 203rd finding (Round 163, task #172 continuation): live reference session shows the 0x00081fc0 self-loop is a per-thread idle park, not a global deadlock - real kernel threads exist and are waiting to be scheduled, corroborating (not contradicting) Round 161's fix theory; PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 still unwritten
