Two other real, citable sources filled the gap: ps2tek's memory-map page (confirms two independent cores, Core1 at exactly `+0x400` from Core0) and PCSX2's historical ZeroSPU2 plugin header (GPL-2.0, same citation tier already used elsewhere in this project - architectural facts/offsets paraphrased, not copied verbatim) for the full per-voice and core-level register table. **Explicitly NOT documented by any source checked**: real power-on/reset values for any SPU2 register, and any specific boot-time "audio ready" polling condition - both stated as genuinely undocumented rather than guessed.

**Implementation** (`include/core/hw/iop_spu2.h`, `source/hw/iop_spu2.c`): added a full, cited, named offset table as macros - per-voice block (24 voices, stride `0x10`: VOLL/VOLR/PITCH/ADSR1/ADSR2/ENVX/VOLXL/VOLXR), per-voice address block (24 voices, stride `0x0C` at core-base+`0x1C0`: SSA/LSA/NAX hi/lo pairs), core-level registers (FMOD1/2, NON, VMIXL/R, MMIX, CTRL, IRQA, KON0/1, KOFF0/1, TSA, TDATA, ADMAS, ENDX0/1, STATX), and shared non-per-core registers (MVOLL/R, EVOLL/R) at their real absolute offsets. Added three address-computing helper functions (`iop_spu2_voice_reg_addr()`, `iop_spu2_voice_addr_reg_addr()`, `iop_spu2_core_reg_addr()`) so calling code can reference registers by real name instead of magic numbers. **Deliberately scoped as naming/addressing only**: the underlying storage remains the pre-existing flat byte-addressable register file - every named offset is still plain read/write passthrough, matching the original scaffold's honest "no envelope generation, no hardware-driven auto-set behavior, no actual audio synthesis" limits. No reset values were changed (the existing memset-to-zero remains the only defensible default, since no real reset values are citable).

**Verification**: new `tests/test_spu2_regs.c` (7 core checks covering ~13 assertions) - Core0/Core1 `+0x400` offset arithmetic, per-voice `0x10` stride, per-voice-address `0x0C` stride at the correct base, all named registers fall within the modeled window and round-trip read/write correctly, voice 23's last field stays inside Core0's block without bleeding into Core1, and the shared MVOLL register lands at the exact real cited absolute address `0x1F900760`. **Full regression suite: 113/113 test files pass, 0 failures.** **Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, same single pre-existing unrelated `strncpy`-truncation warning, unchanged by this round. No host-native boot-trace re-run needed this round (zero behavioral change to any read/write path, pure additive naming/addressing - same low-risk category as Round 135's original SIO2 scaffold before Round 146 added real behavior on top of it).

**This closes the user's "fix all audio peripherals first" directive as stated**: the peripheral half (Round 184's real controller protocol) and the audio half (this round's real SPU2 register map) are both now grounded in cited, real hardware layouts instead of opaque scratch blobs. Genuine audio synthesis/output and dynamic hardware-driven register behavior (real ENDX auto-set, KON/KOFF actually triggering envelope generators, DMA-to-SPU2 data pipeline, Wii AESND output) remain explicitly out of scope, honestly unaddressed - a much larger, separate feature, consistent with this file's original scope note and this project's standing non-fabrication discipline.

### 226th finding (Round 186, task #352): implemented real AddIntcHandler (EE syscall 16/0x10) - corrects an earlier round's factual error about its syscall number, and closes a previously-undiscovered silent-halt gap

**Context**: user directive "implement addintchandler". This is architecturally the exact real per-cause EE interrupt-handler registration mechanism the 111th/126th findings identified as the most-cited candidate blocker for the still-open PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 splash-screen gap.

**Research (via subagent, real ps2sdk github.com/ps2dev/ps2sdk source, fetched this round)**: `ee/kernel/include/syscallnr.h` gives definitive, exact real syscall numbers: `__NR_AddIntcHandler` = **0x10 (16)**, `__NR_AddIntcHandler2` aliased to the same number, `__NR_RemoveIntcHandler` = **0x11 (17)**. This **corrects a factual error in this project's own Round 53-era comment**, which claimed "18 (0x12) is shared between AddIntcHandler and AddDmacHandler depending on context" - re-verified directly against real ps2sdk source this round: AddIntcHandler (16) and AddDmacHandler (18) are two entirely distinct, non-overlapping syscall numbers, each with its own consecutive Add/Remove pair (16/17 for Intc, 18/19 for Dmac, already correctly implemented since Round 180/195-196). Independently cross-confirmed against the Play! PS2 emulator's own public syscall dispatch table (`Source/ee/PS2OS.cpp`), which hard-codes `0x0010->osAddIntcHandler`/`0x0011->osRemoveIntcHandler`, matching ps2sdk exactly. Real C signature (ps2sdk `kernel.h`): `s32 AddIntcHandler(s32 cause, s32 (*handler_func)(s32 cause), s32 next)` - registers a callback for one of the EE's 16 real INTC causes (this project's own existing `EE_INTC_IRQ_*` constants already match the real cause layout). A real ps2sdk sample (`ee/rpc/remote/samples/remote.c`) shows `AddIntcHandler(INTC_VBLANK_S,...)`/`AddIntcHandler(INTC_VBLANK_E,...)` as a common early real-program pattern - directly relevant to this project's own long-running VBLANK/display-setup investigation thread.

**Gap found and fixed**: syscall 16/17 were completely unhandled in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` - no case matched them anywhere, so they fell through to the generic `halt("SYSCALL (no BIOS syscall table implemented)")` fallback. This means any real boot code that ever called AddIntcHandler would have **stopped the entire emulated machine outright** - a previously-undiscovered, silent, severe potential blocker distinct from (and more dangerous than) the already-known register-value gaps this project has spent 185 rounds chasing.

**Fix**: per this project's own established, repeatedly-validated task #180 lesson (do not bypass a real kernel-table-mutating syscall in software and guess at its internal bookkeeping - let it vector as a genuine MIPS Syscall exception so the real, already-resident BIOS kernel handler code runs and installs its own real per-cause handler-table entry), added a `sysnum == 16 || sysnum == 17` block calling `ee_raise_exception(st, EE_EXC_CODE_SYS, this_pc, in_delay_slot)`, placed immediately after the existing, architecturally-identical 18/19 (AddDmacHandler/RemoveDmacHandler) block. Also corrected the erroneous Round-53-era comment in place (near the sysnum==18 handler) to state the real, now-verified distinct syscall numbers instead of the wrong "shared" claim.

**Verification**: new `tests/test_ee_syscall_addintchandler.c` (16 checks across 4 syscall numbers) - confirms syscalls 16 and 17 no longer halt, correctly set `Cause.ExcCode` to Syscall (8), record the correct EPC (pointing at the SYSCALL instruction), and vector to the real general-exception offset (`0xBFC00380`, BEV=1 reset default) - plus a regression check confirming the pre-existing 18/19 (AddDmacHandler/RemoveDmacHandler) behavior is completely unaffected by this addition. **Full regression suite: 114/114 test files pass, 0 failures.** **Host-native boot-trace check**: re-ran the same pure-BIOS-boot diagnostic (200M EE instructions) used in Rounds 183-185 - identical resting point (`EE pc=0x8000cff4`, `IOP pc=0x00118f98`) to the established baseline, confirming this fix introduces no regression; the current 200M-instruction pure-BIOS-boot trajectory does not itself reach a point where real code issues syscall 16/17 within this budget (consistent with this project's own established pattern of syscall-table gaps only manifesting many rounds after being fixed, once earlier blockers clear first - same as AddDmacHandler's own Round 180 fix, whose effect wasn't immediately visible either). **Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, same single pre-existing unrelated `strncpy`-truncation warning, unchanged by this round.

**Not yet resolved, correctly scoped for a future round**: whether this fix, combined with other still-open work, eventually allows real boot code to reach and successfully execute an `AddIntcHandler(INTC_VBLANK_S,...)`-style call and progress toward PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 remains to be observed via further host-native tracing (would need either a longer instruction budget than this sandbox's ~40s wall-clock ceiling allows in one run, or a checkpoint/resume mechanism) - correctly left open rather than claimed prematurely.

### 227th finding (Round 187, task #353): full EE syscall-table audit redone - found and fixed an entire real thread-management syscall family (14 numbers) that was silently machine-halting, correcting an earlier, wrong "no gap found" audit

**Context**: Round 186 discovered syscalls 16/17 (AddIntcHandler/RemoveIntcHandler) were completely unhandled - a severe, silent, machine-halting gap. This directly contradicted an EARLIER audit (task #179, 53rd finding, "EE syscall table audited (no gap found)"), which was therefore demonstrably wrong or incomplete. The user confirmed ("ofc") redoing that audit properly rather than trusting the old conclusion.

**Method**: extracted the complete, current list of explicitly-handled `sysnum` values from `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` via direct grep (`-124, -120, -67, -5, 6, 7, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 32, 34, 47, 48, 60, 61, 64, 65, 66, 68, 69, 100, 118, 119, 120, 121, 122, 124`), then fetched (via subagent, real source) the COMPLETE, non-curated real `ee/kernel/include/syscallnr.h` table from `github.com/ps2dev/ps2sdk` - both the positive (normal-context) numbers and the negative ("fast"/interrupt-context `i`-prefixed) aliases - 148 total `__NR_*` macros collapsing to 135 distinct real numeric slots after merging same-number aliases (e.g. `AddIntcHandler`/`AddIntcHandler2` share one real slot). Cross-referenced the two lists directly (not from memory or assumption).

**Result**: confirmed this project's existing `-124` and `-5` handling are legitimate, already-documented BIOS-internal/undocumented numbers (not present in the real public header at all - consistent with this project's own established 56th finding for `-5`). Confirmed all other currently-handled numbers are real, correctly-numbered matches. Found a large real gap: the great majority of ps2sdk's 135 real syscall slots are NOT handled by this project and would fall through to the machine-halting `halt("SYSCALL (no BIOS syscall table implemented)")` fallback if ever reached. Given the size of that full gap, this round prioritized (per the task's own explicit instruction) the single most plausible-to-be-hit-during-real-boot category not yet covered: **EE kernel thread-management primitives**, directly motivated by this project's own already-cited task #163 live-PCSX2 evidence of 12 concurrent real OSDSYS threads during a genuine boot. This project already handles `CreateThread` (32) and `StartThread` (34) with fixed placeholder returns (since it has no real concurrent scheduler), but the entire REST of the real thread-lifecycle/scheduling family was found completely unhandled: `DeleteThread` (33), `ExitThread` (35), `ExitDeleteThread` (36), `TerminateThread` (37), `DisableDispatchThread` (39), `EnableDispatchThread` (40), `ChangeThreadPriority` (41), `RotateThreadReadyQueue` (43), `ReleaseWaitThread` (45), `SleepThread` (50), `WakeupThread` (51), `CancelWakeupThread` (53), `SuspendThread` (55), `ResumeThread` (57) - all real, cited numeric slots from ps2sdk's `syscallnr.h`.

**Fix**: unlike CreateThread/StartThread (which need software placeholder values because this project cannot actually run a second concurrent thread body), every syscall in this newly-found gap only needs to mutate or query the real kernel's own thread-control-block/ready-queue state, which lives in EE-visible RAM and is maintained entirely by the real BIOS-resident kernel handler code. This project cannot safely guess that internal layout in software - the same already-established task #180 lesson applied identically to syscalls 6/7/16/17/18/19/124. Added a single combined `sysnum == 33 || ... || sysnum == 57` block in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` (placed immediately after the Round 186 AddIntcHandler/RemoveIntcHandler block) calling `ee_raise_exception(st, EE_EXC_CODE_SYS, this_pc, in_delay_slot)` so the real BIOS's own kernel handler runs and does its own real thread-state bookkeeping, rather than halting the whole emulated machine (the previous behavior for all 14 of these numbers).

**Verification**: new `tests/test_ee_syscall_thread_family.c` (59 checks: 4 assertions each across all 14 newly-fixed syscall numbers, plus a 3-assertion regression check confirming syscalls 32/34 (CreateThread/StartThread) still use their pre-existing placeholder-return behavior, NOT the new exception path) - all pass. **Full regression suite: 115/115 test files pass, 0 failures.** **Host-native boot-trace sanity check**: re-ran the same pure-BIOS-boot diagnostic (200M EE instructions) used since Round 183 - identical resting point (`EE pc=0x8000cff4`, `instrs=199900564`; `IOP pc=0x00118f98`, `instrs=24762501`) to the established baseline, confirming zero regression (expected - the current 200M-instruction trajectory doesn't itself reach a point where real code issues any of these 14 syscall numbers within this budget, matching the same pattern already observed for Round 186's AddIntcHandler fix). **Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, same single pre-existing unrelated `strncpy`-truncation warning, unchanged by this round.

**Explicitly NOT resolved this round, correctly scoped for future rounds**: the full real syscall table still has a large number of genuinely unhandled real numbers beyond this thread-management batch - notably the interrupt/DMAC-enable pair `_EnableIntc`(20)/`_DisableIntc`(21) (asymmetric with the already-handled `_EnableDmac`(22)/`_DisableDmac`(23)), the TLB family (`PutTLBEntry`=85, `GetTLBEntry`=87, `ProbeTLBEntry`=88 - this project already has a working COP0 TLB implementation via direct MIPS instructions, but not via these syscall wrappers), the EventFlag family (`CreateEventFlag`=80 through `iSetEventFlag`=83), the Alarm family (`_SetAlarm`=24/`_ReleaseAlarm`=25/`SetAlarm`=252/`ReleaseAlarm`=254), and the full negative "fast"/interrupt-context alias family (`iSetAlarm`, `iSignalSema`, `iEnableIntc`, etc.). These are deliberately left unaddressed this round rather than attempting an oversized, harder-to-review single change - the next round should continue this same audit-driven, prioritized-by-real-boot-plausibility approach.

### 228th finding (Round 188, task #354, real source fix): implemented real _EnableIntc(20)/_DisableIntc(21) - closes the asymmetry Round 187 flagged next to the already-handled _EnableDmac/_DisableDmac pair

**Context**: Round 187's audit deferred this specific gap for a follow-up round: `_EnableIntc`(20)/`_DisableIntc`(21) were unhandled (silently machine-halting) while the structurally-similar `_EnableDmac`(22)/`_DisableDmac`(23) pair sitting immediately next to them in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` was already correctly implemented since Round 176.

**Research**: real ps2sdk signature (`ee/kernel/include/kernel.h`): `s32 _EnableIntc(s32 cause)` / `s32 _DisableIntc(s32 cause)` - `cause` is the same real EE INTC source enum already cited for AddIntcHandler (Round 186). Unlike syscalls 16/17 (which mutate a BIOS-internal per-cause handler table this project cannot safely model), this syscall's real effect is narrowly scoped: ensure one bit of the real INTC_MASK register (`include/core/hw/ee_intc.h`'s `ee_intc_state_t.mask` field) ends up set or clear - a register this project already fully owns and models. `ee_intc.h`'s own header comment (citing PCSX2's `HwWrite.cpp`) documents that a real MMIO write to `INTC_MASK` XOR-toggles the written bits (a real hardware quirk) - but that quirk applies to direct program writes to the hardware register address, not to this kernel-level convenience syscall's net effect, which is a plain end-state set/clear (the same distinction already established and cited for `_EnableDmac`/`_DisableDmac`'s relationship to DMAC_STAT's own toggle-quirk).

**Fix**: added a `sysnum == 20` block (sets `intc->mask |= (1u << cause)`) and a `sysnum == 21` block (clears `intc->mask &= ~(1u << cause)`) in `ee_core.c`, placed immediately before the existing `sysnum == 22` (_EnableDmac) block. Implemented via DIRECT software model (matching the already-established _EnableDmac/_DisableDmac precedent), NOT the "raise a real exception" pattern used for 16/17/33-57 - the correct category boundary being whether this project already owns the real register/state being mutated (yes, for INTC_MASK) versus needing BIOS-internal bookkeeping it cannot see (no, for handler tables or thread-control-blocks). No citable exact real return-value convention was found for `_EnableIntc`/`_DisableIntc`, so both return 0 (success), an honest placeholder matching the same already-established `_EnableDmac`/`_DisableDmac` convention rather than a fabricated specific value.

**Verification**: new `tests/test_ee_syscall_enableintc.c` (13 checks) - confirms both syscalls set/clear the correct real INTC_MASK bit for multiple causes (GS=0, VBLANK_S=2, VBLANK_E=3), confirms neither halts nor vectors through the exception path (correctly distinguishing this fix's category from Round 186/187's exception-raising fixes), an explicit enable-then-disable sequence on the same cause round-trips correctly, and a regression check confirming `_EnableDmac`(22) is unaffected. **Full regression suite: 116/116 test files pass, 0 failures.** **Host-native boot-trace sanity check**: re-ran the same pure-BIOS-boot diagnostic (200M EE instructions) used since Round 183 - identical resting point (`EE pc=0x8000cff4`, `instrs=199900564`; `IOP pc=0x00118f98`, `instrs=24762501`) to the established baseline, zero regression. **Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, same single pre-existing unrelated `strncpy`-truncation warning, unchanged by this round.

**Still-open real syscall gaps, correctly scoped for future rounds** (per Round 187's own list, minus this round's fix): the TLB syscall-wrapper family (`PutTLBEntry`=85, `GetTLBEntry`=87, `ProbeTLBEntry`=88), the EventFlag family (`CreateEventFlag`=80 through `iSetEventFlag`=83), the Alarm family (`_SetAlarm`=24/`_ReleaseAlarm`=25/`SetAlarm`=252/`ReleaseAlarm`=254), and the full negative "fast"/interrupt-context alias family.

### 229th finding (Round 189, task #355, real source addition + methodology correction): GS->Wii output pipeline proven correct end-to-end in isolation; corrected a silently-broken diagnostic hook; new timing data on when real BIOS touches GS registers

**Context**: direct user directive - "bypass the bios boot path and force so we can fix any issues inside so we can trace any other things which are holding pmode etc back", following a discussion of whether the 120+-round-unmoved PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 blocker (94th finding, Round 62, through the 223rd finding, Round 183) means the GS->Wii output pipeline itself might be broken, versus the boot trace simply never reaching the code that would write those registers. This was a genuinely open question - every prior round tested this exclusively THROUGH the real boot trace, never in isolation.

**Part 1 - output pipeline isolation (the main ask)**: bypassed BIOS/EE/IOP entirely. Force-wrote a known RGB test pattern into GS memory using `gs_mem_write_psmct32` (grep-verified this round to be the exact same function `gif.c`'s real rasterizer uses - confirmed `gif.c` never calls the separate `_swizzled` addressing variant, so this uses the actual live write-side convention, not a hypothetical one). Force-wrote realistic real `PMODE`/`DISPFB1` register values directly into `gs_state_t` (bit layout already cited in `gs_decode_dispfb`'s own doc comment: PMODE bit 0=EN1, DISPFB1 bits 0-8=FBP in 2048-word units, bits 9-14=FBW in 64-pixel units). Then ran the EXACT SAME control-flow sequence `main.c`'s `run_real_boot_flow()` executes every frame once `display_active` becomes true: PMODE bit check -> `gs_decode_dispfb` -> `gs_blit_psmct32_to_xfb` -> `gs_rgb8_pair_to_ycbcr`. Verified the resulting synthetic XFB buffer contains exactly the correct expected YCbCr-encoded pixels, with correct row bounds (no off-by-one, no out-of-bounds writes). **Result: all 15 checks pass.** This is a NEW, permanent regression test (`tests/test_gs_output_pipeline_isolation.c`) - the individual leaf functions already had unit coverage (`test_gs_output.c`), but the combined, register-gated production sequence itself never did.

**Conclusion for Part 1**: the real production display pipeline is functionally CORRECT end-to-end when fed realistic register values, at the full C-level control-flow granularity (everything except the actual Wii video hardware / `gccore.h`, which this code has no dependency on). This closes 120+ rounds of ambiguity: the remaining gap is conclusively that real/emulated BIOS boot code never reaches the point of writing PMODE/DISPFB1 - NOT a broken output mechanism.

**Part 2 - a methodology gap found and fixed along the way**: while building this test, discovered that the "boot-trace sanity check" GS-write-counting hook (`round183_log_gs_write`, originally wired into a scratch copy of `gs.c` for the 223rd finding's Round 183 measurement) was **never actually connected to the live, committed `source/hw/gs.c`** - `gs_mmio_write64()` never calls it. Every re-run of `gs_trace_bios.c` since Round 184 (used as the "no regression" sanity check in Rounds 184-188) printed "Total GS register writes: 0" / "PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 writes: 0" - but this was a dead-hook artifact, not a live measurement; the counter was structurally incapable of incrementing. This did NOT invalidate any prior round's actual conclusions (Rounds 184-188's own STATUS.md citations correctly only claimed pc/instruction-count equality, never re-claimed the write-count), and Round 183's ORIGINAL measurement (properly instrumented via its own dedicated scratch copy) remains valid and has now been independently re-confirmed (see Part 3) - but this round is documenting the gap honestly rather than silently continuing to reuse a broken instrument.

**Part 3 - corrected, timestamped re-measurement**: rebuilt a properly-instrumented scratch copy (`/tmp/round189_scratch`, hook correctly wired into `gs_mmio_write64()`, never committed - same established never-merge-diagnostic-hooks discipline as Round 183) and re-ran the full 200M-EE-instruction pure-BIOS-boot trace, this time also timestamping each write against the EE's own instruction counter. **Result: exactly the same 8 GS register writes as Round 183's original measurement** (`CSR=0x200`, `SMODE1` x2, `SYNCH1`, `SYNCH2`, `SYNCV`, `SMODE2=3`, `SRFSH=8`) - confirms Round 183's finding was correct and remains unchanged. **New data this round**: all 8 writes occur at EE instruction #15,410,636 of 199,900,564 total - **7.7% of the way through the run** - and then GS is completely untouched for the remaining **92.3% of the trace** (184.5M+ further EE instructions). This means the real BIOS's CRTC/video-timing-generator setup (SMODE1/2, SRFSH, SYNCH1/2, SYNCV - the electrical/sync configuration that real hardware needs before enabling a display circuit) runs once, early, and completes - it is NOT "almost reaching" PMODE by running out of instruction budget. Whatever code path would eventually enable the display and write DISPFB1 is either never reached at all in this trace, or is gated behind a condition this trace's 200M-instruction budget never satisfies - the EE spends the overwhelming majority of its execution in code that has nothing to do with GS at all.

**Verification**: new `tests/test_gs_output_pipeline_isolation.c` (15 checks, all pass). **Full regression suite: 117/117 test files pass, 0 failures.** **Host-native boot-trace sanity check**: identical resting point (`EE pc=0x8000cff4`, `instrs=199900564`; `IOP pc=0x00118f98`, `instrs=24762501`) to the established baseline - zero regression. **Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, same single pre-existing unrelated `strncpy`-truncation warning, unchanged by this round.

**Reframing for future rounds**: this round shifts the open question from "is PMODE ever written" (already well-established as "no," and now also proven that this ISN'T because of a broken pipeline) to a sharper one: "what is the EE actually doing for the 92.3% of the trace between the CRTC setup at 7.7% and the resting point at pc=0x8000cff4, and is pc=0x8000cff4 a genuine tight polling/wait loop the EE has been stuck in since very early in the boot (consistent with landing at the exact same pc/instruction-count across 6+ rounds of unrelated source changes), or does it represent real, slowly-varying forward progress." Disassembling/characterizing the code around pc=0x8000cff4 specifically (rather than more generic syscall-table audits) is the most direct next step toward finding the real blocker.

### 230th finding (Round 190, task #356, investigation only, no source change): full semantic decode of the resting loop - confirms it's the already-documented "0x8000CC68 wall" family, and corrects a mid-investigation assumption about which specific check is blocking

**Context**: direct continuation of Round 189's finding that the EE spends 92.3% of its 200M-instruction trace in code untouched by GS activity, resting at `pc=0x8000cff4` - unchanged across 6+ rounds. This round characterizes that resting behavior precisely.

**Step 1 - PC-visit histogram**: instrumented a host-native diagnostic to record every distinct EE `pc` value visited across the full 200M-instruction trace. Result: only **6,603 distinct PC values visited in the entire run**, with the top 20 most-visited addresses all hit **~2,323,758 times each** (~1.16% of all steps apiece) - conclusively confirming this is a genuine, bounded, repeating loop region (not slow/varied forward progress through different code each time), consistent with (and now quantified precisely for the first time) the "stable, bounded, repeating loop region" framing already established qualitatively in Round 179.

**Step 2 - full semantic decode**: wrote a fresh, standard-MIPS-ISA instruction decoder (public instruction encoding tables, not copied from any BIOS content) and decoded the hot address ranges. Per this project's own standing non-fabrication/no-literal-transcription convention, only architectural/behavioral facts are recorded here, not raw instruction listings. Findings: the loop region is the SAME address family already named in Rounds 172-183 (`0x8000CFD0`/`0x8000CCAC`/`0x8000CC68`) - confirmed via decoded control flow, not just proximity. Specifically: a subroutine at the `0x8000CF80` family checks the real DMAC_STAT register (masking bit `0x80`) and the real INTC_STAT register (masking bit `0x2`, the SBUS cause) - architecturally exactly matching Round 178's own citation of "checks both INTC_STAT bit 1 and DMAC_STAT bit 0x80". When the INTC_STAT/SBUS check passes, it calls a helper subroutine whose entry point resolves to the exact address (`0x8000CC68`) Round 178/179 already identified as the JAL target from this call site. That helper subroutine's real behavior (newly decoded this round, not previously characterized at this level of detail) is a **debounce/stabilization read loop against the real SIF_SMFLAG register** (`0x1000F230`, this project's own `source/hw/sif.c`/`ee_core.c` already model this address) - it reads SIF_SMFLAG, and if a second read matches the first, returns immediately with that value; if not, it keeps re-reading (with padding delay between reads) until two consecutive reads agree, then returns the stable value. The ~20-22-word runs of zero-valued instruction words Round 179 flagged as an inconclusive, ambiguous signal (too close in magnitude to the known-legitimate Round 131 spin-wait's own 20-word runs to use as a detection heuristic) are now **explained**, not just observed: they are the real padding/delay spans between the debounce subroutine's repeated SIF_SMFLAG reads - a legitimate structural feature of this real code path, not evidence of anything broken.

**Step 3 - runtime value-watching (the corrective finding)**: instrumented the diagnostic to record, on every visit to `pc=0x8000cff4` (the exact resting instruction, a conditional branch on the debounce subroutine's masked return value), the actual runtime value being tested and whether the branch was taken. **Result across all 2,323,756 observed visits**: the masked value is **always exactly `0x00070000`**, and the branch ("something pending, take the non-fallthrough path") is taken **100.0000% of the time, every single visit, with zero variance**. Cross-checked against the live SIF_SMFLAG register value at the end of the run: also exactly `0x00070000` - the real `BOOTEND|CMDINIT|SIFINIT` bits this project's own `mark_iop_boot_complete()` (`source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`) sets once IOP module loading finishes, confirming those bits are genuinely visible to and correctly detected by real EE-side BIOS code at this exact check.

**This corrects an assumption made mid-investigation this round**: the natural first read of "EE parks at pc=X, and X is a conditional branch checking a wait condition" is "the condition at X must never become true, that's the blocker." That is demonstrably NOT the case here - this specific check succeeds and branches forward on literally every one of its 2.3 million observed evaluations. The loop's REAL gating condition, if any, lies either downstream of this check's forward-branch target (a jump to `0x8000CDF8`, not yet traced) or in one of the OTHER, separate condition checks within the broader outer per-frame loop (the already-partially-decoded `0x8000F764`-`0x8000F870` region, which tests several other struct-field/register conditions - `s0`, `s1`, `s2`, `s4`, `s5`, `s6`, `s7`, `fp` - whose real semantic origin has not yet been traced back to a citable source this round).

**No source change this round** - correctly scoped: no safe, citable fix was identified, and per this project's own standing discipline, an uncertain/guessed fix is worse than an honest "not yet resolved." Applying a "fix" targeted at the `0x8000cff4` check specifically would have been based on a wrong premise (this check is not failing) and could easily have introduced a regression without addressing the real gating condition.

**Not yet resolved, correctly scoped for a future round**: trace the real control flow from `0x8000CDF8` onward, and/or trace the semantic origin of the `s0`/`s1`/`s2`/`s4`/`s5`/`s6`/`s7`/`fp`-based condition checks in the `0x8000F764`-`0x8000F870` outer loop - these are the next concrete targets, now that the SIF_SMFLAG/DMAC_STAT/INTC_STAT check at `0x8000cff4` has been conclusively ruled out as the blocker.

## 231st finding (Round 191, task #357): `0x8000CDF8` fully traced - both internal conditional blocks confirmed dead code; the subroutine converges into the SAME already-long-documented `0x8000F768`/`RAM[0x80020B54]`/`AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)` blocker thread (94th-223rd findings, Rounds 64-183) - no new fixable bug inside CDF8 itself, but a real unification of two previously-separate investigation threads

**Method.** Directly continuing Round 190's corrective finding (the `pc=0x8000cff4` SIF_SMFLAG-debounce check succeeds 100% of the time and branches to `0x8000CDF8`, never traced before this round): extended this project's fresh, self-written MIPS decoder (`/tmp/round190_diag/decode_region.c`, standard public MIPS ISA bit-field decoding, not transcribed from BIOS bytes) to cover `0x8000CDA0`-`0x8000CE80` (the `0x8000CDF8` subroutine body) and `0x8000CE90`-`0x8000CF80` (its continuation/epilogue), then built a runtime-value watcher (`/tmp/round190_diag/watch_cdf8.c`) logging `$a0`/`$v0`/`$a1`/`$v1` and hit counts at 8 key addresses inside the subroutine across the full 200M-EE-instruction trace.

**What the decode + watch data show.** `0x8000CDF8` takes a flags argument in `$a0` (confirmed always exactly `0x00070000`, the SIF_SMFLAG boot-complete value from the 190th/`mark_iop_boot_complete()` thread) and has two internal conditional "extra processing" blocks:
- Bit 30 (`0x40000000`) test at `0x8000ce08`: since `0x70000` lacks this bit, the branch always skips the inner block (0 hits recorded at `0x8000ce18` across all 2,323,756 calls) - the dead code there would have called `0x8000CD48`, ACK'd SIF_SMFLAG bit 30, and jumped to the convergence point.
- Sign-bit (`BGEZ`) test at `0x8000ce44`: since `0x70000` has the sign bit clear, this always branches away from the inner block too (0 hits at `0x8000ce54`/`0x8000ce74`) - that dead code would have read a real IOP-RAM-window address (`0xBC0003E4`), ACK'd SIF_SMFLAG bit 31, and called `0x80001F00`.

Both blocks are therefore **confirmed dead code for this project's actual trace** - the function always takes the "nothing special" path. Extending the decode past the convergence point (`0x8000ce98`) shows it is simply the subroutine's own epilogue: `LD s0,16(sp)` / `JR ra` / `ADDIU sp,sp,48` - i.e. `0x8000CDF8` is not itself a wait/gate at all, it is a short flag-ACK helper that restores its saved register and returns to its caller.

**The unification.** Tracing forward from where this subroutine returns leads directly into `0x8000F750`-`0x8000F880` - decoded fresh this round and found to be **the exact same code** this project's docs have already investigated in exhaustive depth as far back as the 94th finding (Round 64): the OSDSYS per-frame retry loop at `0x8000F768`-`0x8000F878`, testing `RAM[s0+0xE28]`/`RAM[s5+0xE30]`/`RAM[s4+0xE3C]`/`RAM[s7+0xE4C]` (offsets 3624/3632/3644/3660 decimal, all relative to the fixed `0x80020000` low-EE-RAM globals block first identified in the 94th finding) and looping back to `0x8000F768` while `RAM[s7+0xE4C]` or `RAM[s0+0xE28]` stay nonzero. This is confirmed by exact offset match: `3660 = 0xE4C`, the precise field the 96th/100th/103rd findings already identified as the per-frame loop's continuation check, and `RAM[0x80020B54]` (`s6+0xB50`-equivalent field in the same struct) is the same gate the 103rd-108th/117th/157th/158th findings traced three real function-levels deep to a genuine EE kernel interrupt-exception vector, ultimately depending on a real `AddIntcHandler` registration for `Cause=0x8800` (Timer+DMAC) that this project's boot trace never reaches (111th finding onward, reconfirmed as recently as the 216th finding, Round 176).

**What this means for task #357.** The user's directive was to trace and, if possible, fix the control flow at `0x8000CDF8`. This round fully traces it: there is no fixable bug inside `0x8000CDF8` itself (both its conditional blocks are correctly-behaving dead code given the real SIF_SMFLAG value observed), and the subroutine's return leads directly into the project's own oldest, most heavily-investigated open blocker - already scoped, across 100+ intervening rounds, as requiring either (a) discovery of what real EE-kernel code should call `AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)` (a large reverse-engineering effort explicitly deprioritized multiple times since the 111th finding, most recently the 216th finding, Round 176), or (b) tracing the sibling `RAM[s0+0xE28]`/`RAM[s5+0xE30]`/`RAM[s4+0xE3C]` checks the 158th finding flagged as still unexplained even after force-writing `RAM[0x80020B54]` alone. This round's real contribution is confirming, for the first time, that the Round 172-190 SIF_SMFLAG-debounce investigation thread and the Round 64-183 OSDSYS-per-frame-loop thread are the SAME single blocker, not two separate ones - closing the possibility that CDF8 hid an independent, more-tractable bug.

**No source change this round** - correctly scoped: `0x8000CDF8` itself has no bug to fix (confirmed via 2,323,756 consistent observations, zero variance), and applying a fix at the downstream `AddIntcHandler`/`RAM[0x80020B54]` gate would repeat the exact same already-tried, already-insufficient experiment from the 158th finding (Round 118) - force-writing that one gate alone was shown NOT to unblock the boot, since further plumbing is missing downstream too. Fabricating a deeper fix without a citable source for the real `AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)` registration path would violate this project's no-fabrication convention.

**Verification.** Regression suite unaffected (no source change to test); this round's diagnostics are entirely scratch-only (`/tmp/round190_diag/`), never touched the committed repo.

**Not yet resolved, correctly scoped for Round 192**: per the 158th finding's own still-open lead, trace the semantic origin/expected-source of `RAM[s0+0xE28]`, `RAM[s5+0xE30]`, `RAM[s4+0xE3C]` (the OTHER three per-frame-loop checks, distinct from the already-deeply-traced `RAM[0x80020B54]`/`RAM[s7+0xE4C]` pair) - this is a comparatively fresh thread relative to the `AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)` mega-effort, and per the 158th finding was never actually chased to its own root cause.

## 232nd finding (Round 192, task #358): Alarm/EventFlag/TLB-wrapper syscall families found unhandled (silent-halt gaps) and fixed; the s0+0xE28/s5+0xE30/s4+0xE3C reverse-engineering thread converges into the same already-deprioritized AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800) mega-effort and is correctly left there

**Live-debugger investigation (task #358's original scope).** Connected to the live PCSX2 reference debugger (paused mid-way through an unrelated, fully-booted commercial game session - 38 real IOP modules loaded, EE pc=0x00081fc0) and disassembled the FIXED, low-address, kernel-resident OSDSYS per-frame function prologue (`0x8000F6E0`-`0x8000F768`) with the native disassembler for the first time this round. This yields one genuinely new fact: the function's very FIRST instruction after its prologue (`0x8000f6fc`, before the retry loop even starts) reads `RAM[0x80020E4C]` and, if zero, branches all the way past the entire retry-loop block to `0x8000F908` - meaning the same single field (`RAM[s7+0xE4C]`, already traced by the 96th-108th findings) gates BOTH whether this code region executes at all AND whether the loop, once entered, keeps repeating. This tightens the picture but does not open a new angle: `s0`/`s4`/`s5`/`s7`/`fp` are confirmed (via the live disassembler, not assumed) to be literally the same fixed `0x80020000` base already established by the 94th finding, meaning `RAM[s0+0xE28]`/`RAM[s5+0xE30]`/`RAM[s4+0xE3C]` are siblings of the exact same struct populated by the exact same class of currently-unreached dispatcher mechanism already traced to depend on `AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)` (111th finding onward). A bounded, honest attempt at directly locating an `AddIntcHandler(0x8800)` call site via binary pattern search (`ori a0,zero,0x8800` encoding, searched across the full 0-2MB physical BIOS-resident range) found zero matches - real negative evidence, but inconclusive, since the cause argument is very likely a small enum/index value rather than the literal runtime Cause-register bitmask this search assumed. Per this project's own repeatedly-applied discipline (216th finding, Round 176: resume the deprioritized effort directly, or continue prioritizing other tractable gaps), and given over 100 rounds have already exhausted the direct approaches available to this project's current tool set, this round correctly does NOT sink further effort into re-attempting the same mega-effort, and instead pivots to a concretely tractable item.

**Pivot: syscall-table audit continuation (proven productive - Rounds 186/187).** Continuing Round 187's own explicitly scoped-but-deferred list, a review of the real ps2sdk `syscallnr.h` (this project's local cached copy) against `ee_core.c`'s currently-handled sysnum list found three more real families completely unhandled (silently halting the whole emulated machine via the generic "no BIOS syscall table implemented" fallback if ever reached):

- **Alarm family**: `_SetAlarm`(24), `_ReleaseAlarm`(25), `SetAlarm`(252), `ReleaseAlarm`(254), and their real fast/interrupt-context forms `_iSetAlarm`(-30), `_iReleaseAlarm`(-31), `iSetAlarm`(-253), `iReleaseAlarm`(-255) - note these "fast" forms are NOT simply the negation of their positive counterpart (e.g. `_SetAlarm`=24 but `_iSetAlarm`=-30, not -24), transcribed exactly as ps2sdk's own header states.
- **EventFlag family**: `CreateEventFlag`(80), `DeleteEventFlag`(81), `SetEventFlag`(82), `iSetEventFlag`(83) - the last one unusually a POSITIVE number in the real header (not a negative "fast" form like most others), transcribed as-is.
- **TLB-wrapper family**: `PutTLBEntry`(85), `_SetTLBEntry`(86), `GetTLBEntry`(87), `ProbeTLBEntry`(88) (Round 187's own note only explicitly named 85/87/88; this round adds 86, the one member of the same real contiguous block that note omitted), plus each member's real negative fast form (-85/-86/-87/-88). These are real kernel-side wrappers around the same COP0 TLB hardware operations this project's EE core already models natively (task #60) - this project owns the underlying hardware correctly, but not the real kernel wrapper's own bookkeeping (index validation, a real kernel-resident software mirror table, real error-code conventions), which has no citable source.

Fixed identically to the established, repeatedly-precedented pattern (task #180's lesson, applied to 6/7/16/17/18/19/33-57/124 already): raise a real MIPS Syscall exception (`ee_raise_exception`) rather than halt, so genuine BIOS-resident kernel code runs and performs its own real bookkeeping, instead of guessing at internal layout this project cannot verify.

**Verification.** New test file `tests/test_ee_syscall_alarm_eventflag_tlb.c`: 82 CHECK() assertions covering all 20 new sysnums (4 checks each: halted==0, Cause.ExcCode==Syscall, EPC correctness, pc vectors to 0xBFC00380) plus a regression check confirming the real, already-modeled native COP0 TLBWI instruction is completely unaffected (different opcode class, no interaction). Full regression suite: 118/118 test files pass (0 build failures, 0 runtime failures). Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.dol`/`.elf` produced (463360/2609068 bytes), same pre-existing benign `strncpy` truncation warning as prior rounds, no new warnings. A bounded (~24M-EE-instruction) host-native boot-trace sanity check confirms neither core halts and the trace continues progressing normally after this round's change (a full run to the known final resting point requires ~200M instructions, beyond this session's per-call bounded runtime; the 24M-instruction checkpoint pc, `0x8000b8b0`, is a normal mid-boot waypoint on the same established trajectory, not a new landmark this round introduces or disrupts).

**Not yet resolved, correctly scoped for Round 193**: the `RAM[s0+0xE28]`/`RAM[s5+0xE30]`/`RAM[s4+0xE3C]` semantic-origin question remains open, converged with (not independent from) the already-deprioritized `AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)` reverse-engineering effort (task #221, open since Round 61). A future round should either commit to a sustained, multi-round live-debugger-assisted push on that specific effort (which would need real conditional-breakpoint tracing of the 32-63 soft-irq registration call sites, not blind pattern search), or continue mining the syscall-table audit for other tractable gaps (this round's own review did not exhaustively re-check the full 0-172 + negative range against the very latest source state - a fresh full pass may still find more).

## Correction to the 231st/232nd findings (Round 193, task #359): the "AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)" framing cited in Rounds 191-192 was ALREADY explicitly closed in the 161st finding (Round 121) - the current, accurate blocker is the separately-documented ICFG-bit-1/SBUS trigger (Rounds 131-183), itself already confirmed exhausted of public-source and live-trace avenues

**How this was found.** The user uploaded an independent live-PCSX2 trace document (`pcsx2_E30_origin_trace.md`) claiming to trace the origin of `RAM[s0+0xE28]`/`RAM[s5+0xE30]`/`RAM[s4+0xE3C]`. Cross-checking its cited base address (`s7=0x002D0000`, no `0x8000`-series virtual prefix, code addresses in the `0x0010xxxx`-`0x0028xxxx` range) against this project's own confirmed base (`0x80020000` virtual/`0x00020000` physical, established via this session's own live disassembly at `0x8000F6C0`-`0x8000F768`) showed a clear mismatch. The user confirmed the trace was captured against a GT3 (Gran Turismo 3) session - a different game's own in-memory object, not this project's OSDSYS/BIOS boot target. This is the same caveat already documented in this project's own 160th finding (Round 120): live-reference-session data from GT3 does not transfer to the bare-OSDSYS boot path this project traces, since GT3 brings its own loaded code and heap layout.

**While re-verifying the citation trail for this correction, a second, more consequential issue surfaced**: re-reading the 161st finding (Round 121) in full shows the "AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)" framing that Round 191's 231st finding (and this session's Round 192, 232nd finding) treated as "the project's oldest, most heavily-investigated open blocker... reconfirmed as recently as the 216th finding, Round 176" was **already explicitly closed and superseded three rounds later, in Round 121 itself**: "this round does not open a new investigative thread - it closes the '0x8800/AddIntcHandler' framing as a downstream symptom of the already-known, already-analyzed task #247 blocker [`Status.EXL=1`]... Continuing to reverse-engineer 'what real code should populate the AddIntcHandler table for cause=0x8800' is not the productive path forward, because no dispatch to that table is even being attempted right now." Task #247 (`Status.EXL=1`) was subsequently root-caused and fixed (165th finding, Round 125 - a real KSEG2/KSEG3 TLB-translation bug) and the boot progressed further. A **new, separate, later-established framing** then emerged (Rounds 131-183, tasks #286-#349): the `0x8000F768`-family wait loop is gated on `DMAC_STAT` bit 0x80 (SIF2 completion - confirmed correctly modeled, Round 177's 217th finding, but never triggered in a bare boot) OR `INTC_STAT` bit 0x2 (SBUS - raised only when the IOP writes real ICFG, physical `0x1F801450`, with bit 1 set). The 216th finding I cited in Round 191 is about *this* ICFG/SBUS framing, not the old "0x8800/AddIntcHandler" one - conflating the two was my own citation error, not a re-discovery of a live thread.

**Current, accurate state of this specific blocker** (superseding Round 191/192's framing): the ICFG-bit-1/SBUS trigger question was investigated exhaustively across Rounds 179-183 (219th-223rd findings) and explicitly concluded exhausted: live-PCSX2 tracing is unusable for this question (220th finding, Round 180 - the connected reference session runs a different real game with no reset tool; 221st finding, Round 181 - a fresh reset reaches an unrelated `0x00081fc0` self-loop in under a second of emulated time, decisively confirmed unrelated software); and a full source-level search of ps2sdk, PCSX2, and a third independent clean-room emulator (`allkern/iris`) found zero occurrences of the real trigger anywhere in public source (222nd finding, Round 182: "No further public source location is left to check; this question cannot be closed without either a live comparable-BIOS trace (avenue closed, Round 181) or real BIOS disassembly (excluded by this project's own clean-room convention)... Future rounds should pivot to other open STATUS.md items... rather than re-searching this exhausted angle."). The 223rd finding (Round 183) reconfirmed PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 unchanged as of that round, the last one to touch this specific thread before Round 191/192's (mis-cited) revival.

**What Round 191/192's actual work still stands as valid.** The `0x8000CDF8` trace (both internal blocks dead code), the GT3-trace mismatch identification, and the Alarm/EventFlag/TLB-wrapper syscall fixes are all independently correct and unaffected by this correction - only the SPECIFIC claim that these findings "reconnect to the AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800) mega-effort" is wrong; they in fact reconnect to the separately-tracked, separately-already-exhausted ICFG-bit-1/SBUS thread, whose own most recent authoritative conclusion (222nd finding) is to pivot elsewhere - which is exactly what Round 192 did (independently, for the right reason) by moving to the syscall-table audit.

**Documenting this correction matters for the same reason the 132nd finding's "CORRECTED below" note and the diagnostic-methodology-gap corrections elsewhere in this project's history matter**: an inaccurate citation, left uncorrected, risks a future round re-opening the already-closed "0x8800/AddIntcHandler" thread a second time under the belief that it's still the standing task #221/#358 lead, wasting a round re-deriving what Round 121 already concluded.

## 233rd finding (Round 193, task #359): full programmatic syscall-table audit finds ~78 more unhandled numbers (Rounds 179/186/187/192's own hand-audits each missed these) - fixed with the established exception-raise pattern

Per this project's own 222nd finding's explicit guidance ("pivot to other open STATUS.md items... rather than re-searching this exhausted angle"), and having corrected Round 191/192's citation error above, this round continued the syscall-table-audit vein that Rounds 186-188/192 already proved productive - but this time via a **script-parsed, not hand-audited**, cross-reference: a Python script parsed every `#define __NR_*` in ps2sdk's real `ee/kernel/include/syscallnr.h` (resolving indirections like `__NR_SetupThread __NR_RFU060`), producing a complete, exact numeric table, then diffed it against every `sysnum ==` literal in the current `ee_core.c`. This is a meaningfully different (and more reliable) method than every prior round's own manual/visual audit (Round 179's first pass, believed complete, was proven wrong by Round 186; Round 187's redo, believed complete, was proven wrong by Round 192; Round 192's own review explicitly flagged itself as non-exhaustive).

## 234th finding (Round 194, task #360): independent cross-verification of the 233rd finding's syscall audit against PCSX2's own source - 79/96 exact matches, all 9 discrepancies resolved in ps2sdk's favor, no behavior change needed

Per the user's explicit directive ("double check that audit if needed reverse eneegie it") following Round 193's 78-number syscall audit, this round independently cross-checked that audit against a SECOND, wholly independent source rather than re-reading the same ps2sdk header again.

**Method.** This project already had a full PCSX2 source checkout cached from an early round (`/tmp/round165_diag/pcsx2_src/pcsx2-master/`, ~Round 165). It contains two genuinely independent syscall references, neither derived from ps2sdk: (1) `pcsx2/R5900OpcodeImpl.cpp`'s `const char * const R5900::bios[256]` - a positional debug-name array (array index = syscall number) used only for cosmetic disassembly-log strings, transcribed in full for indices 0-127 into `/tmp/round194_pcsx2_names.txt`; (2) `pcsx2/R5900OpcodeTables.h`'s `enum Syscall : u8` - a small set of explicit numeric constants that PCSX2's own HLE dispatcher (`pcsx2/R5900OpcodeImpl.cpp`'s `BIOS()` switch, lines ~920-1200) actually branches on at runtime. A script built a dictionary of all 96 syscall numbers this project has implemented across Rounds 187/192/193 and diffed each against the transcribed positional array.

**Result.** Every constant in the behaviorally-used `enum Syscall` (SetGsCrt=2, ExecPS2=7, SetVTLBRefillHandler=13, StartThread=34, ChangeThreadPriority=41, RFU060=60, SetOsdConfigParam=74, GetOsdConfigParam=75, SetOsdConfigParam2=110, GetOsdConfigParam2=111, sysPrintOut=117, sceSifSetDma=119, Deci2Call=124, GetMemorySize=127) matches ps2sdk's numbering exactly - strong independent corroboration that this project's entire audit methodology (built on ps2sdk's numbering) is sound. The positional debug-name array matched on 79 of 96 numbers checked, with 8 numbers outside its 0-127 range (128/130/131/133/134/135/252/254 - no data either way) and exactly 9 real discrepancies: 59 (mine: RFU059, PCSX2: JoinThread), 84-90 (mine: xlaunch/PutTLBEntry/_SetTLBEntry/GetTLBEntry/ProbeTLBEntry/ExpandScratchPad/Copy, PCSX2: RFU084_ClearEventFlag through RFU090_iReferEventFlagStatus - an extended EventFlag Clear/Wait/Poll/Refer API), and 116 (mine: SetSyscall, PCSX2: RFU116).

**Resolving the discrepancies.** All 9 fall entirely outside PCSX2's own behaviorally-used `enum Syscall`/dispatcher switch (confirmed by re-reading the full `case Syscall::` list in `R5900OpcodeImpl.cpp`'s `BIOS()` function: only the 14 numbers listed above are ever behaviorally exercised: none of 59, 84-90, or 116 appear) - meaning even PCSX2's own maintainers never verified or exercised these specific names; they are inert debug strings only. Checking ps2sdk's own `ee/kernel/include/*.h` and `ee/kernel/src/*.c` for any trace of "JoinThread", "ClearEventFlag", "WaitEventFlag", "PollEventFlag", or "ReferEventFlagStatus" (case-insensitive) found **zero hits anywhere** - ps2sdk, the most comprehensive actively-maintained open-source PS2 SDK reimplementation, has no such API under any number. Conversely, ps2sdk explicitly and unambiguously defines `__NR_RFU059` at 0x3b (59) and `__NR_SetSyscall` at 0x74 (116) - exactly the numbers this project already implemented. This is strong evidence PCSX2's cosmetic `bios[256]` array contains a real, longstanding, but functionally-inert transcription inaccuracy in this specific range (never corrected across PCSX2's 20+ year history precisely because it's never behaviorally exercised), and that ps2sdk's numbering - and thus this project's Round 192/193 implementation - is correct.

**No source-code change this round.** `ee_raise_exception(st, EE_EXC_CODE_SYS, this_pc, in_delay_slot)` is the correct, name-agnostic behavior for every one of these 9 numbers regardless of which semantic label is right - the fix does not depend on knowing the real function name, only on recognizing "this is a real, currently-unmodeled kernel syscall, so vector to a real exception rather than halt." This round is a verification/corroboration round, not a behavior-changing one; no `ee_core.c` comment text was found to be incorrect enough to warrant editing (the comments already cite ps2sdk as the source, which this round confirms was the right choice).

**Verification.** No source change -> no new regression suite run or Wii rebuild needed this round (docs-only, per this project's own established convention for investigation rounds). All cross-check work is scratch-only (`/tmp/round194_pcsx2_names.txt`, inline Python), never touched the committed repo.

There is no reverse-engineering result that overturns any of Round 193's 78 fixes.

## 235th finding (Round 195, task #361): implement real analog-mode (DualShock "Read Buttons AND analog inputs") support for the SIO2 pad protocol - the peripheral-completeness increment the user's "go to gs if helpful" framing authorized

Per the user's own explicit criterion from the prior round ("wont make sense to go to gs if the other issue blocking it... ofc you can go to gs if its helpful"), this round first assessed whether GS/audio/peripheral work independent of the still-exhausted ICFG-bit-1/SBUS blocker (222nd finding, Round 182) was available, rather than defaulting to GS. This is real, tractable, fully independent of the ICFG/SBUS blocker (a controller-protocol completeness gap, not a boot-order gap), and directly answers the user's own conditional.

**Research first.** Fetched psx-spx's "Controllers and Memory Cards" page directly this round (same page already cited for the existing digital-pad and memory-card protocols) and confirmed the real, cited analog-mode facts: controller ID `5A73h` ("Analog Pad, in normal analog mode; LED=Red") sent LSB-first exactly like the existing `5A41h` digital ID; the digital-switches halfwords are unchanged in format; after the existing 2 switch bytes, analog mode does NOT stop the transfer - it sends 4 more bytes (`adc0`=RightJoyX, `adc1`=RightJoyY, `adc2`=LeftJoyX, `adc3`=LeftJoyY, each `00h`=one extreme/`80h`=Center/`FFh`=other extreme) before the real cited "transfer stops here for analog pad (in analog mode)" point; real cited power-up default is digital mode ("On power-up, the controllers are in digital mode"). One real gap was found and left honestly unfilled: this project could not locate a byte-exact table for the real command `43h` ("Enter/Exit Configuration Mode", the real software mechanism DualShock pads use to toggle analog mode) in what was fetched - the source's own table of contents lists that section but its body table was not present in the retrieved content, so no bytes were fabricated for it. Per this exact same source's own explicit recommendation for emulators ("It is essential that emulators and any third-party hardware have a way of manually toggling analog mode... as certain games like Gran Turismo 1 will not attempt to enter analog mode on their own"), analog mode is toggled here via a plain host-side API mirroring the real hardware's own manual "Analog button" mechanism, rather than guessing at the uncited `43h` sequence.

**Implementation** (`include/core/hw/iop_sio2.h`, `source/hw/iop_sio2.c`): extended `pad_t` with `analog_mode` (default 0, real cited power-up value) and 4 axis bytes (`axis_rx/ry/lx/ly`, default `0x80` = real cited Center). New public API: `iop_sio2_pad_set_analog_mode()`/`iop_sio2_pad_is_analog_mode()`/`iop_sio2_pad_set_analog_axes()`/`iop_sio2_pad_get_analog_axes()`. `pad_process_command()`'s existing `0x42` READ-command handler now emits the real cited `5A73h` ID instead of `5A41h` when analog mode is on, and continues past the swlo/swhi bytes to emit the 4 real cited `adc0-adc3` bytes (each gated by the same `if (n < N) return` short-transfer pattern already used throughout this function) instead of stopping - exactly matching the two different real cited "transfer stops here" points for digital vs. analog mode. Digital-mode behavior is completely unchanged (regression-verified).

**Verification.** Extended `tests/test_sio2_pad.c` with 9 new checks (30 total, up from 21): default-off analog mode and default-Center axes; ID switches to `5A73h` and all 4 axis bytes match set values once analog mode is enabled; a short 5-byte transfer in analog mode still stops cleanly without reading past what was clocked (mirrors the existing digital-mode partial-transfer check); disabling analog mode reverts the ID to `5A41h` (regression check against Round 184's original digital-only behavior). All 30 checks pass. Full regression suite: 119/119 test files pass (0 build failures, 0 runtime failures) - re-derived the project's own object-file-based build methodology this round (compile all `source/**/*.c` except `main.c`/`ppc_dynarec.c` - Wii-only, needs libogc/devkitPPC headers - into host object files once, link each test against its own file plus every object except whichever source file(s) it self-includes, avoiding duplicate-symbol errors). **Honest scope, unchanged from before this round**: DualShock2-specific extensions (`5A79h` "all analog/digital inputs enabled" ID, the extra analog-button pressure halfwords) and the real `43h`/`44h`/`45h` configuration-mode command sequence remain open, uncited gaps for a future round if ever needed - not fabricated here. `docs/ROADMAP.md`'s "Pad/memory card" checkbox is updated to reflect that both halves (digital+analog pad via SIO2, memory card via SIO2) now have real, cited protocol implementations.

## 236th finding (Round 196, task #362): direct instrumentation finally traces the real ICFG write sites in this project's OWN boot - corrects the prior "exhausted" framing with genuine new evidence; bit 1 (SBUS trigger) confirmed never set across 240M EE instructions, but for the first time we know exactly why

Per the user's explicit push-back on the 222nd finding's "exhausted" conclusion ("it must be called... it reads then it stops... we need to figure out where it stops"): the prior rounds' "exhausted" framing (219th-222nd findings, Rounds 180-182) was based on two avenues only - searching PUBLIC source (ps2sdk/PCSX2/allkern-iris) for the real trigger, and attempting a LIVE comparable PCSX2 session (unavailable). A THIRD avenue was never actually tried: directly instrumenting this project's OWN interpreter, which is running the REAL BIOS (never committed, per this project's standing security rule) - i.e., stop asking "what does public source say should happen" and instead ask "what does our own emulator's own execution of the real ROM actually do." This round did exactly that, and it changes the picture substantially.

**Method (three layers, each scratch-only, never committed - all Round 196 tools live in `/tmp/round196_diag/`, `/tmp/round196_scratch/`).**

1. **Static clean-room scan.** Wrote a small MIPS-I decoder (standard, publicly-documented R3000A opcode fields - not derived from any Sony source) and scanned the full 4MB real BIOS ROM image for `LUI $reg,{0xBF80,0x9F80,0x1F80}` followed by `SW $src,0x1450($reg)` - the generic compiler idiom for writing a fixed absolute address (ICFG). Found 6 real candidate sites, cross-referenced via this project's own ROMDIR-walking logic (`bios_loader.c`'s own signature-scan algorithm, reapplied here) against the named module list: they fall inside **LOADCORE**, **IOPBOOT**, and **UDNL** - three real, named PS2 BIOS modules already well-known to this project's history (LOADCORE especially, from the Round 124-132 registration-walk investigation).

2. **Dynamic instrumentation.** Added a single temporary diagnostic line to a throwaway copy of `iop_mem_write32()` (never touched the committed `source/core/iop/iop_core.c`) logging every write to physical address `0x1F801450` with the current IOP PC. Ran this project's own established `system_init()`/`ee_core_step()`/`iop_core_step()` boot loop (same harness as every prior round's `boot_sanity.c`) for **240,000,000 EE instructions** - 20x further than any prior round's bounded sanity check, and beyond the ~200M-instruction "resting point" this project's history has repeatedly referenced as the boot's steady state. Result: **ICFG is written exactly 64 times**, from only **2 distinct real IOP program-counter locations**, values only ever `0x00000000` or `0x00000001` - **bit 1 (0x2) is never once set**.

3. **Disassembly of both real writer functions** (dumped the actual executing RAM bytes - the modules get copied/relocated into IOP RAM before running, which is why the executing addresses differ from the static ROM offsets above - and decoded them with the same clean-room MIPS-I decoder):
   - **Site A** (`~0x00102608-0x001026E0` in IOP RAM, also reachable via a computed `jr` jump from a second call site at `~0x00102700`, and confirmed via ~64 total appearances to be called repeatedly throughout boot): a standard **cache-flush utility** - reads ICFG, clears bit 0, does a 16-word-stride zeroing loop over a data range while COP0 Status has cache-isolate bits set (the real, standard R3000A "invalidate D-cache" idiom - it also touches the real R3000 Cache Control Register at physical `0xFFFE0130`, a well-documented, non-Sony-specific piece of MIPS/PS1-family architecture), then **restores the exact original ICFG value it read at entry**. Net effect on ICFG: zero - bit 0 is toggled and restored, nothing is permanently changed. This function is almost certainly the real BIOS's equivalent of the well-known `FlushCache()` kernel call, incidentally touching ICFG bit 0 as an undocumented side effect of a cache-control sequence, not as its purpose.
   - **Site B** (`~0x00117A44-0x00117B28` in IOP RAM): a genuine **IOP subsystem bring-up routine**. Reads ICFG, conditionally re-sets bit 4 (0x10), then unconditionally sets bit 0 (0x1) and writes it back (this is the write this round's instrumentation actually caught with `val=1`) - then calls onward into a cluster of further init subroutines (`~0x117DB0`, `~0x1187D8`/`~0x1187E8`/`~0x118800`/`~0x118808`, `~0x1179DC`) whose call pattern (zero a small struct, pass a size/type constant of 42/0x2A, etc.) strongly resembles a real kernel-object-creation sequence (e.g. `CreateEventFlag`-style). Immediately before this, the SAME broader routine also touches two OTHER real, cited nearby registers: it clears `IOP DMA9_CHCR` (`0x1F801528`) and `IOP DMA10_CHCR` (`0x1F801538`), then ORs the literal value `0x8800` into `IOP DPCR2` (`0x1F801570`, "DMA Priority Control register 2") - all three addresses independently confirmed via BOTH PCSX2's `IopHw.h` (`HWx_DMA9_CHCR`/`HWx_DMA10_CHCR`/`HW_DMA_PCR2`) and ps2sdk's `iop_regs.h` (`A_IOP_D9_CHCR`/`A_IOP_D10_CHCR`/`A_IOP_DPCR2`).

**Important correction, made honestly and immediately rather than left for a future round to catch**: the `0x8800` value written to DPCR2 in Site B is a **coincidental numeric match**, NOT a reconnection to this project's long-running "`AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)`" thread (111th finding onward, closed Round 121/161st finding). DPCR2 is a real IOP DMA-controller enable/priority register (standard PS1/PS2 architecture: each DMA channel gets a 4-bit priority+enable nibble; `0x8800` = bits 11 and 15 set, i.e. enabling DMA channels 9 and 10 - exactly the two channels whose CHCR registers this same routine just cleared/reset immediately before). The old `0x8800` thread was about a completely different register on a completely different CPU (the EE's own COP0 Cause register bitmask, hypothesized, never confirmed). These are two unrelated `0x8800` values that happen to share a numeric literal - flagging this explicitly, by name, so no future round repeats the Round 191/192 citation-conflation mistake with this new coincidence.

**Honest, direct answer to the user's question.** The ICFG-writing code IS called - repeatedly, by name, now disassembled in full - and none of it ever sets bit 1. This is a real, substantial, first-time answer (previous rounds could only say "we don't know if/where it's called"; this round shows exactly where, what both call sites do, and that bit 1 genuinely never gets set across the longest bounded trace this project has ever run - 240M EE instructions, well past the established resting point). Two honest possibilities remain open for the ACTUAL bit-1 trigger: (a) it requires IOP code this project's current module-loader configuration never reaches at all in a bare/diskless boot (a real, different gap from "the write site is unknown" - now it's "the write site, if any, must be in code we don't yet execute"), or (b) real hardware genuinely never sets bit 1 on a diskless/bare boot either, and the `0x8000F768` OSDSYS wait loop's SIF2-completion half (DMAC_STAT bit 0x80, already confirmed correctly modeled per the 217th finding) is the one meant to fire in this exact scenario, not the ICFG/SBUS half - i.e. the two independent trigger conditions this project's own docs have tracked since Round 177 (task #342-344) may not be equally reachable in a bare boot, and this round's evidence leans toward SIF2 being the real path forward rather than ICFG/SBUS specifically.

**No source-code change this round** - correctly scoped as an investigation round: no citable fix presents itself (this round found WHERE ICFG is touched and confirmed bit 1 isn't among the touched bits, which is new information, not a bug to fix - the existing `iop_icfg_mmio_write32()` model is already 100% correct per its own PCSX2 citation, it simply has never yet been asked to raise INTC_SBUS because no real code in this trajectory writes that specific bit).

**Not yet resolved, correctly scoped for a future round**: (1) trace the call chain further from Site B's `~0x117DB0`/`~0x1187D8`-`~0x118808` cluster to identify what real kernel object(s) it's creating, and whether any LATER code (not yet exercised in a 240M-instruction window, or gated behind a module this project's loader doesn't yet run) is the genuine ICFG-bit-1 writer; (2) given (b) above, the SIF2-completion path (`DMAC_STAT` bit 0x80) may be the more promising half of the original two-condition OSDSYS wait-loop gate to pursue next, since it's the ONE HALF of that gate this round's evidence doesn't rule out as unreachable.

## 237th finding (Round 197, task #363): full disassembly-traced root cause of the current OSDSYS boot blocker - the exact field, the exact clearing function, its exact sole caller, and the exact gate condition that caller depends on, which is never satisfied because this project's DMA model has no inbound (IOP-to-EE) RAM-write path at all

Per the user's explicit "do both" directive (continue Site B's IOP call chain AND pivot to the SIF2-completion path), this round pursued the SIF2/blocker-tracing half to a definitive conclusion using the same own-interpreter-instrumentation method validated in Round 196, plus a full 32MB EE RAM static scan/disassembly pass never attempted before.

**Step 1 - the Round 178 shortcut fires, but doesn't help.** Confirmed via direct instrumentation that the existing experimental `ee_check_boot_unblock_sbus_wait()` shortcut (Round 178, task #344) DOES fire during the real boot trace, artificially satisfying the SBUS half of the original `0x8000CFD0` gate. This does not unblock the boot - proving the CURRENT actual resting point is a different, later gate than what Round 196's framing assumed, and that Round 196's 240M-instruction ICFG trace, while accurate, was answering a question that had already been made moot by this pre-existing shortcut.

**Step 2 - found the real current resting loop and its exact exit condition.** Disassembled the actual current per-frame retry loop (`0x8000F768-0x8000F8xx`, the same OSDSYS milestone Rounds 190-192 have circled). Its real exit condition, read directly off the disassembly: falls through (exits) only when `RAM[0x80020E4C]==0 AND RAM[0x80020E28]==0`; otherwise loops back to `0x8000f768`. Direct memory reads confirm `RAM[0x80020E28]`, `[0x80020E30]`, `[0x80020E3C]`, and `[0x80020B54]` (all four fields Round 192's task #358 flagged but never fully resolved) are ALL currently `0` (satisfied) - **`RAM[0x80020E4C] = 0x24` (36 decimal) is the sole remaining blocker.**

**Step 3 - found the one function that clears it.** A full static scan of the entire 32MB EE RAM dump (taken after a 240M-EE-step run) for `SW $rt, 0xE4C($rs)` instructions found exactly 3 candidates project-wide. One, at `~0x8000E9B0-0x8000EAB8`, is a genuine SIF/RPC reply-processing callback: validates an incoming packet header, bounds-checks against 17/257, calls a data-copy helper, sets a completion flag, and - via a small switch on a status byte - zeroes `RAM[s0+0xE4C]` at `0x8000eaa8`. This is the only code in the entire 32MB RAM image that can ever clear the blocking field.

**Step 4 - found its one caller, and that caller is itself a bigger dispatcher.** A full-RAM `JAL`-target scan found exactly one call site targeting that callback: `0x800100b8`. Disassembling the surrounding function (entry at `0x8000FFD0`, a real stack-frame prologue - call it "Function F") shows it is the real "process one incoming SIF-RPC-queue message" handler: takes a header pointer and context pointer as args, validates the header's size field against 1025/1024, and dispatches via a jump table (base `0x80013830`) on a state byte read from the context struct - one case (`0x80010090`) reads/rewrites the E4C field directly (sets it to 33, never to 0), and a DIFFERENT case (`0x800100b4`) is the one that actually calls the E4C-clearing callback and stores its return code as the next state.

**Step 5 - proved Function F itself is never reached, and found exactly why.** A hit-counter instrumented directly into the interpreter (checking `ee->pc==0x8000FFD0` on every one of 240,000,000 EE steps) fired **zero times**. A full-RAM `JAL`-target scan for Function F's own address found exactly one caller: `0x8000F3D0`, itself gated by a condition disassembled directly: `bne $3,$2,...` where `$3 = RAM[0x80020E3C]` and `$2 = 1` - i.e. **Function F is only ever called when `RAM[0x80020E3C]` is exactly `1`.** Our confirmed-zero value for that field (Step 2) directly and completely explains the zero hit count - this is not a coincidence, it is the same fact observed from two independent directions (static gate disassembly and dynamic hit-counting), which is as close to proof as this project's tooling can get without a live reference session.

**Step 6 - proved nothing in this project's current emulated system ever writes that field, and identified the structural reason.** Patched the single, central `ee_mem_write32()` function (the ONE code path all EE-side RAM writes funnel through, confirmed by direct source inspection) to log any write to `0x80020E3C` from ANY source - regular EE instructions, HLE shortcuts, everything that goes through this function. ## 238th finding (Round 198, task #365): implemented the missing inbound (IOP-to-EE) DMA write capability identified by Round 197 - a real, tested, citable engine primitive, honestly verified to NOT by itself change the current boot trace since no producer is wired to it yet

SIF0 (`DMA_CHANNEL_SIF0`, physical base `0x1000C000`) is the real, standard, already-cited-throughout-this-file "fromIOP" channel - this is not new/invented terminology, it's the same real hardware fact `dma.h`'s own existing doc comments have described since this channel constant was first added.
