## 249th finding (Round 209, task #366/#371): wired real disc mounting into main.c's ACTUAL persistent boot flow (previously only exercised in throwaway diagnostics) - closes a real gap the user directly identified; and an honest caveat: live DebugServer interaction (pause/breakpoint/continue) destabilized the user's actual PCSX2 session and caused it to crash

**The user's own direct observation was correct, for a more basic reason than initially suspected.** Asked whether "the game is a binary and we don't have a real ISO/BIN loader - maybe it doesn't even try to use the drive, but crashes booting the image" - checked `source/main.c`'s `run_real_boot_flow()` (the actual function that runs on the real Wii `.dol` build, as opposed to this project's many throwaway host-native diagnostics) and confirmed: **it has NEVER called `iop_cdvd_mount_iso()` or `iop_cdrom_legacy_mount_iso()` at all**, in any prior round. Only ever loads a BIOS from `sd:/pcsx2/bios/*.bin`. So while this project's real ISO9660 parser (`iso_loader.c`, Round 139/170) and both real disc-register interfaces (Round 145, Round 206) work correctly when exercised directly, the actual persistent Wii build has had literally no disc to read since disc support was first added - a genuine, concrete gap, not a crash.

**Fixed this round.** `run_real_boot_flow()` now attempts `iop_cdvd_mount_iso()` and `iop_cdrom_legacy_mount_iso()` once, against `sd:/pcsx2/games/game.bin` (falling back to `game.iso`), mirroring the existing BIOS search-path convention. Mounted on BOTH real register interfaces since Rounds 205-207 have not yet established which one (if either) real BIOS/kernel code actually uses - giving the real boot every real chance to succeed regardless of path. A missing disc is logged, not fatal (matches real PS2 hardware, which also boots fine with no disc inserted, just without a disc-boot fast path) - only a real BIOS remains mandatory to proceed.

**Verification.** `main.c` cannot be host-native syntax-checked directly (depends on `<gccore.h>`/libogc, Wii-only, an existing, already-documented limitation) - so the real verification is a clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: `make clean && make` succeeded, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, with only the two already-known, pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings (`iop_core.c:482`, `iop_module_loader.c:225`), no new ones. Full host-native regression suite re-run in full (all 120 `tests/*.c` files, rebuilt test runner since the prior session's tooling was lost to an intervening sandbox reset): **120/120 pass, zero regressions** - expected, since no `source/hw/*.c`/`source/core/*.c` file changed this round, only `main.c` itself, which sits outside the host-native test suite's coverage by design.

**Separately, an honest operational caveat from this same round: live DebugServer interaction can destabilize the user's actual, actively-used PCSX2 session, up to and including crashing it.** Per the user's own explicit request ("beides" - continue both the SIF_SMFLAG-loop thread and disc-loader question), this round attempted to use Round 208's newly-reachable DebugServer connection to arm a fresh live boot trace. In doing so: (1) setting a breakpoint appears to have left the emulator PAUSED in a way that blocked the user's own attempt to resume normal play from their own UI - the user reported "wenn ich versuche den emulator laufen zu lassen wird er von claude blockiert" ("when I try to let the emulator run, it gets blocked by Claude"). Clearing all breakpoints/watchpoints and issuing `pcsx2_continue()` did restore normal running (`Paused: false`, cycles advancing) at that point. (2) Shortly after, attempting to arm a fresh watchpoint produced `ECONNRESET`, and the connection then became fully unreachable (`ECONNREFUSED`) - the user confirmed "jetzt emulator ist gecrasht" (the emulator crashed).

**Honest interpretation.** This project's own DebugServer/PINE connection has, throughout this session, been treated as if it were a passive, read-only reference oracle - but this round's experience shows it is NOT safely passive when the user's own PCSX2 window is their real, actively-used instance (as opposed to a dedicated, otherwise-idle reference session): pausing, breakpoint installation, and rapid continue/step/clear-breakpoint cycling in close succession appear to have left the emulator core in a state it could not recover from. This is reported as a genuine, concrete operational risk for any future round's live-debugging work, not a source-code bug in this project's own emulator (PCSX2 itself is a separate, third-party program) - and not something this round attempts to root-cause further, since doing so would require deliberately reproducing a crash in the user's real, actively-used session again.

**Concrete, scoped guidance for future rounds.** Live DebugServer/PINE interaction with the user's PCSX2 should only be attempted with the user's explicit, per-session confirmation (matching the precedent already set this round via `AskUserQuestion`), kept as brief and surgical as possible (arm exactly what is needed, capture the hit, clear and release immediately), and the user should be given the option to use a separate, dedicated PCSX2 instance for future investigation work if they want to avoid any risk to their own active session going forward. This is a real, practical lesson learned, not a hypothetical concern.

**No BIOS/game data incorporated or affected.** The main.c change reads a user-provided disc path from the SD card at runtime; nothing about the crash or the disc-mount fix touches this project's own standing rule against committing/pushing/rsyncing real BIOS or game data.

## 250th finding (Round 210, task #366/#172): built an independent, standalone live-boot-monitor tool (patch to the separate third-party `PCSX2-MCP` project, not this repo) and used it to capture a full, real reset-to-gameplay cycle live - DISPLAY1 confirmed never written even across a freshly-observed complete reboot, and a previously-documented self-loop address (Round 157's `0x00081fc0`) resurfaces as a recurring, stable execution point

**Context.** Per the user's own follow-up request ("erweitere auch damit er display1 und co auslesen kann alles"), and a separate, more detailed written spec the user provided (`PCSX2_MCP_Debug_Auftrag.txt`, a 5-phase GS/GIF/DMAC debug-system spec), this round extended the user's local `PCSX2-MCP` installation (a separate, third-party tool that bridges Claude to the user's live PCSX2 - not part of this repo, delivered to the user as standalone patch files, not committed here) with: a `cpu:"ee"|"iop"` parameter exposed on every relevant tool (previously only supported internally, never surfaced); a GS/GIF/DMA register-inspector tool family (`pcsx2_gs_read`, `pcsx2_gif_read`, `pcsx2_dma_read`, plus interval-based JSONL tracers for each); a crash-safe, log-only `pcsx2_boot_analyzer`/`pcsx2_boot_analyze` pair (never uses pause/step/continue, per the operational lesson from Round 209's crash); and a standalone Python client, `monitor.py`, that talks directly to the DebugServer's documented TCP/JSON protocol (no Node/MCP dependency) and does live polling, JSONL logging, CSV export, and the same stall-heuristic analysis. All GS/GIF/DMAC register addresses used are the standard, publicly-documented EE hardware register map (matching ps2sdk/PCSX2 conventions, same sourcing standard already established for this project's own GS/CDVD address citations) - no BIOS ROM bytes were transcribed into any of this tooling.

**Live capture, run by the user against their own actively-played PCSX2 session (real BIOS + real Tekken Tag Tournament demo disc).** Two `monitor.py live` runs, ~27s and ~49s respectively, both read out live via the DebugServer connection with zero pause/step/continue calls (read-only polling only, consistent with Round 209's crash-avoidance guidance). Both captures show **DISPLAY1 remaining exactly `0x0000000000000000` for the entire duration**, corroborating Round 223's static finding and Round 208's mid-execution live snapshot from a third, independent angle and tool.

**A genuine, live-observed full reset cycle.** In the second capture, PC is seen paused at `0x00081fc0` for ~11 seconds, then jumps to **`0xbfc00000`** - the literal EE reset vector - while still paused, for a further ~6 seconds. The user confirmed this was an intentional manual reset triggered from PCSX2's own UI (not caused by this project's tooling, which only ever reads memory/status). Upon resume, the boot **fully replays and reaches real game code again within ~7 seconds**: `0x80005b84` (kernel-space, brief) -> `0x00081fc0` -> `0x00200cb0` -> real user-space Tekken code (`0x005189a0` and others, in the same low-address range Round 171/334/335 already identified as the real ELF's loaded code region). **DISPLAY1 stayed at `0x0` throughout this entire observed reset-and-reboot sequence, including well after execution resumed in real game code** - the first time this project has live-observed the display-write question across a complete, freshly-triggered boot cycle rather than only a static snapshot or a mid-execution one.

**A recurring, stable set of execution addresses.** Both captures independently show the same handful of addresses recurring with multi-second dwell times before the PC moves on: `0x005189a0`, `0x00205200`, `0x00216560`, `0x00400760`, `0x003993b8`/`0x003993c0`, and `0x00081fc0`. Their consistent reappearance across two separate capture sessions suggests these are real, stable code locations (menu/idle/polling logic in the actual game code) rather than capture noise. Notably, `0x00081fc0` is an address this project has already investigated once before: Round 157 ("investigate the real task #181 wall itself (`0x00081fc0` self-loop)"). This round does not re-open or re-verify that prior investigation's conclusions - it only notes the address's reappearance here as a cross-reference worth checking against Round 157's own notes in a future round, since the two observations may or may not be describing the same underlying loop.

**Honest interpretation and scope.** This round adds real, live, tool-independent corroboration that DISPLAY1 (and by extension PMODE/DISPFB1, part of the same GS display-config write this project has tracked since the 94th/126th/223rd findings) is never written by this specific real BIOS+game combination, across both ongoing execution and a freshly-observed complete reboot - strengthening, not newly establishing, the already-long-standing conclusion that the boot never reaches a real GS display-configuration call. It does **not** identify what code should write DISPLAY1, why it doesn't, or whether the `0x00081fc0` recurrence is causally related to that gap - those remain open. The GS/GIF/DMA/boot-analyzer tooling itself is new and available for future rounds (both as MCP tools, once a fresh Cowork session picks up the patched server, and directly via `monitor.py`), but was only used this round for the DISPLAY1/reset observation above - the GIF/DMA read-outs and `pcsx2_boot_analyze`'s automated milestone/flag report have not yet been exercised against a real capture.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** All tooling changes live in the separate, third-party `PCSX2-MCP` project (delivered to the user as patch files, `index.ts`/`index.js`/`monitor.py`), not in this repo. Correctly scoped as a docs-only, live-investigation round.

## 251st finding (Round 211, task #366/#172): extended `monitor.py` to detect DMA2(GIF)/PATH3 activity - confirmed inactive across two more live captures (~19s total); and this round's live-observed `0x00081fc0` recurrence is cross-referenced against Round 157, with an important scope correction to that prior investigation

**Context.** The user reviewed Round 210's live captures and proposed a concrete, well-reasoned next diagnostic step: since `DISPLAY1` has now been repeatedly confirmed at `0x0`, stop re-observing that fact and instead trace backwards through the pipeline that would need to feed it - DMAC channel 2 (GIF) state, GIF unit activity, interrupts, and SIF - starting with the most basic question: does a PATH3 transfer ever even start. One correction was made to the user's plan before acting on it: `PMODE`/`DISPFB1`/`DISPLAY1`/`CSR`/etc. are GS **privileged** registers (`0x12000000+`), written directly by the EE via ordinary store instructions - they are architecturally unreachable via GIF A+D packets, which only ever target GS **context/rendering** registers (`PRIM`, `TEX0`, `FRAME`, `ZBUF`, ...). This is standard, public Sony GS Users Manual/ps2sdk-gsKit architecture, not derived from any BIOS disassembly, and it means a GIF-packet decoder could never find a `DISPLAY1` write regardless of boot state - so the useful question from the user's plan is narrowed to "does GIF/PATH3 activity happen at all," not "does it ever target the display registers."

**Extended `monitor.py`** (the standalone Python client delivered in Round 210, separate `PCSX2-MCP` project, no server-side change needed) with a `gif_dma2_activity()` helper that tracks, cumulatively across a whole `live` session or a post-hoc `analyze` run: whether DMA channel 2's `CHCR.STR` bit was ever seen set to `1`, and whether `GIF_STAT`/`GIF_CNT` were ever seen nonzero. Both `live` and `analyze` now print an explicit summary and, if DMA2 never started, an explicit "cause sits before GS/GIF" flag - directly operationalizing the user's proposed diagnostic step using registers `monitor.py` already polled every sample but never explicitly evaluated for this question. Verified via `py_compile` and a synthetic JSONL round-trip before delivery.

**Two live captures, run by the user against their own real, actively-played session (~6s and ~13s).** In both: **DMA channel 2's `CHCR.STR` was never set to `1`, and `GIF_STAT`/`GIF_CNT` stayed exactly `0x0` for the entire duration** - no PATH3 transfer was started even once, in either capture.

**Honest scope caveat.** Both captures' PC values (`0x00400760`, `0x003993c0`, `0x0035c698`, `0x00082220`, `0x00081fc0`, `0x005189a0`, `0x0050e6ac`, `0x005102d8`, `0x0020fef0`, `0x00205200`, `0x00216560`) sit in the real, already-loaded Tekken ELF's code region (the same low-address range Rounds 171/334/335 already identified) - this is **steady-state gameplay/menu execution**, not the initial BIOS reset-to-splash window. So this result establishes "GIF/DMA2 is idle at this point in execution," corroborating but not conclusively proving "GIF/DMA2 is never used during the initial boot." A capture spanning the moment right after `0xBFC00000` (as Round 210's second capture partially did, though without this DMA2/GIF instrumentation active at the time) would be needed to close that gap fully.

**A reproducible rotation among known spin addresses.** The second capture's PC visibly round-robins through six distinct addresses with multi-sample (multi-second) dwell time at each before moving on: `0x00082220` -> `0x00081fc0` -> `0x005189a0` (longest dwell, ~10 samples) -> `0x0050e6ac` -> `0x005189a0` -> `0x005102d8` -> `0x005189a0` -> `0x00081fc0` -> `0x0020fef0` -> `0x00205200` -> `0x00216560`. Combined with the first capture's `0x00400760`, this means **all five of the addresses the user originally listed as "reproducible spin addresses," plus `0x00081fc0`, all reappeared live in this round's two short captures** - strong corroboration that these are real, stable, reproducible code locations (consistent with a scheduler or kernel round-robining between several distinct wait-conditions), not capture artifacts.

**`0x00081fc0` cross-referenced against Round 157 - with an important scope correction.** Round 157 disassembled `0x00081fc0` as a genuine dead self-loop (`nop`x6 then branch-to-self) and characterized it as the EE idle thread parked while `INTC_MASK`=0 (an exhaustive, multi-round investigation across Rounds 157-160 found no write to `INTC_MASK` in any observable window). **Critically, Round 157-160's investigation was run against a different, unrelated live reference PCSX2 session** (real BIOS + a different real disc, later conclusively identified in Round 160 as running distinct real software - most likely OSDSYS's own idle thread, given its 38-module IOP load versus this project's own 29-module boot) - that investigative avenue was explicitly closed as "not comparable" to this project's actual target (the Tekken Tag Tournament Demo boot). This round's `0x00081fc0` sighting is different in kind: it was observed **directly in the user's own actual game session** - the real subject of this entire porting project - not an unrelated comparison session. Since `0x00081fc0` is a low, fixed physical address and shares the exact same "nop-sled + branch-to-self" signature Round 157 already disassembled, the most plausible explanation is that this is real, shared Sony BIOS/kernel idle-thread code resident at a fixed location independent of which disc is booted - meaning Round 157's `INTC_MASK`-starvation characterization plausibly *does* apply to the actual game this project targets, not only to the unrelated session it was first observed on.

**Honest limits of this claim.** This is a plausibility argument from address-plus-signature reappearance, not a re-verification: no `pcsx2_disassemble` or `INTC_MASK`/`I_STAT` read was performed during this round's dwell at `0x00081fc0` (only the existing GS/GIF/DMA/status registers `monitor.py` already polls were read). The claim is "consistent with Round 157's mechanism," not "proven identical" - a live disassemble-and-register-check the next time PC parks at `0x00081fc0` would confirm or refute it directly.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** All tooling changes live in the separate `PCSX2-MCP` project (`monitor.py` extension only, no server/TS rebuild required). Correctly scoped as a docs-only, live-investigation round.

## 252nd finding (Round 212, task #366/#172): user-provided real PCSX2 debugger screenshots at the actual BIOS splash screen reveal the real BIOS drives the picture through GS Circuit 2, not Circuit 1 - and this project's own Wii-side blit code was hardcoded to read only Circuit 1, a real, confirmed bug now fixed

**Context.** Following up on Round 211's monitor.py work, the user provided six screenshots of a real PCSX2's own built-in debugger (Registers panel: GPR/CP0/FPR/VU0f/VU0i/GS tabs) taken at the actual, real BIOS splash screen - the first time this project has had register-level ground truth for what a *successful* boot's GS state actually looks like, as opposed to a mid-boot or stalled snapshot.

**The key values, read directly from the GS tab:**
- `PMODE = 0000000000000066`
- `DISPFB1 = 0`, `DISPLAY1 = 0000000000000000` (exactly zero)
- `DISPFB2 = 00000000000014A0`, `DISPLAY2 = 001FF9FF0181227C` (both nonzero, structured)
- `CSR = 00000000551B400C` (bits 2/3, HSINT/VSINT, both set - real video timing actively running)

**Decoding PMODE (standard, public Sony GS Users Manual bit convention - bit0=EN1, bit1=EN2 - the same sourcing tier already used throughout this project's GS work):** `0x66` = `0110 0110` binary -> **EN1 (bit0) = 0, EN2 (bit1) = 1**. This real BIOS+splash-screen state has **Circuit 1 explicitly disabled and Circuit 2 driving the actual picture**. `DISPFB2`'s FBW field decodes to 640 pixels (a genuine, recognizable real PS2 resolution), confirming this isn't a degenerate/garbage value.

**Why this matters:** `DISPLAY1`/`DISPFB1` reading exactly zero has been treated as evidence of "GS setup never happened" since the 94th finding (Round 62) and re-confirmed in the 126th (Round 115) and 223rd (Round 189/183) findings, and again in Round 210/211's live captures. This new, real reference data shows that a **successful, real, working boot legitimately never touches Circuit 1 at all** - `DISPLAY1`/`DISPFB1` staying zero is not necessarily evidence of failure; it may simply mean this BIOS's splash screen exclusively uses Circuit 2. This doesn't retroactively invalidate the many rounds establishing that PMODE *itself* stays at `0x0` in this project's own boot trace (a stronger, circuit-independent statement - nothing display-related is written at all) - but it does mean any future round that gets far enough to see PMODE become nonzero must check `DISPFB2`/`DISPLAY2`, not just `DISPFB1`/`DISPLAY1`, before concluding display setup hasn't happened.

**A real, confirmed bug found and fixed as a direct result.** Checked `source/main.c`'s `run_real_boot_flow()` - the actual code driving the real Wii build's screen output. Its per-chunk display check already correctly evaluated `display_active` as true when *either* EN1 or EN2 was set (`gs->pmode & 0x3`), but the blit call immediately after it was hardcoded: `decode_dispfb(gs->dispfb1, &bp_words, &bw_pixels)` - always Circuit 1, regardless of which circuit PMODE actually enabled. Given this round's real evidence that the actual target BIOS uses Circuit 2 exclusively, this meant that even a future, hardware-accurate boot that correctly reached real GS display setup (writing `PMODE`/`DISPFB2`/`DISPLAY2` the way real hardware does) would have produced **no picture on the Wii at all** - the blit would silently read Circuit 1's still-zero registers and skip itself (`bw_pixels > 0` check fails), even though the game/BIOS had done everything right. This was a real, previously-undiscovered bug in this project's own code, not a re-statement of the boot-blocker investigation.

**Fix.** `gs_state_t` (`include/core/hw/gs.h`) and `gs.c`'s register map already modeled `dispfb2`/`display2` correctly at their real addresses (`0x12000090`/`0x120000A0`) - only the `main.c` call site needed changing. Now checks `en1`/`en2` individually and blits from `gs->dispfb1` if EN1 is set, else `gs->dispfb2` if EN2 is set (EN1 preferred if both are somehow set, matching real hardware's Circuit-1-primary convention). Both the inline comment and the file's top-of-file doc block were updated to explain why, citing this round's real evidence.

**Verification.** `main.c` remains host-native-untestable (depends on `<gccore.h>`/libogc, an existing, already-documented limitation reconfirmed this round - attempting to run the tests/README.md-documented per-test build commands surfaced that several are now stale/incomplete relative to current source dependencies, unrelated to this change; fixing that stale documentation is out of scope for a targeted main.c fix that suite structurally cannot cover anyway). Real verification: a clean `make clean && make` Wii/devkitPPC rebuild succeeded, producing `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol`, with only the two already-known, pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings (`iop_core.c:482`, `iop_module_loader.c:225`) - no new warnings or errors.

**Honest scope.** This fix is currently *inert* in practice: this project's own boot trace still doesn't reach the point of writing `PMODE` to a nonzero value at all (per the many rounds since the 94th finding), so neither circuit's blit path is exercised yet. Its value is forward-looking and preventative - a real, concrete bug that would otherwise have silently produced a black screen the moment this project's boot investigation finally succeeds, now closed before that happens. It does not resolve task #172's actual blocker-finding goal, and does not change any of this round's or prior rounds' `DISPLAY1`-based observations about this project's own boot state - those remain accurate descriptions of `gs->pmode` staying zero, a stronger and still-valid statement.

**Source-code change this round.** Modified: `source/main.c` only (Circuit1/Circuit2 selection logic + doc comments). No other files changed.

## 253rd finding (Round 213, task #366/#172): monitor.py's GS/DMA/GIF/INTC readings are confirmed non-functional - the whole 0x10000000-0x1FFFFFFF hardware register range is unreadable via DebugServer.cpp's read_memory path, retroactively flagging Round 211/212's DMA2/GIF/INTC-based conclusions as unconfirmed

**Context.** Continuing Round 212's `--watch-display2` work, a fresh live capture with both `--watch-chcr` and `--watch-display2` armed again showed zero hits and all-zero DMA2/GIF/INTC readings, identical to every prior capture. The user pushed back that this didn't match what PCSX2's own debugger was visibly showing on their screen (hex values populated in the GS register tab), which prompted a direct comparison rather than accepting the tool's output at face value.

**Root cause, found by reading the actual uploaded `DebugServer.cpp` source (not guessed):** every GS/DMA/GIF/INTC value `monitor.py` has ever reported comes from the generic `read_memory` command, whose server-side handler is:
```cpp
u32 byte = cpu->read8(addr + i, valid);
if (!valid) byte = 0;
```
This is the same `R5900DebugInterface::read8()` used for RAM/BIOS reads - not a dedicated GS-state accessor. `set_memcheck`/`CBreakPoints::AddMemCheck` (the write-watch mechanism from Round 212) is a related but separate code path, also suspect for the same class of address.

**Live-verified, not just theorized.** The user directly compared PCSX2's own built-in **Memory** view (a hex dump, same underlying debug-interface read path) against its separate, dedicated **GS register tab** at the same live moment. Jumping the Memory view to `0x12000080` (DISPLAY1) showed `??` (unmapped/invalid) for every byte, while the GS tab simultaneously showed real, structured nonzero values at that exact address. A second check at `0x1000A000` (D2_GIF_CHCR, a DMAC address, not GS) showed the identical `??` result. This proves the gap isn't GS-specific - the **entire hardware register range `0x10000000`-`0x1FFFFFFF`** (DMAC, GIF, INTC, GS - everything `monitor.py`'s `read_gs`/`read_gif`/`read_dma`/`read_intc` and both write-watches rely on) is invisible to `cpu->read8()`/`read_memory`, the same conclusion the DebugServer.cpp source read predicted but now confirmed against PCSX2's own UI rather than inferred.

**What this retroactively invalidates.** Every DMA2(GIF)/GIF_STAT/I_STAT/I_MASK/D_ENABLER reading and both write-watches (`--watch-chcr`, `--watch-display2`) across Round 210, 211, and 212's live captures reported a fixed zero regardless of real emulator state - not evidence that DMA channel 2 was never started, that GIF was never active, or that I_MASK was never unmasked. The 251st finding's (Round 211) "DMA channel 2 (GIF) was never started" conclusion and Round 212's CHCR/DISPFB2/DISPLAY2 write-watch "0 hits" results must be treated as unconfirmed, not as negative evidence, until a proper fix exists.

**What remains valid.** The 252nd finding (Round 212) and its `main.c` Circuit1/Circuit2 fix are **unaffected** - that finding was read directly from PCSX2's own GS register tab in user-provided screenshots, a completely different (and confirmed-working) internal data path than `read_memory`. `status` (PC/paused/cycles) and the GPR/FPU/VU register-read tools are also unaffected - plain EE/IOP CPU-context reads go through a different, working path (`read_registers`), not the one implicated here.

**Fix path (not yet implemented, no source to guess from).** `DebugServer.cpp` would need a new command that reads from PCSX2's internal GS/DMA/INTC state structs directly - the same source its own GUI tabs use - instead of routing through `cpu->read8()`. The exact internal API for that isn't known without more of the PCSX2 core source; not guessing at function names without a citation, per this project's standing rule.

**Action taken.** Added a hard, printed warning to `monitor.py`'s `live`/`analyze` commands and its module docstring, and a corresponding warning section in `ANLEITUNG.md`, so future runs (and future rounds of this project) don't misread these zeros as real telemetry again.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** All changes live in the separate `PCSX2-MCP`/`monitor.py` project. Docs-only, self-correcting round.

## 254th finding (Round 214, task #366/#172): monitor.py's DMA/GIF/INTC reads are real and working again via Pine IPC (no PCSX2 rebuild needed) - GS-privileged registers besides CSR are confirmed unreadable via any bus mechanism (real hardware property, not a tooling gap)

**Context.** Following Round 213's finding that `read_memory` (DebugServer.cpp) can't see the `0x10000000`-`0x1FFFFFFF` hardware register range, the user asked to "build our own version" of the third-party `PCSX2-MCP` tool. Before committing to a full PCSX2 source rebuild (Visual Studio 2022 + Qt6 + CMake/Ninja - hours of toolchain setup), the actual `hkmodd/PCSX2-MCP` upstream repository was checked directly: it confirmed the project's own `DebugServer.cpp` is identical to upstream (the bug is real, not something introduced locally), and that the repo also ships a **Pine IPC client** - PCSX2's own official, built-in binary protocol (port 28011, not a custom patch, already compiled into any PCSX2 build; only requires "Settings -> Advanced -> Enable Pine IPC" to be checked).

**Live-tested, not assumed.** A standalone `pine-test` command was added to `monitor.py` (separate `PCSX2-MCP` project, no changes to this repository) reading PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1/DISPFB2/DISPLAY2/CSR plus D2_GIF CHCR/QWC/MADR, GIF_STAT/GIF_CNT, I_STAT/I_MASK, D_ENABLER via Pine's `read32` opcode. The user ran it twice against two real, independent live sessions (a BIOS-boot moment and an actively-played Tekken session).

**Result: DMA/GIF/INTC reads work correctly via Pine.** D2_GIF_CHCR/MADR, GIF_STAT, I_STAT, and I_MASK all returned real, distinct, plausible values that differed meaningfully between the two captures (e.g. `I_STAT` was `0x0` at the BIOS-boot moment and `0x8` - decodes to `VBLANK_E` per the standard EE INTC bit convention - during the Tekken capture; `I_MASK` was nonzero in both, `0x100a` and `0x1006`, decoding to `SBUS`/`VBLANK_E or VBLANK_S`/`TIMER3`). This directly updates the 251st finding's (Round 211) "I_MASK stayed 0x0 for the entire capture" characterization - that was an artifact of the broken `read_memory` path, not a real state. `GIF_STAT=0x4` (nonzero) during the Tekken capture is likewise new, real signal that was previously always hidden as zero.

**Correction to an initial overclaim, caught and fixed the same round.** DMA channel 2's `CHCR` read `0x1` (BIOS-boot capture) and `0x5` (Tekken capture) via Pine. This was initially mis-read as "CHCR.STR=1, DMA channel 2 is running" using bit 0 - **incorrect**. Per the standard, public ps2sdk `dmac.h` convention (and this project's own pre-existing `analyze_sample()` code, which already correctly used `(chcr >> 8) & 1`), **STR is bit 8, not bit 0** - bit 0 is `DIR` (transfer direction). Re-checked against bit 8: both captured `CHCR` values have `STR=0`. **DMA channel 2 was NOT confirmed started by this data** - the 251st finding's "DMA channel 2 (GIF) was never started" conclusion is not contradicted after all; if anything, this is now confirmed with real (not broken-path) data rather than the previously-unconfirmed zero reading. This correction was caught and communicated within the same round, before it was written into permanent documentation, by actually running the project's own bit-decode code against the captured values rather than eyeballing the hex.

**A genuine, real hardware-architecture finding.** PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1/DISPFB2/DISPLAY2 all read back the *exact same* value as CSR in both live captures via Pine - not zero, not garbage, but a real, live value that happened to always equal whatever CSR currently was (differing between captures the way CSR's status bits would, while CHCR/MADR/GIF_STAT/I_STAT/I_MASK in the same captures all read distinct, non-aliased values - ruling out a client-side bug). This is consistent with a real, citable PS2 hardware property: **CSR is the only GS-privileged register the EE bus can read back; PMODE/DISPFBx/DISPLAYx are write-only from the EE's side** (the EE writes configuration into the GS; the GS consumes it internally; there is no bus read path back). This is offered as a reasoned, evidence-based hypothesis matching the observed pattern, not a claim backed by PCSX2 core source access. It explains why PCSX2's own GS register tab (which reads the emulator's internal state directly, not via the bus) is the only place `DISPFB2`/`DISPLAY2` were ever visible (Round 212's screenshots) - no scriptable mechanism (DebugServer or Pine alike) can reach that same internal state without an actual PCSX2 source patch.

**Action taken.** `monitor.py`'s `read_gs`/`read_gif`/`read_dma`/`read_intc` now use Pine (port 28011, new `--pine-port` argument) instead of the broken `read_memory` path for GS/DMA/GIF/INTC reads; `DebugServerClient` remains in use only for status/PC and breakpoints/memchecks. The GS block now reports only `CSR` (with SIGNAL/FINISH/HSINT/VSINT bit decoding) instead of the previous six misleadingly-identical fields. `analyze_sample()`/`cmd_live()`/`cmd_analyze()` were updated accordingly - the old DISPLAY1/DISPLAY2-based flags were replaced with CSR HSINT/VSINT-based ones, with an explicit note that this is not a substitute for checking PCSX2's own GS tab.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** All changes live in the separate `PCSX2-MCP`/`monitor.py` project. A real DebugServer.cpp rebuild is no longer believed necessary for DMA/GIF/INTC telemetry (Pine already provides it); it would still be required if real, scriptable DISPFB2/DISPLAY2 telemetry is wanted beyond what PCSX2's own GS tab already provides - not pursued this round since Pine closed the more urgent gap.

## 255th finding (Round 215, task #366/#172): DebugServer memcheck watches (`--watch-chcr`/`--watch-display2`) do not reliably survive a PCSX2 VM Reset - live-confirmed crash, isolated to the memcheck mechanism specifically; reset-to-gameplay sequence captured as real corroborating evidence for Round 131/157

**Context.** Following Round 214's Pine-IPC fix, the user was walked through capturing a reset-spanning `monitor.py live` session to gather real telemetry across a manual VM Reset - the natural next step now that DMA/GIF/INTC reads are trustworthy. The first attempt (`reset_capture.jsonl`, captured with `--watch-chcr --watch-display2` both active) reported back: "once i hit reset it crashes the emulator and closes the connection."

**Investigation.** `reset_capture.jsonl` (233 lines) was analyzed first: it showed 4 apparent resets survived cleanly (detected via large real-time gaps of 15-43s, cycles resetting near zero, and PC landing in low BIOS addresses - `0x8000b8a0`, `0x80005b84`, `0x00082220` twice) with no in-file crash signature - the file simply ends normally at line 233, meaning the actual crash happened after the last logged sample, not inside a captured reset. The user was asked for the actual error text and pasted the real traceback: three `[!] Could not remove {chcr,dispfb2,display2} memcheck during cleanup` errors (each `[WinError 10054] Eine vorhandene Verbindung wurde vom Remotehost geschlossen`), followed by an unhandled `ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054]` raised from inside `client.list_memchecks()`. `WinError 10054` means the **remote host** (PCSX2 itself) closed the socket - i.e. PCSX2 crashed or the DebugServer connection died server-side, not a bug in `monitor.py`'s own Python code.

**Isolation test.** To separate "memcheck mechanism" from "reset in general" as the cause, the user was asked to repeat the exact same reset-spanning capture procedure with `--watch-chcr`/`--watch-display2` **omitted**. Result (`reset_capture2.jsonl`, 61 lines): "nope no crash." Two clean resets were captured (at lines 21 and 46), both landing at the **exact same** `PC=0x80005b84` immediately post-reset. CSR briefly read `0x00000000`/`0x0000600c` right at the reset moment before settling back into the normal `0x551bXXXc`-pattern steady state. Within ~0.5s of each reset, PC transited through `0x00081fc0` (the Round 157 self-loop address - a nearby, not identical, match, correctly hedged as such). Within a further ~1-1.5s, PC reached real running game code in the `0x005xxxxx` range. Total reset-to-gameplay time was under 2 seconds in both cases, with no dropped connection either time.

**Conclusion.** The DebugServer memcheck/watch mechanism (`set_memcheck`/`CBreakPoints::AddMemCheck`, the write-watch feature added in Round 212) is what does not reliably survive a PCSX2 VM Reset - not Pine IPC, not the reset process in general, and not `monitor.py`'s own Python code. This is a real instability in the community `DebugServer.cpp` patch's interaction with PCSX2's own `VMManager::Reset()`, outside what can be root-caused or fixed without patching and rebuilding PCSX2 itself (out of scope without the source access a full rebuild would require).

**A genuine, real byproduct: a reproducible reset-to-gameplay execution trace.** Both clean resets in `reset_capture2.jsonl` landed at the identical `PC=0x80005b84`, then transited `0x00081fc0` within ~0.5s, then reached real game code within ~1.5-2s total - a highly reproducible, real, live-captured sequence that directly corroborates this project's own prior investigation addresses from Round 131 (`0x80005E60-0x80005EB4` SBUS_SMFLG spin-wait region) and Round 157 (`0x00081fc0` self-loop), as nearby-but-not-identical matches. This is valuable corroborating evidence for task #172's blocker-finding work, though not yet acted on further this round.

**Action taken (mitigation, not a root-cause fix).** Added an explicit, prominent warning to `monitor.py`'s `--watch-chcr`/`--watch-display2` `argparse` help text, documenting the live-confirmed crash risk and recommending against combining these flags with manual Resets until the underlying `DebugServer.cpp` memcheck/reset interaction is fixed upstream. Mirrored the same warning into `ANLEITUNG.md`. Pine-only polling (no watch flags) is unaffected by this bug and remains the safe default for reset-spanning captures.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** All changes live in the separate `PCSX2-MCP`/`monitor.py` project. Docs-only round; the reset-to-gameplay telemetry is recorded here as corroborating evidence but task #172 itself was not further advanced this round - that is flagged as the next round's work.

## 256th finding (Round 216, task #366/#172): live breakpoint trace proves the Round 157/215 self-loop at 0x00081fc0 is a genuine unconditional infinite loop, exited only via a hardware interrupt/exception - real EE general-exception dispatch table extracted (Cause.ExcCode-indexed, base 0x80012380); the exact interrupt source that breaks the loop remains unidentified

**Context.** Round 215 flagged the reproducible reset-to-gameplay trace (`PC=0x80005b84` -> `0x00081fc0` -> real game code) as corroborating evidence worth following up. This round used the newly-connected `pcsx2-mcp` live MCP tools (a direct DebugServer+Pine connection to the user's actual running PCSX2, no more manual `monitor.py` copy-paste) to set a real code breakpoint at `0x00081fc0` and catch it live.

**The loop itself, disassembled directly.** The breakpoint hit immediately post-reset, with all EE GPRs still zero (genuine fresh-reset state) and `Status=0x70030C11` (IE=1, IM2/INTC=1, IM3/DMAC=1 - interrupts fully armed). Disassembly of `0x00081fa0`-`0x00081ffc` shows: `dmove v1,t0` / `teq zero,t0` (a sanity trap) / two nops, then **six `nop`s at `0x00081fc0`-`0x00081fd4` followed by an unconditional `b ->0x00081fc0`** - a real, dead, data-independent infinite loop with no branch condition whatsoever. By MIPS semantics this construct can only ever be exited by an asynchronous exception (interrupt) whose handler redirects the saved return address away from the loop - there is no other mechanism.

**Empirical confirmation the loop is interrupt-broken.** Removed the `0x00081fc0` breakpoint (it was re-triggering every single loop iteration and stalling `continue()` - a real gotcha worth noting for future live sessions: a breakpoint sitting inside a tight loop must be cleared before `continue()` will ever get past it) and set a new breakpoint at `0x80000180`, the EE general exception vector (`Cause.IV=0` in the captured `Status`/`Cause` state means interrupts and synchronous exceptions share this single vector - confirmed, not assumed, from the live `Cause` register). `continue()` ran only ~3900 cycles before hitting `0x80000180` - and `EPC` at that point was `0x00083a94`, **not** anywhere in the `0x00081fxx` loop region. This proves real execution left the loop and progressed to real code well before this particular exception fired.

**What the second breakpoint actually caught (and what it didn't).** Disassembling around `EPC=0x00083a94` revealed a completely ordinary syscall trampoline table - repeating `li v1,N` / `syscall` / `jr ra` / `nop` blocks for consecutive syscall numbers (`-0x77, 0x78, -0x78, 0x79, ...`), a completely mundane, expected part of kernel call machinery. This means the second breakpoint hit caught a **later, unrelated ordinary syscall**, not the specific interrupt that broke the `0x00081fc0` loop itself - that interrupt (and whatever ran between leaving the loop and reaching this syscall trampoline) happened during the ~3900-cycle gap and was not directly observed. **This is explicitly not claimed as "the trigger" found** - only that the loop-exit mechanism is confirmed to be interrupt-driven, not the specific interrupt identified.

**Real, citable ground truth extracted regardless: the actual EE general-exception dispatch table.** The handler at `0x80000180` does: save `t9`, `mfc0 t9,Cause`, `andi t9,0x7c` (masks `Cause` bits 2-6, the ExcCode field, pre-scaled by 4 for a word-table stride), `lui k0,0x8001` / `addu k0,t9` / `lw k0,0x2380(k0)` (loads a handler pointer from table base `0x80012380 + maskedExcCode`), then `jr k0`. This is a real, live-verified, ExcCode-indexed jump table - useful ground truth to cross-check against this project's own EE exception-vectoring implementation (Round 63, Round 178) for structural correctness, not yet done this round.

**Housekeeping note for future live sessions.** `I_STAT` read as all-zero (`0x1000f000`, 32 bytes) at the moment of the first breakpoint hit - expected, since this is the very first instant post-reset before any interrupt has fired yet, not a regression of Round 214's Pine-read fix.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source - this is a live-reference-only investigation round. No fix was implemented since the exact interrupt source (needed to know what our own port's boot flow would need to model to reach this same escape) was not conclusively identified.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative round, using the live `pcsx2-mcp` connector (not `monitor.py`) for the first time this project.

## 257th finding (Round 217, task #366/#172): self-modifying-code hypothesis for the 0x00081fc0 loop ruled out; the loop-exit mechanism is confirmed fully deterministic across independent resets (identical EPC/Cause), but the precise mechanism remains unidentified - honestly left open rather than guessed at

**Context.** Round 216 confirmed the `0x00081fc0` loop is a genuine unconditional infinite loop (structurally, by disassembly) that real hardware nonetheless exits, but only caught a later, unrelated syscall at the exception vector - not the loop-breaking event itself. This round retried with a tighter, two-pronged live capture.

**Hypothesis tested: self-modifying code.** An alternative to "an interrupt breaks the loop" is that the loop's own instruction bytes get overwritten by some other boot-stage DMA/memcpy, and the CPU simply falls into new, real code once that happens - no interrupt required. Tested directly: armed a write-watchpoint across the full loop body (`0x00081fc0`-`0x00081fd8`, log-only... actually break-action, per the tool's `action` parameter) alongside a breakpoint on the general exception vector (`0x80000180`), then had the user reset and let both race. **Result: the write-watchpoint recorded 0 hits both times it was tried.** Nothing ever writes to the loop's own memory. Self-modifying code is ruled out as the mechanism.

**A process note worth recording.** The first attempt at this race gave a false result: it stopped mid-loop at `0x00081fd4`, which looked like it might be significant, but `pcsx2_list_breakpoints` revealed the real cause - a batch of **stale temporary breakpoints** left behind by an earlier `pcsx2_step(count=40)` call (one per loop address, `0x81fc4` through `0x81fdc`), never cleared, contaminating the run. Cleared all breakpoints/watchpoints and re-armed cleanly before trusting any result. Worth remembering for future live sessions: `pcsx2_step` with a `count` leaves temp breakpoints behind that `pcsx2_clear_all_breakpoints` is needed to remove before a clean `continue()` race.

**Deterministic reproducibility, confirmed across two independent resets.** With the contamination cleared, the clean race gave: exception-vector breakpoint hit, `EPC=0x00083a94`, `Cause=0x00000020` (ExcCode=8, Syscall) - **the exact same EPC and Cause value as Round 216's capture**, and a `Count` value within ~700 of Round 216's (`0x024D7D76` vs `0x024D7DA2`). This is not noisy, timing-dependent async-interrupt behavior - this is a fully deterministic code path, reached identically every single time from a fresh reset. That is new information: it argues against "an unpredictable interrupt happens to fire and breaks the loop" and more toward "this is expected, deterministic boot sequencing" - but the exact mechanism by which a structurally-unconditional infinite loop is deterministically exited (confirmed not self-modified) was not identified this round. Manually decoding the exact MIPS semantics of the `teq zero,t0` guard immediately before the loop, and whether `0x00081fa0`-`0x00081fbc` is genuinely code or is being misdecoded data, remain open - flagged honestly as unresolved rather than guessed at further.

**Housekeeping.** PCSX2 was left running normally (not paused) after every capture this round, including a final `pcsx2_clear_all_breakpoints` + `continue()` before ending the session.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source - live-reference-only investigation. No fix implemented.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative round.

## 258th finding (Round 218, task #366/#172): correction - 0x00081fb0/0x00081fb4 (previously disassembled as "dmove v1,t0"/"teq zero,t0") are actually a static two-entry pointer table, not instructions; the adjacent 0x00081fa0/0x00081fa4 words are confirmed genuinely written during boot (previously misread as "lb"/"sd" instructions too) - retracts Round 217's "teq trap" hypothesis

**Context.** Round 217 flagged, as a real possibility rather than a conclusion, that some of the disassembled bytes just before the `0x00081fc0` loop (`0x00081fa0`: "lb at,0x5DE8(zero)", `0x00081fa4`: "sd ra,-1(ra)") "don't read like real code" and might be misdecoded data. This round checked that directly, alongside re-verifying whether `0x00081fb0`/`0x00081fb4` (disassembled as "dmove v1,t0" / "teq zero,t0" back in Round 216 and treated as a possible trap-guard in Round 217's "Next" pointer) are real code.

**Method.** Read the raw memory words at `0x00081f80`-`0x00081fff` directly via Pine (`u32_array`, bypassing the disassembler entirely) from the currently-running live session (deep in OSDSYS, not right after reset), and compared byte-for-byte against the exact raw words captured immediately post-reset in Round 216/217.

**Confirmed: `0x00081fb0`/`0x00081fb4` are data, not code.** Both captures (post-reset and now, mid-boot) show the identical, unchanging values `0x00081fec` and `0x00081ff4` at these two addresses. Those are not plausible instruction encodings that happen to look like addresses - they **are** addresses, and specifically addresses pointing directly into this same code block: `0x00081fec` is the `li v1,-0x5` instruction (the syscall(-5) stub entry, confirmed real code, unchanged across every capture) and `0x00081ff4` is the `nop` immediately after that stub's `syscall`. This is a real, static, two-entry pointer table (something like `{handler_addr, skip_addr}`), not the "dmove v1,t0" / "teq zero,t0" instructions PCSX2's own disassembler rendered them as when asked to decode that address range as code. **This retracts Round 217's proposed "teq trap gates loop entry" hypothesis** - there is no trap guard; that instruction never existed, it was a data value that happens to disassemble into a plausible-looking (but wrong) MIPS encoding.

**Confirmed: `0x00081fa0`/`0x00081fa4` are also data, and are genuinely rewritten during boot.** Round 216/217's post-reset capture showed `0x80015de8` and `0xffffffff` at these two addresses (disassembled at the time as "lb at,0x5DE8(zero)" and "sd ra,-1(ra)"). This round's live read, taken from the currently-running session well past boot, shows **different** values: `0x80000360` and `0x00000000`. Real static code never changes its own encoding at rest between two clean captures; this proves the region is data, and that data is actively written by something during the boot sequence (a plausible real mechanism: it looks like a kernel-internal "last known handler" or module-registration slot, consistent with this project's own prior `boot_info` struct work from Round 134 and similar). Two consecutive live reads taken moments apart both show the same stable `0x80000360`/`0x00000000`, meaning it is written once (not continuously ticking) - consistent with a one-time boot-sequencing side effect, not a live counter.

**What this does and doesn't change.** Round 217's core result - that a write-watchpoint on the **loop body itself** (`0x00081fc0`-`0x00081fd8`) recorded 0 hits - stands unaffected; that specific address range genuinely never gets rewritten. What's now clear is that the wider block this loop sits inside is not pure static code the way it first appeared - it interleaves real instructions (the loop itself, and the `0x00081fe0`+ code, both confirmed byte-stable across every capture) with small data fields that do change. This doesn't yet explain the loop's deterministic exit mechanism (still the open question from Round 216/217) but it does correct a real misreading in this project's own docs, and narrows what's left to investigate: the correlation between "this nearby data gets written once during boot" and "the loop deterministically exits after ~3800 cycles" is observed but not yet proven causal.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source. Correction recorded honestly rather than silently, per this project's standing practice (matching the CHCR/STR correction style from Round 214).

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative/self-correcting round.

## 259th finding (Round 219, task #366/#172): direct proof real execution reaches 0x00081fe0 (the loop's real escape path) via a genuine asynchronous interrupt (Cause.ExcCode=0, IP3/DMAC) - the write-watchpoint on the 0x00081fa0/0x00081fa4 data pair stayed at 0 hits during this window, meaning that data is written later, not during the loop-exit itself

**Context.** Round 218 corrected the misreading of `0x00081fb0`/`0x00081fb4` as instructions (they're a static pointer table) and confirmed `0x00081fa0`/`0x00081fa4` genuinely change value during boot, proposing a targeted watchpoint on that specific pair as the next move. This round did exactly that: raced a write-watchpoint on `0x00081fa0`-`0x00081fa8` against the general-exception-vector breakpoint (`0x80000180`), from a fresh, deterministic reset.

**Result.** The write-watchpoint recorded 0 hits again - that data pair is **not** written during the roughly-3800-cycle window between the loop being entered and execution moving well past it. Whatever writes `0x00081fa0`/`0x00081fa4` (confirmed to happen at some point during boot, per Round 218) happens later than this specific window, not as part of escaping the loop.

**The real find: `EPC=0x00081FE0`.** The capture paused (after the exception-vector breakpoint fired and, per this tool's own execution model, continued a short distance further) at `PC=0x00084058`, with `EPC=0x00081FE0` and `Cause=0x00000800`. Decoding `Cause`: `ExcCode = (0x800>>2)&0x1F = 0`, which is a genuine asynchronous **Interrupt** (not a Syscall - every prior capture in this loop investigation showed `ExcCode=8`/Syscall; this is the first confirmed real interrupt). `Cause` bit 11 (IP3) is set, consistent with this project's own established EE Cause.IP convention where IP3 corresponds to the DMAC-class interrupt line. Most importantly: **`EPC=0x00081FE0` is direct, hardware-recorded proof that the CPU's PC had legitimately reached `0x00081fe0`** - the `lui sp,0x0008` instruction immediately following the loop's pointer table - at the moment this interrupt was recognized. This is the address Round 216 identified as otherwise-unreachable dead code (unreachable by fall-through, since the loop's branch at `0x00081fd8` unconditionally returns to `0x00081fc0`, not `0x00081fe0`). This round provides the first direct, hardware-level evidence that real execution does reach it - confirming the loop is genuinely escaped via legitimate control flow, not stuck.

**Following the trail forward.** By the time this pause was captured, `PC` had progressed to `0x00084058`, disassembling as unambiguous, sensible real code: a function prologue (`addiu sp,-0x90` / `sd s0,...` / `sd ra,...`) immediately followed by a byte-flag load-and-branch (`lbu v0,(a3)` / `andi a1,v0,0xff` / `beqz a1,->0x00084158`). This is real, substantive mainline BIOS/kernel logic, not another dead end - the loop's escape path leads somewhere legitimate.

**Honest scope.** The exact step-by-step path from the interrupt vector (`0x80000180`) through to `PC=0x00084058` was not directly observed (no intermediate breakpoints were set for that specific span) - only the two endpoints (`EPC=0x81fe0` at the interrupt, and the eventual resting `PC=0x84058`) are confirmed. It's not yet established whether `0x84058` is reached via the interrupt handler's own code, via a normal RFE-then-continue through `0x81fe0`'s `jalr ->v1` call, or some combination. That's real, well-scoped future work, not claimed as solved here.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source. Live-reference-only investigation.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative round.

## 260th finding (Round 220, task #366/#172): decoded the 0x00081fe0 trampoline's real structure (reuses the loop's own address as a scratch stack pointer, jumps via v1 to real kernel code with a real return address) - and confirmed pcsx2_step's stale temporary breakpoints are a recurring gotcha, not a one-off, causing repeated false-pause/inflated-cycle results this round

**Context.** Round 219 proved real execution reaches `0x00081fe0` via a genuine interrupt. This round set out to trace the path forward from there toward the `PC=0x84058` resting point observed previously, using `pcsx2_step` for fine-grained tracing.

**Real structural finding: the trampoline's stack-pointer trick.** Register reads at `PC=0x00081fe4` (the `jalr ->v1` instruction, paused before execution) showed `v1=0x00212B28` and `sp=0x00080000`. Combined with the full disassembly (`lui sp,0x0008` at `0x81fe0`, then `jalr ->v1` / `addiu sp,0x1fc0` as the delay-slot pair at `0x81fe4`/`0x81fe8`), this resolves cleanly: `sp` is set to `0x00080000`, then the delay-slot `addiu` finalizes it to `0x00080000 + 0x1fc0 = 0x00081fc0` - **the exact address of the now-finished loop**. This is a real, sensible technique: once the wait-loop's job is done, its own memory region is repurposed as a small scratch stack for whatever `v1` points to, rather than wasting a separate allocation. `ra=0x80001824` at the same moment confirms this whole `0x00081fc0`-`0x00081ff8` block is being invoked as a real subroutine from genuine kernel code, not free-standing boot-time padding.

**Tooling caution, now confirmed a second time.** Round 217/218 already flagged that `pcsx2_step(count>1)` leaves temporary breakpoints behind that must be cleared before trusting a subsequent `continue()`. This round hit the same issue again, worse: after two separate `step(count=20)` calls, `pcsx2_list_breakpoints` revealed leftover temp breakpoints at both `0x00081fe4` and `0x00081fe8`. Because `0x00081fe0`-`0x00081fe8` is a generic trampoline (likely invoked repeatedly throughout normal boot, not just once), these stale breakpoints kept re-triggering on *later, unrelated* invocations of the same code - producing wildly inflated `Count`/cycle deltas between tool calls (one gap was ~76 million cycles) and PC readings that looked like a false "infinite 2-instruction loop" between `0x81fe0` and `0x81fe4` at first glance. That apparent loop was a tooling artifact, not real CPU behavior - confirmed once the stale breakpoints were cleared and `continue()` allowed the emulator to run freely again immediately. **Standing rule for future sessions: always call `pcsx2_clear_all_breakpoints` immediately after any `pcsx2_step` call with `count>1`, not just once at the start of a round.**

**Also confirmed this round (unrelated, incidental):** hitting Reset while the emulator is core-paused via the DebugServer connection can appear as "Reset doesn't work" from the user's side - the reset actually does happen at the hardware level (observed `Cycles: 0` at `PC=0xBFC00000`, the literal boot ROM entry vector), but the core stays paused until an explicit `continue()` is issued. This is a real, minor UX interaction worth knowing: a user reporting "Reset won't work" while a live debug session is attached may simply need the session to `continue()` first.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source. Live-reference-only investigation, plus a documented tooling caution.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative round.

## 261st finding (Round 221, task #366/#172, connects task #181/#216/#219/#221): real syscall(-5) dispatch target identified - it's a per-device probe function, the same template as Round 219's 0x84050 code, confirming syscall(-5) is genuine working kernel dispatch machinery, not a dead-end halt

**Context.** Round 220 left off wanting to trace `v1`'s actual call target from the `0x00081fe0` trampoline without repeating the `pcsx2_step` tooling issue. This round set a single breakpoint directly at that target address (`0x00212B28`, avoiding the trampoline's own repeatedly-hit address) and let a fresh reset run to it.

**Clean hit, no tooling artifacts.** `pcsx2_status` showed `PC=0x00212b28`, `Cycles=51784661` (a real, later point in boot than the loop region). `pcsx2_get_backtrace` returned two frames: `#0 entry=0x00212b28 pc=0x00212b28 sp=0x00081fc0` and `#1 entry=0xffffffff pc=0x00081fec sp=0x00082050`. A direct register read confirmed `ra=0x00081FEC` and `sp=0x00081FC0` exactly.

**This closes a real loop back to task #181.** `PC=0x00081FEC` is the `li v1,-0x5` instruction identified all the way back in task #181/Round 157/216 as the "syscall(-5)" stub sitting right after the wait-loop. This round proves, via a real hardware backtrace and register state (not inference), that **syscall(-5) is genuine, functioning kernel dispatch machinery** - its handler ends up calling through the `0x00081fe0` trampoline into `0x00212B28` as a normal function call, using the loop's finished memory as scratch stack (confirmed: `sp=0x00081FC0` matches Round 220's prediction exactly). Task #181's framing of this as a "halt" or "wall" no longer holds - it's a working, real syscall whose destination is now identified.

**The destination is a per-device probe function - and it's the same template Round 219 already found.** Disassembling `0x00212b28` onward:
```
addiu sp,-0x90 / lui v1,0x0047 / sd s0,0x70(sp) / sd ra,0x80(sp)
addiu s0,v1,-0x29e8 / lw a3,-0x29e8(v1) / lbu v0,(a3) / andi a1,v0,0xff
beqz a1,->0x212c30
```
This is **structurally identical**, instruction-for-instruction, to the function Round 219 found at `0x00084050` (`addiu sp,-0x90` / `lui v1,0x0009` / `sd s0,...` / `sd ra,...` / `addiu s0,v1,-0x3ce8` / `lw a3,-0x3ce8(v1)` / `lbu v0,(a3)` / `andi a1,v0,0xff` / `beqz a1,->0x84158`) - only the `lui`/`addiu` immediate constants differ (computing different base pointers: `0x0046D618` here vs `0x0008C318` there). This is a real, recognizable pattern: **a shared per-device/per-module probe-function template, compiled once per device instance with a different base-address constant baked in** - read a byte flag from a small per-device structure, branch away early if it's zero (device absent/inactive), otherwise continue (both captures stopped at the `beqz`, so the "continue" path wasn't observed this round).

**Connects to this project's own prior device-table work.** This pattern (a per-device flag/table probed via a small, repeated compiled template) is exactly the shape of thing task #221 (93rd finding, "device-table reverse-engineering deprioritized") was chasing before being re-scoped away as too speculative without more evidence. This round provides real, live, hardware-verified evidence of what that device-table structure actually looks like in practice - a concrete reason to reconsider resuming task #221 with this as a starting point, though not undertaken this round.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source. Live-reference-only investigation.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative round, but a substantive one - connects task #181, #219, and #221 into a single coherent picture for the first time.

## 263rd finding (Round 223, task #366, first live-hardware test of the exact question Round 242 scoped as needing one): live breakpoints at Function G (`0x8000f318`) and the `RAM[0x80020E34]` setter helper (`0x8000dca8`) never fire across at least one full real BIOS reset-to-steady-state boot, corroborating - from a completely independent, empirical direction - Round 240-242's static "no discoverable caller" conclusion; also hit and safely recovered from the already-documented Round 215 memcheck-vs-Reset instability a second time

**Context.** Round 222 corrected the framing risk from the `0x00081fc0` investigation and proposed testing whether this project's own `0x8000cff4` SIF_SMFLAG loop family has a real, undelivered-interrupt dependency. Rather than guess, this round went to Round 242's own explicitly-scoped next step: "a genuine live PCSX2 reference-session boot capture... with a watchpoint armed on `RAM[0x80020E34]` before boot starts, which would give a direct, empirical backtrace answer that static analysis alone cannot provide" - now possible for the first time, since the live `pcsx2-mcp` DebugServer connection (unavailable in Round 242/243) is reachable this session.

**First attempt: repeated the exact bug the 255th finding (Round 215) already documented.** Armed write watchpoints on `RAM[0x80020E34]` and `RAM[0x80020E3C]` and asked the user to hit Reset. This is precisely the "memcheck + manual Reset" combination Round 215 explicitly warned against. Result: the same failure mode - after the Reset, `pcsx2_continue()` and even `pcsx2_step()` stopped advancing the CPU state entirely (PC and cycle count frozen across repeated calls), consistent with Round 215's "DebugServer memcheck watches do not reliably survive a PCSX2 VM Reset" finding. **Recovered safely**: `pcsx2_clear_all_breakpoints()` followed by `pcsx2_continue()` immediately restored normal execution (confirmed via `pcsx2_status` showing `Paused: false` and cycles climbing again, PC in real running code) - no crash, no lasting harm to the user's session, but a real mistake on this round's part: this exact risk was already written down in this project's own docs and should have been checked before arming watchpoints across a Reset.

**Second attempt: pivoted to breakpoints (not watchpoints/memchecks) at the two real, statically-identified function entry points instead of the raw memory addresses.** Set regular breakpoints at `0x8000f318` (Function G, per the 241st finding) and `0x8000dca8` (the `RAM[0x80020E34]` setter helper, per the 240th finding) - a tool combination already proven safe across resets throughout Rounds 216-221. Asked the user to hit Reset again.

**Result: both breakpoints survived the reset cleanly (no freeze, no crash) and neither ever fired.** Observed via `pcsx2_status` across the reset: cycle count dropped sharply (consistent with a genuine VM reset occurring) then climbed back up over real elapsed time to the hundreds-of-millions/low-billions range, with PC settling into real running code (`0x0061bbe0`, then `0x005189a0` - both far outside the `0x8000xxxx` low-memory kernel region these breakpoints target) and `Paused: false` throughout. `pcsx2_list_breakpoints` confirmed both breakpoints remained armed (`✅`) the entire time. A breakpoint hit would have shown `Paused: true` with PC at the exact breakpoint address, per the exact same signal used successfully in Rounds 216-221 - this never happened.

**Why this matters.** This is the first REAL, live-execution (not static-disassembly) data point on whether Function G and its associated `RAM[0x80020E34]` setter are ever reached during an actual, full, real-BIOS boot-to-menu sequence on genuine PCSX2. The result - neither is ever hit - independently corroborates Round 240-242's static conclusion (exhaustive `JAL`/`J`/register-construction/`$gp`-relative/literal-data scans of all 11 real EE-side ROM modules found zero callers for Function G) from a completely different angle: real execution, not just disassembly. It does not prove Function G is unreachable under every possible boot mode (this was one full boot-to-interactive-menu sequence, on a "PS2 BIOS (Japan)" session with no specific game/disc verified loaded at the time of the reset), but it is a genuine, honest, non-fabricated data point in the same direction as every static finding since Round 200.

**What this means for task #366 and for Round 222's proposed interrupt-delivery-gap hypothesis.** This round does not resolve task #366's open question (what, if anything, calls Function G on real hardware). It does add real weight to the possibility raised in Round 200-202: either this specific BIOS/OSDSYS trajectory genuinely never exercises this subsystem in a normal boot-to-menu flow, or it requires a program/disc-specific trigger this round's generic "boot to the BIOS menu" scenario didn't include. This also means Round 222's proposed hypothesis (an undelivered interrupt breaking `0x8000cff4`'s loop, by analogy to Round 219's finding) remains untested by this round - the live session available this round was the BIOS menu itself, not a comparable moment to our own emulator's own `0x8000cff4` resting point, and no watchpoint could safely be armed on `SIF_SMFLAG`/`INTC_STAT` this round given the freshly-reconfirmed Round 215 instability.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source. Standing rule reaffirmed with a second real incident: never arm a DebugServer watchpoint/memcheck across a user-initiated Reset - use breakpoints on known code addresses instead, which have now been proven safe across resets in Rounds 216-221 and again this round.
