Next (Round 224): either (a) with the live session in a stable, known post-boot state, attempt a citable, in-place investigation of the `0x8000cff4`-equivalent interrupt-delivery question directly in this project's own source (`source/hw/sif.c`, `source/hw/ee_intc.c`, `source/hw/iop_intc.c`, `source/hw/iop_dma.c`) rather than continuing to lean on the reference session for it, since Round 223 shows the reference session's BIOS-menu state isn't a clean stand-in for our own emulator's specific resting point; or (b) if a live session showing an actual disc-based game boot becomes available, retry Round 223's breakpoint approach during that boot specifically, since Function G's role may be game/disc-triggered rather than generic-menu-triggered.

## 264th finding (Round 224, task #366/#172, direct source-code investigation per Round 223's "Next" option (a)): this project's entire SIF-RPC reply mechanism (Rounds 191-212) delivers reply data via direct EE-RAM writes, never via a real SIF0 DMA transfer - a genuine, newly-identified architectural gap, honestly scoped as an unverified hypothesis for the Function-G/E34 blocker, not a confirmed fix

**Context.** Round 223 corroborated (via a live breakpoint test) that Function G (`0x8000f318`) and its `RAM[0x80020E34]` setter are never reached during a real boot, matching four rounds of static analysis. Round 200's own finding already flagged that this chain is "architecturally consistent with the real SIF/RPC system-command dispatch machinery" - i.e. plausibly triggered by genuine incoming SIF-RPC traffic. This round investigated this project's OWN source directly (not the reference session) to check whether a real, structural gap exists in how SIF-RPC replies are delivered.

**What this round found, reading `source/hw/iop_dma.c`, `source/hw/sif.c`, and `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` directly.** This project's EE syscall 119 (`sceSifSetDma`) implementation has an explicit, already-honest comment (written in Round 176, task #176) stating: "STILL NOT modeled: the IOP-side SIFCMD packet handler actually interpreting what arrives... nothing currently reads the copied bytes back on that end." Cross-checking this against the actual reply mechanism built across Rounds 191-212 (the "SIF reply-queue" work, `ee_core.c`) confirms the gap is real and still present: every single RPC/system-command reply this project synthesizes (BIND/CALL RENDs, MCSERV/SPU2/IOPHEAP replies, `sceSifDmaStat`, etc. - grepped across ~30 reply call sites in `ee_core.c`) is delivered via a **direct `ee_mem_write32()` call straight into the EE's own reply buffer** (e.g. line 1413's `ee_mem_write32(st, ee_recvbuf + 0x24u, ...)`), not via `dma_channel_receive_quadwords()` (the real inbound-DMA primitive Round 198 built specifically for this purpose) or any other DMA-channel-mediated path. **Confirmed via `grep`: zero call sites in `ee_core.c`'s entire SIF-RPC reply machinery reference `dma_channel_receive_quadwords` at all** - the primitive Round 198 built exists and is tested, but is currently used only by Round 199's IOP-side SIF0-CHCR-kick path (`iop_dma_sif0_try_transfer()`), which the 239th finding already confirmed our own boot trace never exercises.

**What this means, architecturally.** This project's SIF-RPC layer is, in its entirety, a host-C-code synthetic shortcut: it recognizes an EE-side syscall pattern (e.g. `sceSifCallRpc`'s underlying `SifSetDma`), decides what a real IOP driver's reply WOULD be, and pokes that reply directly into EE RAM - correctly matching the real reply DATA SHAPE (extensively cross-referenced against real ps2sdk/PCSX2 source across dozens of prior rounds) but never producing the real SIDE EFFECTS a genuine SIF0 hardware DMA transfer would: no `DMAC_STAT` completion bit gets set for the SIF0 channel, no `Cause.IP3` interrupt fires for this specific transfer, and no genuine IOP-side execution of the real interpreted BIOS SIFCMD/SIFMAN driver code ever happens. Real BIOS/kernel code that specifically watches for those hardware-level signals (as opposed to just reading the reply bytes themselves) would not observe them under this project's current model.

**Honest scope - this is a real architectural observation, not a confirmed root cause.** This round does NOT establish that Function G's unreachability is actually caused by this gap. Two things remain genuinely unverified: (1) whether Function G's real trigger chain depends on a genuine SIF0 DMA completion signal specifically (as opposed to depending on RAM content alone, which this project's synthetic replies already deliver correctly), and (2) whether this project's current boot trace ever even reaches the point of issuing the SPECIFIC RPC call(s) that would be relevant to this chain in the first place, given the trace's resting point (`0x8000cff4`/`0x8000F768`) is architecturally early - per the 231st finding, part of OSDSYS's own startup/init sequence, quite possibly before any RPC traffic this mechanism would react to has even been sent. Asserting this gap IS the `0x8000cff4` blocker without checking both of these would repeat exactly the kind of premature-connection mistake Round 222 was written specifically to correct.

**Action taken.** None to this repository's source. This is a real, citable, grounded-in-source-code finding (not fabricated or guessed), but implementing a fix (routing the existing 30+ reply call sites through a real SIF0 DMA-completion path instead of direct memory writes) would be a substantial architectural change, and per this project's standing discipline, should not be attempted until the two open verification points above are checked - otherwise there is a real risk of an large, invasive change that doesn't move the boot trace forward at all, mirroring Round 198/199's own honestly-reported "built the capability, boot trace unchanged" results.

**No source-code change to this repository this round.** Docs-only investigative round. Next (Round 225): before implementing anything, verify whether this project's own boot trace ever reaches a real `sceSifCallRpc`/`SifSetDma` call site downstream of the current `0x8000cff4` resting point (i.e., does progress past this loop even depend on RPC reply delivery at all, or is the loop's own exit condition self-contained within OSDSYS's init sequence, unrelated to RPC traffic) - this determines whether pursuing the DMA-completion-signal gap is actually on the critical path, or a real but currently-irrelevant architectural gap to fix later.

## 265th finding (Round 225, task #366/#172, real fix per user's direct "fix the real dma transfer" directive): implemented dma_channel_note_reply_delivered() and wired it into the two highest-traffic SIF-RPC reply paths - and corrects an inaccuracy in Round 224's own framing along the way

**Context.** The user asked directly to stop investigating and fix the real DMA transfer gap Round 224 flagged. Before touching source, re-verified Round 224's claim by reading `dma_channel_signal_done()`'s call sites directly (not from memory).

**Correction to Round 224.** Round 224 stated "zero call sites in ee_core.c's entire SIF-RPC reply machinery reference dma_channel_receive_quadwords" - true, but its broader framing ("no real DMAC_STAT completion bit gets set... no genuine Cause.IP3 interrupt fires") was WRONG. Direct inspection found `dma_channel_signal_done(DMA_CHANNEL_SIF0)` already called at 4 real sites: `sif_cmd_iop_send_rpcinit_ready()`, `sif_cmd_iop_send_rpc_bind_rend()` (the single highest-traffic reply path - every BIND/CALL completion), and unconditionally at the end of EE syscall 119's handler (covering the MCSERV/PADMAN/SPU2/IOPHEAP/LOADFILE/cdvdman reply branches). `ee_check_dmac_interrupt()` was also independently verified correct: it real-mindedly checks `dma_dmac_interrupt_pending()`, `Status.IE/EIE/EXL/ERL`, and `Status.IM3` before raising `Cause.IP3` and vectoring a real exception - this whole chain was already working. Round 224's overstatement is corrected here rather than left uncorrected.

**What was genuinely missing, confirmed by direct code inspection.** None of these reply sites ever touched the SIF0 channel's own `MADR`/`QWC`/`quadwords_transferred` hardware-register state - they wrote reply bytes via `ee_mem_write32()` (correct, byte-exact, already-cited data) and separately signaled completion, but left the channel's own register state exactly as it was before. Real BIOS/kernel code that reads those specific hardware registers directly (rather than only reacting to the DMAC_STAT IRQ) would see stale state after a synthetic reply landed.

**What was implemented.** `dma_channel_note_reply_delivered(int channel, uint32_t dest_addr, uint32_t nbytes)` in `source/hw/dma.c`/`include/core/hw/dma.h`: a companion to Round 198's `dma_channel_receive_quadwords()` that performs the exact same real bookkeeping (MADR advanced past the delivered data, QWC decremented and clamped at 0, `quadwords_transferred` incremented, `dma_channel_signal_done()` called) without redoing the byte copy (already done by the caller) and without requiring the channel's MADR to already equal the destination first (this project has no citable evidence that real EE-side code pre-programs SIF0's MADR to these specific synthetic reply-buffer addresses). Wired into the two highest-traffic call sites: `sif_cmd_iop_send_rpcinit_ready()` (24-byte `sr_pkt` reply) and `sif_cmd_iop_send_rpc_bind_rend()` (48-byte `SifRpcRendPkt_t` reply, every BIND/CALL completion). The remaining syscall-119 branch replies (MCSERV/PADMAN/SPU2/IOPHEAP/LOADFILE/cdvdman) still use the older bare `dma_channel_signal_done()` call - deliberately not touched this round since correctly attributing each branch's own destination/size to the single shared trailing call point is a larger, more error-prone change; explicitly scoped as open below.

**Verification.** New `tests/test_dma_reply_delivered.c` (10 checks): 48-byte and 24-byte reply sizes correctly advance MADR (with correct round-up-to-quadword behavior for the non-quadword-aligned 24-byte case), QWC decrements and clamps at 0 rather than underflowing, the lifetime counter advances, real `DMAC_STAT` completion is signaled, invalid channel indices are safe no-ops, the function does NOT touch EE RAM contents (bookkeeping only - the caller's own `ee_mem_write32()` calls already wrote the bytes), and channels don't cross-contaminate. All 10 pass. **Full regression suite**, run fresh against a complete, corrected source-file compile list (not the stale per-file database earlier rounds' harness used - see honest note below): **121/121 test files pass, 0 failures**, including the full `test_ee_core.c` suite (exercises `ee_core.c`, the file with both call-site edits) and the new test. **Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced (2624708/467936 bytes), only the same two pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings this project has documented for many rounds (`iop_core.c:482`, `iop_module_loader.c:225`), zero new warnings.

**Honest note on the regression harness itself.** This round built a fresh compile-and-run driver (per-test self-include detection to avoid duplicate-symbol errors, a complete "kitchen sink" source-file list covering every `source/hw/*.c` and `source/core/**/*.c` file except the GX-dependent `gs_wii_output.c`) rather than reusing any prior session's harness (this project's own `/tmp` scratch tooling does not persist across sandbox resets, as multiple earlier rounds have already noted). This is believed to be a more complete/accurate regression check than several earlier rounds' harnesses (which had documented false-positive `COMPILE_FAIL` gaps from stale per-file source lists) - the 121/121 clean result is reported as-is, not adjusted to match any earlier round's specific pass count.

**Honest scope - what this does NOT establish.** This round does not claim (and Round 224 did not establish) that this MADR/QWC bookkeeping gap has any bearing on the `0x8000cff4` blocker specifically - Round 224's own honest scoping already flagged that connection as unverified, and this round did not re-investigate it. This is a real, independently-motivated correctness improvement to the SIF-RPC reply mechanism (making the channel's own hardware-register state consistent with what a real transfer would leave behind), delivered because the user asked for the DMA-transfer gap to be fixed - not a claimed fix for the OSDSYS boot blocker.

New test file added. Full mandatory workflow completed this round.

## 269th finding (Round 230): monitor.py can now wait for PCSX2 to start (enables real cold-boot captures)

**Context**: the user tried exactly the workflow both 267th/268th findings called for - start
`monitor.py live` before launching PCSX2 - and hit `ConnectionRefusedError` immediately, since the
script always assumed DebugServer/Pine were already listening. Both real captures so far accidentally
attached mid-session because of this, not by choice.

**Implemented**: `wait_for_connection(host, port, label)` (new helper) retries a plain TCP connect on a
~1s interval (printing a dot per attempt, one confirmation line once connected) instead of raising
immediately. `DebugServerClient`/`PineClient` both gained a `wait=` constructor param that routes
through this helper. `live` now passes `wait=True` by default - `--no-wait` restores the old fail-fast
behavior for scripted use where PCSX2 is guaranteed already running.

**Verified**: a mock TCP listener that only starts accepting connections 2.5s after the client began
waiting - `wait_for_connection()` correctly blocked and connected within the expected window (2.71s
observed). No live PCSX2 available in this sandbox to test the full `live` flow end-to-end, but the
underlying retry primitive both `DebugServerClient`/`PineClient` now share is confirmed correct.

**What this actually unblocks**: the user can now start `monitor.py live` first, then launch PCSX2 (or
trigger a fresh VM Reset), and the tool will pick up the connection the moment both servers come up -
the workflow needed to finally capture an actual cold boot instead of an already-running game, which is
what both prior real captures (267th/268th findings) missed.

No emulator source files changed this round - `monitor.py` is project tooling (`pcsx2-mcp-patch/`),
not part of the git-tracked emulator core, so no regression suite or Wii rebuild applies here.

## 270th finding (Round 231): root-caused why captures keep missing the boot - Fast Boot + poll interval too coarse

**Context**: the user reported doing a genuine PCSX2 reset (confirmed by a real 102.3s DebugServer
reconnect gap in the terminal log they pasted) immediately before this capture, yet the very first
sample still showed fully-initialized hardware state.

**The evidence**: sample 1, taken well under a second after the DebugServer connection succeeded,
already shows `D_ENABLER=0x00001201`, `I_MASK=0x00001002`, and CSR's `HSINT`/`VSINT` bits set. A genuine
cold boot starts with `D_ENABLER=0`, `I_MASK=0`, and no video timing until BIOS init configures the GS -
none of that ever appears in any of this project's four real captures so far (267th-270th findings).

**Root cause identified**: this is not a tooling failure to detect the reset - it's a timescale mismatch.
With PCSX2's Fast Boot enabled (skips the BIOS splash animation), a small game/demo's entire boot can
complete in well under a second of real wall-clock time on modern hardware - PS2 originally ran at
~294MHz EE / ~37MHz IOP, and a modern PC executes the same instruction count vastly faster with no
animation delay to pad it out. `monitor.py live`'s default 0.5s poll interval (plus normal reconnect
overhead) is coarser than the boot window itself - the entire boot is finishing inside the gap between
polls, not failing to be triggered.

**Fix given to the user**: (1) disable Fast Boot in PCSX2 so the BIOS logo actually plays for several
real seconds, giving the polling loop an observable window; (2) use a much tighter `--interval` (e.g.
`--interval 0.05`) to increase sample density regardless. Not yet implemented as a monitor.py change -
this is a PCSX2-side settings/usage fix, not a script bug. If a future capture with Fast Boot disabled
still misses the boot, that would point back at the tool itself and be worth revisiting.

No source files changed this round - diagnostic analysis of user-provided real capture data only.

## 271st finding (Round 232): add EE/IOP v0/v1 GPR tracking to monitor.py

**Context**: the user reported seeing something meaningful flash by in PCSX2's own debugger UI on IOP
v0/v1, but manually clicking Pause always missed it by the time it took effect - a real timing race
(PS2-speed emulation vastly outruns human reaction plus UI click latency), not a mistake on their part.

**Implemented**: `DebugServerClient.read_gpr(cpu, names)` reads specific named GPRs (standard MIPS ABI
names - `v0`/`v1`/etc, confirmed real names this DebugServer build uses from earlier live register-dump
citations) via `read_registers(cpu, category=0)`'s `"GPR"` block. Wired into `live`'s per-sample loop:
`EE.v0`/`EE.v1`/`IOP.v0`/`IOP.v1` are now polled and logged every sample, best-effort, alongside
everything else already tracked. `--no-gpr` disables it.

**Why this beats trying to catch it live**: a fleeting register value doesn't need a human to win a race
against real execution speed if every poll already has it in the log - whichever sample happens to land
on the right instant preserves it permanently in the JSONL, checkable after the fact instead of by eye.

**Verified**: a mock DebugServer returning the real `{"GPR": {"regs": [{"name":"v0", "display":...}]}}`
response shape (matching the patched `index.ts`'s own `regs.GPR?.regs` access pattern) round-trips
correctly through `read_gpr()` - including a `v0=0xfffffffb` (-5) value chosen deliberately to match
Round 221's already-cited real `syscall(-5)` dispatch finding, confirming the extraction logic handles
negative-as-unsigned-hex values correctly. No live PCSX2 available in this sandbox for a true end-to-end
test.

No emulator source files changed this round - `monitor.py` is project tooling, not part of the
git-tracked core.

## 272nd finding (Round 233): independent live cross-confirmation of the all-zero-GPR/self-jump idle-thread signature

**Context**: the user was trying to catch a fleeting IOP register state in PCSX2's own debugger UI
(having reported "even if i pause it goes away"). Two screenshots later, with the exact PC identified,
this turned out not to be a fleeting one-shot value at all - it's a stable, real idle-thread parking
loop, and its disappearance on Resume is just the scheduler moving on, not a rare race.

**What was caught** (PCSX2's native IOP/R3000 debugger, live session, Gran Turismo 3 - A-Spec, cold
boot per the user's report): PC parked at `0x0000B694`, disassembling to `j 0x0000B694` - a real,
unconditional self-jump. Every GPR reads `0x00000000` except `k0=0000B694` (mirrors PC) and
`k1=01430A0D` (uninterpreted scratch). Tracing backward in the same disassembly dump: `0x0000B674`
calls a PCSX2-symbolicated real kernel function, `thbase[33]::DelayThread`, with its delay-slot
instruction (`ori a0,a0,0x4240` combined with the preceding `lui a0,0x000F`) setting the argument to
`0x000F4240` = 1,000,000 (microseconds - a 1-second sleep), inside a loop (`0x0000B67C: j 0x0000B674`)
that polls `*s0` until nonzero. Once that polling function returns (`jr ra` at `0x0000B68C`), execution
falls straight through into the self-jump at `0x0000B694`.

**Why this matters**: this is an *independent* real-hardware/real-PCSX2 confirmation, on a different
game (GT3, not Tekken) and a completely different address than anything in this project's own boot
trace, of the exact same signature already documented for this project's own EE-side investigation - an
unconditional self-jump combined with an all-zero GPR file is the genuine, universal real PS2-kernel
idle-thread-body shape, not an artifact specific to one game, one CPU, or one investigation. It
independently strengthens (without repeating) that earlier citation.

**Practical guidance given to the user**: since this is a stable parking point (not a race-condition
flicker), a real breakpoint at IOP `0x0000B694` will now catch it deterministically on demand, rather
than needing to out-react PCSX2's own scheduler by manually timing Pause.

**Scope note**: this GT3 address has no established connection to this project's own
`0x8000cff4`/`0x00118f98` blocker (different game, different address, different CPU state entirely) -
recorded here purely as a valuable independent cross-confirmation of a general kernel-behavior pattern,
not as progress on the blocker itself. No source files changed this round.

## 273rd finding (Round 234): real BIOS Circuit-2 GS setup routine caught live on a genuine Tekken cold boot

**Context**: the user set write watchpoints on PMODE (`0x12000000`) and DISPFB2 (`0x12000090`) in
PCSX2's native debugger to catch the exact real BIOS write this project's own boot trace never reaches
(94th/126th/183rd/271st-adjacent findings: our own emulator halts at EE `0x8000cff4`/IOP `0x00118f98`
without ever writing these registers). The user reported the emulator "keeps stopping from alone" with
both breakpoints showing `Hits: 0`, even after a genuine reset, and this persisted after ruling out
"Pause on Focus Loss" and window-focus timing.

**Root cause of the confusing symptom**: PCSX2's native debugger UI's "Breakpoints" panel `Hits` column
does not reflect memory watchpoint activity - these are tracked as a separate internal list entirely
(confirmed via this session's live DebugServer connection: `pcsx2_list_breakpoints` returned "No
breakpoints set" while `pcsx2_list_watchpoints` simultaneously showed the same two entries very much
active, still reading `0 hits` in its own listing despite provably firing). The two watchpoints were, in
fact, working the whole time - the "runs a second, stops" pattern was real and correct: the loaded game
(Gran Turismo 3) was already well past its own boot and rewrites PMODE/DISPFB2 on essentially every
frame during normal double-buffered display flipping, so the watchpoint halted the VM almost every
frame. Removing both watchpoints and issuing Continue immediately confirmed this: cycle count advanced
by 1.09 billion cycles in a single step with zero further auto-stops, versus ~5-10 cycles per step while
armed.

**The real capture**: switched the loaded title to Tekken Tag Tournament [Demo] (`SCED-50041`), which
was sitting at a genuine `PC=0xbfc00000`/`Cycles=0` cold-reset state, then re-armed the same two write
watchpoints and resumed. It halted once, after 226,286,117 real cycles, at EE `PC=0x0050b420` -
`0xfc640000` = `sd a0,(v1)` with `v1=0x12000000` (PMODE) and `a0=0x66` about to be written. This is the
first time in this project's history that a genuine real-BIOS PMODE/DISPFB2 write has been captured live
(all prior sessions only ever observed our own emulator's trace, which never reaches this point).

**Full routine, disassembled** (`0x0050b410`-`0x0050b45c`, straight-line, no branches/loops): loads five
8-byte values from a table at `a3` (`=0x0051D3E0`, offsets `0x00/0x08/0x10/0x18/0x20`) and writes them
in order to PMODE (`0x12000000`), SMODE2 (`0x12000020`), DISPFB2 (`0x12000090`), DISPLAY2
(`0x120000A0`), and BGCOLOR (`0x120000E0`). Reading the live table memory at `0x51D3E0` gave the exact
real values: `PMODE=0x66`, `SMODE2=0x03`, `DISPFB2=0x1400`, `DISPLAY2=0x001bf9ff0183227c`,
`BGCOLOR=0x000000`.

**Why this matters most**: `PMODE=0x66` decodes to `EN1=0` (Circuit 1 **disabled**), `EN2=1` (Circuit 2
**enabled**), `MMOD=1`, `AMOD=1`, `SLBG=0` - real hardware boots showing output exclusively through GS
Circuit 2, never Circuit 1. This is an exact, live, real-hardware confirmation of the premise behind
task #388's already-landed fix ("main.c hardcodes Circuit1 blit, real BIOS uses Circuit2") - that fix
was reasoned from indirect evidence; this is the first direct real-BIOS register capture proving it
correct. `SMODE2=0x03` (`INT=1`, `FFMD=1`) is the standard NTSC interlaced/field-mode value. `DISPFB2`
and `DISPLAY2` are non-zero, real, structured values (not zero/garbage), consistent with a genuine
configured framebuffer and display-timing setup, not a stub or placeholder.

**Call stack at the halt** (6 frames, EE): `0x0050b410` (this routine) <- `0x0050a9a0` (`beqz s0,...`
guard) <- `0x005000c4` (`dmove a0,s0` - passes the same table pointer forward) <- `0x005002f8` (`jal
0x00518990`) <- `0x00500488` (`lw v0,-0x7D30(gp)` - global lookup) <- outermost frame `j 0x00518140`.
Confirms this is invoked once, unconditionally-on-a-guard, from OSDSYS's own boot-time display-init
path - not from any game-specific code (address range is shared BIOS/OSDSYS code, independent of which
disc is mounted).

**Next step this unlocks**: compare this exact PMODE/SMODE2/DISPFB2/DISPLAY2/BGCOLOR value set against
what our own emulator's Circuit-2 output path (post-task-#388) currently assumes/hardcodes, and correct
any mismatch - this is now a citable, exact real-hardware reference rather than an inferred one. No
emulator source files changed this round (live-debugging + documentation only).

## 274th finding (Round 235): compared Round 234's live capture against this project's existing Circuit-2 code and against Round 212's earlier screenshot data - no bug found, existing fix reconfirmed; also corrects a transcription error in Round 234's own entry

**Self-correction first.** Round 234's `DISPLAY2` value was mis-transcribed as `0x1bf9ff0183227c00`
(18 hex digits - one byte too many). Re-parsing the original 40-byte hex dump programmatically gives
the correct little-endian 8-byte value: `0x001bf9ff0183227c`. Fixed in all three docs files. The error
was caught by re-deriving the value with a script instead of trusting the original by-hand read, before
building anything on top of it - the same discipline this project has applied to prior self-corrections
(e.g. the 253rd/254th findings).

**Comparison against this project's own source.** Checked `source/main.c`'s Circuit-2 selection logic
and `source/hw/gs_wii_output.c`'s `gs_decode_dispfb()` (the two places that would need to match real
hardware for a picture to actually appear) against the newly-captured real values. Both already handle
this correctly: `gs_decode_dispfb(0x1400, ...)` gives `FBP=0, FBW=640px` - the field-decode logic (FBP =
bits 0-8 x2048, FBW = bits 9-14 x64) needs no change. `main.c`'s `en1`/`en2`-based circuit selection
(task #388/252nd finding, Round 212) already prefers `dispfb2`/`display2` when `EN2` alone is set, which
is exactly this capture's real `PMODE=0x66` state. **No source-code bug was found this round** - the
existing fix was reasoned correctly from indirect/screenshot evidence in Round 212, and this round's
direct live capture confirms it rather than correcting it.

**Cross-check against Round 212's earlier screenshot values** (`PMODE=0x66`, `DISPFB2=0x00000000000014A0`,
`DISPLAY2=0x001FF9FF0181227C`, taken at the real BIOS splash screen): `PMODE` matches exactly. `DISPFB2`
differs only in its FBP field (`0` here vs `160` there) - both decode to the same `FBW=640px`. This is a
real, expected difference, not a discrepancy: Round 234's capture is the framebuffer's very first BIOS
write (base address 0, `Cycles=226,286,117` from a `Cycles=0` cold reset), while Round 212's was taken
later, at the already-showing splash screen, after the BIOS had relocated the buffer to word offset
`160*2048`. `DISPLAY2` differs by a few bits in its packed DX/DY/MAGH fields (`0x001bf9ff0183227c` vs
`0x001ff9ff0181227c`) - consistent with minor real CRTC-timing-register differences between the two
captured moments, not an error in either reading.

**New information this round adds beyond Round 212's screenshots**: `SMODE2=0x03` and `BGCOLOR=0x000000`
were not previously captured (Round 212's screenshots only covered the GS register tab's PMODE/DISPFBx/
DISPLAYx/CSR fields). `SMODE2`'s `INT=1`/`FFMD=1` is the standard NTSC interlaced/field-mode value.
`BGCOLOR=0` (black) matches the expectation of a boot-time background before content is drawn. This
round also has the exact disassembled routine and 6-frame call stack producing these writes (Round 234),
which Round 212's screenshots never had access to - only the resulting register values, not the code
that set them.

**Conclusion.** This closes out the comparison the user asked for: real hardware and this project's
existing Wii-output code already agree. No further action needed on the Circuit-2 path itself. No
emulator source files changed this round (comparison + doc correction only).

## 275th finding (Round 236): surveyed other independent PS2 emulator/BIOS projects for boot-blocker leads - no new fix found, but real, citable validation that this project's IOP-module struggle is a known-hard, widely-documented category of difficulty, not a sign of a wrong approach

**Context.** The user asked whether other PS2 emulator ports (Xbox, Android, etc.) publicly document how far they get through boot, as a source of leads for this project's own persistent EE `0x8000cff4`/IOP `0x00118f98` resting point.

**Surveyed, with results:**
- **XBSX2** (Xbox/Xbox Series homebrew port): confirmed to be a direct UWP port of upstream PCSX2 itself, not an independent implementation. Not a new information source - this project already works from PCSX2's own upstream source directly (task #10/#11), so XBSX2's boot behavior is definitionally identical to what's already available.
- **DobieStation** (independent, from-scratch, cross-platform LLE emulator, PSI-Rockin): its own public wiki ("Making a PS2 Emulator: From Bits to Pixels") states directly: *"HLE of the PS2 becomes incredibly difficult once you start implementing the Input/Output Processor (IOP), as nearly every game will have patches for the many IOP modules. Play!, an HLE emulator, has made good progress but is still inferior to PCSX2, which uses LLE."* This is a real, independent, citable confirmation from a mature, working PS2 emulator project that IOP module handling is specifically and widely known to be the hardest part of PS2 emulation - directly matching this project's own multi-hundred-round history concentrated on exactly that subsystem (LOADCORE/ModuleInfo_t/SIFCMD/SIFINIT, findings #124/#132/#151-167 and many since). DobieStation's own compatibility notes ("a large portion of the PS2's library can boot or get to menus... some titles can even go in-game") also confirm that even for a mature, several-years-old independent emulator, "reliably reaching a menu/splash" is a genuine milestone, not a given - this project not yet reaching it is consistent with the field's normal difficulty curve, not evidence of a wrong architecture.
- **"Writing a PlayStation 2 BIOS in Rust"** (rust-console, a clean-room, from-scratch BIOS reimplementation - not an emulator, but documentation of the real IOP loader's exact mechanics): its IOP-boot chapter documents the real IRX (`.iopmod` section, export table magic `0x41C00000`, import table magic `0x41E00000`) format and the real "stub patching" linking mechanism - each imported function starts as a two-instruction do-nothing stub (`jr $ra` / `li $zero,NN`) that gets overwritten in place with a direct `j <target>` jump once the real exporting module's address is known. **Checked against this project's own `source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`**: `link_imports_one()` (line ~479) already implements exactly this mechanism, and its own inline comment already cites "the cited PS2 BIOS book" - meaning this project had already independently arrived at and correctly implemented this exact real mechanism in an earlier round, and this book is confirmation of prior work, not a new fix.
- **Neutrino** (rickgaiser): checked and ruled out as directly relevant - it's a backing-store/disc-image loader environment (DVD/HDD/memory-card virtualization for real PS2 hardware), not a CPU/BIOS emulator, so it has nothing to say about EE/IOP boot semantics.
- **Play!** (jpd002, genuine independent HLE PS2 emulator): confirmed to exist and be under active development on GitHub, but its actual IOP-module HLE source (`Source/Iop_*.cpp` files, referenced by DobieStation's own citation above) could not be fetched in this round - GitHub's code search API requires authentication and the repository's file browser is JavaScript-rendered, neither reachable with this session's tools. This remains a real, not-yet-exploited lead: Play!'s actual module list would show exactly which IOP kernel modules a *working* HLE boot needs to implement, which could be compared line-for-line against this project's own module coverage. Flagged for a future round with browser-capable tooling.

**Conclusion.** No new technical fix was found this round - this was a reconnaissance round, not an implementation round, and it's reported honestly as such. The most valuable outcome is the DobieStation citation: it independently confirms, from a real working PS2 emulator project's own public writing, that this project's persistent IOP-module-focused difficulty is a known, widely-shared hard problem in PS2 emulation generally, not a sign this project has taken a wrong turn. The one concrete unexploited lead (Play!'s real module list) is recorded for a future round.

No source files changed this round (research/comparison only).

## 276th finding (Round 237): direct source access to Play! (jpd002/Play-) - independent cross-validation of this project's SIF system command IDs, plus a real module-boot-order checklist; one architectural dead-end honestly ruled out

**Context.** Following Round 236's survey (which couldn't reach Play!'s actual source), the user provided
the real `Play--master.zip` source archive directly. This round examines it against this project's own
already-implemented SIF protocol and IOP module set.

**Independent cross-validation, the most valuable result this round.** Play!'s `SifDefs.h` defines:
`SIF_CMD_SETSREG = 0x80000001`, `SIF_CMD_REND = 0x80000008`, `SIF_CMD_BIND = 0x80000009`,
`SIF_CMD_CALL = 0x8000000A`. This project's own `include/core/hw/sif.h` independently defines
`SIF_CMD_SET_SREG = 0x80000001`, `SIF_CMD_RPC_END = 0x80000008`, `SIF_CMD_RPC_BIND = 0x80000009`,
`SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL = 0x8000000A` - an **exact four-way match**, arrived at completely independently (this
project's values came from live PCSX2-debugger reverse-engineering across Rounds ~53-71/the 63rd/68th/71st
findings; Play!'s came from years of its own real-hardware-testing-driven development). Two unrelated
projects independently reverse-engineering the same real hardware protocol and landing on identical
numeric IDs and semantic roles is about as strong a confirmation as this kind of research can produce.
One open item honestly remains open on both sides: Play!'s own source comments that command `0x80000004`
is used but its exact purpose is unknown ("no clue... could be FlushCache or something like that") -
this project has no citation for that command ID either; not resolved by either project.

**A real, useful module-boot-order checklist.** Play!'s `CIopBios::Reset()` registers its HLE modules in
a fixed order: ioman, stdio, sysmem, modload, sysclib, loadcore, thbase, thmsgbx, thsema, thfpool,
thvpool, thevent, heaplib, timrman, intrman, dmacman, secrman, vblank, cdvdman, sifman, sifcmd, fileio,
cdvdfsv, mcserv, poweroff, usbd, iomanX. Cross-checked against this project's own coverage: every one of
these categories already has a real or HLE counterpart in this project (IOP interrupt controller/timers/
DMA, threading (task #339's TCB model), LOADCORE, SIF (sif.c), CD-ROM/CDVD, memory card, SIO2/pad, SPU2).
No missing subsystem category was found by this comparison - this project's coverage breadth already
matches a real, working HLE emulator's own module list.

**An architectural dead end, honestly ruled out.** Checked Play!'s `Iop_SifMan.cpp` for how it models the
real `SIF_STAT`/`SIFINIT` handshake flag this project's own 131st finding (Round 91) had to fix - Play!'s
`SifInit` is a bare named no-op with no internal status-flag state at all. This is because Play!'s HLE
architecture wires the EE/IOP RPC bridge directly in software rather than modeling two real chips
independently polling a shared hardware status register - an architectural difference from this project's
LLE-style real-BIOS-bytes approach, not a hidden trick this project is missing. No further comparison
value available here without modeling an HLE bridge this project doesn't have and doesn't want (it would
defeat the point of running the real BIOS).

**Not pursued further this round, structurally different subsystem.** `Iop_Loadcore.cpp`'s `LoadModule`/
`StopModule`/etc. turned out to be Play!'s *remote, mid-game* dynamic-module-loading RPC service (games
calling `sceLoadModule` during play), not the real BIOS's own early-boot module bring-up (which happens
before any RPC service exists) - not directly comparable to this project's own boot-time LOADCORE work.

**Conclusion.** No new bug or fix identified this round, but a real, valuable independent confirmation
that this project's SIF system-command layer is byte-exact-correct, and that its overall IOP module
coverage is not missing any category a working emulator needs. No source files changed (comparison only).

## Round 238 (277th finding) - task #407 continuation, real forward progress out of the outer-loop wall

**Context.** Continuing the standing autonomous authorization ("fix everything you need to do... as long
it works and gets us out of this loop crap"). Resumed the still-open, more-precise question left after
Round 190-193's own investigation of the EE's persistent outer-loop rest (address family
`0x8000CC68`-`0x8000F874`, first documented in the 230th finding): the already-merged Round 178 pragmatic
SBUS shortcut had fired and its effect (INTC_STAT bit 1 set) persists, and `ee_intc_pending()` correctly
returns true - but a fresh host-native diagnostic this round (scratch driver, real BIOS + real Tekken Tag
Tournament Demo disc, never committed) captured the live COP0 state at rest: `Status=0x70030C00` ->
`IE=0, EXL=0, ERL=0, EIE=1, IM2=1, IM3=1`. Reading `ee_check_intc_interrupt()` (`source/core/ee/ee_core.c`)
confirmed its gate requires `(Status & (IE|EXL|ERL|EIE)) == (IE|EIE)` - i.e. **IE=1 is mandatory** - so
despite being pending, unmasked, and otherwise fully qualified, the interrupt was never actually delivered
because `Status.IE` never leaves 0 anywhere in the trace.

**Ruled out as the cause: this project's own EI/DI implementation.** Read the `funct 0x38`/`0x39` (EI/DI)
cases in `ee_core.c` - both correctly toggle only `Status.EIE` (bit 16), never `Status.IE` (bit 0), which
is the real, documented R5900 hardware behavior (matches PCSX2's own `COP0::EI()`/`COP0::DI()`). Not a
bug. On real hardware, `Status.IE` is instead set by a direct kernel `MTC0` write to the whole Status
register (typically once, during kernel/scheduler thread-dispatch bring-up) - and this project's own MTC0
handler already performs a raw, unmasked `cop0[rd] = rt32` write for Status, so that mechanism already
works correctly if/when real BIOS code reaches it. The open question (not resolved this round, and not
claimed to be) is *why* that real MTC0 write is never reached - most plausibly a bootstrap chicken-and-egg:
the code that performs it may live inside the very interrupt handler this pending-but-undelivered
interrupt would invoke.

**Fix implemented: `ee_check_boot_unblock_ie_gate()`.** Same pragmatic-shortcut category and labeling
convention as Round 161's `ee_check_boot_unblock_selfloop()` and Round 178's
`ee_check_boot_unblock_sbus_wait()` (see the full doc comment in `ee_core.c` for the complete
authorization/reasoning trail). Sets `Status.IE=1` exactly once per boot (static latch), and only when
ALL of the following already-true, real conditions hold: a genuine pending+unmasked interrupt
(`ee_intc_pending()`), `EIE=1`/`EXL=0`/`ERL=0`, `IM2` set, and the EE resting somewhere in the documented
outer-loop address family (`0x8000CC00`-`0x8000FA00`) as a safety bound. Called from both existing
per-step call sites alongside the Round 178 shortcut.

**Verification - genuine, previously-unreached forward progress.** Re-ran the host-native diagnostic
(20M-slice budget, same real BIOS + real disc) with this change:
```
EE  pc=0x800014FC halted=0 instr=159900564
IOP pc=0x00118F98 halted=0 instr=19762501
EE_INTC stat=0x0000080E mask=0x00001002 (bit1/SBUS set=1)
COP0 Status=0x70030C00 Cause=0x00008C00  IE=0 EXL=0 ERL=0 EIE=1 IM2=1 IM3=1
```
The EE has moved **entirely out of** the `0x8000CC68`-`0x8000F874` family it had rested in since Round 190
and is now oscillating in a **new, different, previously-unreached** address family: a tight loop at
`0x800014EC`-`0x800014FC` (7 distinct PCs, ~11-12 hits each) plus new activity at `0x8000B8A0`-`0x8000B8B8`
and `0x9FC42548`-`0x9FC42560` (the latter is a KSEG1-mirrored real BIOS ROM address, phys ~`0x1C42548` -
genuine BIOS ROM code, not RAM). This is the first time in this project's history the EE has left the
Round-190-documented outer-loop family at all. Note `Status.IE` reads back as 0 again in the final
snapshot - consistent with the shortcut firing once, the EE briefly executing with interrupts enabled
(reaching new code), and then either the ISR or subsequent kernel code clearing IE again (e.g. on
entering a nested exception context) before settling into this new resting loop - not a sign the shortcut
failed to fire (the PC/loop-family change and the INTC_STAT bit1 latch are the real evidence it worked).

**Regression.** Full 121-file suite: 120/121 direct `PASS`. The 1 remaining
(`test_ee_syscall_full_audit_sweep.c`) hit the harness's 5-second subprocess timeout, but re-run standalone
with a longer timeout it completes in ~7.8s (almost entirely `sys` time, not CPU-bound `user` time - a
sandbox/harness artifact, not a real regression) and reports `ALL CHECKS PASSED (0 failures)`. Effective
result: **121/121 logical pass, 0 real failures**, honestly noting the harness-timeout artifact rather
than silently re-running until it passes or hiding it.

**Wii/devkitPPC rebuild.** Clean `make clean && make`, exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced
(2625556/468192 bytes), only the same two pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings this project
has documented for many rounds (`iop_core.c:482`, `iop_module_loader.c:225`), zero new warnings.

**Status of task #407.** Genuine forward progress achieved and verified, but the boot is **not yet at a
splash screen** - it has reached a new, uncharacterized resting loop. Per this project's own long-standing
pattern ("fix a wall, reach a new wall, document it, iterate"), the next round's job is to characterize
this new `0x800014EC`/`0x8000B8A0`/`0x9FC42548` loop family the same way Rounds 190-193 characterized the
one this round finally escaped.

## Round 239 (278th finding, docs-only) - the new resting loop is a real kernel debug-print-then-panic trap; probable root cause tied to the already-known CreateThread/StartThread gap

**Context.** Continuing task #407 with the live PCSX2 DebugServer session (still connected from earlier
this session, paused mid Circuit-2 GS setup at `pc=0x0050b420` - Pine/game-info wasn't available this
round, so the "same session" match is inferred from the paused PC landing exactly inside Round 234's own
disassembled Circuit-2 range, not Pine-confirmed). Used the live native disassembler as a ground-truth
oracle for the new post-Round-238 resting address family (`0x800014EC`-`0x80001500`,
`0x8000B8A0`-`0x8000B8B8`, `0x9FC42548`-`0x9FC42560`) discovered in Round 238's own host-native diagnostic.

**`0x9FC42548` (real BIOS ROM, KSEG1) is a bounded Count-based delay loop, not a blocker.** Disassembly:
`mfc0 v1,Count` / `mfc0 v0,Count` / `subu v0,v1` / `sltu v0,a0` / `bnez v0,->0x9FC42548`. A textbook
"busy-wait N cycles" utility (compares elapsed COP0 `Count` against an `a0` threshold) - bounded, resolves
on its own, not a wait condition of interest.

**`0x8000B8A0` is a real bzero/memset loop, not a blocker.** Disassembly: `sq v0,(s0)` (128-bit zero
store) / `addiu s0,0x10` / `sltu v0,s0,a0` / `bnez v0,->0x8000B8A0` - a standard EE-optimized "zero N
bytes with quadword stores" kernel utility, self-terminating, matches the histogram's low (1-2) hit count
for this address (transiently visited during bring-up, not the final rest).

**`0x800014EC`-`0x80001500` is the real thing worth documenting: a genuine kernel debug-print-then-freeze
trap, not a polling loop.** Disassembly of the lead-in (`0x800014D8`-`0x80001504`):
```
dmove a1, a0            ; save the real numeric argument before it's overwritten
lui   a0, 0x8001
addiu a0, 0x2493        ; a0 = 0x80012493 (a real format-string pointer)
jal   ->0x80007340
nop
nop x5
b     ->0x800014EC       ; unconditional - the actual final resting shape
```
Reading real memory at `0x80012493` (ASCII) returns an actual embedded kernel debug-string table:
`"# INT: INTC (%d)\0# INT: DMAC (%d)\0# INT: CPU Timer\0# Syscall: undefined (%d)\0"`. `0x80012493` lands
exactly on the start of `"# INT: INTC (%d)"` - so this is specifically the kernel's **default/fallback
handler for an unhandled INTC-category interrupt**, not DMAC/Timer/Syscall. Disassembling the callee
`0x80007340` confirms it's a real varargs-style kernel print function (classic prologue: saves
`a1`/`a2`/`a3`/`t0`-`t3` to a stack save area, then sets `a1` to point at that save area - i.e. builds a
`va_list` for a format-string printer). So the real, concrete shape is: **kprintf("# INT: INTC (%d)",
irq_number); then spin forever** - a genuine kernel panic/trap body, exactly analogous in shape (and
almost certainly in purpose) to the already-documented `0x00081fc0`/idle-thread nop-sled-plus-branch-to-
self signature from Rounds 157/180/181/233, but this one prints a diagnostic first.

**Why this happens: tied to the already-known, already-self-documented CreateThread/StartThread gap.**
`ee_core.c`'s own syscalls 32 (CreateThread) and 34 (StartThread) are honestly documented as placeholder
stubs - "this project has no real multi-thread scheduler... the target thread's function body never
actually executes concurrently under this project's model." Round 238's diagnostic showed `EE_INTC
stat=0x0000080E` - **four** interrupt lines simultaneously pending and never acknowledged (SBUS, VBLANK_
START, VBLANK_END, TIMER2). The most coherent explanation tying both this round's finding and the
original Round-190-238 wall together: the real BIOS/kernel's boot design spawns a separate thread (via
CreateThread/StartThread) whose job is to call `AddIntcHandler` (already correctly implemented per Round
186/task #352) for these specific lines and continue further bring-up - but since that thread's body
never actually runs under this project's current single-thread-only architecture, none of these lines
ever gets a real handler registered. When the real, periodic hardware interrupts (VBLANK ticks especially)
start arriving, the kernel's own generic INTC dispatcher correctly and repeatedly falls through to this
exact "no handler installed" debug trap - genuine, real BIOS behavior given the precondition (no handler
registered), not an emulator bug in the trap-invocation itself. This is presented as the most coherent
supported hypothesis, not a fully proven trace (the precise causal link from "CreateThread stub" to "this
specific call site" was not walked instruction-by-instruction this round).

**Scope decision.** Implementing a real EE-side multi-thread scheduler is a substantial, multi-round
feature (cooperative or full preemptive thread bring-up, TCB model, context save/restore, scheduler
ready-queue) - not a one-round pragmatic shortcut in the spirit of Round 161/178/238's narrow fixes. Per
this project's own established discipline of not forcing a large architectural feature into a rushed
single-round hack, this round is scoped as investigation/characterization only (no source change, no
regression/rebuild required per this project's docs-only carve-out). The next task should scope out what
a minimal real EE-side thread model would need to look like (likely mirroring task #339's already-
completed real IOP TCB model, Round 174, as a template) to actually let the real boot-time helper thread's
body execute and register these interrupt handlers for real.

## Round 240 (279th finding) - correction to Round 239, CreateThread/StartThread experiment, and honest negative result

**Correction to Round 239's own citation.** Round 239 (278th finding) described task #339/Round 174 as
having implemented "a real IOP thread/TCB model" and recommended it as a template for a new EE-side
scheduler. Re-reading Round 174's own 214th finding this round shows that framing is wrong: Round 174's
own text explicitly retracts it - *"Round 173's 'genuine IOP thread/TCB gap' framing is retracted as the
diagnosis for this specific wall... No thread/TCB model was needed for this wall."* Round 174's real fix
was an IOP_IRQ_DMA dispatch-fallback bug, not a thread model. **There is no real thread/TCB model anywhere
in this codebase, on either the EE or IOP side** - confirmed by grepping the whole tree for `tcb`/`TCB`/
`thread_t` and finding no such struct. This correction is made transparently, per this project's own
established practice (Round 213/214, Round 235) of catching and documenting its own errors quickly.

**Research (real ps2sdk source, fetched fresh this round via `raw.githubusercontent.com`, not guessed):**
`ee/kernel/include/kernel.h`'s real `ee_thread_t` struct (the `CreateThread` input, `sizeof` implied 0x24):
`status(0x00)/func(0x04)/stack(0x08)/stack_size(0x0C)/gp_reg(0x10)/initial_priority(0x14)/
current_priority(0x18)/attr(0x1C)/option(0x20)` - confirms this project's own existing
`ee_thread_status_t` comment (task #353) already had the right offsets for the first 9 fields (that struct
just has 3 extra trailing fields). `ee/kernel/include/syscallnr.h` gives the real thread-lifecycle numbers:
`CreateThread=0x20(32)`, `DeleteThread=0x21(33)`, `StartThread=0x22(34)`, `ExitThread=0x23(35)`,
`ExitDeleteThread=0x24(36)`, `TerminateThread=0x25(37)` - all already matching this project's own existing
numeric handling.

**Experiment (task #408 first angle, tested before building any hand-rolled synthetic scheduler).**
Noticed an inconsistency: every OTHER real thread-lifecycle syscall in this file's own already-existing
family (33/35/36/37/39/40/41/43/45/50/51/53/55/57) is deliberately routed to a genuine MIPS Syscall
exception, on the well-established principle "don't fabricate kernel-internal bookkeeping, let the real,
unmodified BIOS-resident kernel handler do its own real work" (task #180's own repeatedly-cited lesson).
Only `CreateThread`(32) and `StartThread`(34) were singled out for fixed placeholder returns instead, on
the assumption that "this project has no real concurrent scheduler [so] it cannot actually spawn and run
the requested thread function." That assumption was never actually tested. Real PS2/MIPS kernel context-
switch code performs its own thread bring-up using only ordinary instructions this interpreter already
executes correctly (loads/stores against its own real, kernel-private, RAM-resident TCB table; `MTC0` to
`EPC`; `ERET`) - so in principle, letting `CreateThread`/`StartThread` ALSO vector like their siblings
should let the real kernel do genuine thread bring-up with zero fabricated software state, exactly as
already happens for the other 14 numbers in this family.

**Change made**: `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` - removed the two placeholder blocks for sysnum 32/34 and
added both numbers to the existing exception-vectoring condition. Updated `tests/test_ee_syscall_thread_
family.c` (whose own header comment explicitly asserted the OLD placeholder behavior as a "regression
check") to test and assert the NEW behavior instead, with a full explanation of the change in the file's
own header comment.

**Honest result: no measurable effect on the actual boot wall.** Re-ran the same host-native diagnostic
used since Round 238/239 (real BIOS + real Tekken demo disc, 20M-slice budget) with this change applied.
**Result was byte-for-byte identical to the pre-change run**: same final `EE pc=0x800014FC`, same
`instr=159900564`, same PC histogram, same `EE_INTC stat=0x0000080E`. This is strong, direct evidence that
**the current traced boot path never actually reaches a `CreateThread`/`StartThread` call site at all**
within this instruction budget - the change had literally nothing to act on. This means Round 239's
hypothesis (tying the INTC panic trap directly to the CreateThread/StartThread stub gap via "a helper
thread never runs its registration code") is **not confirmed by direct measurement** - it may still be
true in a longer trace, or the real cause of the unregistered INTC handlers may be something else entirely
that doesn't route through these two syscalls at all. Reported as a genuine, informative negative result,
not adjusted or reframed to look like a success.

**Regression**: full 121-file suite re-run clean: **121/121 pass, 0 failures** (including the updated
`test_ee_syscall_thread_family.c`, now asserting the new exception-vectoring behavior for 32/34). **Clean
Wii/devkitPPC rebuild**: exit 0, same two pre-existing benign `strncpy` warnings, zero new warnings.

**Decision on keeping the change**: kept, despite the null result on the current wall. Reasoning: it
removes a special-case that was never verified to be necessary, brings `CreateThread`/`StartThread`
into consistency with their own sibling syscalls in the same family, and is a strictly more honest
position (trusting real, unmodified kernel code) than fabricating placeholder return values whose
correctness this project could never actually verify either. It is not a "fix" for task #407/#408 - the
real INTC-handler-registration gap remains open, and the next step is still to determine, from a genuinely
longer trace or from live-session evidence, whether `CreateThread`/`StartThread` are EVER reached at all
during a real boot, and if so, whether the real kernel's own context-switch code (now reachable, not
short-circuited) behaves correctly against this project's existing COP0/exception/ERET model or exposes a
new, real gap.

## Round 241 (280th finding, docs-only) - live-session confirms CreateThread/StartThread genuinely fire on real hardware during this exact game's boot

**Context.** Direct follow-up to Round 240's open question: does the real Tekken Tag Tournament Demo boot
ever actually call `CreateThread`/`StartThread` at all, or does Round 239's causal hypothesis rest on a
syscall pair that's never really exercised? Reconnected to the same live PCSX2 DebugServer session (still
paused mid this exact game's own execution, `pc=0x0050b420`/`0x0050b448` region - the already-documented
Circuit-2 GS setup vicinity). Set a conditional breakpoint at the real kernel Syscall vector
(`0x80000180`, `v1==32 || v1==34`) to try to catch a live call - continuing only advanced a handful of
cycles per call (this session's real-time execution rate through this specific code region is very slow
via the DebugServer bridge), making a live catch impractical within a reasonable number of tool calls.

**Answered a different way, just as conclusively: `pcsx2_get_threads` (real EE thread table).** The live
session already has **10 real threads** (TID 0-9), not 1: TID 0 at the already-known real idle-thread
address (`0x00081fc0`, matches Rounds 157/180/181/233's own finding), TID 3 at `0x00501b2c` (status=1/
READY, in the game's own code - almost certainly the actively-scheduled thread near the current pause
point), and TIDs 1/2/4-9 at real, distinct, non-idle, non-zero entry points (`0x00210e78`, `0x00210e68`
shared by five of them, `0x0061b668`, `0x007c45e8`), most in status=4 (THS_WAIT). A single-thread kernel
model could never produce this table - **these 10 threads can only exist because `CreateThread` (and
`StartThread`) genuinely executed multiple times for real, on real hardware, during this exact game's
actual boot and early execution.** This directly answers Round 240's open question: yes, real code
absolutely does call these syscalls in a real boot of this project's own target game - the reason this
project's own host-native diagnostic never reaches one within its tested ~160M-instruction budget is that
this project's own emulator is still stuck earlier (the Round 238/239 INTC panic-trap wall), not because
the syscalls are irrelevant or hypothetical.

**Revised standing for task #408.** Round 239's causal hypothesis (an unrun helper thread explains the
unregistered INTC handlers) remains unconfirmed at the *instruction* level (still no direct trace showing
our own emulator reaching a real `CreateThread` call site), but is now **more plausible, not less** - real
boot genuinely depends on multi-threading working, confirmed independently of this project's own source.
The next step is unchanged in kind but sharper in priority: push this project's own boot trace further
(a longer host-native run, and/or resolving whatever keeps it parked at the post-238 INTC trap) to reach

now-real-exception-vectoring change lets real kernel code bring up a second thread correctly against this

## Round 242 (281st finding) - reverted Round 238's IE-unblock shortcut: live evidence shows real hardware never visits the panic trap it produces

**Context.** Direct follow-up to the still-open task #408 priority (push the boot trace toward a real
`CreateThread` call site) and the user's explicit "yup implement and fix it" instruction. Before building
anything new on top of Round 238's `ee_check_boot_unblock_ie_gate()` shortcut, checked whether that
shortcut itself is actually correct, since Round 239 had already conclusively identified where it leads:
the real BIOS kernel's own "unhandled INTC interrupt" debug-print-then-freeze trap at `0x800014EC`
(embedded debug string `"# INT: INTC (%d)..."` at `0x80012493`, confirmed via live disassembly in Round
239). A shortcut that "escapes" one wall only to force the EE into a different wall real hardware never
visits is not real progress.

**Live-oracle test.** Reconnected to the user's real, running PCSX2 DebugServer session (same live Tekken
Tag Tournament Demo instance used in Rounds 234/241). Set a breakpoint at `0x800014D8`, the exact first
instruction of the panic-trap body, with the explicit question "does real hardware ever hit this during
normal play?" Called `pcsx2_continue()` and polled `pcsx2_status()` repeatedly, observing the EE cycle
counter and PC move through a wide, apparently-normal range of real execution: `pc=0x8000af90` at ~2.14B
cycles, then an apparent VM reset (a previously-documented quirk, Round 215's 391st finding) dropping to
`pc=0x00081fc0`/~194M cycles, then climbing to `pc=0x003993c0` at ~3.55B cycles - roughly 3.3+ billion real
EE cycles of ordinary, successful live gameplay in total. A final `pcsx2_pause()` (landed at
`pc=0x00400760`) plus `pcsx2_list_breakpoints()` confirmed the `0x800014d8` breakpoint was still armed the
entire time and **never fired once**. That is strong, direct evidence: real, correctly-functioning PS2
hardware does not take this path under normal operation. Round 238's shortcut was therefore not "unblocking
a real interrupt into a real handler" - it was forcing `Status.IE=1` under conditions real hardware
apparently does not consider sufficient, and routing the EE into a resting state (the panic trap) that is
itself artificial, not a byte-for-byte match for real behavior.

**Root-cause reasoning for why the shortcut over-fires.** Real hardware most plausibly only flips
`Status.IE=1` once the kernel's own real INTC dispatch table already has a handler registered for the
specific line being unblocked (an ordering constraint: register-handler-then-enable, not enable-then-hope-
a-handler-shows-up). Round 238's gate checked only "is a real interrupt pending+unmasked+otherwise
qualified", never whether a handler was actually registered for it via `AddIntcHandler` (syscall 16, Round
186's own real implementation) - so it could and did fire before real registration happened. Checked
whether this project's own `ee_core.c` keeps any host-side (C-level) table of which INTC lines have
registered handlers, which would let the gate check this precondition directly instead of guessing: it does
not, and per this project's own established discipline (task #180: don't fabricate kernel-internal
bookkeeping, let real BIOS code run) that this project has repeatedly cited and followed throughout the
230+ prior findings, adding one now just to patch this shortcut back up would be exactly the wrong
direction - it would mean shadowing real BIOS-resident state in synthetic C state, the opposite of letting
real code run.

**Decision: reverted, not patched.** `ee_check_boot_unblock_ie_gate()` (the whole function, its doc comment,
its two call sites in `ee_core.c`) has been removed outright. This is a deliberate, disciplined reversal,
not a discovery of a bug in the shortcut's C code - the code did exactly what its own doc comment said it
would do. The problem is that what it does turns out not to match real hardware behavior, per direct live
evidence. Removing it restores the honest, already-well-characterized Round 190/193 outer-loop wall as
this project's real current boot frontier - a known, if still-open, wall, rather than a new wall that
real hardware never visits.

**Verification.** Host-native diagnostic (same `/tmp/round238_diag/driver.c` scratch harness, real BIOS +
real Tekken demo disc, 20M-slice/~160M-instruction budget) re-run against the reverted source: EE now rests
at `pc=0x8000CCAC`, squarely back inside the `0x8000CC00`-`0x8000FA00` outer-loop family (matching Round
190/193's own landmark PCs), with `EE COP0 Status=0x70030C00` -> `IE=0 EXL=0 ERL=0 EIE=1 IM2=1 IM3=1` -
exactly the pre-Round-238 state, confirming the revert is clean and complete (no partial/mixed state).

**Bonus correction (folds in a loose end from Round 239).** The same diagnostic run's `EE_INTC stat=
0x0000080E mask=0x00001002` snapshot was re-examined arithmetically: `stat & mask = 0x080E & 0x1002 =
0x0002` - only **bit 1 (SBUS)** is actually both pending and unmasked (i.e. actually contributes to
`Cause.IP2` / is "deliverable"). Round 239's STATUS.md text describing this as "four interrupt lines
simultaneously pending and never acknowledged" is corrected here: bits 2/3/11 (VBLANK_START/VBLANK_END/
TIM2) are latched in STAT (real hardware behavior - STAT accumulates regardless of MASK) but are not
unmasked in MASK, so they do not actually drive interrupt delivery. Separately, MASK bit 12 (`0x1000`,
`INTC_TIM3`) is set - per the real ps2sdk kernel header's own comment (confirmed via fresh fetch in Round
240), this is "Reserved by the EE kernel for alarms (do not use)", i.e. legitimately used internally by the
real kernel's own alarm/scheduler-tick mechanism, not a bug or a stray unmasked line.

**Regression**: full 121-file suite re-run clean: **121/121 pass, 0 failures**. No test referenced
`ee_check_boot_unblock_ie_gate()` directly (it was never given its own dedicated unit test, unlike the
`sbus_wait`/`selfloop` shortcuts), so no test file required updating for this revert. **Clean Wii/devkitPPC
rebuild**: exit 0, same two pre-existing benign `strncpy` warnings, zero new warnings.

Task #408's priority is restored to where Round 237 left it: the Round 190/193 outer-loop wall itself,

## Round 243 (282nd finding, docs-only) - located the real candidate kernel subroutine that sets Status.IE=1, and confirmed via direct instrumentation that this project's own boot trace never reaches it

**Context.** Direct continuation of task #408 (the Round 190/193 outer-loop wall, restored as the real
frontier after Round 242's revert) and Round 238's own still-open question: "why is the real kernel MTC0
write that sets `Status.IE=1` never reached in this project's own trace?" Round 238 could only observe that
`Status.EI`/`DI` (funct 0x38/0x39) correctly touch only `EIE` (bit 16), never `IE` (bit 0) - matching real
R5900 hardware, where `IE` is instead set by a direct kernel `MTC0` write, typically once, during kernel
bring-up - but never located that real write in the actual BIOS.

**Method - static, clean-room ROMDIR extraction (same established convention as Round 200).** Reused this
project's own `bios_loader.c` ROMDIR-walking algorithm (RESET+ROMDIR name-signature scan, then sequential
16-byte-aligned module packing from file offset 0) via a scratch Python re-implementation against the real
BIOS (never committed, `/tmp` scratch only) to re-locate the `KERNEL` module: file offset `0xb3200`, size
`0x13bf0` (80880 bytes) - exactly matching Round 200's own citation. Confirmed the module maps 1:1 to EE
virtual address `0x80000000` (file offset X -> VA `0x80000000+X`) by cross-checking two already-published,
independently-verified landmarks against freshly-extracted bytes: the real debug string at `0x80012493`
("`# INT: INTC (%d)...`", Round 239's own finding) and the real `JAL` target at `0x800014e4` resolving to
exactly `0x80007340` (Round 239's own finding) - both matched byte-for-byte on the first try, confirming the
mapping and the extraction pipeline before using it for anything new.

**New static search.** Scanned the entire 80880-byte `KERNEL` blob for the real MIPS `MTC0 $rt, Status(c0_12)`
instruction encoding (`word & 0xFFE0F800 == 0x40806000`, standard public COP0 instruction format, not
transcribed from any BIOS content) - found 44 real occurrences. The overwhelming majority (37 of 44, `rt=$k0`
or `rt=$at`) are `mfc0/AND -28/mtc0` triplets - a real, standard "disable interrupts + force kernel mode"
critical-section-entry pattern (`-28` = `0xFFFFFFE4`, clearing `IE`/`EXL`/`KSU` bits), each paired with a
matching restore - normal kernel scaffolding, not a bring-up write. One (`rt=$k0` at `0x80002870`) is inside
a real exception-handler epilogue immediately before `ERET`. The remaining candidates were individually
disassembled with a small MIPS decoder built for this round and cross-verified via `pcsx2_disassemble`'s
own "perfect" native disassembler against the live session (exact match, word-for-word, including
correctly identifying the `SYNC` instructions this round's own decoder had initially left unclassified).

**The real finding: a genuine `Status.IE=1` bring-up subroutine, at `0x80000840`.**
```
0x80000828: j    ->0x80000880        (adjacent jump-table trampoline slot, unrelated function)
0x80000830: j    ->0x80000840        (jump-table trampoline slot for this function)
0x80000840: lui  v0, 0x0001
0x80000844: mfc0 at, Status
0x80000848: ori  v0, 0x8001
0x8000084c: or   at, v0              # at |= 0x00018001
0x80000850: mtc0 at, Status          # writes IE(bit0)=1, IM7(bit15)=1, EIE(bit16)=1
0x80000854: SYNC
0x80000858: mtc0 zero, Count
0x8000085c: SYNC
0x80000860: jr   ra
```
This ORs in exactly `IE` (bit 0), `IM7` (bit 15), and `EIE` (bit 16) without disturbing any other Status
bits, then resets the Count register and returns - architecturally exactly the kind of one-shot "kernel is
now ready to take interrupts" bring-up call Round 238 hypothesized must exist somewhere. The adjacent
function at `0x80000880` (reached via the sibling trampoline at `0x80000828`) is a companion
"clear IM7, reset Count, preserve Compare" utility - the two look like a matched enable/disable pair for
this specific line, not a random coincidence.

**Confirmed via direct instrumentation: never reached in this project's own trace.** The same host-native
diagnostic harness used throughout Rounds 238-242 (`/tmp/round238_diag/driver.c`, unchanged, real BIOS +
real Tekken Tag Tournament Demo disc, ~160M-instruction budget) tracks every *distinct* EE PC ever visited
in a run (`hist_n`, uncapped below its 4096-slot limit) - the full run visits only **87 distinct addresses**
in total across the entire ~160M instructions. Address `0x80000840` (and its `0x80000828` trampoline) is
not among them. This is a direct, load-bearing measurement, not an inference from a "top-N" display: with
only 87 total distinct PCs ever touched, this project's own boot trace demonstrably never executes this
function at all, at any point, within the tested budget - not during initial bring-up, and not later.

**Static callsite search: not called via any direct JAL/J anywhere in the low kernel.** Scanned the entire
`KERNEL` blob for any `J`/`JAL` instruction whose resolved target is `0x80000828`, `0x80000830`, or
`0x80000840` - found exactly one hit, the trampoline's own `j ->0x80000840` at `0x80000830` (i.e. the stub
itself). No other code anywhere in the 80KB low-kernel blob calls into this function by a direct, static
branch. Combined with the paired trampoline-stub structure (two adjacent 8-byte `j; nop` slots, `0x80000828`
and `0x80000830`), this is architecturally consistent with a real, well-known PS2 convention: a small,
fixed-address table of `j real_target; nop` stubs so other code (or other modules, compiled independently
of the kernel's exact internal layout) can call a stable low address that indirects to wherever the real
implementation currently lives. This means the real caller must reach this function via a **register-
indirect call** (a `JALR` through a computed table-slot address), which a simple immediate-operand grep
cannot find - identifying that caller is scoped as a next step, not resolved this round.

**Live-session check attempted, result inconclusive (not counter-evidence).** Set breakpoints at both
`0x80000840` and `0x80000828` on the live, real, currently-running PCSX2 DebugServer session (same Tekken
Tag Tournament Demo instance used in Rounds 234/241/242) and let it run freely for approximately 2.4
billion further real EE cycles (including through what looked like another VM-reset event, the same
previously-documented quirk from Round 215). Neither breakpoint fired. Unlike Round 242's panic-trap test
(which exhaustively tested a *repeating* condition over billions of cycles, making a non-hit strong
evidence against the path ever being taken), this is a plausible one-shot kernel bring-up call - the live
session was already deep in active, ongoing gameplay when first connected many rounds ago, long past any
real early-boot bring-up sequence, so a non-hit here is fully consistent with "this already ran, correctly,
before this session was ever observed" and is explicitly **not** being read as evidence the function is
unused or wrong. Session breakpoints cleared afterward; no other change made to the live session.

**Standing for task #408.** This is genuine forward progress on the specific open question Round 238 left
unresolved: a real, disassembled, cross-verified candidate for the missing `Status.IE=1` kernel bring-up
write now has a concrete address (`0x80000840`) and a concrete reason this project's own trace never
reaches it (it's called only indirectly, through a jump-table slot whose real caller is not yet identified,
and this project's boot never gets far enough to make that call). No source change this round - this is a
static/live research finding, not yet an implementable fix. **Next step, correctly scoped for a future
round**: identify what real code is supposed to call through the `0x80000828`/`0x80000830` table slots (most
likely via a fixed low-memory function-pointer table whose base address needs locating - a `LUI`/`ORI`/
`ADDIU` sequence elsewhere in the kernel or in a different module computing a table-base-plus-offset address
before a `JALR`, or a live-session data/backtrace trace from inside this function outward to its caller)
and then determine whether this project's own current resting point (`pc=0x8000CCAC` family) is upstream or
downstream of that real call site.
