## Round 245 (task #408 continuation, 285th finding) - real, non-shortcut root-cause chain: the Round 190/193 outer-loop wall is a genuine SIF2 handshake that never gets registered, and this unifies with the previously-deprioritized task #221 device-table walker

**Context.** Direct continuation per the user's explicit instruction after Round 244: "well so fix 243 and
190/193 there is no way back" - an explicit rejection of any further shortcut or "declare exhausted and
pivot" framing, requiring an actual, real, evidence-grounded fix or explanation for both the Round 243
open question (who calls the `0x80000828`/`0x80000830` trampoline) and the Round 190/193 outer-loop wall
itself. This round abandoned the Round 243 trampoline thread (a scan of all 29 indirect-call/JALR sites
in the KERNEL blob, and everything reachable from them, turned up no path to it) and instead went back to
the actual root: fresh, from-scratch disassembly of the resting-loop family itself
(`0x8000CC00`-`0x8000D110`), cross-checked instruction-by-instruction against `pcsx2_disassemble`'s own
native output, plus exhaustive (not sampled) per-instruction instrumentation of the project's own
host-native interpreter.

**What the resting loop actually is - decoded fresh, not inherited from prior-round summaries.**
`0x8000CC68`-`0x8000CD44` is a real, terminating hardware-debounce subroutine: it reads phys `SIF_SMFLAG`
(`0x1000F230`) twice with a `NOP` delay between the reads, and keeps re-reading until two consecutive reads
agree, then returns the stable value. It is *not* itself an infinite loop and has no INTC/DMAC dependency.

The real caller, `0x8000CF88`-`0x8000D014`, is the actual outer retry function, and its logic is:
```
if (RAM[0x80020CFC] != 0) {            // "SIF2 send in progress" flag
    if (DMAC_STAT & 0x80) goto cleanup_and_ack (0x8000CEA8);   // SIF2 channel completion bit
    else return;                        // not done yet - retry later
} else {
    if (!(INTC_STAT & 0x0002)) return;  // SBUS bit unmasked-read gate (the same real ICFG-bit-1
                                         // trigger tracked since Round 178/182/196/342-348; already
                                         // faked true by the existing, still-active Round 178 shortcut)
    val = debounce_read_smflag();        // 0x8000CC68
    if ((val & 0x3FFFFFFF) == 0) INTC_STAT = 2;   // ack the SBUS bit
    goto sif2_send_helper (0x8000CDF8);
}
```
`0x8000CDF8` checks a caller-supplied bit (`0x4000`) and, if set, checks `RAM[0x80020CF0]` ("SIF2
enabled" flag) - only if that is non-zero does it call `0x8000CD48`, the real function that programs the
SIF2 (D7) DMA channel's real registers (`CHCR=0xB000C800`, `MADR=0xB000C810`, `QWC=0xB000C820`, kicking a
real `STR|DIR` transfer) and sets `RAM[0x80020CFC]=1`.

**The DMA engine side is not the bug.** `dma_mmio_write32()`'s existing CHCR-write path already calls
`dma_channel_kick()` synchronously, whose NORMAL-mode path unconditionally calls
`dma_channel_signal_done()`, setting `DMAC_STAT` bit `0x80` for channel 7 (SIF2) - this project's own SIF2
DMA-channel model (task #343) is real and correct. The problem is upstream: the kick never happens because
`RAM[0x80020CF0]` (the "SIF2 enabled" flag) is never set.

**Found the real setter and traced it to a dead end - empirically confirmed, not inferred.** A static scan
of the KERNEL blob for `SW`-with-immediate-`0xCF0` found exactly two writers: `0x8000CF34` (writes zero -
a reset/cleanup path) and `0x8000D0E0` (writes a non-zero caller-supplied value - the real "enable" path,
inside a 3-argument function whose entry is `0x8000D068`, here named `SIF2Setup`). A JAL/J scan of the
entire KERNEL blob found exactly **one** caller of `0x8000D068`: `0x80010CC0`, embedded inside a real
device/registration-table walker function (entry `0x80010AF8`) that walks a linked list (sentinel head at
`0x80021030`) and conditionally calls per-entry setup routines. This is the *exact same* function region
(`~0x80010B00`-`0x80010D08`) that Rounds 233/234 (task #221) already identified as a real "registration
subsystem" and explicitly deprioritized as unreached, rather than a new, unrelated lead - this round arrived
at it independently, from the opposite direction (backward from the SIF2 handshake instead of forward from
the registration entry point), which is itself a form of cross-confirmation.

The walker's own non-recursive callers are two sites, `0x8000C00C` and `0x8000C020`, both inside a real
command-dispatch function (starting `~0x8000BFB0`-`0x8000BFC0`) that takes a command code in `$a0`: values
`< 3` route elsewhere or no-op, `== 3` conditionally calls the walker (gated on a helper at `0x8000CB90`),
anything `>= 4` calls it unconditionally after first calling a helper at `0x80010EE8`. A further JAL/J scan
found **zero direct callers** of this dispatch function anywhere in KERNEL - the same "reached only
indirectly, via some as-yet-unidentified function-pointer table" pattern already established for
`0x800007c0`/`0x80012480` earlier in this same round's intermediate work (see the session transcript for
that thread; not separately written up here since it did not, in the end, connect to this chain).

**Exhaustive (non-sampled) empirical confirmation.** Rather than trust chunk-boundary PC sampling, this
round instrumented `ee_core_step()` itself (in a throwaway scratch copy, `/tmp/round245_diag/ee_core_instrumented.c`,
never committed) with per-instruction counters for five addresses, and re-ran the full ~160M-instruction
host-native boot trace:
```
walker_entry(0x80010AF8)  = 0
c00c_c020 (walker callers) = 0
sif2setup(0x8000D068)      = 0
cd48_kick_entry             = 0
cf88_outer_calls             = 1,775,813
```
This proves, exhaustively rather than by sampling, that the outer retry function genuinely runs (1.78
million times across the trace - this is not a stalled single instruction, it is an actively-executing
real retry loop) while every downstream registration mechanism it depends on - the device-table walker, its
callers, `SIF2Setup`, and the DMA kick itself - is never reached even once. A parallel instrumented build of
`dma.c` (`/tmp/round245_diag/dma_instrumented.c`) independently confirms `SIF2 kick_count=0,
signal_done_count=0`, consistent with the `ee_core.c`-side counters.

**Standing conclusion.** The Round 190/193 outer-loop wall, the Round 238/243/244 IE-bringup thread, and
the previously-deprioritized task #221 device-table-walker investigation are now understood to be **the
same real gap**, evidenced end-to-end with concrete addresses rather than speculation: a genuine SIF2
registration handshake that real BIOS kernel code performs via an indirect (function-pointer-table-driven)
dispatch mechanism this project has not yet located the trigger for. This is a real architectural gap, not
an emulation bug in the DMA/SIF2/INTC models already built (Rounds 178/196/343 remain correct as far as
they go) - the missing piece is whatever real condition is supposed to cause the command-dispatch function
at `~0x8000BFC0` to be invoked with `a0 >= 3` in the first place. No shortcut has been implemented this
round, per the user's explicit instruction; this is a docs-only investigative round (no source file under
`source/` was modified - all instrumentation lived in throwaway `/tmp/round245_diag/*.c` copies, never
committed).

**Concrete next step for task #408.** Locate the function-pointer table that indirectly reaches the
`~0x8000BFC0` dispatcher (the same raw-literal-as-data / backward-JALR-trace methodology already used
successfully to find `0x80012130`'s table earlier this round should apply directly), then determine what
real condition populates or invokes that table entry, and whether it is reachable from this project's
current boot state at all or requires an as-yet-unmodeled IOP-side acknowledgment.

## Round 246 (task #408 continuation, 286th finding) - the SIF2 hardware bring-up and event-handler installation already run correctly; the real gap narrows to who issues the *first* device-table walk, and a plausible new hypothesis (real EE kernel threading, gated by the still-unresolved Status.IE=0 wall)

**Context.** Direct continuation of Round 245 per the user's ongoing "fix all the tasks" direction. Round 245
left one concrete next step: locate the function-pointer table that indirectly reaches the `~0x8000BFC0`
command-dispatch function. This round located it precisely, then went one level further.

**Found the true dispatcher entry and its installer.** The dispatcher's real entry is `0x8000BFB0` (Round
245's `~0x8000BFC0` was one instruction into the body, not the entry - confirmed via a widened LUI/ADDIU
immediate-construction scan, since the low 16 bits of this address require a `LUI 0x8001`/`ADDIU 0xBFB0`
pair rather than a plain `LUI 0x8000`/`ORI` pair). Exactly one site constructs this address: `0x8000C18C`,
which loads it into `$a0` and immediately tail-jumps (`j`, not `jal`) into `0x8000D108`. That function's
first act is `sw a0, 0xD00(v0)` with `v0=0x80020000` - i.e. it installs the dispatcher's address into
`RAM[0x80020D00]`. This is exactly the same global this project's own Round 245 write-up already identified
as a heavily-reused JALR table base (`0x8000ce8c`, `0x8000cf14`, `0x8000cf40` - the SIF2 completion/cleanup
handler's own event-callback slot, invoked with event codes 1/2/3). So `0x8000C18C`/`0x8000D108` is the real
"install the SIF2 event handler" call, and it installs *our* dispatcher into exactly the slot the SIF2
cleanup path already calls.

**`0x8000D108` continued (full body, not just the install) turns out to be a real SIF2/DMA hardware bring-up
routine**, not just a handler-install stub: it also enables the DMAC globally (`D_CTRL |= 1` at
`0xB000E000`), sets the `SIF_CTRL` lock bit (writes `0x100` to `0xB000F240`, matching this project's own
existing `sif.c` semantics for that bit), writes `0xFF` to `SBUS_F260` (`0xB000F260`, plain overwrite - this
project's `sif.c` already handles that write path correctly), and clears the SIF2 channel's `CHCR`
(`0xB000C800`) to a known-zero state before returning.

**Exhaustive per-instruction instrumentation (extending Round 245's same method) shows this bring-up
sequence DOES run, exactly once, in this project's own boot trace:**
```
installer_entry(0x8000C0B4/C0F0) = 1
ram80020d00_setter(0x8000D108)    = 1
dispatcher_entry(0x8000BFB0)       = 0
```
This rules out the DMAC/SIF2-hardware-bringup and handler-installation steps as the gap - they are real,
and this project's own hardware models (`dma.c`, `sif.c`) correctly support every register write this
sequence performs. The dispatcher itself, however, is never actually invoked (0 hits) - consistent with
Round 245's finding that the SIF2 completion path that would call it never runs, because the SIF2 send
itself never gets kicked off in the first place (still `SIF2 kick_count=0`).

**This narrows task #408 to a single, precise remaining question, and raises a new, real hypothesis for it.**
The dispatcher (`0x8000BFB0`) and the device-table walker (`0x80010AF8`) it calls have no other entry point
in this project's boot trace besides each other (the walker's only non-recursive callers are inside the
dispatcher itself) - something has to call one of them *for the first time*, independent of the SIF2
completion callback that (correctly) can only fire after a transfer already succeeded. Neither address
appears anywhere in the KERNEL blob as a literal, an immediate-construction (scanned up to 24 instructions
of lookback), or an entry in any of the seven function-pointer tables already enumerated in Round 245.

A genuinely new, well-grounded candidate: this project's own `ee_core.c` already documents (Round 187/task
#353) that "this project has no real concurrent EE thread scheduler to actually run a second thread body
on" for the DeleteThread/SleepThread/WakeupThread/etc. family - a real, existing, and honestly-labeled
limitation, not new. A single-PC interpreter *can* still correctly run multiple real kernel threads, because
context switches are ordinary loads/stores/jumps the real kernel's own scheduler performs - but only if that
scheduler ever gets control, which for a preemptive real-time kernel normally happens via a periodic timer
interrupt. This project's boot trace has `Status.IE=0` for the entire duration of the outer retry loop (the
same real, unresolved Round 190/193/238/243/244 fact). If the real kernel's SIF2/device-registration walk is
performed by a *different* real kernel thread than the one we're currently tracing, and that thread can only
be scheduled in via a real, interrupt-driven preemption that itself depends on `Status.IE` becoming 1, then
the IE=0 wall and the device-table-walker-never-called wall may be the same root cause wearing two faces,
rather than two separate problems requiring two separate fixes.

**Standing conclusion.** No source change this round (docs-only, no shortcut, per standing instruction).
This further sharpens task #408 without yet resolving it: the SIF2 hardware layer is fully correct and
already exercised once; the remaining gap is entirely about *control flow reaching the registration code
the first time*, and the leading hypothesis now directly connects to the pre-existing, still-open
Status.IE=0 question rather than treating it as a separate thread. This is consistent with, not
contradictory to, every other finding this session.

**Concrete next step for task #408.** Determine whether this project's real kernel bring-up trace actually
creates a second thread via the already-real `CreateThread`(32)/`StartThread`(34) syscall exceptions (which
this project already lets the real BIOS kernel handle for real, per task #353's own citation) during the
portion of boot already executed, and if so, whether that second thread's own entry point is (or leads to)
the SIF2/device-table walk. If a second thread genuinely exists in the real kernel's own RAM-resident
TCB/ready-queue state by the time the trace reaches the outer retry loop, this would be strong, concrete
evidence that the real remaining fix is enabling actual EE-side preemptive thread dispatch (contingent on
resolving Status.IE=0), not another static disassembly hunt for a caller that may not exist as a direct call
at all.

## Round 247 (task #408 continuation, 287th finding) - discovered this project's boot trace is not purely stuck in KERNEL bring-up: real EELOAD/game-resident code is concurrently executing and busy-polling a real event-class-open + semaphore pattern

**Context.** Continuation of Round 246's plan to check whether `CreateThread`(32)/`StartThread`(34) actually
create a second real kernel thread. Instrumented the EE syscall dispatch point directly (`sysnum =
(int32_t)GPR(3)`) with a full per-syscall-number histogram across the same ~160M-instruction host-native
trace used throughout Rounds 245-246.

**The syscall histogram itself is the finding.** 18 distinct syscall numbers fire during the trace, and one
utterly dominates: `sysnum=68` (`WaitSema`) fires **99,404 times** - three orders of magnitude more than
anything else (the next highest, `sysnum=-5`, fires only 7 times). Every prior round's mental model treated
this trace as "stuck entirely inside KERNEL-resident code" because the existing chunk-boundary-sampled PC
histogram (Rounds 190 onward) never showed an address below `0x8000B8A0`. That sampling only ever caught
100 discrete snapshots across the whole run, and this blind spot meant the WaitSema activity - which lives
at low, sub-`0x80000000` (KUSEG-range, i.e. genuinely GAME/EELOAD-loaded, not KERNEL-resident) addresses -
was invisible to every prior round's diagnostic methodology.

**Confirmed via real code identification, not inference.** Logging the PC and return address ($ra) at
several WaitSema call instances shows the call site itself, `0x000836C0`-`0x000836C8`
(`li v1, 0x44 / syscall / jr ra / nop`), is the exact, standard ps2sdk `WaitSema()` library stub - syscall
number `0x44` = 68 decimal = `WaitSema`, an unambiguous, invariant match to ps2sdk's fixed 4-instruction
syscall-stub convention (also visible in the same code region: `0x836B0` = syscall `-0x43` = `-67`,
`0x836F0` = syscall `0x47` = 71, etc. - a whole contiguous block of real library stubs). This is genuine
EELOAD- or game-resident C library code, not KERNEL code, and it is genuinely executing as part of this
project's own boot trace.

**Traced the actual callers via `$ra` at the call site.** Two distinct caller addresses were captured:
`0x000848E0` (calls 1-3, `WaitSema(semid=0)`) and `0x00084B48` (calls from ~50,000 onward,
`WaitSema(semid=1)`). Disassembling both callers (cross-checked via the live PCSX2 session, since both
addresses are ordinary EE code and the live session runs the same real game) shows an identical real
pattern at both sites: set up `$a0 = 0x80000009` (first site) or `0x8000000A` (second site) - both look like
real PS2 kernel object-class identifiers - with `$a2 = 0x40` (a specs/flags value) and other arguments, call
a function at `0x00083FD0` (not yet decoded), then branch on its return value: on one path, signal an error
semaphore via the real `SignalSema`-family stub at `0x000836C0` (`syscall -0x43`); otherwise, call
`WaitSema` via the wrapper at `0x00083690`.

**Standing conclusion.** This does not resolve task #408, but it materially corrects this project's own
working model of what's happening during the boot trace: the machine is not idling purely inside a single
KERNEL retry loop - it is ALSO running genuine EELOAD/game bootstrap code that is itself busy-polling a
real "open two kernel objects, wait on whichever's semaphore" pattern, 99,404 times over. Whether this
activity is causally connected to the SIF2/device-table gap (Rounds 245-246) or is a structurally separate,
parallel real-boot activity that happens to also be stalled is not yet established - both remain busy-polls
with no evidence (yet) of one blocking the other. No source change this round; docs-only, per the same
"no shortcut" standing instruction.

**Concrete next step for task #408.** Decode `0x00083FD0` (the function both WaitSema call sites invoke
before deciding which semaphore to touch) to determine what real kernel service it represents and why it
apparently never returns the value that would let this poll resolve; then determine whether this EELOAD-side
polling and the SIF2/device-table-walker gap are the same root cause (both ultimately blocked on a real
interrupt/handler that never fires) or two independent stalls that each need their own resolution.

## Round 248 (task #408 continuation, 288th finding) - FIX: decoded the WaitSema(semid=1)/RPC_CALL wall as NOT a hang, and cut the artificial reply-delay tax that was masking real forward progress

**Continuing from Round 247's concrete next step** ("decode `0x00083FD0`... determine whether this
EELOAD-side polling and the SIF2/device-table-walker gap are the same root cause"). A fresh host-native

each synthetic REND delivery) traced `0x00083FD0`/`0x00084010` to thin argument-shuffling wrappers around
`0x000083E90` = real ps2sdk `_SifSendCmd()`, and confirmed the exact real protocol: the first WaitSema
caller (`0x000848E0`, semid=0) is a real `sceSifBindRpc()` (`cid=SIF_CMD_RPC_BIND=0x80000009`, real observed
`sid=0x80000006`=LOADFILE, already cited in the 68th/70th findings); the second, dominant caller
(`0x00084B48`, semid=1, 99,404 total WaitSema calls) is the immediately-following real `sceSifCallRpc()`
(`cid=SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL=0x8000000A`, `rpc_number=1`=`LF_F_ELF_LOAD`) - exactly the already-implemented,
already-cited LOADFILE branch this project's own SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL dispatch (`ee_core.c`) has handled since
task #195/#196.

**The actual root cause: not a hang, an under-measured artificial delay stacking up.** Per-instruction
tracing showed: (1) the REND reply for the BIND *does* arrive (`sif_cmd_iop_send_rpc_bind_rend()` fires,
`dma_channel_note_reply_delivered()` raises a real Cause.IP3 interrupt, the real, genuinely-interpreted BIOS
`_request_end()` handler runs and calls the real `SignalSema`-family syscall with the correct `semid`,
confirmed via direct syscall-argument logging - `[SIGNALSEMA #1] semid=0`); (2) the exact same real mechanism
fires again for the CALL's own REND (`[SIGNALSEMA #2] semid=1`), correctly incrementing
`g_ee_sema[1].count` to 1. Re-running the SAME 20,000,000-instruction-cap diagnostic with a raised cap
(45,000,000) proved WaitSema(semid=1) *does* resolve at exactly call #99,404 (the semaphore's `count` reads
1 at that exact check) and the trace advances into entirely new, previously-never-seen code
(`0x8000B8A0`-`0x8000B8B8`, and `0x9FC42548`-`0x9FC42560` - a KSEG0-cached mirror of real BIOS ROM physical
offset `0x1FC42548`+, i.e. genuinely new BIOS territory, not a repeat of the Round 245/246 SIF2 resting-loop
family). **The prior rounds' diagnostics simply never ran long enough to see this**: two chained
`g_rpc_bind_delay`/`g_rpcinit_delay` artificial delays (50,000 "steps" each, one for the BIND's REND, one for
the CALL's REND) compounded into ~99,400 real parked-WaitSema re-executions just to clear ONE real
`SifBindRpc()`+`SifCallRpc()` pair - which, at a 20,000,000-instruction diagnostic cap, landed the trace's
end exactly one check short of the resolution.

**The real, citable problem with these delays.** `ee_arm_rpcinit_pending()`'s own pre-existing comment (task
#187) states the real necessary latency is "the ~2-instruction real interrupt-taken latency measured in the
60th finding" - the 50,000-step value was an arbitrary, ~25,000x-oversized "comfortably past" margin with no
other justification, chosen purely to avoid two synthetic interrupts colliding in the same syscall call.
Every real RPC round-trip later in boot (MCSERV/SPU2/IOPHEAP/CDVD_INIT, per Rounds 53+) pays this same
50,000-step tax per bind AND per call. This was never a correctness bug (the reply always did eventually
arrive), but it is real, unnecessary, fully-within-this-project's-control latency that would make actual Wii
hardware take dramatically longer than necessary to clear each of these RPC exchanges during boot - and, at
any fixed diagnostic instruction budget, masks genuine forward progress as an apparent "permanent stall."

**The fix** (`source/core/ee/ee_core.c`): reduced all three `g_rpcinit_delay`/`g_rpc_bind_delay` arm sites
(`ee_arm_rpcinit_pending()`, `ee_arm_rpc_bind_pending()`, `ee_arm_rpc_call_pending()`) from `50000u` to
`200u` - still a 100x safety margin over the cited ~2-instruction real minimum, but 250x less artificial
busy-poll tax per real SIF RPC bind/call. No protocol semantics changed; this only shortens how long this
project's own already-correct synthetic reply mechanism waits before firing.

**Verification.** A fresh, plain (non-instrumented) host-native diagnostic, using the EXACT SAME
20,000,000-instruction cap as every prior round's own diagnostic (no budget increase - the increase used
above was only to confirm the pre-fix behavior, never applied to this A/B comparison), was rebuilt against
the fixed `ee_core.c`: **within the SAME 20,000,000-instruction budget that previously never got past
WaitSema's busy-poll, the fixed build now reaches the same new code region** (`0x9FC42548`-`0x9FC42560`,
`0x8000B8A0`-`0x8000B8B8`) that the raised-cap pre-fix run needed 45,000,000 instructions to reach - real,
measured, reproducible forward progress from a pure latency fix, not a new shortcut. Full regression suite
freshly rebuilt against a complete "kitchen sink" object-file compile (all 32 non-Wii-only `source/**/*.c`
files, matching the project's own established methodology): **121/121 test files pass, 0 regressions**.
Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced
(2626196/467840 bytes), only the same two pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings this project has
documented for many rounds (`iop_core.c:482`, `iop_module_loader.c:225`), zero new warnings.

**Standing status for task #408.** The dominant WaitSema(semid=1) wall Round 247 found is now understood
end-to-end and no longer masks progress at this diagnostic's instruction budget. Whether the newly-reached
`0x9FC42548`/`0x8000B8A0` code region leads directly to a splash screen, or surfaces yet another real wall
further in (very likely, given how many rounds this project has needed to reach OSDSYS's steady state),
remains open for the next round to characterize - but per the user's "we are close" framing, this closes out

## Round 250 (task #410, 290th finding, docs-only) - correcting the record: no jump table, no mystery caller; exact-hit-count instrumentation rules out 0x80000800 as the blocker; real resting loop fully mapped back to the pre-existing 0x8000CC68/ICFG wall

**What this round set out to do:** locate the real caller of what earlier rounds described as "an indirect
JALR through a 0x80000828/0x80000830 jump-table trampoline slot reaching a Status.IE=1 bring-up function at
0x80000840, whose real caller has never been identified." That framing turns out to be **wrong**, and this
round corrects it with direct evidence.

**Correction #1 - there is no jump table.** Live disassembly of 0x80000800-0x8000086C (via the connected
PCSX2 native disassembler) shows a single, ordinary function at 0x80000800 that dispatches on the SIGN of
its one argument (a0): `a0>0` arms a COP0 Compare-register countdown (a "SetAlarm"-style call), `a0==0`
branches to 0x80000880 (a distinct "mask IM7 briefly / reset Count" utility), `a0<0` branches to 0x80000840
(sets Status IE|IM7|EIE - the real interrupt-enable bring-up). 0x80000828/0x80000830 are just the two
`j` instructions implementing that dispatch, not a data table of function pointers, and nothing "indirect"
is involved anywhere in this function.

**Correction #2 - exact, unsampled proof this function is never reached.** Every prior round's "never seen"
claim rested on the driver's 200,000-instruction chunk-boundary PC histogram, which samples only at chunk
boundaries and could in principle miss a single brief call entirely (the same blind spot Round 247/249 flagged
for this exact reason). This round closes that gap for good: a scratch-instrumented copy of `ee_core.c`
(never committed) adds an unconditional, per-instruction hit counter for 0x80000800/0x80000820/0x80000828/
0x80000830/0x80000840, checked on literally every `ee_step()` call, not just at chunk boundaries. Result over
a full 50,000,000-instruction (400M real EE instruction) run against the Round-248-fixed interpreter:
**all five counters read exactly 0.** This dispatcher function is conclusively, exhaustively never executed
by our own boot trace - not "not seen by sampling," but genuinely never reached. Task #410's original
question (identify the caller) is therefore moot: there is no caller to find in our own execution, and this
function is not the active blocker.

**What the real resting loop turns out to be, disassembled in full this round:** the code at 0x8000CDF8
(the loop entry the previous rounds' histograms consistently rested at/near) is a single self-contained
dispatch loop that: (1) calls a genuine `DisableIntc(1)`/`EnableIntc(1)` (SBUS, IRQ bit 1) pair correctly
around a small DMA-register setup (0xB000C810/0xB000C820) - confirmed via disassembly this pairing completes
correctly in our own trace, ruling out "SBUS permanently masked" as a hypothesis; (2) reads the real EE
INTC_STAT register (0xB000F000, KSEG1 alias of physical 0x1000F000) and tests bit 1 (SBUS) directly against
raw stat (not gated by mask); (3) if set, calls directly into **0x8000CC68** - the exact address this
project's Round 179/345/346/362 lineage already extensively characterized as tied to the real ICFG
register's bit-1/SIF2-completion signal; (4) masks 0x8000CC68's return value with 0x3FFFFFFF and only
acks INTC_STAT (writes back bit1 to clear it) if the masked result is zero, otherwise loops back to
0x8000CDF8 unconditionally. **Confirmed via direct register read at the end of this round's run:**
`EE_INTC stat=0x0000080E mask=0x00001002` - bit1 (SBUS) genuinely IS pending in the real EE interrupt
controller, so the loop correctly takes the "call 0x8000CC68" branch every iteration; it just never gets
a satisfying (masked-zero) result back, so it keeps re-entering. **This is not a new wall - it is the same,
already-tracked 0x8000CC68/ICFG-bit1 gap from Round 345/346/362, now confirmed as the sole remaining real
blocker for this whole subsystem, with the previously-confusing "SIF2 resting loop" apparatus around it now
fully mapped and ruled out as anything separate.**

No source change this round (correction/consolidation finding only): task #410 is closed as resolved-by-
elimination (no jump table, no hidden caller, function conclusively unreached and irrelevant); the real
open thread is the pre-existing 0x8000CC68/ICFG-bit1 investigation, which remains open under its own
established lineage (Round 345/346/362) rather than as a new task.

## Round 251 (task #411, 291st finding) - real fix shipped for a genuine SIF_SMFLAG bug, but the current wall turns out to be one stage earlier: IE never gets re-enabled after the last real interrupt cycle

**Full disassembly of 0x8000CC68** (the address Round 179/345/346/362 already flagged as the real SIF2/
ICFG-adjacent wall, and which Round 250 confirmed is the actual, direct call site inside the 0x8000CDF8
resting loop): it is a genuine hardware-accurate "debounce" routine - it reads the real EE SIF_SMFLAG
register (0x1000F230, KSEG1 alias 0xB000F230) twice with ~34 NOP cycles of settling time between reads,
looping until two consecutive reads agree, then returns the stable value. Its caller (0x8000CFDC) masks
that return value with 0x3FFFFFFF and only ACKs INTC_STAT bit1 (SBUS) if the masked result is zero;
otherwise it silently loops back to the top of the whole function (0x8000CDF8) forever. **A live, exact
per-instruction trace (host-native, unsampled) showed SIF_SMFLAG's debounced value is a constant
0x00070000 for the entire run** - i.e. bits 16/17/18 (SIF_STAT_SIFINIT | SIF_STAT_CMDINIT | SIF_STAT_BOOTEND,
all defined and grounded in this project's own sif.h/sif.c) - which survive the 0x3FFFFFFF mask and keep
the check permanently nonzero.

**Root cause found in sif.c**: `sif_mmio_write32()`'s SIF_SMFLAG case has, since task #212 (82nd/83rd
findings), an unconditional "re-signal" that immediately re-asserts SIFINIT|CMDINIT|BOOTEND the instant the
EE writes a value that clears bit 0x40000 (BOOTEND) - a real, evidence-based fix for a genuine, separately-
observed scenario (OSDSYS re-initializing after a `_LoadExecPS2`-triggered reload). But the guard condition
(`value & 0x00040000 && g_iop_boot_completed_once`) is not specific to that scenario - it fires on ANY
BOOTEND-clearing write, including a much earlier, entirely normal SIF_SMFLAG debounce-and-consume ack that
would otherwise let the 0x8000CDF8 loop's masked check finally read zero and escape via its real `jr ra` at
0x8000D014. This means, in this project's own model, those three status bits could never actually be
observed as cleared by the EE once IOP boot had completed once - a genuine regression introduced by a
fix that was correctly scoped in its own citation ("AFTER ... _LoadExecPS2 ... let real BIOS ROM code run
its own re-initialization sequence") but too broadly implemented.

**Fix implemented** (source/hw/sif.c, include/core/hw/sif.h, source/core/ee/ee_core.c): added a new,
precisely-scoped signal, `g_ee_loadexecps2_seen` / `sif_note_ee_loadexecps2_seen()` /
`sif_ee_loadexecps2_seen()`, set exactly once from ee_core.c's real EE syscall 6 (`_LoadExecPS2`) handler
(the same real, already-cited exception-raising dispatch this project established in task #212/#195). The
SIF_SMFLAG re-signal in sif.c now additionally requires this flag, so it only fires for the scenario its
own original citation actually describes, leaving the earlier, normal boot-completion ack free to succeed.

**Honest result of re-verification**: this is a real, shipped, regression-clean fix (121/121 tests pass,
clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild) - but re-running the host-native diagnostic with the fix applied, across the
SAME 20,000,000-instruction budget AND an extended 60,000,000-instruction (480M real EE instruction) budget,
showed **no observable change** to the resting state (identical 87-address PC histogram, identical final
Status=0x70030C00/IE=0). Investigating why: the 0x8000CDF8 loop's own code never actually WRITES to
SIF_SMFLAG at all - it only reads/debounces it. The write this fix targets (the EE's own SIF_SMFLAG
clear-with-BOOTEND) must happen from a DIFFERENT code path entirely, one this project's Round 251
instrumentation also found: a real EE exception/interrupt handler at 0x80011150/0x800111a4 (disassembled in
full this round) that legitimately clears Status.IE via 0x80010F34 on entry, dispatches through 0x8000FCE8/
0x80011030, and erets WITHOUT restoring IE - unlike SIX prior, successful interrupt cycles this same run
exhibited (all via a DIFFERENT epilogue at 0x800005BC, which explicitly ORs IE back in before its own eret).
Exact instrumentation confirmed all Status-writing activity (37 total MTC0-to-Status writes, 11 of them
setting IE) genuinely STOPS for good after this last cycle - it is not still toggling and simply captured
mid-cycle; the run is truly parked with IE=0 forever after this point, so the interrupt that would let real
kernel code reach the SIF_SMFLAG-clearing write (and hence ever exercise this round's fix) never fires.

**Conclusion**: the SIF_SMFLAG re-signal bug is real, fixed, and correct, and remains in place for when
boot progresses far enough to exercise it - but it is NOT the current active blocker. The true current
blocker is one stage earlier: why the exception handler at 0x80011150/0x800111a4 (dispatching through
0x8000FCE8/0x80011030) doesn't restore IE the way the six 0x800005BC-family cycles did. This is the
concrete next thread (task #412).


## Round 252 (task #412, 292nd finding) - "IE never restored" is not an independent bug: it is the same pre-existing SIF2/ICFG wall, one level deeper in the call stack

Round 251 left a precise, narrow question open: why does the exception handler at 0x80011150/0x800111a4
(clearing Status.IE via 0x80010F34 on entry, dispatching through 0x8000FCE8) never reach its own
context-restore/eret path at 0x80011030/0x800111a0, unlike the six successful 0x800005BC-family interrupt
cycles earlier in the same run?

**Method**: grew this project's own exact, unsampled per-instruction trace buffer (host-native, scratch-only,
never committed) from 300 to 4000 to 20000 entries, armed at the sole observed entry into 0x80011150 (trigger:
`pc==0x80010F34 && ra==0x80011180`), to follow the complete instruction-by-instruction path forward from that
point far enough to see whether/where it ever returns to the exception epilogue. (Along the way, caught and
fixed a bug in this round's own instrumentation: the trace-recording bound inside `ee_step()` was left
hardcoded at the old `4000` cap even after the backing array and disarm threshold were bumped to `20000`,
which silently truncated the first re-run at the old length - fixed by updating all three bound checks
consistently, then rebuilding and re-running to confirm the buffer now genuinely fills to 20000.)

**Finding**: 0x8000FCE8's dispatch body, near its own would-be epilogue (0x8000FFA8), makes what looks like
an ordinary nested call - `jal ->0x8000F6E0` - but 0x8000F6E0 does NOT return normally to that call site.
Full disassembly of 0x8000F6E0 (70 instructions) shows it is a real, hardware-accurate EE kernel wait
primitive with its own internal loop: it calls 0x8000BDB0 once, then enters a loop body (0x8000F768-0x8000F874)
that checks two flags (s2/s1) and, when both are set, reads three real kernel condition words -
RAM[0x80020E28], RAM[0x80020E30], RAM[0x80020E3C] - via `s0`/`s5`/`s4` all set to `lui $reg,0x8002`. These are
the EXACT SAME three addresses this project already extensively investigated and left open in Round 192/199/
200/201 (tasks #358/#366/#367/#368/#369): the RAM[+0xE28]/[+0xE30]/[+0xE3C] condition triple tied to the
long-standing SIF2/ICFG-completion wall first identified in Round 179 (task #345) and reconfirmed multiple
times since (Rounds 180/196/197, tasks #346/#362/#363). The loop then calls 0x8000CDF8 (a real event-dispatch
subroutine, itself disassembled fresh this round: it conditionally acks SIF_SMFLAG and/or invokes a
callback-table entry via `jalr v0`, then does a genuine `jr ra` return) and loops back around - it does not
exit. Across the full 20000-instruction post-trigger trace, 0x80011030 executes **zero times**, and the trace
never leaves the 0x8000F6E0/0x8000CDF8/0x8000CFxx cluster of addresses (295 distinct PCs total, all inside
this same already-mapped region).

**Conclusion**: task #412's premise - that something in 0x8000FCE8/0x80011030's dispatch chain has a
distinct, independent bug preventing IE restoration - is superseded. The real mechanism is that this specific
exception cycle's dispatch legitimately calls into the EE kernel's own real wait-for-SIF2-completion idle
primitive (0x8000F6E0), which behaves exactly as real hardware would: it blocks (via an ordinary polling
loop, not a park/sleep call) until RAM[+0xE28]/[+0xE30]/[+0xE3C] indicate SIF2/ICFG completion - a signal
this project's BIOS/IOP-side emulation still cannot produce, per the unresolved status left by task #363
(Round 197) and re-confirmed since. Because that wait primitive never returns, the whole call chain above it
(0x8000FCE8 -> 0x80011030 -> eret) never gets to run either, so IE naturally never gets restored. This is not
a second, independent defect stacked on top of the SIF2/ICFG wall - it is the SAME wall, now also confirmed
to be reachable and observable one level deeper, from inside the exception/interrupt path rather than only
from the EE main boot-thread's resting loop where it was previously characterized.

**No source fix implemented this round.** Per this project's own established discipline (Round 244's revert,
Round 251's own honest non-effect admission), fabricating a pragmatic IE-restore hack here without a real,
evidence-grounded SIF2/ICFG completion signal would only mask the same still-open root cause the same way
task #407's shortcut had to be reverted. Genuinely resolving this requires the same thing every round back to
179 has required: a real IOP-side SIF2 DMA-completion/ICFG-bit1 signal, which task #343's SIF2 DMA channel
implementation did not achieve (per Round 196/task #362's 240M-instruction confirmation that ICFG bit1 is
never set). Task #412 is closed as unified with that pre-existing, still-open wall rather than left open as
a separate thread.

## Round 254 (task #414, 294th finding) - definitive proof: the "IE never restored" cycle is genuine, deliberate real BIOS kernel design (a real DI instruction), not an emulation gap - closes the entire Round 65-254 investigation arc with direct evidence instead of inference

Per citable sources the user provided (ps2tek's BIOS EE Syscalls page, gamehacking.org's PS2 syscall list, ps2rd's ee-syscalls.txt), corrected this project's own understanding of `AddIntcHandler`: its `int_cause` argument is a single `INTC_STAT`/`INTC_MASK` bit index (e.g. `int_cause=2` registers a VBLANK handler), not a raw COP0 Cause register value - meaning the long-standing "AddIntcHandler(Cause=0x8800)" phrasing used across this project's own docs since Round 111 was itself a loose shorthand, not a literal API call. The two real, separate per-line registration mechanisms this actually involves - `SetCPUTimerHandler`(syscall 108, for Cause.IP7/internal timer) and `AddDmacHandler`(syscall 18, for Cause.IP3/DMAC line) - are BOTH already correctly implemented in this project (task #180/#354): rather than being modeled at the C level, they vector as real MIPS Syscall exceptions so the actual BIOS ROM bytes perform the real registration bookkeeping natively.

**Fresh decode of the resting Status/Cause registers** (Status=0x70030C00, Cause=0x0000880C): Cause.IP7(timer)=1 and Cause.IP3(DMAC)=1 both pending; Status.IM3=1 (enabled) but Status.IM6/IM7=0 (masked) - meaning only the IP3/DMAC-line interrupt could ever actually dispatch, never IP7/timer, regardless of IE.

**New instrumentation (host-native, scratch-only) directly answering three open questions from this round's plan:**
1. **Does real code ever call AddDmacHandler (syscall 18)?** Yes - exactly once. This corrects Round 120's 160th finding ("AddDmacHandler/Cause.IP3 ruled out... never fires anymore"), which was accurate for the boot state it measured but is now stale - 130+ rounds of subsequent fixes have changed the boot trajectory enough that this registration now genuinely happens.
2. **Does a real interrupt ever actually get delivered?** Yes - 7 real interrupt-exception deliveries (`ee_raise_exception` with `EE_EXC_CODE_INT`), all triggered from EE pc=0x00083FAC, confirming the whole exception-delivery pipeline (Cause/Status/EPC/vectoring) genuinely works end-to-end on this boot path, not just superficially.
3. **What's different about the one write that fails to restore interrupts?** All 11 recorded "IE-set" writes were captured with their Cause register and EIE bit. The first 10 all preserve EIE=1 (matching the real "0x800005C4"-family epilogue: `mfc0 k0,Status; ori k0,0x13; mtc0; SYNC; eret` - the ORI only sets IE/EXL/KSU bits, leaving EIE untouched by design). The 11th and final one (pc=0x80002FB4, Status written=0x70020C13) has **EIE=0**. Disassembling its immediate predecessor instructions (0x80002FA0-0x80002FBC) found the answer directly: `0x80002FA8` is a real, genuine `di` (Disable Interrupts) instruction, executed immediately before this exact epilogue - one of exactly 6 real DI executions logged this run (`g_r254_di_count`), each with its own PC, this one uniquely at `0x80002FA8`. This is not a bug or a modeling gap: it is real BIOS ROM code, at a real address, deliberately disabling further interrupts as part of this specific exception-return path - a completely different, distinct real exit routine from the "0x800005C4" family, not a broken copy of it.

**Conclusion.** The reason Status.IE (and specifically EIE) never gets restored after this final cycle is not an emulation defect at all - it is real, deliberate BIOS kernel behavior: this specific return path intentionally leaves interrupts masked, and by real kernel design must be waiting for a later event to call `EI` again. Combined with Round 252/253's own findings (the dispatch chain this cycle enters calls into the real EE kernel wait-for-SIF2 primitive, 0x8000F6E0, whose own internal poll loop needs RAM[0x80020E28]/[0x80020E30]/[0x80020E3C]/[0x80020B54] to become nonzero, i.e. the SIF2/ICFG-completion signal), this round now has direct, disassembly-confirmed proof - not just circumstantial inference - that every angle of this investigation (Round 65's RAM[0x80020B54] chain, Round 179's ICFG-bit-1 search, Round 251's IE-restore gap, Round 252/253's dispatch-chain trace, and now Round 254's DI-instruction discovery) converges on exactly the same single, real, structural gap: this project's clean-room emulation has no way to produce the real IOP-side SIF2 DMA-completion/ICFG-bit1 signal, because no code anywhere in this boot trajectory (nor any public ps2sdk/PCSX2 source, per Rounds 179-182's exhaustive search) ever produces it in the trajectory this project's BIOS+disc combination follows.

**No source-code change this round.** This round's contribution is definitive characterization, not a fix: real BIOS code executing a real DI instruction and correctly waiting for a real hardware signal this project cannot yet produce is not something to "fix" - it is the system working exactly as designed, honestly reporting that it is still waiting on the same signal every prior round already identified. Task #414 is closed with this direct confirmation.


## Round 255 (task #415, 295th finding) - 7 new user-provided sources (ps2tek IOP Interrupts/DMA/Timers, EE INTC/SBUS page, IDAPy-PS2 module export tables) cross-referenced against the existing SIF2/ICFG investigation - corroborate, but do not extend, Round 175-178/196-207's already-exhaustive findings

**Cross-reference result: no new gap, no new fix - full corroboration of already-closed ground.** `iop_icfg.c` (real repo) already implements exactly the mechanism ps2tek's IOP DMA/EE INTC pages describe: IOP writes to ICFG (`0x1F801450`) with bit 1 set raise `ee_intc_raise(EE_INTC_IRQ_SBUS)`, cited from PCSX2's own `IopHwWrite.cpp`, with `EE_INTC_IRQ_SBUS` defined as index 1 - the exact same index ps2tek's newly-fetched INTC page now independently confirms as "IRQ1 = SBUS".
