## Round 269b (task #423, 310th finding, docs-only) - decisive proof: OSDSYS's real main loop is correctly idling, not stuck - it is genuinely waiting for an input/auto-boot stimulus this project's boot trace has never supplied

Direct continuation of Round 269's device-table work, tracing forward from the confirmed-successful `0x80010A08` call (`0x8000F808`-`0x8000F864`) into the code immediately after it, disassembled fresh live from the running BIOS:

```
0x8000f864: jal ->0x8000CF88          ; real per-frame dispatcher (the SBUS/SIF2 wait loop)
0x8000f86c: lw  v0, 0xE4C(s7)         ; s7 = 0x80020000 -> checks RAM[0x80020E4C]
0x8000f870: bnez v0, ->0x8000F768     ; nonzero -> loop back to top of frame
0x8000f874: lw  v0, 0xE28(s0)         ; s0 = 0x80020000 -> checks RAM[0x80020E28]
0x8000f878: bnez v0, ->0x8000F768     ; nonzero -> loop back to top of frame
0x8000f87c: ...                       ; only reached if BOTH flags are zero
0x8000f880: jal ->0x8000F130          ; real further-progress code (unexplored)
0x8000f888: jal ->0x8000BE28          ; real further-progress code (unexplored)
```

Instrumented both branch conditions with exact per-instruction register capture (methodology per Round 250's precedent) across a fresh 36M-instruction run: **`s7` and `s0` are both `0x80020000` on every one of 8 sampled visits, and the fall-through path past both branches (`0x8000F87C`) is reached 0 times** - meaning `RAM[0x80020E4C]` and/or `RAM[0x80020E28]` stay nonzero on every single pass, and `0x8000BE28`/`0x8000F130` (the real menu/further-boot-progress code this project has not yet explored) are never reached even once.

**This is not a bug - it is the real, correctly-modeled OSDSYS idle main loop.** The per-frame dispatcher at `0x8000CF88` (SBUS/SIF2 wait), the two flag checks, and the loop-back to `0x8000F768` together constitute the genuine "sit at the menu/splash screen, wait for something to happen" state real PS2 hardware also enters with no game auto-boot trigger satisfied. Re-confirmed alongside this run: SIO2 write count is 0 (matches Round 267's finding, now at 3x the previous instruction budget) and `dispatch_ncmd()` call count remains 0 (matches Round 269's finding). Taken together, these three independent zero-counts triangulate on the same conclusion: **nothing in this project's boot-flow test harness has ever supplied a pad-input event, a disc-insert/auto-boot signal, or any other real stimulus that would cause OSDSYS to advance past its idle loop** - not because any of those mechanisms are unimplemented (SIO2's real pad protocol has been complete and correctly cited since Round 184/195; CDVD's S-command/N-command protocol has been complete since Round 261) but because the boot-flow driver itself never exercises them.

**Honest conclusion for "implement everything for OSDSYS menu."** The blocking gap this round identifies is not missing kernel/hardware emulation logic - it's that reaching a real menu render or real game auto-boot requires the test harness to simulate a real stimulus (a pad button press, most plausibly) into an already-idling, already-correct loop, which is a different kind of work (test/harness-level, not kernel-emulation-level) from anything else this 269-round investigation has done. This is now a concrete, well-evidenced next thread rather than a guess, and is the natural Round 270 starting point.

## Round 270 (task #423, 311th finding, docs-only) - correction to Round 269b: the two loop-back flags are one-time state, not a repeatedly-gated wait; the real repeatable decision point is inside 0x8000CF88 itself

Write-trapped `RAM[0x80020E4C]` and `RAM[0x80020E28]` (the two fields Round 269b found gate the `0x8000F86C`-`0x8000F878` loop-back) directly in the emulator core to find every real write, across the same 36M-instruction run:

```
[wtrap 0] pc=0x8000F6E0 addr=0x80020E4C val=0x00000024
[wtrap 1] pc=0x8000F2E8 addr=0x80020E28 val=0xA00214B0
[wtrap 2] pc=0x8000F5DC addr=0x80020E28 val=0xA00214C0
```

Both fields are written a small, fixed number of times early (a plain integer `0x24` for the first; two successive KSEG0 pointers, `0xA00214B0` then `0xA00214C0`, both into low EE RAM, for the second) and never written again or cleared to zero for the rest of the run. **This means Round 269b's framing needs correcting**: `0x8000BE28`/`0x8000F130` are not a "next milestone" being blocked on a repeatedly-checked wait condition - they are a genuine one-time OSDSYS root-state bootstrap that has already run once (earlier than this round's 8-sample capture window) and correctly never re-runs, exactly as real hardware would only initialize its root menu state once. Owning this correction explicitly rather than letting the prior round's framing stand uncorrected.

**Where the real repeatable decision actually lives**: the per-frame dispatcher `0x8000CF88` itself, specifically its post-SMFLAG-read branch (already disassembled in Round 265/266: masks the debounced SMFLAG result and branches to `0x8000D008` if relevant bits are "still set" vs. writes an ack to `INTC_STAT` at `0x8000D000` otherwise). That branch, not the `0x8000F86C` pair, is the actual per-frame fork point that would differ based on real user/menu input - it has not yet been traced for which real SMFLAG bit values would send it down the `0x8000D008` path versus the ack path, or what `0x8000D008` itself leads to. That is the concrete, corrected next thread.

## Round 271 (task #423, 312th finding, docs-only) - the real per-frame SMFLAG dispatcher is also confirmed correct and fully resolved; the low-level SIF/SBUS/SMFLAG handshake chain is now exhaustively traced end-to-end with no remaining blocker found in it

Direct continuation of Round 270: disassembled `0x8000CDF8` fresh (the function `0x8000CF88` tail-calls into after a successful SMFLAG debounce-read - confirmed via delay-slot analysis that this is a genuine compiler tail-call, not an anomaly: `0x8000D004`'s `ld ra,0x10(sp)` combined with `0x8000D010`'s `addiu sp,0x20` in the jump's delay slot restores the caller's own frame/return address before jumping, so `0x8000CDF8`'s eventual `jr ra` correctly returns all the way back to `0x8000F864`, not a stack-corrupting bug).

`0x8000CDF8` decodes as the real, generic "dispatch on debounced SMFLAG bits" handler: bit 30 set (with `RAM[0x80020CF0]` also nonzero) re-kicks a SIF0 DMA transfer via `0x8000CD48` and writes `0x40000000` to a real SIF register at phys `0x1000F230`; bit 31 set (with `RAM[0x80020CF0]` zero) reads a value from phys `0xBC0003E4` and dispatches through a real function-pointer callback stored at `RAM[0x80020D00]` (a `jalr` call, `0x8000CE88`) - almost certainly a generic registered-callback slot for menu/event notification, matching this session's earlier finding about `RAM[0x80020B60]`'s handler-table pattern.

**Instrumented and measured which path this project's boot trace actually takes**: captured the raw (undebounced-mask) SMFLAG value at every entry to `0x8000CDF8` across a fresh 36M-instruction run - **all 8 samples read exactly `0x00070000`**, both bit 30 and bit 31 clear on every occurrence. `0x00070000` is precisely the `SIF_STAT_SIFINIT|CMDINIT|BOOTEND` value this project's own `mark_iop_boot_complete()` already writes (real, cited since early in this investigation) - meaning the real kernel dispatcher is correctly recognizing this project's own real boot-completion signal and correctly determining, per real PS2 kernel logic, that neither the SIF0-re-kick nor the callback-dispatch special case applies to it (0 hits on both paths this run). This is not a blocker - it is the dispatcher working exactly as real kernel code should for the SMFLAG value it is actually given.

**Consolidated conclusion across Rounds 269-271**: three independent, increasingly deep points of the OSDSYS per-frame flow have now been directly measured and found correct and fully resolved - the device-table check (`0x80010A08`, returns success), the main-loop state flags (`RAM[0x80020E4C]`/`RAM[0x80020E28]`, one-time-set as designed), and the SMFLAG-bit dispatcher (`0x8000CDF8`, correctly no-ops on this project's real completion value). None of this low-level SIF/SBUS/SMFLAG handshake chain is blocking further progress. Combined with the standing zero-counts re-confirmed across every round this window (SIO2 register writes: 0; `dispatch_ncmd()` calls: 0), the only remaining unexplored lever toward a real menu render or game auto-boot is the harness-level one Round 269b first identified: this project's boot-flow test driver has never simulated a real pad-button-press event or supplied whatever real signal would trigger CD-ROM auto-boot detection. That remains the sole concrete next thread; no further low-level kernel/SIF tracing is indicated until that is tried.

## Round 272 (task #423, 313th finding, REAL FIX SHIPPED + honest negative result) - wired real Wii pad input into the emulated PS2 controller port; tested and falsified the "pad press unblocks OSDSYS" hypothesis

**Experiment first.** Before shipping anything, tested Round 269b-271's remaining hypothesis directly: does simulating a real, continuously-held PS2 Cross (confirm) button from boot start change anything about the traced boot sequence? Used this project's own already-implemented, real host-side pad API (`iop_sio2_pad_connect()`/`iop_sio2_pad_press()`, Round 184/195) in a scratch diagnostic, holding Cross from the very first instruction across a fresh 36M-instruction run. **Result: no measurable difference from the no-press baseline whatsoever** - SIO2 register writes stayed at exactly 0, `dispatch_ncmd()` calls stayed at 0, every previously-captured trace address/value (device-table return, main-loop flags, SMFLAG dispatch value) was byte-identical. This falsifies the hypothesis cleanly: the real kernel code never even attempts to poll the controller port within this instruction budget, so supplying a button state has nothing to act on. The blocker is not "no button was pressed" - it's that the SIO2-polling code itself is never reached.

**Shipped anyway, for a different, real reason.** `source/main.c`'s real boot-flow loop (`run_real_boot_flow()`) scans the real Wii GameCube-style controller every frame (`PAD_ScanPads()`/`PAD_ButtonsHeld()`) but never forwarded that state anywhere - the emulated PS2 controller port has sat permanently unconnected-but-idle (Round 184's cited default) for the entire project. Added `wii_pad_to_ps2_pad()`, a small, explicitly-labeled port-level **design-choice** mapping (not a hardware citation - there is no real "Wii-to-PS2 pad" mapping to cite, since no such pairing ever existed on real hardware) from libogc's real `PAD_BUTTON_*`/`PAD_TRIGGER_*` bits to this project's real, psx-spx-cited `IOP_PAD_BTN_*` digital-pad bits (Wii A/B/X/Y -> PS2 Cross/Circle/Square/Triangle, matching physical ring position; D-pad direct; L/R -> L1/R1; Z -> Select), and calls `iop_sio2_pad_connect()` once plus `iop_sio2_pad_set_buttons()` every frame in the main loop. This makes real Wii Remote/GameCube-controller presses actually reach the emulated PS2 controller-port protocol for the first time - a real, correct, useful feature for actual interactive use once further boot progress is made in a future round, shipped honestly labeled as a design choice rather than a fix for the traced idle-loop (which it measurably is not).

**Verification.** `main.c` remains host-native-untestable by this project's own established, already-documented limitation (`<gccore.h>`/libogc dependency) - real verification is a clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: `make clean && make` succeeded (`pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced, 2623368/468448 bytes), only the two already-known, pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings (`iop_core.c:482`, `iop_module_loader.c:225`), no new warnings. Full host-native regression suite re-run in full: **121/121 test files pass, 0 failures** (one test, `test_ee_syscall_full_audit_sweep.c`, needs slightly more than the runner script's 5-second default subprocess timeout to complete - confirmed pass with 0 failures when run standalone with a longer timeout; pre-existing runner-script limitation, unrelated to this round's change, not a regression).

**Honest scope note.** "Implement the auto-boot trigger" cannot be honestly done this round: this project has now tested the most plausible candidate (real pad input) and found it has zero effect, and has no other real, cited candidate mechanism to point to. Fabricating one now would violate the same no-fabrication discipline this project has held for 272 rounds. The real next step, if this thread is picked back up, is finding what real condition (a different SIF/SBUS signal not yet identified, a real MECHACON disc-presence event, or something else) actually causes the traced kernel code to first poll the controller port or attempt a disc read - not yet known.

## Round 273 (task #423, 314th finding, docs-only, MAJOR CLARIFICATION) - confirmed OSDSYS's real ELF genuinely loads AND executes in the current disc-mounted trace; the "idle loop" traced since Round 265 is proven to be OSDSYS's own post-init code, not separate bootstrap glue; USB is not present in this BIOS's ROMDIR

Prompted by the user pointing at ps2sdk's storage-device documentation (`deepwiki.com/ps2dev/ps2sdk/3.2-storage-devices`) and asking whether USB/memory-card drivers are implemented.

**Real ROMDIR scan (direct read of the real BIOS's own bytes, not fabricated).** Confirmed this project's real SCPH-10000 BIOS ROM contains `SIO2MAN`, `MCMAN`, `MCSERV`, `PADMAN`, `CDVDMAN`, `CDVDFSV` as genuine ROMDIR entries - matching real PS2 hardware. **USB (`USBD`/`USBHDFSD`) is NOT present anywhere in this BIOS's 76-entry ROMDIR** - confirmed via exhaustive listing, not just a targeted lookup. This specific early BIOS revision does not ship USB mass-storage drivers ROM-resident, so USB isn't a real lever for this project's target hardware.

**Bigger discovery: this project already has a full, real, working ELF loader for OSDSYS itself, built around Round 50 (task #195/#196), and it genuinely fires in the current trace.** `sif_loadfile_elf_load()` (`ee_core.c`) is the real, existing machinery: it answers the real LOADFILE SIF RPC (`sid=0x80000006`, `rpc_number=1`=`LF_F_ELF_LOAD`) by reading a real ROMDIR-named ELF directly out of the loaded BIOS image and copying its real `PT_LOAD` segment bytes into EE RAM at the segment's real `p_vaddr`. Instrumented this function directly (exact per-call capture, not sampling) across a fresh, larger-budget run (288,000,000 real EE instructions - the emulator core's actual host-native throughput turns out to be far higher than earlier rounds' budgeting assumed, ~9.7M instr/sec on this hardware, not the ~1.3-1.5M/sec estimate carried since Round 261): **exactly one call happens, at EE instruction ~30,006,788, with `romname="OSDSYS"`, and it succeeds.**

**Confirmed EE PC genuinely reaches and executes OSDSYS's real code**, not just a loaded-but-dead ELF: instrumented every EE PC visit to OSDSYS's real loaded range (`0x00200000`-`0x00480000`, matching the 71st/72nd findings' own citation of the ELF's `p_vaddr`/`memsz`) - **205,915 visits, starting at `0x00200008`, the ELF's own real `e_entry`** (byte-verified independently this round via a small Python MIPS decoder applied directly to the real ROM's OSDSYS payload - not inferred). Disassembled the first 20 real instructions at the entry point directly from the ROM bytes: it is a completely ordinary, unremarkable C-runtime `_start`/crt0 BSS-clear loop (`v0`=BSS start `0x0028D200`, `v1`=BSS end `0x004702B0`, ~1.9MB, a plain `while (v0 < v1) { *v0 = 0; v0 += 16; }` pattern) - not a stuck wait condition, just standard startup work.

**Traced what happens after OSDSYS's own init completes: it calls back into the exact same low-address per-frame dispatcher (`0x8000CF88` region) this project's Rounds 265-271 already spent five rounds characterizing.** The mid-run progress sample (taken well after the LOADFILE call, at real-instruction ~168,000,000) shows EE PC back at `0x8000CCB8`, inside that same dispatcher. **This is a valuable correction, not a contradiction, of Rounds 265-271's work**: those rounds were examining real, genuine, POST-LOAD OSDSYS application behavior all along (OSDSYS's own idle loop genuinely calling a shared low-address kernel service routine each frame), not separate BIOS-resident bootstrap glue as an earlier, looser framing this round initially worried about. Every finding from Rounds 265-271 (device-table check succeeds, main-loop flags are one-time state, SMFLAG dispatch correctly no-ops) stands, now with the added confirmation that it's genuinely OSDSYS's own code exercising that machinery.

**Re-verified Round 272's negative pad-press result under this corrected, much larger observation window.** With OSDSYS now confirmed to get ~258,000,000 real instructions of its own post-init runtime in this same run (far more than the ~6,000,000-instruction window a smaller, earlier-cap test could have given it), and Cross held from boot start the entire time (same `iop_sio2_pad_press()` mechanism as Round 272): **SIO2 register writes remain at exactly 0.** This substantially strengthens, rather than undermines, Round 272's conclusion - it is not an artifact of too short a test window.

**Answering the user's question directly.** The real memory-card/pad/SIO2 modules (`SIO2MAN`/`MCMAN`/`MCSERV`/`PADMAN`) genuinely exist in this project's own BIOS ROM and are real, loadable ROMDIR entries via the exact same `sif_loadfile_elf_load()` machinery that just proved itself working for OSDSYS - but in this run's full 288M-instruction trace, **zero LOADFILE requests were made for any of them** (only the single OSDSYS request). This is not because the machinery is missing - it demonstrably works - but because OSDSYS's own idle-loop code, in the portion of its execution this project's boot trace reaches, never issues the RPC request that would trigger loading them. USB drivers are absent from this BIOS entirely, so they were never going to be the answer regardless.

**Concrete next thread**: now that OSDSYS is confirmed genuinely running (not stuck at entry), the real open question is what specific condition inside OSDSYS's OWN loaded code (not the shared low-address kernel dispatcher, which is already exhaustively traced) would cause it to issue a LOADFILE request for `PADMAN`/`SIO2MAN`/`MCMAN` - this requires disassembling OSDSYS's own ELF code further (now directly readable from the real ROM bytes, same technique used this round for its entry point), not the low kernel addresses this investigation has focused on since Round 265.

## Round 274 (task #423, 315th finding, REAL FIX SHIPPED - major breakthrough) - found and fixed a real bug in this project's own SetupThread (syscall 60) implementation that was silently crashing OSDSYS's own real code on every single boot; unblocks real PADMAN/MCSERV/IOPHEAP/SPU2 RPC activity for the first time in this session's entire investigation

Directly following the user's "disassemble everything until you find the right solution once its done implement it" instruction, continuing from Round 273's confirmation that OSDSYS's real ELF genuinely loads and runs.

**Coverage-mapped OSDSYS's own executed code (not the shared kernel dispatcher).** Instrumented every EE PC visit within OSDSYS's real loaded range with a full address/visit-count map (not just sampling): OSDSYS's crt0 BSS-clear loop runs, its brief post-init sequence executes linearly, calls `FlushCache` (syscall 100, already correctly modeled) via a small trampoline, then calls a substantial real function at `0x00204D68` (544-byte stack frame, real register-save prologue) - which the coverage map showed executing **exactly 2 instructions, ever, across a 336-million-instruction run**, before EE PC permanently resettles in the already-exhaustively-traced low-address kernel dispatcher for the rest of every run tested.

**Root-caused it directly, not by guessing.** Captured the real exception state right after those 2 instructions: `Cause=0x8820` (ExcCode 3, real MIPS AdES - Address Error on Store), `EPC=0x00204D6C` (exactly the second instruction, a real stack-relative register save), `BadVAddr=0x00004FD0`. Captured the function's own `$sp` at entry: **`0x00004FF0`** - a near-zero address, ~20KB into a 32MB address space, nowhere near a sane stack location. Traced this back one level further: `$sp` came from `SetupThread` (syscall 60)'s own return value, captured directly at its real call site (`0x00200064`): **`$a1(stack_base)=0xFFFFFFFF` (-1), `$a2(stack_size)=0x5000` (20480)**.

**Found the real bug, in this project's own code, not PS2 hardware.** This project's syscall-60 handler (Round 171, task #172) computes `sp_top = stack_base + stack_size` as a plain unsigned 32-bit add with no bounds/overflow check. For `stack_base=0xFFFFFFFF`, this overflows: `0xFFFFFFFF + 0x5000 = 0x100004FFF`, truncated to `0x00004FFF`, 16-byte-aligned to `0x00004FF0` - exactly the observed value. OSDSYS's real, unmodified, factory Sony code then genuinely crashes the instant it tries to use this bogus stack - a real, reproducible bug in this project's own emulation of a real kernel API, not any kind of PS2 hardware/architecture gap. No real PS2 console has ever crashed running its own shipped OSDSYS, confirming this had to be an emulation bug, not a genuine hardware wall.

**Fetched real ps2sdk sources to check for a citable, exact meaning of `stack_base=-1`** (`ee/startup/src/crt0.c`, `ee/kernel/include/kernel.h`, psdevwiki's EE Syscalls page): confirmed real ps2sdk-built programs never pass `-1` (their crt0 always passes a real linker-computed `_stack` symbol) - OSDSYS is real, Sony-internal code that predates/differs from the public ps2sdk toolchain, and no public source documents the kernel's exact internal handling of this specific sentinel value. Rather than fabricate an unverified byte-exact Sony behavior, the fix applies the one part that IS certain regardless of interpretation: a correct kernel stack-setup routine must never hand back a pointer produced by silently wrapping around zero. Implemented: when `stack_base == 0xFFFFFFFFu`, substitute a safe, explicitly-derived default (top of this project's own already-modeled 32MB `EE_RAM_SIZE`, minus a conservative safety margin, 16-byte aligned) instead of performing the raw overflow-prone addition - honestly labeled in the code as a principled substitution, not a claimed citation.

**Verified the fix directly, not just "no crash."** A host-native scratch diagnostic with the identical fix applied showed dramatic, real forward progress: `$sp` at the same function entry is now `0x01FF0000` (sane, high, valid RAM); the same 2-instruction death point now continues normally and raises a real, *expected* Syscall exception elsewhere (`Cause` ExcCode 8, not an address error) as OSDSYS's own code goes on to do real work; **EE PC visits to OSDSYS's own range rose from 205,915 to 185,950,767** (a ~900x increase in real OSDSYS code execution) in a smaller instruction budget than before; **OSDSYS's own code-coverage footprint rose from 45 to 1,849 distinct addresses**; and **total real SIF RPC calls dispatched rose from 1 (only the initial OSDSYS load) to 16**, including genuine binds/calls to `SIF_SID_PAD_BIND_ID1_OLD` (`0x8000010F`, real PADMAN, ee/rpc/pad/src/libpad.c-cited) **twice**, `SIF_SID_MCSERV` (`0x80000400`, real memory-card RPC service), `SIF_SID_IOPHEAP` (`0x80000003`), `SIF_SID_SPU2DRV` (`0x80000601`, multiple calls), and six further real `LF_F_MOD_LOAD` (LOADFILE `rpc_number=0`) requests beyond the initial ELF load - directly answering this round's original question: OSDSYS, once it can actually run past this crash, DOES genuinely request the real PADMAN and MCSERV modules the user asked about.

**Verification (mandatory workflow).** New test `tests/test_ee_syscall_setupthread.c` (20 checks): confirms ordinary finite `stack_base`/`stack_size` pairs are computed identically to before (no regression - two independent non-sentinel cases checked), and the new `0xFFFFFFFF` sentinel case produces the safe, 16-byte-aligned, high-RAM default regardless of `stack_size` (two cases), with neither case ever raising a spurious exception (syscall 60 is real, direct-return). All 20 checks pass. Full regression suite: 122/122 test files pass, 0 failures (`test_ee_syscall_full_audit_sweep.c` needs slightly more than the runner script's 5-second default timeout - confirmed independently passing with 0 failures given more time, same known, pre-existing, unrelated runner limitation noted in earlier rounds). Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`.dol` produced (2623448/468448 bytes), only the same two pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings, zero new warnings.

**This is the most significant real fix of this entire multi-hundred-round investigation.** Every prior round back to Round 265 characterized the low-address per-frame kernel dispatcher as "OSDSYS's genuine, correctly-functioning idle loop, waiting for a real stimulus" - that characterization was an honest, evidence-based read of the SYMPTOM, but the actual ROOT CAUSE was a silent crash in this project's own SetupThread emulation, immediately after OSDSYS's own code started running, on every single boot this entire session. The user's specific push to "disassemble everything until you find the right solution" is what surfaced it - static, sampling-based, or higher-level tracing (as used in Rounds 265-273) could not have found this without the exact per-instruction coverage map and register capture this round performed.

## Round 275 (task #423, 316th finding, docs-only) - with the SetupThread crash fixed, OSDSYS now runs 185M+ instructions further and reaches a genuine WaitSema park that real SignalSema activity does not resolve; a new, real, well-evidenced blocker, not fabricated

Direct continuation of Round 274's fix, re-tracing forward to see how far OSDSYS now progresses.

**Honest scope for this round**: this is a new, genuinely tractable, well-evidenced next blocker - not a return to the "no evidence, architecturally out of reach" territory Rounds 265-271 (correctly) concluded before Round 274's fix. ## Round 276 (task #423, 317th finding, REAL FIX SHIPPED) - id 0 was a red herring; found and fixed the real permanently-blocked semaphore (a genuine, previously-unimplemented SIF RPC service, CD_SERVER_NCMD) behind Round 275's WaitSema park

Direct continuation of Round 275's scoped next step: trace the semaphore create/delete lifecycle to find the real blocker.

**Semaphore ID 0 turned out to be a red herring.** Instrumented every real `CreateSema`/`DeleteSema` event for `semid==0` specifically (capped at first 32, then widened to 40, then 400 after each cap turned out to be saturated): found **63 real create/delete pairs for id 0 alone**, all `max_count=1`/`init_count=0`, cleanly completing in tight bursts, the last one finishing at instruction ~30,364,157 - **far before** the sustained park Round 275 measured continuing through instruction 200,000,000. This project's own `WaitSema` trampoline at `0x00210F84` is generic, shared code (a single `addiu v1,68 / syscall / jr ra` stub) reused by every real `WaitSema(semid)` call site in OSDSYS's own ELF, not tied to any one semaphore - so "PC parked at 0x00210F84" alone doesn't identify which semaphore is actually blocked.

**Found the real blocked semaphore via a full table scan.** Added a debug accessor (`ee_core_debug_get_sema_table()`, diagnostic-only, not part of any real emulation path) to dump every one of the real 256-slot `g_ee_sema[]` table's `in_use`/`count`/`wait_threads` fields directly, rather than continuing to guess at a single ID. Result, at the end of a 216,000,000-instruction run: only 3 semaphore slots in use (ids 0, 1, 2) - and **id 2 alone has `wait_threads=185,633,661`**, confirming it, not id 0, is the real, permanently-parked wait.

**Traced id 2's real creator and the real, unimplemented service behind it.** Id 2's creation (return address `0x00213620`) traced back through a generic "build+send SIF RPC call, then create/wait/delete a completion semaphore" dispatcher at `0x00212AA8` (confirmed via direct disassembly of the real ROM bytes: `a0=0x8000000A`, this project's own already-cited `SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL`, `a2=64`, real `RPC_PACKET_SIZE`). This project's own SIF RPC call capture (previously capped at 16 entries - exhausted long before this call ever fired; widened to 64 with an added instruction-count timestamp this round) caught the real call responsible, landing exactly in the park window: **`sid=0x80000595`, `rpc_number=10`, at instruction 30,366,039** - about 300 instructions before id 2's `WaitSema` first parks. `0x80000595` is real, freshly-fetched `CD_SERVER_NCMD` (`ee/rpc/cdvd/src/ncmd.c`, bound by `_CdCheckNCmd()`) - a genuinely different, previously entirely unimplemented real CDVDFSV RPC service from the already-handled `SIF_SID_CDVD_INIT` (`0x80000592`), which only covers the disc-init bind. `rpc_number=10` is real `CD_NCMD_CDDASTREAM` per the same fetched source's `CD_NCMD_CMDS` enum - plausibly OSDSYS probing disc type as part of its real disc-browser startup.

## Round 279 (task #423, 320th finding, REAL FIX SHIPPED) - found and fixed a second, later instance of the same real hardware-signal gap as Round 161's fix: VBLANK masked off exactly where OSDSYS's own code needs it to unblock a real PollSema retry loop

**Confirmed `PollSema` itself is correctly implemented** (non-blocking count-check-and-decrement, real ps2sdk-cited semantics) - the spin is the real CALLER's own retry loop (traced to `0x0020D478`-`0x0020D4A0`, disassembled directly), not an emulation bug in the syscall. Captured the real semaphore ID being polled (`semid=1`) and its live state: `in_use=1, count=0` - never signaled. Since this project's own model has no hardware-driven auto-signal hook (the only code that can ever call `SignalSema`/`iSignalSema` is real EE code executing those exact syscalls), some other real EE code path - most plausibly a real VBLANK-interrupt-driven handler, given `ee_check_vblank()` already raises `EE_INTC_IRQ_VBLANK_START`/`END` every real frame - must be the intended signaler. Direct register capture confirmed the real blocker: **`INTC_MASK=0x00001002`** (SBUS+TIMER3 only) - VBLANK's bits (2/3) not set, so no real VBLANK interrupt exception can ever be taken, even though the hardware signal itself fires every frame. This is the exact same real-hardware-signal-gap category as the existing Round 161 fix (`ee_check_boot_unblock_selfloop`), re-encountered later in OSDSYS's own real control flow.

**Live-experiment-verified before shipping anything.** A scratch diagnostic that force-enables VBLANK at this exact condition dropped the observed `PollSema` call count from **1,885,160 to 2-3** in the same run, and EE PC genuinely moved on to new, real kernel code (a real interrupt-driven dispatch/delay routine around `0x800014E8`, disassembled and confirmed to be a real, ordinary NOP-padded delay loop following a real function call - not itself a bug) it had never reached before. Real, measured forward progress, not merely a changed loop count.

**Shipped, following the exact same fix shape and honesty discipline as the existing Round 161 precedent.** New `ee_check_pollsema_vblank_unblock()`: force-enables ONLY the `VBLANK_START`/`END` mask bits, only once per boot (latched), only at this exact, live-traced condition (`PollSema` call site, with the specific polled semaphore still `count==0`) - not a blanket "always unmask everything" shortcut. **`0x80007340` is not new code - it is the exact generic real BIOS "kernel print-then-freeze panic dispatcher"** this project already identified and extensively documented in Rounds 239/242/244 (see this file's own `ee_core.c` comments near line 780-810), reached there via two different, both-since-reverted interrupt-forcing shortcuts. Live-read the actual format string this call passes, directly from EE RAM at `0x80012493`: `"# INT: INTC (%d).\n"` - a real BIOS diagnostic message meaning "an INTC-level interrupt fired with no handler registered for it," followed by the same real, honest, unconditional freeze loop real hardware itself would enter in this situation (this project's own disassembly confirms the loop truly never exits - not an artifact of the interpreter, a genuine `beq zero,zero` self-branch).

**Root cause: Round 279's fix force-unmasked VBLANK before real code had installed a handler for it.** This project's own `AddIntcHandler` (syscall 16) implementation deliberately vectors as a real MIPS exception rather than faking kernel bookkeeping (task #180 discipline, see the syscall-16 comment block in `ee_core.c`), specifically so that real BIOS-resident kernel code performs its own genuine per-cause handler-table registration. Round 279's shortcut force-set the VBLANK_START/END mask bits at a live-traced `PollSema` spin without checking whether real code had ever reached that registration step - manufacturing an interrupt condition real hardware's own kernel dispatch table cannot service, which is precisely what the `"# INT: INTC (%d)"` panic reports. Since this exact panic dispatcher was already established (Rounds 238/242/244, ~3.3 billion real EE cycles of ordinary gameplay tracing) as a path real hardware essentially never visits during normal operation, Round 279's fix reproduced a synthetic, unearned version of the same known dead end - not genuine forward progress, despite the real, measured drop in `PollSema` call count that made it look like progress at the time.

This restores the honest `PollSema(0x00210F90)` spin (Round 279's own starting point) as the project's real current frontier. Round 161's original, differently-triggered VBLANK-mask fix (a different PC, a different real condition, and one that has since led to genuine measured forward progress across Rounds 275-278) is unaffected and remains shipped - this revert is scoped to Round 279's fix alone.

## Round 284 (task #423 continuation, 325th finding, docs-only investigation) - the real TIM3 interrupt fires 8 times right after thread creation, then goes silent for the rest of the run despite staying unmasked - the timer source itself appears to stop, not the mask

Directly continuing Round 283's own "concrete next thread": whether the real timer interrupt (bit 12 of `INTC_MASK`, real hardware source TIM3 per the EE INTC's standard 16-source layout: 0=GS,1=SBUS,2/3=VBLANK_S/E,4/5=VIF0/1,6/7=VU0/1,8=IPU,9-12=TIM0-3,13=SFIFO,14=VU0WD) actually fires during the `PollSema` spin.

**Instrumented every real INT-class exception (`EE_EXC_CODE_INT`) actually TAKEN** (not merely pending in `INTC_STAT`) from the moment `StartThread(2)` returns onward, capturing the interrupted PC (`EPC`) and instruction count for each. Ran the same corrected (Round-280-reverted) scratch build.

**Result: exactly 8 real interrupts taken, all within a narrow ~18,000-instruction window right after thread creation** (instructions 30364563 through 30382458 - all within roughly 0.01% of the run's total length), every one interrupting the main thread at the identical `EPC=0x00212A84` (consistent with the main thread still looping in the semaphore-pair setup helper's own early code, before it ever reaches the well-characterized `0x0020C3A0` `PollSema` call site). **Then zero further real interrupts for the remaining ~146 million instructions of the run** - effectively the entire `PollSema` spin phase.

**Critically, `INTC_MASK` never changes.** The "Final hardware state" dump at the end of the run still shows `mask=0x00001002` - the exact same value throughout, TIM3's bit still set/unmasked. Since the mask bit remains set the whole time, the absence of further interrupts after the first 8 is not a masking issue - it points at the real TIM3 *hardware timer itself* (its own COUNT/MODE/COMP registers, tracked separately from the INTC mask) no longer reaching its compare threshold and requesting a new interrupt, which would be a genuine, different real hardware layer than anything the last several rounds (279-283) have examined.

**This is a strong new, concrete lead**, and a plausible root cause for the entire chain this investigation has been following since Round 279: if TIM3 is real hardware's actual intended mechanism for periodically re-checking `PollSema`-blocked threads (a real, common RTOS pattern - a periodic timer tick driving scheduler reconsideration), then a gap in this project's own EE Timer (`ee_timers_tick()`, already cited in the per-instruction epilogue) that causes TIM3 to stop generating compare-match events after its first several firings would fully explain both Round 281's "AddIntcHandler never called" and Round 282/283's "thread 2 never runs" findings as downstream symptoms of the same single upstream gap.

**Honest scope of this finding.** This identifies WHEN and WHERE the real interrupt stream stops (TIM3, ~18,000 instructions post-thread-creation) but not yet WHY - that requires reading this project's own live `T3_COUNT`/`T3_MODE`/`T3_COMP` register state across the same window to see whether the counter itself stalls, wraps without re-arming, or whether real code deliberately reconfigures/disables the timer channel partway through (which would be legitimate real behavior this project should not "fix"). No fix shipped this round.

## Round 285 (task #423 continuation, 326th finding, docs-only investigation, CORRECTS Round 284) - T3 was misidentified: the real timer is healthy and hasn't overflowed yet; the 8 observed interrupts were real SBUS/SIF-completion events, not T3

Directly continuing Round 284's own "concrete next thread" - and this round's job, per the user's explicit "let's track down T3 and fix it" - was to determine whether T3 genuinely stalls or is intentionally reconfigured. The honest answer is neither of Round 284's framings: **T3 was never the real source of the 8 observed interrupts, and T3 itself has no bug.**

**Instrumented every real `ee_intc_raise()` call originating from T3's own compare-match/overflow logic** in `ee_timers_tick()`, plus every real MMIO write to T3's `MODE` register. Result: **zero** `ee_intc_raise()` calls from T3 across the entire run - directly disproving Round 284's assumption that the 8 observed `EE_EXC_CODE_INT` events were T3-sourced. T3's `MODE` was written exactly once (at bus-tick 15,416,581, real value `0x0483`: `CLKS=3` (HBLNK-divided), `CUE=1` (counting), `OVF_ENABLE=1`, `CMP_ENABLE=0`, `REPEAT_IRQ=0`, `COMP=0xFFFF` - matching the already-cited Round 87 finding that all four EE timers get armed with `COMP=0xFFFF`, i.e. configured for overflow-only, not compare-match).

**Directly read T3's live register state at several points during a run** (`ee_timers_get_state()`, via the driver's own periodic progress print): `count` grows steadily and correctly - `0x01CA` → `0x06BE` → `0x0BAC` → `0x109B` → ... - confirming T3 is ticking exactly as its `MODE` configures it, with `CUE` staying set and no configuration change. **The real math**: T3 is HBLNK-clocked (divide-by-18,743, real, already-cited NTSC constant) and 16-bit (overflows at count `0xFFFF`+1 = 65,536 HBLNK-divided ticks). That requires **65,536 x 18,743 ≈ 1.229 billion raw EE cycles** (~4.17 real seconds at the real 294.912MHz EE clock) from the moment `CUE` was set to reach its first overflow. Every diagnostic trace this investigation has run so far caps out around 150-190 million EE instructions (a deliberate limit to fit the ~45-second synchronous diagnostic budget) - roughly 6-8x too short to ever reach T3's real overflow point. **T3 has never once overflowed in any trace this investigation has produced - not because of a bug, but because no trace has run long enough in real EE-cycle terms.** There is nothing to fix in T3's own emulation; `ee_timers_tick()`'s CLKS/CUE/OVF_ENABLE/REPEAT semantics are already correctly, honestly implemented per their own extensive existing citation trail.

**The real source of the 8 interrupts Round 284 captured is SBUS** (`EE_INTC` bit 1, real cause: `ee_check_intc_interrupt()`'s `ee_intc_pending()` gate, delivered via `IP2`/`Status.IM2` - both confirmed set the whole run per Round 286's Status snapshots below). Cross-referencing the 8 interrupt instruction numbers against the already-captured real RPC call log (Round 274) shows an exact, tight correlation: the last 4 real RPC calls in this boot sequence (`sid=0x80000592` CDVD_INIT at instr 30363474, `sid=0x80000595` CDVD_NCMD at 30366039, `sid=0x80000400` MCSERV at 30374383 and 30382671) directly bracket all 8 captured interrupts (30364563 through 30382458) - each interrupt pair sits between two consecutive real RPC exchanges. This is real, correct SIF/RPC-completion signaling, not a hardware bug - and it genuinely stops the moment real RPC traffic stops (the last real RPC call completes at instr 30382671, just 213 instructions after the 8th and final captured interrupt).

**Also verified (Round 286 sub-finding, folded in here): EE Status never becomes the blocker.** Captured `cop0[12]` (Status) both at each of the 8 interrupts and via periodic snapshots every 2 million instructions from instruction 2,000,000 through 120,000,000+. Before real code finishes its own boot-time interrupt bring-up (`<30,000,000` instructions), `IE=0/EIE=0` (correctly, real hardware boot-time default). From instruction 32,000,000 onward, Status is **perfectly stable** at `0x70030C11` (`IE=1, EXL=0, ERL=0, EIE=1, IM2=1, IM3=1, IM7=0`) for the entire remainder of the trace - real interrupt delivery machinery stays correctly armed and healthy throughout the whole `PollSema` spin. `IM7=0` (COP0 Count/Compare's own IP7 line) stays masked throughout, which is also consistent and correct - this project's kernel is using the peripheral `T0-T3`/`EE_INTC` path, not the internal COP0 timer, for whatever real periodic mechanism it relies on.

**Net conclusion for this whole investigation arc (Rounds 279-285).** Every interrupt/scheduling mechanism examined so far is confirmed healthy and correctly modeled: `PollSema` (correct), `StartThread`'s synchronous return (correct, real RTOS behavior), `AddIntcHandler` (never called - genuinely absent from this trace, not a project bug), EE Status/interrupt-enable machinery (stays correctly armed), SBUS interrupts (real, correctly tied to RPC completion, correctly cease when RPC traffic ends), and now T3 (correctly ticking, simply hasn't had enough simulated real time to overflow). No further source-level bug has been found in this chain. The honest remaining open question is whether T3's eventual real overflow (~4.2 real seconds in) is genuinely what real hardware relies on to break this specific idle pattern, which this project's tooling cannot yet verify empirically (would require a single trace roughly 7-8x longer than any run performed so far, likely requiring either a raised `TOTAL_CAP` run outside the standard 45-second synchronous diagnostic budget, or new tooling to checkpoint/resume a long run across multiple tool calls).

**Verification.** No source change this round - `ee_timers.c` needed no fix; this was a corrective investigation. No regression suite or Wii rebuild required, matching the established docs-only-round precedent.

**Concrete next thread**: either (a) find a way to run a single diagnostic trace long enough (~150-170 million TOTAL_CAP, likely requiring new checkpoint/resume tooling to survive across multiple 45-second tool calls) to empirically observe whether T3's real overflow is what finally breaks OSDSYS out of the `PollSema` loop, or (b) step back and look for a different, closer real event this project's trace already reaches but hasn't yet interpreted as the intended real unblock signal, since a ~4.2-second real hang before any visible boot progress would be an unusually long, conspicuous real-hardware wait for what is otherwise a very fast-booting BIOS sequence.


## Round 286 (task #423 continuation, 327th finding, docs-only investigation, DECISIVE) - built real checkpoint/resume tooling, confirmed T3's real overflow ALSO hits the same panic-freeze dispatcher - the root blocker is structural, not timing

Directly continuing Round 285's own "concrete next thread" - per the user's explicit "do both to be sure" directive: (a) build real checkpoint/resume tooling to run a single logical trace long enough to reach T3's real overflow, and (b) use it to settle whether that overflow is genuinely what unblocks OSDSYS.

**Built real checkpoint/resume tooling** (`driver_checkpoint.c`, scratch-only, never committed). Technique: compile `-no-pie` and always launch via `setarch $(uname -m) -R` (disables ASLR), which makes the executable's own `.data`/`.bss` segment (bounded by the standard glibc linker symbols `__data_start`/`_end`) and the two big EE/IOP RAM buffers (switched from `memalign()` to a fixed-address `MAP_FIXED` mmap, gated behind a scratch-only `-DR285_CHECKPOINT_FIXED_ADDR` build flag) land at byte-identical virtual addresses across separate process launches of the same binary - empirically verified before relying on it (`addrtest.c`, ran twice under `setarch -R`, identical addresses both times). A checkpoint is then a raw `fwrite` of those three fixed-address byte ranges to a file; resume re-runs the exact same init sequence (which necessarily recreates fresh state at those same fixed addresses) and overwrites it with the checkpoint bytes before continuing. **Verified byte-perfect round-trip fidelity** on a small test (2,000,000 slices, dump, resume, confirmed the "before" state after resume exactly matched the "after" state before dumping: same PC, same instruction count, same INTC/T3 register state) before trusting it for a long run.

**Chained 9 resume calls into one continuous logical trace spanning 1,279,147,211 real EE instructions** - roughly 6.7x further than any prior trace in this entire investigation (previous traces capped around 150-190 million instructions due to the ~45-second synchronous diagnostic budget; this trace spans the equivalent of ~4.34 real seconds of PS2 EE execution at 294.912MHz). Total wall-clock: about 4.5 minutes across 9 tool calls, each individually within budget.

**T3 DID overflow, exactly where the Round 285 math predicted.** At real EE instruction 1,247,147,211 (predicted: ~1,243,924,486 - within 0.3%), T3's `MODE` register flipped from `0x00000483` to `0x00001C03`: `EQUF` (bit 11, compare-match flag) and `OVFF` (bit 12, overflow flag) both set, confirming `count` genuinely passed through `0xFFFF` and wrapped; `OVF_ENABLE` auto-cleared per the real one-shot semantics already correctly implemented in `ee_timers_tick()`. `INTC_STAT` changed from `0x0000080C` to `0x0000180C` (TIMER3's bit, 0x1000, now set) - a real, genuine, correctly-timed overflow interrupt was raised, exactly as designed.

**The result is decisive: EE PC landed at `0x800014F4`, then permanently froze at `0x80001504`** - the EXACT same address range Round 280 already identified as the real BIOS "kernel print-then-freeze" panic dispatcher. Read the interrupted state directly out of the raw checkpoint file bytes (parsing the checkpoint's own embedded headers in Python, independent of any compiled binary, to sidestep a `.data`/`.bss` layout-mismatch snag hit when a recompiled inspector binary's own static layout had shifted): the instructions at `0x800014DC`-`0x800014E4` are byte-identical to Round 280's earlier capture (`lui a0,0x8001; addiu a0,a0,0x2493; jal 0x80007340`), and the string at the resulting address (`0x80012493`, read directly from the checkpointed EE RAM bytes) is, byte-for-byte, **`"# INT: INTC (%d)"`** - the exact same message Round 280 found. A follow-up resume (3,000,000 more slices) confirmed the freeze is permanent: PC stayed in the loop, and `PollSema` total calls stayed frozen at exactly 16,852,294 (unchanged), even though T3's own count kept ticking (irrelevant now - the CPU never leaves the freeze loop again).

**This settles the open question definitively, in the negative.** Round 285 asked whether the earlier interrupt-storm-then-silence pattern was a real hardware wait this project's traces just hadn't been long enough to see through. It was not a wait-and-it-resolves-itself situation: **the genuine, correctly-timed, un-forced T3 overflow interrupt leads to the exact same dead end as Round 279's premature shortcut did.** This proves the real root blocker is structural, not a timing/patience problem: **any interrupt this project's hardware model ever correctly raises - regardless of source or timing - will hit this same "no handler registered" panic, because `AddIntcHandler` is never called by any real code path this project's boot trace reaches (Round 281's finding, now doubly confirmed).** No amount of extending the trace further will change this outcome; the actual fix has to be finding why real code never gets far enough to register a handler in the first place.

**This redirects the investigation back to Round 282/283's still-open thread.** OSDSYS's own second real thread (`CreateThread`/`StartThread`, entry point `0x0020C260`) is the most plausible remaining candidate for containing the real `AddIntcHandler` call this trace has never reached - it's real, in-process code that's never been observed executing (Round 282), and `StartThread` correctly returns synchronously without forcing a switch to it (Round 283, real RTOS behavior). The real next question is a scheduling/dispatch one, not an interrupt-timing one: what real condition would cause the kernel's own scheduler to actually context-switch to thread 2, and can this project's trace ever reach that condition.

**Verification.** No source change this round - `ee_timers.c`/`ee_core.c`'s production code needed no fix; the `-DR285_CHECKPOINT_FIXED_ADDR` mmap changes are scratch-only, gated behind a macro never defined in the real build, and were verified via `grep` to confirm zero occurrences of `R285_CHECKPOINT_FIXED_ADDR` outside `/tmp/round257_diag`. No regression suite or Wii rebuild required, matching the established docs-only-round precedent.

**Concrete next thread**: trace what real condition (if any) this project's boot sequence ever reaches that would cause the kernel's scheduler to dispatch thread 2 - likely requires instrumenting the real thread-ready-queue/dispatch bookkeeping the kernel's own `StartThread` handler already performs (per Round 283's trace through `0x80003040`-`0x800059B8`) to find what data structure records thread 2 as ready, and whether ANY real code path in this project's model ever consults it again.

## Round 287 (task #423 continuation, 328th finding, docs-only investigation, KEY REFRAME) - real ps2sdk source confirms T3/INTC_TIM3 is reserved by the EE kernel itself for its internal Alarm mechanism, installed via InitAlarm() during standard _InitSys() bootstrap - redirects the investigation to the earliest boot stage, not OSDSYS's thread 2

Directly continuing Round 286's own "concrete next thread" - before diving further into thread-2 dispatch mechanics, fetched the real, authoritative ps2sdk `ee/kernel/include/kernel.h` (https://github.com/ps2dev/ps2sdk/blob/master/ee/kernel/include/kernel.h) to check whether this project's existing citations about TIM3/Alarm syscalls (Round 192) connect to the panic dispatcher this investigation keeps hitting.

**Direct quote, real source, not inferred:**
```c
enum {
    INTC_GS, INTC_SBUS, INTC_VBLANK_S, INTC_VBLANK_E,
    INTC_VIF0, INTC_VIF1, INTC_VU0, INTC_VU1, INTC_IPU,
    INTC_TIM0, INTC_TIM1, INTC_TIM2,
    // INTC_TIM3,       // Reserved by the EE kernel for alarms (do not use)
    INTC_SFIFO = 13, INTC_VU0WD
};
...
extern void InitAlarm(void); // Run by _InitSys
```

**This is decisive, sourced context this investigation didn't have before.** T3/`INTC_TIM3` is not an ordinary, program-configurable peripheral timer from real software's point of view - it is explicitly reserved by the real EE kernel itself for its own internal Alarm dispatch mechanism (the same `SetAlarm`/`ReleaseAlarm`/`_SetAlarm`/`_ReleaseAlarm` family this project already vectors as real exceptions, per Round 192's citation). Real hardware's kernel installs a handler for it automatically via `InitAlarm()`, which the same header documents as "Run by `_InitSys`" - i.e. standard C-runtime/kernel bootstrap that runs before ANY real PS2 program's own code, whether a homebrew ELF or Sony's own OSDSYS. This means on real hardware, T3 should essentially NEVER be genuinely "unhandled" - by the time any program's own code (let alone a busy-poll loop deep in OSDSYS) could ever cause a T3 overflow, the kernel's own internal handler has normally been installed for a very long time already, as one of the very first things that happens after power-on.

**This reframes Round 286's finding.** It's not just that "AddIntcHandler is never called by OSDSYS's own late-boot code" (Round 281/282's framing, which pointed at OSDSYS's never-dispatched thread 2) - it's that **the real EE kernel's own foundational bootstrap, which every real PS2 program depends on and which should install T3's handler extremely early (likely within the first few hundred thousand instructions after the IPL hands off, well before OSDSYS's own ELF even loads), appears to never run, or never reach this specific step, anywhere in this project's modeled boot sequence.** Round 281's own zero-AddIntcHandler-calls finding already covered the ENTIRE trace (including its earliest portions), so this isn't a new data point - it's a more precise, better-sourced explanation of what that zero means: the gap is likely at the very foundation of kernel bring-up, not specifically tied to OSDSYS's thread 2 (though thread 2 remains a plausible, still-unverified secondary candidate).

**Honest scope.** This is research, not yet a new live trace - the next step is to go back to the very earliest portion of this project's boot trace (before OSDSYS's ELF loads, within the BIOS/IPL's own bootstrap code this project already has extensively characterized in much earlier rounds) and look for whatever real code corresponds to the kernel's own `_InitSys()`/`InitAlarm()`-equivalent bring-up, to determine whether it's reached at all, and if so, why the resulting `AddIntcHandler` call (or whatever real, lower-level mechanism `InitAlarm()` actually uses) doesn't happen.

**Verification.** No source change this round - research/citation only. No regression suite or Wii rebuild required, matching the established docs-only-round precedent.

**Concrete next thread**: trace the earliest portion of this project's boot sequence (the BIOS/IPL bootstrap stage, well before OSDSYS's own ELF loads) for evidence of real kernel-level bring-up code that should install T3's internal alarm handler - check whether this project's trace ever reaches that code, and if so, disassemble exactly what it does and why no `AddIntcHandler`-class registration results. If that earliest-stage code is confirmed present and correctly executing, the investigation returns to Round 282/283's OSDSYS-thread-2 angle as the remaining candidate; if it's absent or diverges, that earliest gap becomes the new primary target - a different, more foundational fix than anything examined in Rounds 279-286.

## Round 289: DECISIVE — full instrumented trace from fresh boot through T3 overflow (1.279B instructions) confirms AddIntcHandler is NEVER called; the "Initialize INTC" loop is not an initialization loop at all

**Context.** Round 288 ended with an open question: does the "Initialize INTC" routine at `0x8000AED0` (confirmed in Round 288 to genuinely execute) lead into a loop that eventually calls the real `AddIntcHandler` syscall, or does it terminate without ever registering a handler? Round 288's own coverage-bitmap instrumentation (`g_r288_cov[]`) had a bug at the time of writing (see below) that made its "first hit" timing report unreliable, so this question was left explicitly open as the "concrete next thread."

**Bug found and fixed before this round's real analysis.** The `g_r287_aed0_instr` "first hit" instrumentation had a dangling-`if` bug: `if (st->pc == 0x8000AED0u) g_r287_visit_aed0++; if (g_r287_visit_aed0 == 1) g_r287_aed0_instr = st->instructions_executed;` — the second `if` was unguarded by the PC check (missing braces) and ran every single instruction, continuously overwriting the "first hit" timestamp with the current instruction count for the entire remainder of any run. This explained why every previous report showed "first hit" exactly equal to the run's own final instruction count regardless of run length. Fixed by adding braces around both statements at both of the two call sites in `/tmp/round257_diag/source_i/core/ee/ee_core.c` (scratch copy only — this instrumentation bug never existed in the real repo, which contains no `R287`/`R288` scratch-only symbols; confirmed via `grep` showing zero occurrences in `source/`). Verified the fix with a small bisection run: corrected "first hit" now reads `instr=15,414,644`, genuinely earlier than the run's own length, unlike the broken pre-fix behavior which always equaled the endpoint.

**Cross-check: this timestamp lines up almost exactly with T3's own MODE-register configuration.** Round 285 independently found (via direct `ee_intc_raise()` instrumentation) that T3's `MODE` register gets written with `CUE=1, OVF_ENABLE=1` at real instruction tick 15,416,581 — only ~1,937 instructions after the corrected "Initialize INTC" first-hit timestamp of 15,414,644. These two events are, for practical purposes, simultaneous. This is strong independent corroboration that `0x8000AED0` really is the authentic kernel INTC/Timer bring-up routine (consistent with Round 287's citation of real ps2sdk `kernel.h`, which documents `InitAlarm()` — called from `_InitSys()` — as the mechanism that reserves `INTC_TIM3` for the kernel's own alarm system): both the T3 hardware configuration and the "Initialize INTC" debug print happen at essentially the same moment in the boot sequence, exactly where real kernel bring-up would be expected to sit.

**Method: chained checkpoint/resume runs with corrected instrumentation, from a fresh boot start, to a full 1.279 billion instructions.** Using the Round 286 checkpoint/resume tooling (`driver_checkpoint.c`, rebuilt as `driver_ckpt6` with the dangling-if fix plus a new lightweight coverage bitmap `g_r288_cov[]` covering the full EE kernel address range `0x80000000`-`0x80030000`), ran a single continuous trace in ~20,000,000-slice increments, checkpointing and resuming between each increment (each resumed run's `[before]` state exactly matches the prior run's `[after]` state, confirming checkpoint fidelity held across the whole chain). Findings at each stage:

- **Instr ~79,000,000** (first checked at this point): kernel-range coverage = 2,974 distinct addresses visited, highest address `0x80011F44`. `AddIntcHandler`/`RemoveIntcHandler` count = 0.
- **Instr 316,032,153 / 473,840,372 / 631,648,591 / 789,456,810 / 947,265,030 / 1,105,073,249** (six further checkpoints, each ~157-158M instructions apart): kernel-range coverage completely unchanged at 2,974 distinct addresses, highest still exactly `0x80011F44`, at every single one of these six checkpoints. `AddIntcHandler` count = 0 throughout. EE PC at each of these checkpoints is in the `0x0020xxxx` range (OSDSYS's own loaded userspace ELF code, matching already-known hot-loop addresses from Round 279/280's PollSema-spin investigation) — **not** in kernel range at all.

**Conclusion — this closes out the open question from Round 288 decisively and negatively.** Across a single continuous, checkpoint-verified trace spanning the genuine kernel INTC/Timer bring-up (`Initialize INTC`, first executed at instr ~15.4M), the entirety of OSDSYS's settled idle/polling loop (spanning from ~79M through beyond 1.1 billion instructions, over 1 billion instructions of real elapsed execution), and T3's real hardware-accurate overflow interrupt and resulting panic-freeze (~1.263B), the real `AddIntcHandler` syscall is **never called, not once**. The "Initialize INTC" routine at `0x8000AED0` is not an "initialization loop" in the sense Round 288 hypothesized — it executes once, touches a small, fixed, bounded set of kernel-range addresses (2,974 distinct addresses, capped at `0x80011F44`), and then permanently hands control back to OSDSYS's own userspace code, which never re-enters kernel code again except involuntarily via exception/interrupt dispatch. This rules out the "just needs to run longer" hypothesis definitively: this is not a timing/patience problem, it is a structural gap — somewhere in the boot sequence, real hardware must reach a code path that installs at least one real interrupt handler (almost certainly via a genuine IOP module load / RPC sequence this port's boot trace never triggers), and the current trace never reaches that path no matter how long it runs.

**Concrete next thread.** Since the gap is structural rather than temporal, further "run it longer" checkpoint work is very unlikely to help. The next productive direction is to investigate what real module-load/RPC activity (IOP-side driver loading, e.g. real `SIFLOADFILE`/`EELOAD`/`LOADMODULE`-family syscalls or their SIF-RPC IOP-side equivalents already partially explored in Round 273-274) would normally occur between kernel bring-up and OSDSYS's idle loop settling, and whether this port's boot trace is skipping or short-circuiting that stage — since on real hardware, IRX driver modules (e.g. `INTCMAN`, `SIFMAN`, `SIFCMD`, pad/mc drivers) are exactly the kind of code that would call `AddIntcHandler` for their own device interrupts, and none of that module-loading activity has been directly confirmed to occur in this trace to date.

The same page also documents syscall `0x73`/115, `SetVSyncFlag(int* vsync_occurred, u64* csr_stat_on_vsync)`, which "sets two kernel pointers used in the DEFAULT INTC interrupt handler when a VSYNC interrupt has occurred" — a real, alternate, handler-free notification pattern (poll a flag the kernel's own always-resident default handler sets) that also doesn't require AddIntcHandler. **Confirmed this project already implements `_EnableIntc`(20)/`_DisableIntc`(21) correctly** (Round 188, task #354, pre-existing production code, unchanged this round): both syscalls directly set/clear the real end-state bit in `ee_intc_state_t.mask`, exactly matching the ps2tek-documented real signature and semantics. `SetVSyncFlag`(115) is handled via this project's established real-exception-vectoring convention (grouped with syscalls 107-123, Round 193) — deliberately NOT modeled in software, letting the real, already-resident BIOS kernel code run instead, consistent with the project's own "don't fabricate unverified kernel bookkeeping" discipline.

**New instrumentation, same rigor as Round 289's checkpoint methodology.** Added scratch-only counters (`g_r292_enableintc_count`/`g_r292_disableintc_count`, logging each `cause` argument, plus `g_r292_setvsyncflag_count` for syscall 115's exception-raise hits) at the exact real call sites, then re-ran a single continuous checkpointed trace from a fresh boot through 1,279,147,211 instructions (the identical endpoint as Round 289's decisive trace, chained in ~20,000,000-slice increments, checkpoint-fidelity-verified at every stage — every intermediate `ee_pc`/`ee_instr` value exactly reproduced Round 289's own historical checkpoints, confirming this rebuild is faithful).

**Result: both alternate mechanisms are equally never exercised.** `_EnableIntc` calls: 0. `_DisableIntc` calls: 0. `SetVSyncFlag`(115) exception-raise hits: 0. All three counters stayed at zero through kernel INTC/Timer bring-up, the full OSDSYS idle-loop plateau, T3's real overflow interrupt (confirmed again at instr 1,263,147,211, `INTC` stat flipping `0x0000080C`->`0x0000180C`, landing in the already-documented panic dispatcher), and the resulting freeze loop. `INTC_MASK` itself was independently confirmed unchanged (`0x00001002`) at every single checkpoint across the entire trace, consistent with all three enabling mechanisms genuinely never firing (not merely under-instrumented).

**This is the strongest form of Round 289's finding yet.** It is not simply that `AddIntcHandler` specifically is never called — of the three real, independently-documented ps2sdk/BIOS mechanisms by which a program could ever cause VBLANK's `INTC_MASK` bit to become set (custom handler registration via `AddIntcHandler`, direct mask-bit enable via `_EnableIntc`, or the kernel-default-handler-plus-polled-flag pattern via `SetVSyncFlag`), none are ever reached by any code path in this project's current boot trace. This rules out the specific concern that Round 289's narrower instrumentation might have been answering the wrong question, and reinforces Round 291's synthesis (the blocked `semid=1` PollSema spin cannot resolve because nothing ever arms VBLANK through any real channel) on firmer ground.

## Round 294: checked the real "EEPROM read path" the user asked about directly - it's not a raw memory read at all, it's the real CDVD S-command config protocol (OpenConfig/ReadConfig/CloseConfig), which this project already modeled and verified working in Round 261; the actual gap is that OSDSYS's own EE-side code never issues the RPC call that would use it

**Motivation.** The user shared two more real sources - Woon Yung/sp193's "Initializing the PS2/PSX" page (the original source behind Round 293's ps2homebrew write-up) and ps2dev/ps2sdk's real `osd_config.h` - and asked directly: "Check and maybe fix if possible the eeprom read path if needed." Round 293 had left this as the open next thread: OSDSYS never reaches `SetOsdConfigParam`, and the natural next question is whether the real EEPROM/config read that's supposed to happen just before it is modeled at all.

**First correction: "EEPROM read" is not a raw memory read on real hardware.** The Google Sites page's own real code sample, FMCB's `EnableHDDBooting()`, shows the actual mechanism:
```c
do{ sceCdOpenConfig(0, 0, 1, &OpResult); }while(OpResult&9);
do{ result=sceCdReadConfig(OSDConfigBuffer, &OpResult); }while(OpResult&9 || result==0);
do{ result=sceCdCloseConfig(&OpResult); }while(OpResult&9 || result==0);
```
These three calls are real CDVD S-commands, independently confirmed on ps2tek's own dedicated `SCMD.html` page: `40h OpenConfig` ("Dobiestation returns zero"), `41h ReadConfig` ("Output is four 32bit words"), `43h CloseConfig`. So "the EEPROM read path" on real hardware is a CD/DVD-controller protocol exchange (EE calls into IOP-resident EECONF/CDVDMAN code, which drives the SCOMMAND/SDATAIN/SDATAOUT register triplet), not a memory-mapped EEPROM access.

**Checked whether this project already models that protocol - it does, and it was already verified working two investigation arcs ago.** `include/core/hw/iop_cdvd.h`/`source/hw/iop_cdvd.c` (Round 261, task #422) already implement `SCMD_OPENCONFIG`/`SCMD_READCONFIG`/`SCMD_CLOSECONFIG` via `dispatch_scmd()`, built from this project's own fresh disassembly of the real, mounted SCPH-10000 BIOS (the real `sceCdSCmd()`-equivalent at IOP `0x0010BB30-0x0010BC7C`) cross-checked against both ps2tek's SCMD page and the user-provided real 2003 `EECONF.C` reimplementation. Round 261's own measurement already confirmed this works: CDVD register reads collapsed from Round 260's 9,993,281 (the S-command block spinning unresolved) down to 55, "the real EECONF config protocol now resolves almost instantly instead of spinning" - this is the IOP-resident `EECONF` module's own internal startup self-check (part of the real IOPBTCONF module bring-up sequence, confirmed all 29/29 modules load in Round 290), running automatically at IOP boot regardless of what EE-side OSDSYS code does later. `ReadConfig`'s 16-byte result is honestly zero-filled (no real config content is modeled, only the real byte count, per the header's own documented scope) - real config *values* were never claimed to be modeled, only the real *protocol*, which is what actually unblocks a real busy-wait/drain loop from spinning forever.

**Checked the second, separate question: does EE-side OSDSYS code ever independently call `sceCdReadConfig()` itself (an EE-to-IOP RPC, not the IOP-internal EECONF self-check above)?** Re-ran the same checkpointed boot trace fresh this round (cold boot, real SCPH-10000 BIOS + real Tekken Tag Tournament disc, 20,000,000 slices / 158,223,934 real EE instructions) and dumped the full, per-call real SIF RPC log (`g_r291_rpc_sid[]`/`g_r291_rpc_num[]`, Round 291's own instrumentation, unmodified). This project's own `sif.h` (cross-checked directly, not assumed) only defines real, cited SIF service IDs for these two CDVD entry points - there is no third, config-specific RPC call anywhere in the trace, and none was expected to exist separately since `sceCdReadConfig()`'s real IOP-side handler is the same EECONF/CDVDMAN code family already reached via `SIF_SID_CDVD_NCMD`.

**Conclusion: no bug found, no fix warranted.** The real "EEPROM read path" - correctly understood as the CDVD S-command config protocol, not a raw memory read - is already modeled from real, cited, disassembly-confirmed semantics, and was already independently verified to work correctly (Round 261). Fabricating a synthetic EE-side call to `sceCdReadConfig()` to "unstick" this would mean inventing unverified OSDSYS behavior this project has explicitly avoided for 294 rounds now - not a real fix.

**Net result: this round narrows, rather than extends, the list of untested hypotheses.** "Does this project model real OSD/EEPROM configuration I/O" (Round 293's stated next thread) is now answered: yes, correctly, at the IOP level, and it isn't the blocker. The open question remains exactly what Round 291 originally framed it as (now understood to sit even earlier in the sequence than Round 291 assumed, per Round 293): what real EE-side userspace code path OSDSYS is supposed to take past its current resting point, and why this trace never takes it.
