Implemented a checkpoint/resume design that restores the flat `[__data_start,_end)` block as before, then explicitly re-points all five of these fields at the *current* process's own freshly-allocated buffers (remembered before the restore) rather than leaving them at the old process's stale values, and re-invokes the two public `_bind_` functions to keep the cached copies consistent. **All five of these are real, confirmed bugs in the checkpoint design and are fixed as far as they go** - but the same-binary resume segfault still occurs, identically, via a `SIGSEGV` handler confirming the fault is still on a genuinely unmapped address, still occurring specifically *during* the very first `read_block_into()` call (the raw `[__data_start,_end)` restore itself - confirmed via `fprintf`-bisected debug tracing that the crash happens before that call even returns, not afterward when a stale pointer might be dereferenced). **Ruled out one more theory this round**: a matched minimal reproduction (a bare, unrelated ~4.7MB static global array, filled via `fopen`/`fwrite`/`fopen`/`fread`/`memcpy` in exactly the same sequence, with no emulator code involved at all) completes with **zero issues** on this same machine/toolchain - conclusively proving this is not a generic sandbox/glibc/fread limitation, but something specific to the real emulator's own accumulated global state, still not identified.

**Net assessment**: no real repository source code was changed this round (`git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm the working tree is unchanged - all driver files were scratch-only and never committed). Real, concrete progress was made on two fronts: a genuinely faster tracing driver (usable in future rounds for ~40-65% more headroom per process) and five real, now-fixed bugs in the checkpoint tool's pointer-handling design (a correct foundation for whoever continues this) - but the core crash remains unsolved, its true mechanism still unknown after two full rounds of targeted investigation. Given the scale of effort now invested (two rounds, multiple independent hypotheses tested and disproven: GOT/ASLR corruption, `fread()` self-corruption, stale embedded pointers) without a resolution, and per this project's own long-standing discipline about disproportionate effort on scratch-only tooling, **this investigation is being set aside again** - not because it's unimportant, but because it has now consumed enough dedicated effort across two rounds to qualify as exactly the kind of sink this project's discipline exists to prevent. The lean driver (without checkpoint/resume, just plain `run` mode) remains a real, usable improvement and will be the default going forward for any single-process trace.

Left as the concrete next investigative target for Round 311: display-setup activity has still not been observed in ~400,000,000 real EE instructions of tracing. The gap to the splash screen appears to be substantially larger than what a single sandboxed process (even the faster lean driver) can reach - the realistic paths forward are either finding a way to control a real, resettable live PCSX2 session in a future session (may require the user to have PCSX2 open and visible, or a different access route), or accepting that this specific boot-trace investigation has reached the limit of what this sandbox environment can practically explore further, and shifting focus to other, more tractable subsystems (GS rasterizer work, VU0/VU1, or other ROADMAP.md items that don't require multi-hundred-million-instruction cold-boot budgets).

Live PCSX2 session not touched this round beyond the read-only `pcsx2_status` check described above.

## Round 311: gained real live-PCSX2 control, performed a genuine cold reset, and obtained a real-hardware calibration bound for the splash-screen milestone

Direct continuation of "everything needed for the splash screen" following the user's "yes take control of the pc" / "if you cant reach the emulator which is open search other ways" direction after Round 310 found live PCSX2 unreachable via the app-name-based `request_access` resolver.

**Found the real access path**: the visible PCSX2 window is titled by its currently-loaded game ("Tekken Tag Tournament [Demo]"), not "PCSX2", which is why every plausible display-name guess failed. A screenshot (via a generically-granted `Explorer` access first, just to see the desktop) confirmed the window was genuinely PCSX2 (System/Settings/View/Tools/Debug/Help menu bar). The actual resolvable app name turned out to be the real executable basename, **`pcsx2-qt.exe`**, found by guessing likely real PCSX2 release binary names rather than display names - `request_access` granted it at full tier immediately once the right name was used.

**Performed a genuine, clean cold reset via the real UI** (`System > Reset`), confirmed unambiguously via `pcsx2_status`: `EE PC: 0xBFC00000` (the real EE reset vector - the exact address this project's own Round 5 finding, `docs/STATUS.md`'s oldest entry, was built around) and `Cycles: 0`. This is the first time this project has had a *live, controllable, genuinely-reset* real PS2 session to compare against, rather than an already-billions-of-cycles-deep session inherited from elsewhere.

**Set watchpoints on GS_PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 (0x12000000/0x12000070/0x12000080) and continued, hoping the debugger would auto-break the instant any got written.** This surfaced two real, now-documented limitations of the third-party `pcsx2-mcp` DebugServer bridge itself (external tooling, not this project's own code): (1) the watchpoints did repeatedly and reliably pause execution back at the same address (`0x0050b420`, a generic MMIO-write helper, most likely hit as part of an early register-sweep/clear pass, given the values observed there were 0) - but `pcsx2_list_watchpoints` always reported `0 hits` regardless, a broken hit-counter in the bridge; (2) `pcsx2_gs_registers` - the bridge's own dedicated tool for reading exactly these registers - continued reporting all-zero values even at a point (~2 billion cycles) where a screenshot conclusively showed the game already rendering full, correct, working 3D gameplay, proving this read path does not reliably reflect PCSX2's actual internal GS register state over an extended live session. Both are genuine bugs/limitations in the external MCP bridge, not in this project's own code - noted here for any future round that reaches for this tool again.

**Worked around both limitations with the one source of ground truth that can't lie: the screen itself.** Cleared the (unreliable) watchpoints, let execution free-run, and periodically checked `pcsx2_status` (for cycle count) alongside screenshots (for actual visual state). Confirmed the emulator had been running heavily throttled (~13,000,000 cycles/sec, roughly 4% of the real 294,912,000 Hz EE clock) while any DebugServer step/pause/watchpoint activity was in play - a well-known category of side effect (debug hooks force the interpreter core instead of the fast recompiler) - resolving once watchpoints were cleared and the session was allowed to free-run normally. **Bisected via alternating `pcsx2_status`/screenshot checks: real GS registers still read zero and no watchpoint fired by 354,002,731 cycles; a screenshot taken shortly after a 708,818,359-cycle check showed the real Tekken Tag Tournament title/splash screen fully rendered** (logo, character portraits, fire background - an unambiguous, real splash screen, not a placeholder). By 1,695,532,173-2,082,044,449 cycles the game had progressed into normal, fully-rendered attract-mode 3D gameplay (walking character model, textured city-street background) - a clean, healthy, un-stuck live session.

**Net assessment - a real, useful calibration bound, with an honest caveat on its precision**: real hardware (as faithfully emulated by real PCSX2) reaches its splash/title screen somewhere in the range of roughly 354,000,000-709,000,000 EE cycles after a genuine cold reset, for this specific game (Tekken Tag Tournament Demo) and its own real BIOS/boot path. This is the *same order of magnitude* as this project's own current scratch-trace reach (~400,000,000 instructions, Round 310), which is a meaningfully different picture than the "possibly wildly short" concern Round 310 raised - it suggests this project's own trace may genuinely be in a plausible ballpark of what's needed, lending real support to "more tracing budget is the right lever" (fix checkpoint/resume, or keep speeding up the interpreter) rather than "there must be a missing/broken feature blocking progress entirely." The caveat: this is not a precise, apples-to-apples number - different game, different BIOS revision/boot path, real EE's dual-issue superscalar execution vs. this project's own scalar per-instruction interpreter, and the throttled/uneven debug-session cycle rate all mean this is an order-of-magnitude comparison, not a strict bound.

**No real repository source code changes were made this round** (`git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm the working tree is unchanged apart from this documentation update) - this was pure investigation/calibration, so the regression suite and Wii rebuild were not re-run. The live PCSX2 session was left clean: all breakpoints/watchpoints cleared (`pcsx2_clear_all_breakpoints`), execution running freely (`Paused: false`), in normal, healthy attract-mode gameplay - not paused, not stuck.

Left as the concrete next investigative target: given the calibration data now supports "more tracing budget" as a plausible, non-wasted direction, Round 312 should resume Task #40's throughput options with renewed confidence - either take another, more careful pass at the checkpoint/resume segfault (perhaps with `strace`/`ltrace`-style tooling if available, since two rounds of pointer-focused hypotheses have now been exhausted without success), or continue hardening/using the Round 310 lean driver for straight `run`-mode progress at the highest achievable slice budget per process.

## Round 312: FIXED the checkpoint/resume segfault (two real, confirmed root causes, three rounds in the making) and used it to push the scratch trace to unprecedented depth (2.64 billion instructions), reaching a new, precisely-identified resting point

Direct continuation of "do whats better" following Round 311's calibration data. Picked Task #42's option (a) - another pass at the checkpoint/resume segfault - this time reaching for a real backtrace instead of more hypothesis-guessing.

**Found `strace`, `addr2line`, `objdump`, and `nm` available in this sandbox (no `gdb`, and no package-manager access to install one - `sudo`/`apt-get` are both blocked).** Without `gdb`, added a `SIGSEGV` handler using glibc's own `backtrace()`/`backtrace_symbols_fd()` (`<execinfo.h>`) to a fresh, from-scratch lean driver built directly against the real repository's `source/`/`include/` (same approach as Round 310's lean driver). This is the single biggest methodology upgrade across all three rounds of this investigation - every prior round's diagnosis (Round 307-310) relied on `fprintf`-bisected tracing and could only narrow the crash down to "somewhere inside this function call"; a real backtrace immediately named the exact crashing call.

**Root cause #1, confirmed via backtrace + `addr2line`**: `ee_mem_ptr()`'s `st->bios->size`/`st->bios->data` dereference (`source/core/ee/ee_core.c:952-953`) faulted on a stack-shaped address. This driver's build command was missing `-no-pie` (every prior round's scratch driver always included it, but this fresh rebuild dropped it without noticing) - meaning the executable itself is position-independent, so its own load base address is re-randomized by ASLR on every separate process invocation. `ee_state_t.bios` is a pointer *into the executable's own global data space* (`&bios`, a file-scope global holding the loaded BIOS image struct) - even after making `bios` a stable global (Round 310's fix for the *equivalent* scratch-driver bug), restoring the raw pointer *value* from an old process is only valid if the *whole executable's own base address* is guaranteed identical between the writing and reading process. Rebuilding with `-no-pie` (disabling ASLR for the main executable, matching every prior round's convention) fixed this specific fault immediately and completely.

**Root cause #2, confirmed via the same backtrace technique**: with `#1` fixed, a *new* fault appeared - now cleanly inside `_IO_printf` itself, called from ordinary `printf()` statements in both the scratch driver's own code and the real repository's own `system.c` diagnostic output (`printf("[!] system_run_interleaved: hit slice cap...")`). This is a real, reproducible finding: **any `printf()`/stdio call made after this checkpoint format's raw `[__data_start,_end)` restore reliably crashes**, regardless of its format string or arguments (confirmed on multiple different call sites, with and without `%s` arguments) - something about the restore leaves the C library's own buffered-stdio machinery in a bad state, not yet understood down to the exact mechanism (glibc's own `libc.so.6` internals are stripped of local symbols, and `gdb` isn't available in this sandbox to inspect further). **Workaround, not a full root-cause fix**: replaced every `printf()` call reachable after a resume - both in the scratch driver's own code and, via a *local, untracked, diagnostic-only copy* of `system.c` (never touching the real, tracked file), with a small helper that formats via `vsnprintf()` into a stack buffer and writes it with a raw `write()` syscall, entirely avoiding the `FILE`-stream/buffered-stdio machinery. This is an honest, labeled workaround for still-unexplained stdio fragility, not a confirmed root cause - flagged here in case it recurs or someone gets `gdb` access to investigate further.

**With both fixes in place, checkpoint/resume worked completely cleanly, repeatedly, across many separate process invocations** - the first time in this project's history this has ever worked. Verified explicitly: chained two small 3,000,000-slice resume calls back-to-back and confirmed the cumulative instruction counter advanced correctly and continuously across both (47,999,343 -> 71,999,263, exactly matching the expected per-chunk delta) - genuine, correct state continuity, not a fresh restart disguised as a resume.

**Used the now-working chain to push this project's own scratch trace to a depth never previously reached: 2,639,996,564 instructions (2.64 billion) across eleven chained 30,000,000-slice runs**, each completing in a real ~19-25 second wall-clock window (well within this sandbox's per-call budget) - a version of the same lean, low-instrumentation driver design from Round 310 for throughput. **The trace passed through three distinct, real phases**, confirmed via both PC sampling and this round's new SIF RPC pending/delivered counters (`g_r303_rpc_pending_sets`/`g_r303_rpc_delivered_count`, already present in the real, tracked `ee_core.c`): (1) the VBLANK-wait busy-poll loop Round 308/309 already characterized, with RPC counts climbing steadily throughout (168 -> 391 pending/delivered) confirming continued real background work, up to roughly 1,440,000,000 instructions; (2) a brief transition through kernel code at `0x8000F768`; (3) settling, from roughly 1,680,000,000 instructions onward, into a new steady state cycling through `0x8000CC9C`-`0x8000CFEC`, with the RPC counters flat at 391 for the remainder (five consecutive 30,000,000-slice chunks, 150,000,000+ instructions with zero RPC growth) - a genuinely different resting point, not the same VBLANK-wait loop.

**Disassembled this new resting point directly from the live trace** (`ee_mem_read32()`-based dump around the final PC, the same technique established in earlier rounds): `0x8000CF88` (`lui v0,0x8002`) through `0x8000CFB4` decode to a real, recognizable poll: read `RAM[0x80020CFC]` (a device-table-adjacent field - `0x80020B60` is the exact base address Round 269's own "OSDSYS device-table mechanism (RAM[0x80020B60], 16 slots)" investigation already named), branch away if zero, then read the real DMA `D_STAT` register (`0xB000E010`) and test bit 7, branching away if clear. **`0x8000CF88` is the *exact* address Round 271's own task description already named**: "trace 0x8000CF88's post-SMFLAG branch (0x8000D008 vs ack path) to find the real repeatable menu-advance decision point." This scratch trace has now reached, via genuine sustained execution for the first time, the precise decision point that round characterized 40+ rounds ago through static/limited-depth analysis alone.

**Net assessment**: this is the single most significant tooling result of the whole "everything needed for the splash screen" effort - checkpoint/resume is genuinely fixed (two confirmed causes, one clean fix and one honest, working-but-not-fully-understood workaround), unlocking effectively unbounded tracing depth for future rounds (each chain link only needs to fit this sandbox's ~40s per-call budget; there is no longer a hard ceiling on cumulative instructions reachable across many links). The trace's new resting point is not an unexplained mystery - it lands precisely on ground this project already mapped in Rounds 269-278 (OSDSYS device-table read + a real DMA-channel-completion poll), meaning Round 278's earlier partial fixes (device-table modeling, pad-press stimulus) got the trace *close* but not *past* this exact loop, and the one-shot `iop_sio2_pad_press()` call this scratch driver issues once at startup (not on any repeated, real-per-frame cadence) is a clear, concrete suspect for why.

**No real repository source code was changed this round** (`git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm the working tree is unchanged - the driver and its locally-patched `system.c` copy were both scratch-only, in `/tmp`, never copied into the tracked repository or committed) - docs-only, so the regression suite and Wii rebuild were not re-run.

Left as the concrete next investigative target for Round 313: determine why the trace stalls at the `0x8000CF88` device-table/D_STAT poll despite Round 278's earlier fixes - the most direct next step is to have the scratch driver issue *repeated* pad-press stimuli (matching a real per-frame/per-poll cadence, not a single one-shot press at boot) and see whether that's sufficient to advance past this loop, cross-referenced against a live-PCSX2 read of the equivalent real memory location if useful.

Live PCSX2 session not touched this round - all investigation reused the new backtrace-equipped lean scratch driver's `run`/`resume` modes.

## Round 313: periodic (not one-shot) pad-press stimulus tested and RULED OUT as the fix for the 0x8000CF88 stall; probed the exact live values the loop polls on and confirmed the stall is structural, not a timing/stimulus issue; found and fixed a real leak-prevention gap in checkpoint persistence before it became a problem

Direct continuation of the user's "push as far as possible to the splash screen" direction, testing Round 312's own concrete next step: whether *repeated* pad-press stimuli (matching a real per-frame cadence) rather than a single one-shot press at boot is enough to advance the trace past the `0x8000CF88` device-table/D_STAT poll.

**Built `driver_r313`**, a fresh copy of Round 312's working (`-no-pie`, safe-printf) lean driver with one change: the single `iop_sio2_pad_press(IOP_PAD_BTN_CROSS)` issued once at startup is now toggled press/release every 2,000,000 slices throughout the run, for the entire duration of the trace (not just once).

**Chained the trace to 3,119,996,564 instructions (3.12 billion) - past Round 312's prior 2.64-billion ceiling for the first time** - across twelve 30,000,000-slice `resume` calls. Result: **the periodic pad-press toggle does not help.** The trace reaches the exact same `0x8000CC9C`-`0x8000CFEC` address range at the exact same depth as Round 312's one-shot-press run (~1.68 billion instructions), and the real SIF RPC pending/delivered counters (`g_r303_rpc_pending_sets`/`g_r303_rpc_delivered_count`) plateau at the identical value (391) and stay flat for the remaining 1.44 billion+ instructions traced this round, regardless of the now-continuously-toggling pad input. This conclusively rules out "just needs more human-like repeated input" as the fix - the earlier one-shot-press design was not the limiting factor.

**Added a direct probe of the two live values Round 271/312's disassembly said this loop polls on**, reading them straight out of live EE memory via `ee_mem_read32()` (no new global state, so this rebuild remained resumable against the existing checkpoint chain without a restart - confirmed by successfully resuming the 3.12-billion-instruction checkpoint with the newly-rebuilt probe-equipped binary): `RAM[0x80020CFC] = 0x00000000` (the device-table slot the loop branches away on when zero - confirmed still zero at 3.12 billion instructions, same as at the loop's first visit) and `D_STAT (0xB000E010) = 0x00A00000` (bits 21 and 23 set - these are the upper-half **mask** bits for DMA channels 5 and 7, i.e. SIF0 and SIF2 completion IRQs are both armed/enabled - but bit 7 itself, the actual SIF2 channel-completion **status** bit the loop branches away on when clear, reads 0). Also dumped all 16 raw device-table slots at `0x80020B60`: several already hold real, plausible OSDSYS-module code addresses (`0x8000c500`, `0x8000d1e0`, `0x8000f318`, `0x80010898`), confirming the table itself is populated with real data - it's specifically the `0x80020CFC` slot (a different, adjacent field, not one of the 16 numbered table entries) and the SIF2 D_STAT completion bit that stay stuck at zero.

**This matches a much older and more deeply-investigated finding already on record in this file** (the historical note that this project's own DMA model is synchronous - `dma_channel_kick()` completes a transfer immediately when the EE-side code issues it - and that the real DMAC channel register this loop is ultimately gating on is never once written by the EE's own code across a full trace): if D_STAT bit 7 never goes high, the only possible explanation under this project's synchronous DMA model is that **the EE's own code never issues the SIF2 DMA kick in the first place** - not a timing race, not a missing IOP response, not a stimulus problem. Something upstream of this loop (most likely gated on the same `RAM[0x80020CFC]==0` condition, which per the historical record traces back to task #221's already-identified, already-deprioritized "device-table entries are genuine embedded IOP IRX/ELF modules" scope) is what prevents the EE from ever reaching the code that would kick the DMA transfer this loop is waiting to see complete.

**Net assessment**: Round 313's contribution is negative-but-valuable - it closes off "more/better stimulus" and "more raw instruction budget" (3.12 billion instructions is already 4-9x Round 311's real-hardware splash-screen calibration bound of 354-709 million EE cycles, and the loop shows zero signs of ever escaping on its own) as viable paths, and pins the remaining gap down to a precise, previously-identified, previously-deprioritized root cause: the `RAM[0x80020CFC]` device-table field and the code path that would populate it and/or trigger the EE-side SIF2 DMA kick. This is real, substantive architecture work (embedded IOP IRX/ELF module handling per task #221), not a quick register fix, and was correctly not attempted speculatively this round per this project's established discipline against unverified fixes.

**A real leak-prevention gap was found and self-corrected mid-round, before any leak occurred.** While setting up persistent checkpoint tooling per the user's "make checkpoints so it survives sandbox resets" request, a `.ckpt` file (containing a raw dump of post-boot EE/IOP RAM) was briefly staged into the persistent outputs folder alongside the driver source/binary. Before finishing, it was recognized that this file almost certainly embeds real, copyrighted PS2 BIOS boot code and/or game-disc sector data that gets copied into RAM during the emulated boot - exactly the class of content this project's standing leak-prevention rule prohibits - and, critically, that **the existing filename-based leak check (`*.bin`/`*.iso`/`*tekken*`) would not have caught it**, since a `.ckpt` file matches none of those patterns. The file was deleted immediately (`allow_cowork_file_delete` + `rm`, verified via `find`/`ls` afterward). Resolved with a safe, deterministic-boot-based alternative instead: only the driver source, its locally-patched `system.c` copy, and a documented rebuild/re-chain procedure (`checkpoint_tool/README.md`) are persisted - since the boot trace is fully deterministic, a future session can regenerate the same depth from a cold boot in about a dozen cheap chained calls without ever needing to persist raw RAM-derived state. This finding should be treated as a standing addition to this project's leak-prevention discipline: **any future file derived from emulated RAM/BIOS/disc state (checkpoints, memory snapshots, save states, etc.) must be treated as high-risk regardless of filename, not just files matching the existing `*.bin`/`*.iso`/`*tekken*` patterns.**

**No real repository source code was changed this round** (`git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm the working tree is unchanged apart from this documentation update and the untracked scratch `driver_r313.c` - the driver and its locally-patched `system.c` copy were both scratch-only, never committed) - docs-only, so the regression suite and Wii rebuild were not re-run.

Left as the concrete next investigative target: this is now squarely back in task #221's scope (embedded IOP IRX/ELF device-table module handling) - trace what real EE code path is supposed to populate/consult `RAM[0x80020CFC]` and issue the SIF2 DMA kick this loop is waiting on, likely requiring the same kind of live-PCSX2 memory-diff comparison Round 311 demonstrated works well (set the equivalent live breakpoint/watchpoint on a real, freshly-reset PCSX2 session and see what real code touches this address, since this project's own static/scratch-trace analysis has now been pushed about as far as it usefully can without that ground truth).

## Round 314: live-hardware ground-truth check corrects the Round 271/312/313 hypothesis about what the 0x8000CF88 dispatcher's resting state means; found a new, earlier, previously-undocumented SIF-handshake spin in this project's own trace; confirmed a hard tooling ceiling on live-hardware early-boot comparison and two new pcsx2-mcp bridge bugs; no fix shipped (root cause still not confidently identified)

Direct continuation of the user's "focus on the pcsx2 investigation... disassemble everything... implement everything once done, don't ask, keep going until the limit is reached" direction, picking up right where Round 313 left off (the `0x8000CF88` OSDSYS device-table/D_STAT decision point).

**Used the still-connected live PCSX2 DebugServer session (`pcsx2-qt.exe`, granted since Round 311) to get real, native-disassembler ground truth on this exact function for the first time**, rather than continuing to rely on this project's own hand-decoded `ee_mem_read32()` hex dumps. `pcsx2_disassemble` gave a clean, complete, correctly-decoded listing of `0x8000CF88-0x8000D000`.

**Correction of the Round 271/312/313 framing.** The earlier characterization ("this loop polls `RAM[0x80020CFC]`, then checks `D_STAT` bit 7 for SIF2 completion") described only ONE of two branches, and - critically - the branch that is NOT taken when `RAM[0x80020CFC]==0` (which is the condition this project's trace, and real hardware, are BOTH actually in). The real control flow, read directly off the native disassembly: `lw v1, RAM[0x80020CFC]; beqz v1, ->0x8000CFC4`. When `RAM[0x80020CFC]==0` (true in every observed case, this project's own trace AND real hardware alike), execution branches AWAY from the `D_STAT` bit-7 SIF2 check entirely and into a completely different check at `0x8000CFC4`: `lw v0, (0xB000F000); andi v0,v0,2; beqz v0, ->0x8000D014` (return). **This means the SIF2/D_STAT framing this project has used since Round 271 describes a branch that isn't even being executed under the observed condition** - a real, substantive correction, not just a rewording.

**Confirmed via a genuine live read of real, working hardware that this is not a stall condition at all.** Paused the live session (already deep in normal, healthy attract-mode gameplay, cycles > 600,000,000, screen actively rendering) and read `RAM[0x80020CFC]` and `0xB000F000` directly: **both are `0x00000000` on real hardware too**, at a point where the game is unambiguously running correctly. This rules out "these being zero" as any kind of real blocker - it's a legitimate, permanently-idle fast-exit path that real hardware also sits in (or repeatedly re-visits and exits from) during and after normal operation, not evidence of missing functionality.

**Independently validated Round 269's 16-slot device-table reconstruction against real hardware for the first time.** Read `RAM[0x80020B60..0x80020B9C]` (16 words) on the live session: indices 3-14 are **byte-identical** to this project's own values at a comparable point in its trace (`0x00000001, 0x00000000, 0x8000c500, 0x00000201, 0x00000000, 0x80010898, 0x0000021f, 0x00000000, 0x8000d1e0, 0x00000230, 0x00000000, 0x8000f318`) - real, matching function-pointer-shaped values, not coincidental noise. This is strong, first-ever live confirmation that Round 269's device-table modeling is genuinely correct, not a fabricated/guessed structure.

**Re-identified the earlier `0x002113D0`-ish resting point this project's own trace visits before ~1,440,000,000 instructions - correction of an initial mislabel made while drafting this entry.** A fresh cold-boot run (no checkpoint chaining, single 30,000,000-slice run, ~240,000,000 instructions) settles at `0x002113E8-0x002113F4`. Disassembled directly (own `ee_mem_read32()` dump): `lui v1,0x1000; ori v1,0xf000` (`v1 = 0x1000F000`), `li v0,4; sw v0,(v1)`, then `lw v0,(v1); andi v0,4; beqz -> retry`. Cross-referencing this project's own already-committed source (`source/hw/ee_intc.c`) shows `0x1000F000` is **`EE_INTC_STAT`**, not a SIF register - bit 2 is the real, standard `VBLANK_START` cause bit, and the write-4-then-poll-for-4 pattern is the ordinary real write-1-to-clear-then-rearm idiom. This is, on closer identification, **the SAME real, already-documented, already-healthy VBLANK-wait busy-poll this file's own Round 308/309 entries already characterized in detail** ("arm INTC_STAT bit 2 [VBLANK_START], loop reading 0x1000F000 until the bit sets, ack, return... healthy, expected real-hardware-shaped behavior, not a new blocker") - not a new or previously-undocumented finding as an earlier draft of this entry incorrectly claimed. Flagging the correction explicitly rather than silently fixing it, since an inaccurate "new finding" claim would otherwise mislead a future round. The genuinely new, corrected finding from this session remains the `0x8000CF88`/`0x8000CFC4` branch re-identification above (register `0xB000F000`/`0x1000F000` is the same real `EE_INTC_STAT`, and the checked bit there - bit 1 - is `INTC_SBUS`, matching this file's own much earlier `13801`-line entry's citation of "`INTC_SBUS`" at the same address, now independently re-confirmed via live real-hardware disassembly and a live real-hardware read).

**Attempted a live, real-hardware comparison at the equivalent early-boot moment - hit a hard, confirmed tooling ceiling, not a PS2 finding.** After a genuine `System > Reset` plus an immediate `pcsx2_pause` (no watchpoint involved this time, learning from the failure mode below), successfully caught real hardware at the true reset vector for the first time this session (`PC=0xBFC00000`, `Cycles=0`) - proving the catch IS possible with the right sequencing. However, **the very next `continue()` immediately followed by `pause()` (zero added wait) already landed at `Cycles=3,865,269,656`** - 3.87 billion cycles, far past not just the target early-boot window but past the entire splash-screen-to-gameplay range Round 311 calibrated. This means the round-trip latency of a single `continue`-then-`pause` tool-call pair, on its own, is enough to blow past the entire region of interest on this unthrottled live session - there is currently no reliable way to catch real hardware inside the sub-1-billion-cycle window using this bridge's `pause`/`continue`/`step` primitives, regardless of sequencing care. This is a new, real, honestly-reported tooling ceiling, not a PS2/emulation finding, and it specifically blocked getting the one piece of ground truth that would have been most valuable this round (whether real hardware's `0x1000F000` bit 2 is set at the equivalent early moment this project's own trace is still waiting on it).

**Found a second new, real pcsx2-mcp bridge bug this round, beyond Round 311's already-documented two (broken watchpoint hit-counters, stale `gs_registers` reads).** Setting a `type:"write", action:"break"` watchpoint on `RAM[0x80020CFC]` left the live session in a state where `pcsx2_continue()` reported success but `pcsx2_status()`/`pcsx2_step()` continued to report the exact same frozen `PC`/`Cycles`/instruction indefinitely across multiple calls (5 consecutive `step()` calls all returned identical `PC=0xbfc00c70` with no advancement) - genuinely stuck, confirmed via the PCSX2 UI's own "Paused" status bar agreeing, not just a bridge-side stale read. Removing the watchpoint entirely (not just clearing its break/log mode) immediately un-stuck it - the next `continue()` worked normally. This is now flagged for any future round reaching for this bridge's watchpoint tooling: **avoid `action:"break"` watchpoints in this session/build, or budget for needing to fully remove (not just clear-all) a watchpoint to recover from a hang.**

**No fix shipped this round.** The real, concrete correction made to this project's own understanding is the `0x8000CF88`/`0x8000CFC4` branch re-framing (register identity `EE_INTC_STAT`, gating bit `INTC_SBUS`, not the previously-assumed SIF2/D_STAT path) - it does not by itself identify a confident, verifiable root cause for the FINAL blocker (the `0x8000CFxx` kernel-dispatcher cycling that persists unchanged from ~1.44 billion to 3.12+ billion instructions, RPC counters flat at 391). Per this project's own well-established discipline against shipping speculative fixes without live-verified evidence (most notably Round 279's VBLANK-force-unmask shortcut, which Round 280 had to revert after tracing its consequences into a genuine, real BIOS panic-freeze dead end) - simply forcing `RAM[0x80020CFC]` or `INTC_STAT` bit 1 (`INTC_SBUS`) nonzero without knowing what real IOP/SIF-side code is supposed to set it would repeat exactly that mistake. `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm the working tree is unchanged apart from this documentation update - the real repository was not touched.

**Live PCSX2 session left clean**: all breakpoints/watchpoints cleared (`pcsx2_clear_all_breakpoints`), execution resumed and running freely (not paused), same healthy attract-mode gameplay state it was in at the start of this round.

Left as the concrete next investigative target: find what real IOP-side code is supposed to set `INTC_STAT` bit 1 (`INTC_SBUS`) - the condition the corrected `0x8000CFC4` branch checks - or, more fundamentally, what causes OSDSYS's own caller loop to keep re-visiting this idle poll for 1.68+ billion instructions with zero SIF RPC growth instead of progressing to its next real stage (matching this file's own many prior Round 265-296 threads on this same underlying question, none of which reached a shippable fix). `source/hw/sif.c` and `source/hw/ee_intc.c` (real, already-modeled, tracked source, cited above as already correctly implementing `INTC_STAT`'s real semantics) remain the right starting point for any future round pursuing this, rather than a live-hardware-only mystery. A fixed/patched live-debugging bridge (able to reliably pause inside the sub-1-billion-cycle window, unlike this round's confirmed 3.87-billion-cycle-per-round-trip ceiling) would also materially help.

## Round 314 (continued): found and SHIPPED a real, verified off-by-one timing bug in the existing SBUS-wait shortcut (`ee_check_boot_unblock_sbus_wait`) - a genuine correctness fix, honestly confirmed to NOT unblock the final boot-progress wall on its own

Direct continuation of this round's live-hardware disassembly work above, following the user's "implement everything once its done, don't ask, keep going" direction once a concrete, well-evidenced bug (not a guess) was found.

**Found a real bug in existing, already-shipped, already-accepted production code.** `source/core/ee/ee_core.c`'s `ee_check_boot_unblock_sbus_wait()` (Round 178, with its one-shot latch removed in Round 262-264 per explicit user direction, confirmed present and active on `main` despite its header comment's stale "EXPERIMENTAL BRANCH ONLY" label) is triggered by `EE_SBUS_WAIT_LOOP_PC = 0x8000CFD0`. This round's live, native-disassembler-confirmed ground truth (see above) shows `0x8000CFD0` is the **`andi v0,v0,2`** instruction - the one that *consumes* a value already loaded into `v0` one instruction earlier, at `0x8000CFCC`'s `lw v0,(s0)` (`s0 = EE_INTC_STAT`). This project's own per-instruction hook dispatch (`source/core/ee/ee_core.c`, main step loop) fires each check function with `st->pc` already advanced to the *next* instruction to be fetched - so triggering on `0x8000CFD0` means the `lw` has *already executed* by the time this function raises `EE_INTC_IRQ_SBUS`, and the `andi` about to run reads the *stale* `v0` register, not the freshly-updated `intc->stat`. The raise is one instruction too late to ever affect the outcome it was written to influence - a genuine, real timing bug, not a design choice.

**Fixed by moving the trigger to the read itself.** Changed `EE_SBUS_WAIT_LOOP_PC` from `0x8000CFD0` to `0x8000CFCC` (the `lw` instruction) so the raise happens *before* `EE_INTC_STAT` is read, letting the read pick up the fresh value the same way a correctly-timed real interrupt would already be visible to it. The function's own pre-existing guards (never fires if the bit's already set; never fires if the real DMAC_STAT half of the OR-condition is already satisfied) are unchanged, so this remains additive and cannot fight or duplicate a real write - only the trigger *timing* changed, not the function's logic or its safety guarantees.

**Verified via the host-native diagnostic driver, chained past the exact depth Round 313's baseline plateaued at.** Rebuilt the scratch checkpoint/resume driver against the patched source and re-ran a fresh cold-boot chain to 2,639,996,564 instructions - the exact same depth as Round 313's own baseline checkpoint. Result, honestly reported: **the fix does not change the outcome at this depth** - `RPC: pending_sets=391 delivered=391` at 2.64 billion instructions, identical to the unpatched baseline; PC still cycles within the same `0x8000CCxx`-`0x8000CFxx` dispatcher-idle-loop address family Round 277 already characterized as normal, healthy idle-loop cycling (visiting `0x8000CC78`, `0x8000CCBC`, `0x8000CDFC`, `0x8000F810`, `0x8000CFE0`, `0x8000CCA8` across the chained runs - all addresses already on that list). The real, corrected SBUS-raise timing is very likely now succeeding (the register-timing bug it fixed was real and directly demonstrated via disassembly), but whatever handler consumes it (`0x8000CC68`, called when the check passes) does not itself produce observable further progress (no SIF RPC growth, no PC escape into new territory) within the budget tested.

**Verification (mandatory workflow, full).** New host-native regression pass: **122/122 test files pass, 0 real failures** (the one runner-reported `FAIL(run) test_ee_syscall_full_audit_sweep` is the same pre-existing, already-documented benign runner-timeout limitation from earlier rounds - independently re-confirmed passing cleanly with `ALL CHECKS PASSED (0 failures)` given a longer timeout). Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild from the cached, previously-documented toolchain (`outputs/build/devkitpro/TOOLCHAIN_SETUP_NOTES.md`, re-linked this round after this session's sandbox reset cleared `/tmp`'s toolchain state - matching the exact env-var recipe that file already documents): `make clean && make` exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.elf` (2,630,280 bytes) / `pcsx2-wii-git.dol` (468,736 bytes) produced, only the same two pre-existing benign `strncpy`-truncation warnings, zero new warnings or errors.

**Honest net assessment.** This is a real, verified, low-risk correctness fix - not a speculative "force a value" shortcut like Round 279's (which had to be reverted). It is shipped on its own merits (a genuine bug, independently demonstrated via live-hardware disassembly and confirmed via regression-clean host-native + Wii builds), explicitly NOT because it was observed to unblock the splash-screen investigation - it did not, at least not within the 2.64-billion-instruction budget re-tested. ## Round 321 (live-hardware, MAJOR FINDING) - live breakpoint/disassembly on the real, live PCSX2 session caught real OSDSYS's actual display-setup routine in the act: it writes PMODE + DISPFB2 + DISPLAY2 (GS output CIRCUIT 2), and legitimately NEVER writes DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 for this boot - correcting this project's own "PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 never written" success-detection criteria, standing since Round 87/94/111/126/127

Direct continuation of Round 320, after the user restored computer-use access to the live PCSX2 window (`pcsx2-qt.exe`) and asked to also check DISPLAY2.

**Set a real, live write watchpoint at PMODE (0x12000000) and DISPLAY1 (0x12000080), triggered a real System > Reset via computer-use, and let the live session run freely (no manual pause timing needed - watchpoints stop the emulator exactly at the trigger regardless of the already-documented continue/pause latency ceiling).** The PMODE watchpoint hit cleanly at EE PC `0x0050b420`, real cycle count 762,357,931 - within the same order of magnitude as Round 311's own splash-screen calibration window (354M-709M cycles).

**Disassembled live (PCSX2's own native disassembler) and read live registers at the exact break point**: the real routine at `0x0050b414-0x0050b45c` is a genuine, real, unremarkable four-register-write sequence:
```
0x0050b414: lui v1,0x1200          ; v1 = 0x12000000 = PMODE
0x0050b420: sd   a0,(v1)           ; PMODE = a0 = 0x66 (bit1=EN2 SET, bit0=EN1 CLEAR)
0x0050b424: ori  v0,0x20           ; v0 = 0x12000020 = SMODE2
0x0050b428: ori  a2,0x90           ; a2 = 0x12000090 = DISPFB2
0x0050b42c: lui  a1,0x1200
0x0050b434: ori  a1,0xA0           ; a1 = 0x120000A0 = DISPLAY2
0x0050b43c: sd   v1,(v0)           ; SMODE2 = ...
0x0050b448: sd   v0,(a2)           ; DISPFB2 = ...
0x0050b450: sd   v1,(a1)           ; DISPLAY2 = ... (real value captured: 0x0183227C)
0x0050b45c: sd   v0,(a0)           ; BGCOLOR (0x120000E0) = ...
```
Re-armed a second, separate watchpoint on DISPLAY2 alone (0x120000A0) and reset again to independently confirm and capture its exact real written value at the moment of the store: **`v1 = 0x0183227C`** - a real, structured, non-zero display-configuration value (DX/DY offset + magnification + width/height fields per the real DISPLAY register format), not zero, not garbage. `pcsx2_get_backtrace` at the PMODE break point showed a real, coherent 6-frame call stack (entries at `0x0050a9a0`, `0x00500268`, `0x005002f8`, `0x00500488`, `0x004162b0`) - genuine function-call-driven code, not corrupted state.

**The critical finding: PMODE's real written value (`0x66`) has bit 1 (EN2) SET and bit 0 (EN1) CLEAR.** Real OSDSYS, for this exact real BIOS + real game disc, configures and enables GS output **CIRCUIT 2** (`DISPFB2`/`DISPLAY2`) for its splash/attract-mode display - and, by construction (`EN1` clear), legitimately **never needs to write `DISPFB1`/`DISPLAY1` at all** for this boot path. This is not "hasn't happened yet" - on real hardware, for this game, it never happens, ever, by design.

**This directly and significantly corrects this project's own, long-standing (Round 87/94/111/126/127, cited and re-cited across dozens of subsequent rounds including this session's own recent work) success-detection framing: "is PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 non-zero yet" as the definition of "reached the splash screen."** That check could never have detected success on this exact real hardware/game/BIOS combination, even if this project's own emulated trace had, hypothetically, reached the real display-setup code at some point in any of the 300+ prior rounds - a real, previously-unnoticed methodological blind spot in this project's own measurement, not evidence about what real hardware does or doesn't do.

**No functional/behavioral source fix was required.** Checked `source/hw/gs.c`'s real MMIO dispatch table directly: it already, correctly, generically maps BOTH `DISPFB1`/`DISPLAY1` (`0x12000070`/`0x12000080`) AND `DISPFB2`/`DISPLAY2` (`0x12000090`/`0x120000A0`) to `gs_state_t`'s own `dispfb1`/`display1`/`dispfb2`/`display2` fields - the GS register model itself has been complete and correct this whole time; only this project's own diagnostic/success-criteria (scratch driver instrumentation, and this file's own repeatedly-cited comments) needed correcting. Added a clear, prominently-placed correction comment in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` (directly before the original Round 87 comment block that first established the now-corrected framing), documenting this finding in full and instructing any future round's own splash-screen check to test PMODE plus BOTH circuits' registers (or gate on PMODE's own EN1/EN2 bits), not `DISPFB1`/`DISPLAY1` alone. Per this project's own established convention (preserve historical reasoning, add a dated correction rather than silently rewriting it - the same pattern used for Round 314's SIF mislabel correction), the original Round 87/94/111/126/127 comment text is left intact immediately after the new correction.

**Verification (mandatory workflow, full - a tracked source file's comment changed).** `gcc -fsyntax-only` clean. Full host-native regression suite: **122/122 test files pass, 0 failures** (a genuinely clean run this time - no runner-timeout flag at all). Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: `make` exit 0 (incremental - only `ee_core.c` recompiled, as expected for a comment-only change), `pcsx2-wii-git.elf` (2,630,560 bytes)/`pcsx2-wii-git.dol` (468,832 bytes) produced, zero errors.

**Practical impact and honest scope.** This finding does NOT, by itself, unblock this project's own current boot-progress wall (the `0x8000CFxx` idle-loop plateau Rounds 314-318 have been investigating remains a separate, still-open question about EARLIER boot progress than this display-setup code, which real hardware only reaches after passing that same stage). What it DOES provide: (1) a corrected, real, evidence-based definition of what "success" actually looks like for any future round that DOES make further progress - checking `DISPFB1`/`DISPLAY1` alone would have silently failed to recognize a real win; (2) independent, further reinforcement (a third live data point, after Round 314 and Round 319/320) that this exact real BIOS+disc combination does reach full real rendering, and now precisely how (circuit 2, `PMODE=0x66`); (3) a concrete, real target address (`0x0050b420`, within OSDSYS's `0x00200000-0x00480000` range) a future round could set a live breakpoint on to directly, empirically measure how many real EE cycles/instructions elapse between OSDSYS's own boot start and this exact real display-setup call - a much more precise calibration than Round 311's screenshot-based bisection.

Live session left clean: watchpoints removed (not just cleared, per the established Round 314 recovery procedure), resumed and running freely at the end of this round.

**The caller identity is not a bug - it's the real, previously-documented call site.** `ra=0x8000F86C` is exactly `0x8000F864 + 8` (jal delay-slot return address), matching this project's own long-established real disassembly of the OSDSYS outer per-frame loop's `jal 0x8000CF88` at `0x8000F864` (first characterized around the 94th/106th findings, re-confirmed many times since, most explicitly in this file's own already-recorded note: *"`ra=0x8000F86C` simply re-calls it in a steady idle loop"*). The tables-empty observation Round 323/324 made in this project's own emulated trace is real and accurately characterized, but is a description of why the emulated trace's own loop never exits, not a lead on what real hardware does differently - real hardware exits (or rather, never enters) via a completely different, still-unidentified control-flow decision made earlier, before ever reaching this per-frame idle dispatcher the way this project's own trace does.

## Round 326 (live-hardware, docs-only, direct continuation of Round 325 / the long-open Round 205-207 thread): direct positive confirmation - real hardware's CDVD N-command register holds 0x06 (ReadCd), proving genuine disc sector reads occur during boot; also found IOP-scoped watchpoint hit-counters are unreliable, extending the already-documented EE-side bridge quirk to the IOP side

Direct continuation of Round 325, picking up the long-open Round 205-207 thread ("re-run the real boot trace... with breakpoints/watchpoints armed on the real CD-ROM/CDVD driver entry points, captured from a fresh reset... remains the concrete next step to directly resolve... not attempted yet") - this project's own docs have flagged this exact live check as outstanding since Round 207/243, roughly 120 rounds ago, and it had never actually been performed until this round.

**Method.** Set write watchpoints (log mode, learning from Round 325's break-mode freeze) on the real IOP-side CDVD N-command register (`0x1F402004`) and S-command register (`0x1F402016`), both per the real ps2tek register map this project already cited in Round 206. Triggered a fresh `System > Reset`. This time the reset did NOT freeze continue/step (log-mode watchpoints, unlike Round 325's initial break-mode ones, did not trigger the DebugServer-halt quirk) - the session progressed on its own, visibly reaching the game's own title/logo screen ("TEKKEN TAG TOURNAMENT", real Namco copyright text) within a short real time.

**Found: both watchpoints report 0 hits, but a direct register read proves a real command WAS issued.** `pcsx2_read_memory(0x1F402004, cpu=iop)` reads back `0x06` at the N-command register - the real, documented `ReadCd` opcode (per ps2tep's N-command table, already cited in Round 206) - not zero, not garbage, a specific meaningful real command byte, stable and reproducible across two separate reads. This directly, positively confirms real hardware DOES issue genuine CD-ROM sector-read commands during this boot (consistent with, and now the first live-hardware confirmation of, the Round 205 Play!-derived SYSTEM.CNF/BOOT2 auto-boot hypothesis and the general expectation that a real disc's data - `SYSTEM.CNF`, the game ELF, or subsequent game asset loads - must be read via exactly this mechanism).

**The watchpoints' 0-hit reading is a tooling artifact, not evidence of no write.** This extends the already-documented EE-side watchpoint/GS-register bridge staleness bugs (Round 311's `pcsx2_gs_registers`, Round 320's plain `pcsx2_read_memory`, Round 311/318/321's watchpoint hit-counter unreliability) to the IOP-scoped watchpoint path specifically, which had not been individually exercised/tested before this round. **Generalizes this project's own tooling-limitations knowledge further: hit-counters on this bridge should never be trusted as a negative result (no evidence of hits does NOT mean no writes occurred) regardless of which CPU (EE or IOP) the watchpoint targets - only a direct register/memory read, or a real breakpoint hit/miss (not a watchpoint), has been shown reliable so far.**

**No fix shipped this round** (live investigation only). `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm no source changes - docs-only. Live session left clean: both watchpoints removed, session running freely.

Left as the concrete next step: since watchpoints on this register are confirmed unreliable, use a real breakpoint (not a watchpoint - matching the already-established Round 314/322 reliability precedent for breakpoints specifically) on the actual IOP code address that issues the N-command write, or use the dedicated `pcsx2_dma_trace_start`/`pcsx2_dma_read` tools (not yet tried this investigation) to directly capture the CDVD DMA transfer this ReadCd command must have produced - either would give real timing data (WHEN, relative to boot, and WHAT data gets read) that this round's snapshot-only register read cannot provide.

## Round 329 (live-hardware, docs-only): real IOP thread snapshot explains the recurring R3000A recompiler exception as a benign self-jump idle loop, and quantifies a substantial real architectural gap - real hardware runs 54 persistent IOP kernel threads at rest, this project's own IOP model halts entirely after module discovery

Offline scratch-driver tooling was unavailable this round (the real BIOS/disc scratch files used by the checkpoint/resume tool were lost to an earlier sandbox reset and were not re-supplied) - pivoted to a live-hardware check using the still-healthy live PCSX2 session.

**Captured real EE and IOP thread lists** (`pcsx2_get_threads`) on the live session: the **EE side has just 2 threads** (TID 0 ready, TID 1 running - a lean, expected real footprint for this demo game). The **IOP side has 54 real threads** - a rich, persistent kernel thread population this project's own IOP model has never had any equivalent of.

**Explained the Round 327/328 recurring "R3000A: Jump to unmapped recLUT page (PC: 0x0000ae94)" exception with real disassembly, closing that open thread.** `pcsx2_disassemble(0x0000ae80, cpu=iop)` shows `0x0000ae94: j ->$0x0000AE94` - a literal, genuine self-referential unconditional jump (the instruction's own target is its own address). This is a real, standard, legitimate real-kernel idle-halt idiom (MIPS I has no dedicated halt opcode; spinning on a jump-to-self is the conventional way a kernel idles while waiting for an interrupt to break out via exception) - **not a bug, deadlock, or corruption in this project's own investigation**. The recurring PCSX2-internal exception at this exact address is now well-explained as a plausible, real PCSX2 recompiler edge case: JIT recompilers commonly have trouble correctly caching/validating self-referential infinite-loop code blocks in their own code-cache page-mapping ("recLUT") logic, and this is exactly that class of block. `pcsx2_get_threads` confirms **TID 1, the currently-RUNNING real IOP thread, sits at exactly this address** - directly explaining why this specific PC is hit so often (it's the genuine, real, currently-active IOP idle thread) and why the exception recurs periodically (every time PCSX2's recompiler needs to re-validate/re-enter this specific self-loop block).

**The ~50 other IOP threads reported at `PC=0x0000aea4` are not stuck or deadlocked either** - disassembly of that address shows `jr ->ra` (a plain leaf-function return) immediately following a small real kernel routine (`li v0,0x20; syscall` at `0xae9c-0xaea0`, a real low-level kernel primitive, most plausibly a sleep/yield-style syscall wrapper given its short leaf-function shape). The shared PC simply reflects that this snapshot caught dozens of real threads at the same instruction offset because they all recently called through this exact common, tiny, real kernel library routine - a real, benign scheduling snapshot artifact, not a hang.

**The substantial, newly-quantified real finding: real hardware's IOP kernel runs a persistent 54-thread real scheduler even at rest**, continuously, as part of ordinary healthy operation. This project's own IOP model, by contrast, has been an honestly-documented simplification since around Round 205 (or earlier) that **halts the IOP entirely once it finishes running every discovered module** - meaning this project's own emulated trace has literally zero ongoing IOP-side thread activity post-module-discovery, versus real hardware's genuinely rich, persistent, always-running 54-thread kernel environment. This is a concrete, now-quantified (54 vs. 0) architectural gap that plausibly underlies several of this investigation's longest-standing open threads at once: the CDVD driver's ongoing real dispatch activity (Round 326's confirmed `ReadCd` command, and any FURTHER real reads a persistent CDVD service thread might issue that this project's halted IOP model could never replicate), the registration-table population question (Rounds 323-325 - a real driver "register" call would need an ongoing real IOP thread to make it, which this project's model doesn't have past module discovery), and more broadly, why this project's OWN emulated trace's control flow diverges from real hardware's the way Round 322/325 already found.

**No fix shipped this round** (this is architectural-scope evidence-gathering, matching this project's own established discipline of not speculatively re-architecting a major simplification without a concrete, scoped implementation plan first). `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm no source changes - docs-only.

Left as the concrete next step, now backed by a real, quantified number for the first time: assess what it would concretely take to keep this project's own IOP model's threads genuinely alive/scheduled past module discovery (rather than halting), even in a simplified form - and whether that is the real, root architectural fix this entire multi-hundred-round investigation has been converging toward, or whether a smaller, targeted subset (e.g., just keeping the CDVD driver's own thread alive and dispatching) would be sufficient to let this project's own trace start exercising the real disc-read/SYSTEM.CNF-auto-boot path Round 326 confirmed real hardware relies on.

## Round 330 (source-review, docs-only, CORRECTION to Round 329): the IOP does NOT halt after module discovery - task #179 (long predating this session) already fixed this to a real, interrupt-responsive `idle` mechanism; the real architectural gap is narrower than Round 329 claimed

Direct continuation of Round 329's own stated next step ("assess what it would concretely take to keep this project's own IOP model's threads genuinely alive/scheduled past module discovery"). Reading `source/hw/iop_module_loader.c` and `source/core/iop/iop_core.c` directly to scope the work **found Round 329's own characterization was materially wrong and needs correcting**, per this project's established self-correction discipline (same pattern as Round 320's correction of Round 319, Round 270's correction of Round 269, etc. - own mistakes get fixed transparently, not left standing).

**Round 329 claimed**: "this project's own IOP model...halts entirely once it finishes running every discovered module." **This is inaccurate as of task #179** (explicitly cited in-code as predating this entire session by a wide margin - the comment reads "task #179 continued (54th finding)"), which replaced an earlier, genuinely-unconditional `halt()` at the module-boot-complete site with a real `idle` flag mechanism: `iop_module_loader_try_handle()`'s three real completion-detection sites (panic-loop bypass, unconditional-trap-stub bypass, genuine loadcore completion) all set `st->idle = 1` (not `st->halted = 1`), and `iop_core.c`'s own scheduler-tick function (~line 1637-1650) explicitly documents and implements the real distinction: **while idle, the IOP skips real fetch/decode/execute (correctly, since the module-loader's own trampoline address isn't real executable code) but keeps running `iop_timers_tick()`, `iop_asyncio_service()`, and `iop_check_vblank()` unconditionally every tick, and re-checks for a genuine pending hardware interrupt on every call via `iop_check_hw_interrupt()`. The moment a real interrupt is found pending, `idle` is cleared and the very next call resumes genuine fetch/decode/execute at the vectored exception address - running whatever real handler code the already-loaded modules installed.** This is a real, correct, interrupt-responsive idle model, not a permanent halt - Round 329's "0 vs 54 threads" framing overstated the gap by implying this project's IOP simply stops dead, when it in fact keeps timers/VBLANK/async-I/O ticking and remains genuinely able to resume real handler execution.

**The real, narrower gap, honestly restated**: real hardware's IOP kernel runs a genuine **multi-threaded scheduler** - 54 concurrently-live real threads (Round 329's own live capture), each independently schedulable, sleeping/waking on their own real semaphores/events/timers, with the kernel's dispatcher actively context-switching between them. This project's own model, even with the real `idle`/un-idle mechanism above, only ever has **one single logical execution context** (the IOP interpreter's own `pc`/register state) that can be either "idle, ticking peripherals" or "actively executing real code at one vectored address" - it has no concept of multiple concurrent threads, a thread-ready queue, or context-switching between several independently-blocked real threads. So the accurate framing is not "0 threads vs 54" (Round 329's overclaim) but **"1 schedulable context vs 54"** - a real, still-significant, but meaningfully smaller and differently-shaped gap than Round 329 described.

**Whether this narrower gap is actually what's blocking the CDVD/registration-table findings (Rounds 323-326) remains open and unverified** - correcting the overclaim does not itself resolve that question. It's plausible that a single reactivatable context is sufficient to eventually run whatever real code populates the registration tables or issues further CDVD commands (if the right interrupt/timer condition is ever met), OR it's possible genuine concurrent multi-threading is structurally required (e.g., if real driver code relies on one thread blocking on a semaphore while another thread's handler signals it - a pattern this project's single-context model cannot represent at all). This round does not resolve which is true - it only corrects the prior round's overstated framing and clarifies exactly what would need investigating to find out (e.g., live-tracing whether real hardware's CDVD driver thread specifically, vs. some other one of the 54, is the one that would need modeling).

**No fix shipped this round** (this is a documentation/analysis correction, not a code change - `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm no source changes). This keeps the project's own docs honest and accurate rather than leaving Round 329's overstated framing to mislead a future round into scoping unnecessary work.

## Round 332 (real fix, shipped): silenced the last remaining pre-existing devkitPPC/GCC warning - strncpy -> memcpy in the ROMDIR name parser, no behavioral change

Direct follow-up to Round 331's clean baseline check, which reconfirmed the one remaining pre-existing build warning (`iop_module_loader.c:225`, `-Wstringop-truncation` on `strncpy(e->name, name, 10)`). This has been flagged as benign in every round that's mentioned it going back many rounds - the very next line already explicitly writes `e->name[10] = '\0'`, so truncation without termination was never actually possible - but a benign warning is still worth cleanly silencing when the fix is this small, safe, and mechanical, rather than leaving it to be re-noted indefinitely.

**The fix**: the local `name[11]` buffer being copied from is *already* explicitly null-terminated (`name[10] = '\0'`) several lines above the flagged call, so all 11 bytes (10 real characters + the guaranteed terminator) can simply be `memcpy`'d directly into `e->name` (itself declared `char name[10 + 1]`) in one step - equally correct, clearer, and not subject to `-Wstringop-truncation`'s static-analysis limitation (which can't prove `strncpy` won't truncate a fixed-length, non-null-guaranteed source, even though the following line already handled that case manually). Purely mechanical, zero behavioral change - same bytes end up in `e->name` either way.

**Verification (mandatory workflow, full - a tracked source file changed).** `gcc -fsyntax-only` clean. Full host-native regression suite (rebuilt fresh after the mid-session sandbox reset per Round 331's own new generic runner): **122/122 pass, 0 failures.** Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild: `make` exit 0, **zero warnings this time** (previously the sole remaining pre-existing warning; now gone), `pcsx2-wii-git.elf` (2,630,616 bytes) / `pcsx2-wii-git.dol` (468,800 bytes) produced - a few dozen bytes different from the immediately-prior build (expected: the actual generated code differs slightly, `memcpy` vs `strncpy` compiles to different instruction sequences), not a red flag.

This is a small, low-risk, purely-cosmetic (but genuinely real and verified) cleanup - not a step toward the boot-blocker investigation, but good hygiene while the repository is in a freshly-reverified-healthy state.

## Round 334 (synthesis, docs-only): consolidating Rounds 322-333 - where the boot-blocker investigation actually stands now

A budget-aware pause point after a dense cluster of rounds (322-333, spanning live-hardware breakpoints/watchpoints, an offline scratch-driver push before its BIOS/disc inputs were lost to a sandbox reset, source-level architectural review, a real correction, and a small shipped hygiene fix). This round collects the thread rather than opening a new one.

**What is now solidly established, with direct evidence (not inference), across this cluster:**

1. **Real OSDSYS uses GS output circuit 2** (`PMODE=0x66`, `DISPFB2`/`DISPLAY2`), never circuit 1, for this real BIOS/disc/game combination (Round 321) - corrects this project's own thirty-plus-round-standing success-detection criteria.
2. **Real hardware never revisits the `0x8000CF88` per-frame dispatcher after early boot** - a live breakpoint across 2.58B real cycles (Round 322) and, independently, live watchpoints on the two registration tables that dispatcher's own exit condition depends on across 4.08B real cycles (Round 325) both came back clean/never-hit, spanning confirmed sustained real gameplay.
3. **This project's own emulated trace, by contrast, genuinely does re-enter that same dispatcher** from the one real, correctly-identified caller (`ra=0x8000F86C`, Round 323) in a tight, unthrottled busy-spin exactly coincident with its own RPC-counter plateau, and the two registration tables really are empty in that trace even at 1.72B instructions deep (Round 324) - this project's own control flow demonstrably diverges from real hardware's, not merely runs slower or differently-timed.
4. **Real hardware does issue a genuine CD-ROM `ReadCd` command (N-command register = `0x06`) during this boot** (Round 326), confirmed stable/unchanged across the entire remainder of a long live session (Round 333) - i.e., a real, one-time, front-loaded disc read early in boot, not a recurring one. The blocker is now precisely: **the specific instant this project's trace is resting at has the IOP's own global interrupt-enable flag turned off, and IOP PC does not appear to be advancing meaningfully across a million-instruction window either way** - two related but distinct open questions (why is IEc off here, and why isn't PC clearly progressing) that need a real disassembly of the code around `0x00118F7C` before further action, rather than a guess.

## Round 339 (correction to Round 338 + real disassembly): the resting IOP PC is NOT frozen - it's a genuine, actively-advancing loop that was being aliased by 50,000-instruction-granularity sampling; real IOP-side interrupts DO fire periodically (Status.IEc does toggle back on), reframing whether/when the Round 338 CDVD interrupt could ever be delivered

Direct follow-up to Round 338, prompted by writing a small (self-authored, public-ISA-spec-based, not copyrighted-BIOS-derived) MIPS-I instruction decoder to properly read the code around the "frozen" PC rather than guess from raw hex, per this project's own standing discipline against unverified conclusions.

**Method.** Dumped a wider (257-word) raw memory window around the Round 338 resting PC and decoded it with a small scratch MIPS-I disassembler (public R3000A/MIPS-I opcode encodings only - no BIOS bytes transcribed, same category of legitimate reference material as this project's existing ps2sdk/ps2tek citations). Found the region is NOT a simple polled-flag spin-loop; it contains real function-call code interleaved with what is very likely a repeated data table (a 3-word pattern - two pointer-shaped values plus a small constant - recurring at regular ~48-byte strides) and comparisons against fixed constant values. Given the ambiguity of a purely linear byte disassembly (real code/data often interleave; a naive linear sweep can't always tell them apart without symbol boundaries), followed up with a finer-grained, single-slice-at-a-time trace (`system_run_interleaved(1)`, confirmed via `source/core/system.c`'s own documented contract - each "slice" is exactly one real `iop_core_step()` call, not a fraction) printing IOP PC, COP0 Status/Cause, and `exception_pending` after every individual real IOP instruction.

**Found: the IOP PC genuinely advances normally** - 0x00118F80 -> 0x00118F84 -> (a real exception fires: PC jumps to the real general exception vector 0x80000080, `exception_pending=1`, `cop0_status` bit 0 correctly clears per real MIPS exception-entry semantics) -> 0x00118F88 -> 0x00118F8C -> 0x00118F90 -> ... continuing forward step by step exactly as expected. **Round 338's "IOP PC stayed frozen at exactly 0x00118F7C across a million-instruction window" claim is corrected**: it was real, honestly-reported raw data (the coarse ~50,000-instruction-granularity samples genuinely did all read the identical address), but the conclusion drawn from it (a true freeze/stall) does not hold - this is a real, aliasing artifact of sampling at intervals close to this loop's own real iteration period, not a genuine stall. Per this project's own established self-correction precedent (Round 320-corrects-319, Round 270-corrects-269, Round 330-corrects-329), this is flagged explicitly rather than silently amended.

The single-step trace also directly caught this loop taking a REAL interrupt mid-stride (the jump to 0x80000080 at the trace's step=2) - meaning **Status.IEc is not permanently stuck at 0 as Round 338's single snapshot suggested; it genuinely toggles back on periodically as part of this loop's own normal, real interrupt-servicing behavior**, exactly as correct real MIPS/IOP kernel code should. This means the CDVD/IRQ2 interrupt Round 338 raised (still pending in I_STAT, since nothing observed in this trace acknowledged/cleared it) is NOT necessarily permanently undeliverable - it plausibly could be delivered on a later pass through this same loop, once IEc happens to be high again AND the real exception-vector dispatch logic's own IRQ-priority-ordering reaches bit 2. This round's tracing did not run long enough to directly confirm that delivery (`exc_pending` was only ever observed going to 1 with a Cause value consistent with the loop's PRE-EXISTING regular interrupt, not confirmed yet to be specifically the CDVD one) - an honestly-flagged open question, not claimed as resolved.

Left as the concrete next step: extend the single-step trace considerably further (thousands to millions of individual `system_run_interleaved(1)` calls, budget permitting, or a coarser-but-still-fine-grained periodic PC sample - e.g. every 100-1000 instructions rather than every 50,000 - to avoid Round 338's aliasing mistake) to determine whether the pending CDVD interrupt is ever actually delivered to the real registered handler (0x00120d60, Round 338), and if so what real code there does with it.

## Round 340 (real, shipped source fix + honest correction): fixed a genuine IRQ low-range priority-starvation gap in iop_check_hw_interrupt() (mirrors the already-shipped Round 174 precedent one level deeper) - but direct re-testing shows this does NOT resolve Round 338/339's specific resting loop, because that loop's "exception" turned out to be an unrelated synchronous Reserved-Instruction trap, not a starved hardware interrupt

**The real, shipped fix.** Round 339 left an open question: does the pending CDVD (IRQ2) interrupt Round 338 raised ever get delivered to its already-real, already-registered handler (0x00120d60)? Extended fine-grained tracing (up to ~90 million further instructions, well past Round 339's short window) directly caught the answer: no, and found why. `iop_check_hw_interrupt()`'s low-range dispatch logic (`source/core/iop/iop_core.c`) computed only the SINGLE numerically-lowest pending+unmasked IRQ bit and attempted dispatch for that one bit alone - if it failed (no real handler registered for it yet), the code fell straight through to the soft range / fixed-vector default, never trying any OTHER pending bit that might already have a real, ready handler. Directly observed: VBLANK_START (bit 0, always the lowest bit whenever a VBLANK is pending - which is essentially always, since this project's own already-correct `iop_check_vblank()` raises it unconditionally every real frame) was simultaneously pending alongside CDVD (bit 2, which DOES have a real registered handler at this point, confirmed via `iop_hle_intr_get_intr_handler(2)`) - and the old code's "only try the lowest bit" logic meant CDVD's ready handler was never even attempted.

This is a genuine architectural gap one level deeper than the one Round 174 already found and fixed (which addressed the LOW-range-vs-SOFT-range boundary: a low-range irq failing no longer blocks the soft range from its own independent chance). Round 340 mirrors that exact, already-proven, already-shipped design precedent one level further in: the low range's own internal dispatch loop now tries EVERY pending+unmasked bit, in ascending real-hardware-priority order, until one actually dispatches, instead of giving up on the whole low range after the first (lowest) bit's attempt fails. No change to real priority ORDER - a lower-numbered bit with a real handler still always wins over a higher-numbered one, exactly as before; this only stops a real, ready handler from being starved forever by an unrelated, still-unregistered lower bit.

**Verification**: 122/122 host-native regression tests pass; clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild (incidentally also fixed one newly-surfaced, pre-existing, unrelated `-Wstringop-truncation` warning in `halt()`'s own `strncpy` - same real category as Round 332's fix, this one a genuine latent non-termination risk rather than just cosmetic, fixed with an explicit terminator write). Both fixes are real, small, mechanical, and fully covered by the existing test suite.

## Round 341 (offline scratch instrumentation, direct continuation of Round 340): confirmed the Reserved-Instruction trap at 0x118F84 is genuine (occurs in a clean, non-injected trace too, not a probe artifact) and precisely located inside the real IGREETING module

**Found: the trap is genuine.** Across the clean 3000-instruction trace, the same Reserved-Instruction trap (`ExcCode=10`, `EPC=0x00118F84`) recurred 187 times - not a probe artifact. Cross-referencing this address against Round 336's own real IOPBTCONF module-list dump precisely locates it: `IGREETING` (a real, cited IOP module - entry `0x118d00`) is the module whose real code contains this address; the very next module in the boot list, `SIFCMD`, doesn't begin until `0x1198d0`, so `0x118F84` falls squarely inside IGREETING's own loaded image, not in any inter-module gap.

**Structural detail (not yet conclusively explained).** The exact same 3-word byte pattern (`0x00112DA0`/`0x001131FC`/`0x000000E4`) recurs identically five times at regular 0x30-byte strides within IGREETING's image (`0x118F20`, `0x118F50`, `0x118F80`, `0x118FB0`, `0x118FE0`) - consistent with five near-identical inlined per-item processing blocks (plausibly IGREETING iterating over several real boot-greeting resources - icons, sounds, or animation elements - each needing its own real function-pointer dispatch). The real, traced control flow does correctly take at least one genuine branch (from `0x118F0C` to `0x118F78`, skipping an intervening real function call at `0x118F70`) but then falls through *linearly* from `0x118F80` into `0x118F84` rather than via any indirect call - meaning either this project's own IOP interpreter is missing a real branch/jump that real hardware would take at this exact point, or the middle word of this triplet genuinely is supposed to be read as **data** (e.g. a real function-pointer table entry, loaded via a real indirect-call sequence like `lw`+`jalr`) that a correct trace would never linearly fetch as an instruction at all.

**One real, already-self-documented candidate root cause, not yet confirmed:** `iop_elf.h`'s own header comment already flags that this project's ELF/IRX loader does **not** compute or set `$gp` (the MIPS o32 ABI global pointer) - a scope limit adopted after the one module byte-dumped at the time (`SYSMEM`) showed no `R_MIPS_GPREL16` relocations. Real MIPS o32 position-independent code commonly loads function pointers via `$gp`-relative addressing for indirect calls; if IGREETING's real code relies on this (unlike SYSMEM) and `$gp` is left at 0/uninitialized, an indirect-call sequence could read from the wrong address - though this project's loader would have hard-failed with "unsupported relocation type" if IGREETING's own `.rel` section contained a `GPREL16`-class entry, and Round 336 already confirmed IGREETING loads with `rc=0` (no error) - meaning if `$gp` really is the issue, IGREETING's own code must rely on the CALLER (not an ELF relocation) to have set `$gp` correctly before jumping in, per the standard o32 calling-convention split of responsibility. This is flagged honestly as a plausible, not yet proven, hypothesis - not a claimed root cause.

No fix attempted this round (still diagnosis; confirming genuineness and precisely locating the module is real, evidenced progress, but resolving it responsibly needs either a section-header-aware disassembly pass (to definitively tell whether `0x118F84` is inside IGREETING's real `.text` or `.rodata`/`.data`, which this project's own already-existing `iop_elf.c` infrastructure could be extended to expose) or direct confirmation of whether `$gp` is genuinely used/needed here - neither completed yet). `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm docs-only, zero source changes this round.
