### Round 403 (task #130, "rework the elf loader and see if there are some bugs") - MAJOR finding: Round 402's corruption is NOT an ELF-loader/relocation bug at all - it's a genuine, reproducible, unbounded IOP call-stack leak happening during organic boot execution, traced to a specific broken NULL-callback dispatch inside THREADMAN's own code

**Method**: built a fresh scratch tree (`/tmp/r402_build`, synced from the current committed repo) and added new scratch-only diagnostics to `iop_module_loader.c`/`.h` (never committed): `r403_romdir_find_payload()` (real ROMDIR payload_off/size lookup), `r403_get_modlist_count()`/`r403_get_module_info()` (full boot-list dump). Cross-checked the actual raw REBOOT ELF bytes directly from `bios.bin` (bypassing this project's own loader entirely) against a from-scratch Python ELF32/MIPS parser to get independent ground truth on REBOOT's real program headers, section headers, and `.rel.text`/`.rel.data` relocation entries.

**Step 1 - ELF loader/relocation logic is correct (disproves Round 402's leading hypothesis)**: manually computed the expected post-relocation word for REBOOT's real `.text` offset 0x10 (a real `R_MIPS_26` relocation, entry `[1]` in `.rel.text`) by hand from the raw pre-relocation file bytes (`0x0C000083`) and this project's own real cited R_MIPS_26 algorithm: result `0x0C04711F` (a valid `JAL 0x0011C47C` - REBOOT's own real `loadcore` import stub). A scratch driver reading IOP RAM at `entry+0x10` **immediately after `system_init()` (0 cycles run, i.e. right after loading+relocation, before any interpreted execution)** confirmed this EXACT expected value is what's actually in memory. This directly disproves Round 402's "ELF loader/relocation bug" hypothesis - the loader is provably correct at load time, byte-for-byte.

**Step 2 - the real bug is a runtime write, not a load-time one**: the same address was re-checked at increasing cycle counts (1K/10K/100K/1M/5M/20M). It stayed correctly `0x0C04711F` through 1,000,000 cycles, then was found corrupted to `0x00112DA0` (Round 402's garbage value) by 5,000,000 cycles - something WRITES over this already-correctly-loaded code DURING boot execution, well after loading completes. A module-range cross-check (all 29 real boot-list modules' load ranges) confirmed NO other module's own PT_LOAD segment overlaps REBOOT's memory range - ruling out a "later module clobbers an earlier one" bump-allocator bug.

**Step 3 - root-caused to a genuine, unbounded IOP $sp (stack pointer) leak**: binary-searching the exact cycle range (coarse 1000-cycle-stride scan, then single-stepping) pinpointed the corrupting write as an ordinary-looking `sw $s2, 0x20($sp)` instruction inside THREADMAN's own module code (IOP pc≈0x111854, well within THREADMAN's real range `0x0010C5D0-0x00113264`) - a completely normal-looking register-save instruction, EXCEPT `$sp` itself had already drifted down to an address inside REBOOT's memory region. Tracking `$sp` itself (not just the target memory) over the preceding cycles showed it decreasing by **exactly 0x30 bytes on every single iteration of a repeating instruction sequence**, with zero variance across at least 9+ consecutive 1000-cycle windows (`0x0011D280 -> 0x0011D0A0 -> 0x0011CEC0 -> ...`, each step exactly -0x1E0 per 1000-cycle window, which single-instruction tracing resolved to exactly -0x30 per loop iteration). This is a genuine, mechanical, monotonic IOP call-stack leak - not random corruption, not an ELF issue - that will eventually overwrite ANY module sitting below wherever it started, given enough boot time; REBOOT and SIFCMD merely happen to be in its path.

**Step 4 - the leaking call site**: single-instruction tracing of one full loop iteration (starting at IOP pc=0x111870) shows a repeating structure: two calls into TIMEMANI's real time-query routine (target `0x00112998`, called twice per iteration, likely reading a 64-bit system-time value's two halves), two more calls to internal THREADMAN subroutines (`0x00112428`, `0x00112460`), and finally an **indirect call via `jalr $ra, $v0`** at pc=`0x001119A0`, where `$v0` and `$a0` are loaded from `[$s0+0x18]`/`[$s0+0x1C]` immediately beforehand (`lw $v0,0x18($s0)` / `lw $a0,0x1C($s0)` - the classic "call a registered callback(arg) from a list/queue entry" pattern). Critically, `$s0` itself was `0x00000000` (NULL) at this point - the loaded "function pointer" (`$v0=0x00000020`) and "argument" simply happen to be whatever raw bytes sit at this project's own low-memory HLE trap/trampoline sentinel region (address `0x18`/`0x1C`), not a real callback at all. This project's own `iop_core.c` "modeled low region" check (`phys_pc < 0x100`, cited in that file's own Round-173-era comment) treats ALL of `0x0-0xFF` as already-handled/excluded from its "wandered into unpopulated memory" halt, even though only a handful of SPECIFIC addresses within that range (`0xA0`/`0xB0`/`0xC0`/`0xE4`/`0xE8`/`0xEC`/`0xF0`) are actually meaningfully modeled - so a call to the unrecognized address `0x20` silently falls through without halting, and the loop keeps going.

**What this establishes and what remains open**: this is a real, precisely-located, 100%-reproducible finding (exact PC, exact leaked byte count, exact triggering pattern), not a guess - but the FULL root cause is not yet closed out. Two open sub-questions for a follow-up round: (1) why is `$s0` NULL here - is this a real THREADMAN alarm/timer/callback queue this project doesn't yet populate (an honest modeling gap - the underlying real queue-walk this loop performs may legitimately need a registered callback this project never installs), or is it a genuine bug in how this project's own call-stack/scheduling drives IOP execution into this function repeatedly without it ever being allowed to complete past this dispatch point; (2) confirm precisely where the net -0x30/iteration is actually lost - is it the JALR-to-0x20 "call" itself never restoring `$sp` (most likely, since the low-address trap fallthrough was never designed to handle a real function-call-with-stack-frame convention), or the enclosing loop's own prologue re-executing without a matching epilogue. No source changes made this round - this is a significant, well-evidenced repositioning of the Round 399/402 investigation, not a fix; a targeted fix should follow directly from resolving sub-question (1)/(2) above, not be guessed at blind.

This finding also means: any future round attempting a real fix here has a very good chance of being the single most impactful bug fix toward the splash screen found so far in this project - a permanently-growing, self-corrupting IOP stack during normal boot execution would eventually corrupt any module in its path, degrading system stability the longer boot runs, regardless of which specific module happens to sit in its way.

### Round 404 ("check all h files" - real ps2sdk iop/system/threadman/include directory) - real thcommon.h/list.h internal kernel source strongly corroborates Round 403's IOP stack-leak root cause

**Source checked**: all 7 files in the real ps2sdk `iop/system/threadman/include` directory (thbase.h, thevent.h, thfpool.h, thmsgbx.h, thsemap.h, thvpool.h, xthbase.h) - the public real THREADMAN API headers. thbase.h/thevent.h/thsemap.h were already incorporated (Round 395); thfpool.h (fixed memory pool)/thmsgbx.h (message box)/thvpool.h (variable memory pool)/xthbase.h (extended thread API, SDK 2.5+) are new, but contain no struct layouts relevant to the Round 403 stack-leak investigation - noted for completeness, no action needed.

**The real prize**: thbase.h's real `SetAlarm(iop_sys_clock_t *sys_clock, unsigned int (*alarm_cb)(void *userdata), void *arg)` signature, cross-referenced via the doxygen page's own internal links, led to the REAL internal kernel struct definitions (`iop/system/threadman/src/include/thcommon.h` and `iop/system/threadman/src/include/list.h` - a modern, open, functionally-real reimplementation of THREADMAN's own internal data structures, not literal Sony source, but structurally authoritative for how a real THREADMAN kernel manages these lists):

- `struct alarm { struct heaptag tag; struct list_head alarm_list; u64 target; unsigned int (*cb)(void *userdata); void *userptr; };` - a real Alarm queue entry: exactly the "callback function pointer immediately followed by a userdata/arg pointer" field pair Round 403 found being loaded from `[$s0+0x18]`/`[$s0+0x1C]` right before the leaking `jalr $ra,$v0` call. Field order and type shape (fn ptr immediately followed by an arg pointer) match exactly, even though the specific byte offsets differ from this particular open reimplementation's own compiler layout (expected: real retail Sony BIOS has its own independent struct packing).
- `struct thread_context` (the single real global THREADMAN state struct) has SEVENTEEN separate `struct list_head` members: `ready_queue[128]`, `thread_list`, `semaphore`, `event_flag`, `mbox`, `vpool`, `fpool`, `alarm`, `alarm_pool`, `sleep_queue`, `delay_queue`, `dormant_queue`, `delete_queue` - i.e. essentially every one of THREADMAN's real subsystems is backed by the same `list_head` convention.
- `list.h`'s real `struct list_head { struct list_head *next, *prev; }` is a classic circular doubly-linked list with a **self-referential sentinel head**: `list_init()` sets `list->next = list; list->prev = list;`, and `list_empty()` checks `list == list->next` - NOT `next == NULL`. This is the standard, well-known "circular list with sentinel" idiom.

**Why this matters**: Round 403 found `$s0` (the alarm-queue entry pointer being walked) was `0x00000000` (NULL) at the exact point of the leaking indirect call, with the "callback"/"arg" fields read from this project's own low-memory HLE sentinel region as an accidental side effect of dereferencing that NULL pointer. The real list-head idiom just confirmed above means a CORRECTLY-initialized, genuinely-empty real alarm list would have its head's `next` pointing back to ITSELF (a valid, non-NULL, self-referential address) - never to `0`. A real walk loop terminates by comparing against the list head (self-reference), not by NULL-checking. If this project's own environment for organically-executing THREADMAN's real init code never correctly ran the equivalent of `list_init()` on its own internal `alarm`/`ready_queue`/etc. list heads (leaving that memory at its raw zero-initialized state instead), a real walk loop that assumes the standard self-referential-sentinel convention would misinterpret "next == 0" as "one more real entry to visit" instead of "back at the head, list is empty" - dereferencing NULL and reading garbage exactly as Round 403 observed.

**What remains open (unchanged from Round 403, now more precisely scoped)**: this is strong corroborating evidence for a specific mechanism, not yet a confirmed fix. The next concrete step (Round 405) is to check whether this project's own organic IOP execution ever runs THREADMAN's real init code far enough to perform the equivalent of `list_init()` on its internal list heads (a real, findable function call in THREADMAN's own module code, distinct from this project's synthetic thread-scheduling HLE in `iop_hle_thread.c`) - i.e. is this an honest gap where THREADMAN's real init never completes/runs, or does something in this project's environment leave already-initialized memory at zero regardless. No source changes this round - purely a citation-gathering and hypothesis-corroboration round, per the user's "check all h files" request.

### Round 405 (task #131, user's "lets go" - direct continuation of the Round 403/404 IOP stack-leak investigation): CONFIRMED via live single-instruction trace - the leaking list-walk's head field is genuinely zero, not self-referential, and this fully explains the exact Round 402 REBOOT-corruption mechanism too

**Method**: built a fresh scratch driver (`driver405c.c`, `/tmp/r402_build`, never committed) that single-steps IOP execution one instruction at a time from the top of the leaking function (pc=`0x00111850`, first found in Round 403/404's disassembly work), logging every change to `$s0`-`$s3` alongside the exact instruction word and PC that caused it - a full, unambiguous data-flow trace through one real iteration of the loop, rather than further static disassembly guessing.

**Finding 1 - confirms `$s2` = `&thctx` exactly, and pins down its real address**: at function entry, `$s2` is set (via `addu $s2,$a0,$zero` at `0x111858`) to the function's own first argument, observed as `0x00112DA0` - i.e. THREADMAN's real global thread-context struct lives at this exact IOP RAM address, confirming Round 405's working hypothesis from the prior (interrupted) analysis pass. This address falls squarely inside THREADMAN's own real module range (`0x0010C5D0-0x00113264`, Round 403), i.e. it is genuine THREADMAN `.data`/`.bss`, not an unclaimed/misattributed region.

**Finding 2 - the exact list-head load and its value, live**: at pc=`0x1118B4` (`lw $s0, 0x45C($s2)`), `$s0` is loaded directly from `thctx+0x45C` and observed to be **exactly `0x00000000`**. Critically, `$s3` - unchanged across the entire traced span, carried in from the caller - is `0x001131FC`, which is exactly `$s2 + 0x45C` (`0x00112DA0 + 0x45C = 0x001131FC`, confirmed by direct arithmetic): i.e. **`$s3` is `&(thctx+0x45C)` itself**, the list head's own address, being used exactly the way real `list_for_each(pos, head)` uses its `head` parameter. The subsequent `beq $s0,$s3,...` (pc=`0x111914`, real loop-termination check comparing the current walk pointer against the head) does NOT branch (`0 != 0x001131FC`), so the loop treats the zeroed field as "one more real node to visit" instead of "empty list, stop" - exactly Round 404's predicted failure mode, now directly observed rather than inferred. This is the first LIVE, INSTRUCTION-LEVEL confirmation (not corroboration) that a THREADMAN list head is holding raw zero instead of the real self-referential sentinel a correctly-initialized empty list requires.

**Finding 3 - the NULL dereference itself, live**: two instructions later (pc=`0x111920`, `lw $s1, 0x0($s0)` = `head->next` per the standard list-node layout), with `$s0` already confirmed `0`, this is a direct, literal `lw $s1, 0(0)` - reading IOP address 0 - and the loop proceeds using whatever this project models at address 0 as if it were a real list node's `next` pointer. This is the precise instant Round 403's downstream `[$s0+0x18]`/`[$s0+0x1C]` garbage callback/arg load (leading to the leaking `jalr` two calls later) becomes inevitable - traced back to this exact single load, not just the general vicinity.

**Finding 4 (bonus, closes out Round 402's separate open question)**: this trace also fully explains Round 402's REBOOT-memory-corruption finding without any further mystery. `$s2` (`= 0x00112DA0`, the thctx pointer) is saved to the stack every single iteration via the function's own ordinary prologue (`sw $s2, 0x20($sp)`, ordinary callee-save, already seen in Round 403/404's static disassembly). Since `$sp` leaks downward by a fixed `0x30` bytes per iteration (Round 403) with no bound, this same ordinary, correct instruction eventually executes with `$sp` pointing inside REBOOT's memory - at which point it deposits the literal, constant value `0x00112DA0` there. This is EXACTLY Round 402's originally-observed "mystery" corruption value (`0x00112DA0`, the first of the recurring 3-word sequence) - not a wild/misdirected store, not a relocation bug, just a completely ordinary register-spill instruction executing at an address it was never meant to reach, over and over, because of the unrelated stack leak. Round 402's second/third recurring words (`0x001131FC`, `0x000000E4`) are consistent with this same mechanism: `0x001131FC` = `$s3` (also callee-saved that same prologue, one word over) and is itself `$s2+0x45C` as shown above; `0x000000E4` remains unexplained by this round's trace (not one of the four registers directly tracked) but is very plausibly a third saved register from the same prologue, a strong candidate for quick confirmation in a future round if ever needed, though it is no longer a mystery in kind - it is understood to be more callee-save spill from the identical mechanism.

**What this establishes**: the root cause chain from Round 402 through 405 is now a single, closed, fully-evidenced mechanism end-to-end: THREADMAN's real internal list head at `thctx+0x45C` is zero instead of self-referential -> its walk loop misreads "empty" as "one more node" -> dereferences NULL -> eventually calls through a garbage function pointer that this project's low-address fallthrough silently absorbs without restoring `$sp` -> `$sp` leaks 0x30 bytes/iteration, unbounded -> ordinary callee-save spills from the SAME loop's own prologue eventually land inside REBOOT's (and any other sufficiently-nearby module's) memory, depositing the constant, now-fully-explained values Round 402 first found. Nothing in this chain is still an open "coincidence" or unexplained pattern - Round 402's finding, Round 403's finding, and Round 404's hypothesis are now one single, real, fully-traced bug.

**What remains open, honestly, for a future round**: WHY `thctx+0x45C` is zero instead of self-referential is still not itself resolved - this round proves the SYMPTOM live but not yet the ORIGIN. Two concrete, non-fabricated candidates for the next round: (1) confirm whether real THREADMAN's own init code (`thcommon.c`'s `_start()`, already confirmed via Round 403's citation to run to completion in this project's boot trace) is actually responsible for initializing this specific field at all, by locating the real init call site for this list (would require finding, in the real disassembly, an instruction sequence that writes `$s2+0x45C` with the value `$s2+0x45C` itself - a self-store - anywhere in the boot trace prior to this function's first execution, and confirming whether that store ever actually happens); (2) if no such store is ever found to occur, determine whether that's because the real init function that should perform it is never reached at all (a genuine, findable control-flow gap in this project's THREADMAN modeling) versus this being a field real THREADMAN legitimately initializes lazily on first real use elsewhere (e.g., only when the first real alarm/timer/etc. is actually registered by some other module, meaning an EMPTY structural state here might be less unusual than it currently looks, and the true bug might instead be in how the walk loop's own termination condition is reached - worth re-examining whether `$s3`'s exact value, sourced from the CALLER rather than this function, is itself correct in the first place). Not applying an unproven, guessed-at "just force list_init() everywhere" patch here is a deliberate, disciplined choice, consistent with this project's established "not fabricated without citation" precedent (Round 403's own explicit statement of the same discipline) - a source-level fix should follow directly from resolving (1)/(2) above, not precede it.

No source changes this round - purely a live single-instruction-trace investigation round (scratch-only, `driver405c.c`, never committed), directly continuing Round 403/404's already-documented methodology at the user's explicit "lets go" instruction.

### Round 406 (task #132, direct continuation of Round 405 per user's "do everything possible to reach the splash screen"): traced the full causal chain three more layers deeper - real list_init() runs correctly; the corruption is a genuine NULL-insert from a real "heaplib" pool allocator that fails for one specific allocation size

**Method**: built a new scratch instrumented copy of `iop_core.c` (`/tmp/r406_build`, never committed) adding a targeted memory-write watch (any store to `thctx+0x430`..`thctx+0x474`, the full span of THREADMAN's sibling list-head members) and several PC-range register watches, then ran the full known-good cold-boot warmup (2,079,000+200,000 cycles, the same window Round 405 used) capturing every relevant write and register state, instead of further static disassembly guessing.

**Finding 1 - `list_init()` genuinely runs correctly, seven times, exactly as expected**: found and disassembled the real 3-instruction `list_init(struct list_head*)` function itself (`0x00112440`-`0x00112448`: `sw $a0,0($a0)` / `jr $ra` / `sw $a0,4($a0)` in the delay slot - byte-exact match for real `list->next=list; list->prev=list;`). Live trace confirms it is called exactly 7 times in a row early in boot, correctly self-initializing 7 consecutive list-head structs at `thctx+0x430` through `thctx+0x464` (8-byte stride) - including our Round 405 target at `thctx+0x45C` (`0x001131FC`), which is confirmed to be set to the correct self-referential value `0x001131FC` at this point. This REVISES Round 405's open question: THREADMAN's real init code does NOT skip this field - it initializes it correctly.

**Finding 2 - immediately afterward, a genuine list_insert() call corrupts it back to zero by inserting a NULL node**: also found and disassembled the real doubly-linked-list "insert-before" primitive (`0x00112498`-`0x001124B4`, the standard 6-instruction real `__list_add`-style shape: `Y.next=X; Y.prev=X.prev; X.prev=Y; (X.prev_old).next=Y`). Live single-instruction tracing (register-level, not just memory writes) caught this function being called with `$a0` (X, the existing list head, `0x001131FC`) correct, but `$a1` (Y, the new node to insert) equal to **`0x00000000`** - a genuine NULL new-node argument. This directly, mechanically explains the exact zero values Round 405 found: inserting a NULL node before a self-referential empty list overwrites both of the head's own pointer fields with 0, exactly matching Round 405's live-captured evidence.

**Finding 3 - traced $a1's NULL back through two more real function layers to a genuine allocator call**: the NULL insert argument (`$a1`) is the return value ($v0) of a real small-object pool allocator function at `0x001124C0` (own real shape: take a pool-hint arg and a size, call a lower-level allocator, zero the result via a second call, and stamp a tag byte at `result+8` - a completely ordinary, real "allocate and construct a pool object" helper), which is itself called from a real caller at `0x00112348`-`0x00112384` that first checks `list_empty()` on a shared free-pool head (`0x00113204`) and, finding it empty, requests a fresh allocation of size `0x28` (40 bytes - a very plausible real size for a `struct alarm`-class object: list_head(8) + target(8) + callback fn ptr(4) + userptr(4) + tag/heaptag fields). Live tracing followed this all the way into the actual lower-level allocator's own real code (`0x0010B860`, a genuine 40+ instruction real function with a normal prologue/epilogue, confirmed via a wide instruction-level trace showing 748 real instruction-steps of it executing for THIS specific call, not a stub or unresolved-import fallback as Round 406's mid-round hypothesis initially suspected) - and this real allocator call, for this specific `size=0x28` request, returns `$v0=0`. A DIFFERENT concurrent call elsewhere in the same boot window (`size=0x50`, 80 bytes) was observed reaching the same allocator function successfully. This is a genuine, size-specific allocation failure inside a real, executing (not missing/stubbed) piece of guest code - not an emulator modeling gap in the sense Round 402/403 found, and not an unresolved-import fallback as briefly suspected mid-round (that hypothesis is explicitly retracted: the code at `0x0010B860` is real, loaded, and does execute, confirmed by direct instruction-level trace).

**What this establishes**: the full causal chain is now traced FIVE real function layers deep, end to end, every link backed by live register/memory evidence rather than static inference: `list_init()` (correct) -> `list_empty()` check on a shared free-pool (correctly detects empty) -> pool-growth call requesting a 40-byte block -> a real lower-level allocator function (genuinely executes, not missing) -> returns NULL for this specific size/pool state -> the NULL propagates back up three call frames -> gets inserted as a "new list node" into an unrelated list (`thctx+0x45C`) without a NULL check -> corrupts that list's self-reference back to zero -> (Round 403/405's already-documented mechanism) a later walk of that corrupted list dereferences NULL, calls through a garbage pointer, and leaks the IOP stack by 0x30 bytes/iteration indefinitely.

**Finding 4 (closes the chain - the true, deepest root cause)**: disassembled `0x0010B860`'s own body in full (~50 real instructions). Its first real action is `lw $v1, 0($a0)` (dereferencing its own first argument, `$a0` - the "pool handle" this function was called with) followed by a loop that walks a free-block list starting from `$a0+8`, searching for a block of the requested size. `$a0` for our failing call is `MEM[0x00113248]` - a single, specific global pointer this project's own THREADMAN-region code reads immediately before every call into this allocator (`0x001124D4`-`0x001124D8`: `lui $a0,0x0011; lw $a0,0x3248($a0)`). A dedicated write-watch on this exact global address across the FULL cold-boot trace (2,079,000+200,000 cycles) found it is written to **exactly 3 times, all three writes storing 0x00000000** - twice by ordinary, generic zero-init passes (`0x0010AF4C`, the same bulk bss-clear loop Finding 1 already identified; `0x0010C74C`, a second, more targeted-looking zero-init) and once more by this project's own already-documented (Round 403/405) IOP stack leak spilling a callee-saved register through this address as an incidental casualty of the SAME unbounded `$sp` drift, not a real init write. **This global pointer is never once set to a real, non-NULL pool/arena address anywhere in this entire boot trace.** When the allocator dereferences it (`lw $v1,0($a0)` with `$a0=0`), it is walking garbage derived from low-memory address 0 and 8, not a real pool structure - the NULL return four calls later is the direct, mechanical, now fully-explained consequence of this one uninitialized global, not a real "out of memory" condition.

**What this establishes, end to end**: the causal chain is now traced SIX real layers deep, from a single root all the way to the visible stack-leak symptom: an IOP-RAM global "heaplib pool handle" (`0x00113248`) is left NULL after boot's generic zero-init passes, with no real init call in this trace ever populating it with a valid pool pointer -> the first real code that needs to grow the alarm/fpool free-list dereferences this NULL handle and, walking garbage, eventually returns NULL from the low-level block-search allocator -> that NULL propagates up through two real wrapper functions -> gets inserted as a "new node" into an unrelated, already-correctly-initialized list (`thctx+0x45C`) without a NULL check -> corrupts that list's self-reference back to zero (Round 405's finding) -> a later walk of the now-broken list dereferences NULL and calls through a garbage function pointer that this project's low-address fallthrough silently absorbs (Round 403's finding) -> the IOP call stack leaks 0x30 bytes/iteration forever, eventually corrupting REBOOT's (and potentially other modules') memory (Round 402's finding, fully explained by Round 405).

**What remains open for Round 407**: WHY the real pool-handle global is never populated - the two concrete, non-fabricated candidates are (1) a real "create/register the heaplib pool" call exists somewhere in THREADMAN's (or a sibling module's) real init code that this project's boot trace never reaches (a genuine, findable control-flow gap - the next step would be searching for real code elsewhere that writes a non-zero value to `0x00113248`-equivalent-computed addresses, or that calls a real "heap-pool-create" API by name/ordinal we haven't yet identified), or (2) this pool is deliberately meant to be created lazily by a DIFFERENT, earlier real caller of the SAME size-40 allocation path that this project's boot trace also never reaches for unrelated reasons (in which case the true gap is further upstream still). This round deliberately stops short of guessing at a fix - consistent with this project's established "not fabricated without citation" discipline (explicitly restated in Round 403/405) - implementing a synthetic/invented pool-creation shortcut here without first finding the REAL missing call site would risk papering over a genuine, larger control-flow gap rather than fixing it.

**Mid-round correction, stated honestly**: this round initially cross-referenced the export table's library name (`"heaplib"`, real bytes confirmed at `0x001129D4`) against real ps2sdk's own `iop/system/alloc/include/alloc.h` (fetched this round from `https://ps2dev.github.io/ps2sdk/alloc_8h.html`), which documents ordinals `4=malloc, 5=realloc, 6=free, 7=calloc, 8=memalign` - an exact numeric match to the ordinal markers this round found at the same export table (`0x1129DC`-`0x112A00`). Taken at face value this would mean the JAL at `0x1129EC` (ordinal 6) is real libc `free(ptr)`, not a size-based allocator - which would undercut Finding 4's "allocation failure" framing (`free(NULL)` is valid, defined, harmless C behavior, not a bug). However, this is flagged as UNCONFIRMED, not adopted: ps2sdk's `alloc.h` is an independently-authored HOMEBREW reimplementation library that merely shares a display name with whatever real retail Sony BIOS library this project's own loaded module actually exports - there is no guarantee the two assign the same function to the same ordinal number, and the directly-disassembled REAL behavior of the function at `0x0010B860` (walks a free-block list searching for a match to a caller-supplied SIZE argument, per Finding 4's own disassembly) does not match `free()`'s usual (no-size-argument, no list-search-by-size) behavior at all. The disassembled real code's own observed behavior is treated as the more reliable signal here, consistent with this project's methodology throughout (prefer directly-observed real behavior over name/ordinal pattern-matching against a differently-authored source) - but the ambiguity itself is recorded honestly rather than silently resolved either way, and re-confirming which real function this actually is (independent of any assumed name/ordinal correspondence) is folded into Round 407's scope.

### Round 407 (task #133, direct continuation per user's "do everything possible... fix everything", using the 3 URLs the user supplied this round): confirmed HEAPLIB is a real, separate, cleanly-completing IOP module; the uninitialized pool-handle global is a genuine lazy-init gap, not a missed module load

**New sources incorporated this round** (all user-supplied): a community PS2 BIOS ROM-contents reference gist (forked from uyjulian's well-known catalogue) confirms `HEAPLIB` is a real, distinct retail BIOS module ("Memory HEAP LIBrary (i.e. thvpool, thfpool)" - i.e. it backs THREADMAN's own fixed/variable memory-pool subsystems, exactly the kind of consumer our Round 406 trace already implicated); a real ps2sdk GitHub issue (#425) documents an actual real-hardware/PCSX2 IOP module termination log showing the real init/termination order (`sysmem, loadcore, excepman, intrman, ssbusc, dmacman, timrman, sysclib, stdio, heaplib, thrdman, thbase, thevent, thsemap, thmsgbx, thfpool, thvpool, vblank, ioman, modload, ...` - HEAPLIB loads and initializes BEFORE THREADMAN, exactly matching this project's own already-loaded module order, see below) plus real HEAPLIB startup console text (`"iop heap service (99/11/03)"`, `"read/write allocate memory 4000"`); a linked real homebrew repro project (`fjtrujy/helloWorldPS2`, `reset_IOP` branch) demonstrating the same real reboot/module-reinit sequence in practice.

**Finding 1 - HEAPLIB is already a correctly-loaded, real module in this project's own boot list, and it is NOT the missing piece**: a new scratch accessor (`r407_get_modlist_count()`/`r407_get_module_info()`, added to `/tmp/r406_build`'s copy of `iop_module_loader.c`, never committed) dumped this project's full real 29-module boot list. `HEAPLIB` is module index 10, loaded at `0x0010B290`-`0x0010BB30` - and Round 406's Finding 4 allocator function (`0x0010B860`) sits squarely inside this exact range, confirming it IS genuine HEAPLIB code (not a coincidental address, and not real libc `free()` from an unrelated homebrew library as Round 406's addendum had flagged as an open, unconfirmed possibility - that specific ambiguity is now resolved in favor of Round 406's ORIGINAL "real allocator" reading, since the function is definitively inside HEAPLIB's own module, and the gist's own real description of HEAPLIB's purpose - backing THREADMAN's pool subsystems - matches a size-parameterized block allocator, not a bare `free()`). Also confirmed: HEAPLIB (module 10) loads immediately before THREADMAN (module 12, with EECONF at 11 in between) in this project's own list - an exact match to the real init order the ps2sdk issue's boot log documents.

**Finding 2 - both HEAPLIB's own module init AND THREADMAN's own module init run to genuine, clean completion (not truncated/bypassed) - and neither one ever touches the pool-handle global**: live single-instruction tracing from HEAPLIB's real entry point (`0x0010B290`) showed it execute 577 real instructions and then genuinely RETURN to the module dispatcher (`pc=0x00100000`) - a real completion, not a trap-stub bypass. Separately, tracing from THREADMAN's real entry point (`0x0010C5E0`) showed it run 10,741 real instructions, calling INTO HEAPLIB's own code 774 separate times along the way (confirming THREADMAN's real init genuinely, heavily depends on HEAPLIB for its own internal allocations - semaphores, event flags, thread control blocks, etc.), before also returning cleanly to the dispatcher and advancing to the next module (VBLANK, `pc=0x00113270`) - exactly matching this project's own already-established module order. Across BOTH of these complete, real init passes, `MEM[0x00113248]` (Round 406's target global) is never written even once - directly ruling out "module init got cut off early" as the explanation.

**What this establishes**: the pool-handle global at `0x00113248` is not populated by either module's bulk/eager initialization - it must be intended for LAZY initialization, on first real use of whatever specific sub-pool it backs (very plausibly the alarm list specifically, distinct from the many OTHER pools/lists THREADMAN's eager init already successfully provisions via its 774 other HEAPLIB calls). This reframes Round 406's open question precisely: the bug is not "a real init call is missing/skipped" in the sense of a whole module or a whole subsystem's setup being dropped - both modules genuinely, verifiably run to completion - it is specifically that the CALLER at `0x00112348` (Round 406 Finding 3, only partially disassembled so far) either lacks, or has a broken, "pool handle is still NULL - create it now" lazy-init check before calling the block-search allocator with a NULL handle.

**What remains open for Round 408**: fully disassemble `0x00112348`'s complete body (only its `list_empty()` check and its unconditional pool-growth call have been decoded so far) to determine whether a real lazy pool-creation branch exists there and fails to fire, or is genuinely absent (which would itself be surprising for real, mature Sony BIOS code, and would need re-examination of whether this project's own boot-timing is reaching this code path earlier/differently than real hardware ever would). No fix applied yet - the exact real mechanism is still one disassembly pass away from being fully confirmed, and this project's discipline is to find the real mechanism before writing a fix, not after.

No source changes this round - purely a live single-instruction trace investigation round (scratch-only, `driver407a`-`driver407e`, `/tmp/r406_build`, never committed) plus incorporation of 3 new user-supplied real sources, directly continuing Round 406's methodology.

### Round 408 (task #134, "finish it"): fully disassembled the missing-NULL-check function; implemented and host-native-tested two candidate fixes; BOTH reverted after live verification showed a real EE boot-progress regression

**Full disassembly of 0x00112348 (Round 406/407's remaining open function)**: confirms no lazy pool-creation branch exists there or anywhere nearby - the function is exactly as narrow as Round 406's partial read suggested:
```
s1 = 0x00113204                      // shared free-pool list head
if (list_empty(s1)) {
    s0 = heaplib_alloc_wrapper(hint=0, size=0x20)   // ALWAYS passes hint=0 - the wrapper's own
                                                      // internal pool-handle read (MEM[0x113248]) is
                                                      // the only source of truth, confirmed unused
                                                      // caller argument (Round 407's "s3 saved but
                                                      // never read" observation, now fully explained)
    counter = MEM[s1+0x14]++;
    s0->id(+0xA) = counter;          // UNCONDITIONAL - no NULL check on s0 at all
} else {
    s0 = MEM[s1+0];                  // reuse an existing free node
    list_remove(s0);                 // via 0x112460
}
return s0;
```
Its own caller (`0x111740`-`0x11176C`) is equally direct: `list_init()` a fresh list, zero a local counter, call `0x112348` for a node, then unconditionally `list_insert(existing_list, new_node=s3)` with zero NULL-checking on `s3`. There is no missing branch to find - real, mature Sony code here simply assumes the pool always already exists by this point, exactly as Round 407 concluded. The real, structural gap remains exactly where Round 407 left it: some other, not-yet-located real code is responsible for the one-time pool creation and populating `0x00113248`, and it never runs (or never reaches that point) in this project's boot trace.

**Two candidate emulator-side fixes were implemented and host-native-tested against the real BIOS/disc scratch driver** (both targeting `source/core/iop/iop_core.c`'s Round-173 low-memory-region check, which Round 405/406/407 already fully traced as the mechanism that lets the resulting bogus indirect call silently leak the IOP stack instead of failing loudly):

1. **Narrow `in_modeled_low_region`'s `phys_pc<0x100` exclusion down to the real, specific HLE sentinel addresses** (0xA0/0xB0/0xC0/0xD0/0xD4/0xD8/0xDC/0xE0/0xE4/0xE8/0xEC/0xF0) instead of the whole range, so a genuinely-unmodeled address like the observed `0x00000020` correctly falls through to the existing "wandered into unpopulated memory" halt. New test (`tests/test_iop_low_region_halt.c`, 4 checks) confirmed this in isolation: jumping to `0x20` now halts with a clear diagnostic; jumping to real sentinels `0xA0`/`0xE8` still behaves normally (no spurious halt) - all 4 checks passed cleanly.
2. Live full-boot verification found the 8-consecutive-zero-word threshold this reuses **never actually accumulates** for this specific case: the real trace reaches `phys_pc=0x20`, executes exactly one zero word, and is then legitimately interrupted (a real, confirmed-live Timer5/scheduler-tick ISR dispatch) before a second consecutive zero step at `0x24` is ever reached - the interrupt's own real handler code resets the counter every single time. So a second variant was implemented: an immediate, one-shot halt for `phys_pc < IOP_HLE_TABLE_A0` specifically (justified since nothing real ever legitimately executes below `0xA0` at all, unlike the `0xE000`-`0x10000` region the original 8-word grace period was designed for). Verified live: this version DOES stop the corruption - `REBOOT`'s memory stays correctly `0x0C04711F` through 20,000,000 cycles - but it halts the entire IOP core at ~2,100,000 cycles, and live comparison against the current committed baseline showed this is a real, measured regression: EE progress drops from its established, many-round resting point (`0x8000CF9C`, confirmed via the unmodified baseline build) all the way back to `0x80005E90` - EE's own forward progress depends on the IOP continuing to service SIF/RPC traffic even while this specific corruption is independently, quietly happening in the background.
3. A third variant replaced the hard halt with a graceful "treat the bogus call as an empty function that returns immediately" recovery (`st->pc = st->gpr[31]; st->next_pc = st->gpr[31]+4`, i.e. synthesize a `jr $ra`) instead of halting - correctly avoiding the total IOP freeze. Live verification confirmed this ALSO stops the memory corruption (`REBOOT`+0x10 stays `0x0C04711F`) - but EE progress STILL regressed to the same `0x80005E90`, not the baseline `0x8000CF9C`. This was unexpected and reveals the fix's side effects are not simply "IOP freezes" - even a non-halting interception of this call measurably changes overall system timing (very plausibly because this specific call site is reached far more frequently, in a tight loop, than its old "wander through several NOPs before an interrupt reclaims control" behavior, changing how the interleaved EE/IOP scheduler apportions execution between the two cores).

**Decision, stated honestly**: both fixes were reverted (confirmed via `git stash`/`git status` - `iop_core.c` is back to its Round 407 committed state; the new test file was removed) after live, host-native, apples-to-apples comparison against the current committed baseline showed a real, measured EE boot-progress regression neither fix's author (this round) fully understands the mechanism of. Per this project's own established discipline (Round 403/405/406/407's repeated "not fabricated without citation," extended here to "not shipped without verified non-regression"), a fix that provably makes the ACTUAL, currently-tracked measure of progress (EE PC advancement) worse must not be committed, even though it demonstrably solves the narrower, isolated memory-corruption symptom it targeted. The corruption itself, while real and now fully root-caused end-to-end across Rounds 402-408, lands in a region (REBOOT's own already-executed code) that nothing on the currently-relevant EE boot-progress path has ever been shown to read back - it is very plausibly a currently-inert, cosmetic-only symptom of the deeper, still-unfixed HEAPLIB pool-handle gap, and chasing it further via symptomatic patches at the interception point is very likely the wrong layer to fix at.

**What remains open for Round 409**: the ONLY fix that would not carry this same risk is the real one - find the actual real code (in HEAPLIB, THREADMAN, or some other not-yet-searched module) that is supposed to populate `0x00113248` with a valid pool pointer, and determine why it never runs in this project's boot trace. That is a substantially larger search (across all 29 real modules' code, not just the two already fully traced) than this round had capacity to complete safely. No source changes shipped this round - all instrumentation, both fix attempts, and their verification were done in scratch trees (`/tmp/r406_build`, `/tmp/r408_verify`-`/tmp/r408_verify4`, `/tmp/r408_baseline`, all never committed) and via a stashed-then-dropped local change to the tracked repo, confirmed reverted via `git status`.

### Round 409 (task #135): found and disassembly-confirmed the TRUE root cause (SYSMEM's real entry point receives the wrong `$a0` argument) - fix implemented and host-native-verified to work exactly as predicted, but REVERTED after exposing a severe, previously-dormant second bug

**Method**: a full static scan of the entire 2MB IOP RAM image (post-boot, all 29 modules loaded) for every `LUI reg,0x0011` instruction followed by a load/store using that register with offset `0x3248` (i.e., every place in loaded code that computes or dereferences the exact address `0x00113248`) found exactly 3 references: 2 reads (inside the `0x1124C0` wrapper, already known) and, critically, ONE WRITE not previously identified - a `SW $v0,0($s3)` at IOP address `0x0010C74C`, sitting in a `JAL` delay slot inside THREADMAN's own init code (`0x0010C740`-`0x0010C74C`, ~0x160 bytes into THREADMAN's real entry at `0x0010C5E0`). Full disassembly of the surrounding code showed this is not "lazy" init at all - it is an EAGER call, right there in THREADMAN's own real init: `JAL 0x001129DC` (THREADMAN's own export ordinal-4 stub, itself a real `J 0x0010B730` redirect into HEAPLIB) with args `(size=0x800, flag=1)`, whose return value the delay slot stores directly into `0x00113248`. This resolved Round 406/407/408's "where does the write happen" question completely: THREADMAN calls HEAPLIB's real "create pool" function once, eagerly, at init time - and the result is always the NULL Round 406 already confirmed, because the pool-creation call itself fails.

**Full disassembly of the pool-creation chain, three levels deep**:
- `0x0010B730` (HEAPLIB ordinal-4, "create pool"): rounds the requested size, calls a lower allocator (`0x0010BAC4`) for the raw block, and - critically - DOES have a real NULL check (`BEQ $s0,$zero,...`) that correctly returns 0 if the raw allocator fails, rather than blindly dereferencing like `0x00112348`'s caller does. This function is not the bug; it is behaving exactly as real, defensive Sony code should.
- `0x0010BAC4` is itself another real import-stub jump table (matching the same `J <addr>; ADDIU $zero,$zero,<ordinal>` pattern already seen for HEAPLIB's own export table), redirecting HEAPLIB's internal ordinal-4 request out of its own module range entirely, into `0x0010032C` - real KERNEL/SYSMEM code, far below any of the 29 loadable modules' own ranges.
- `0x0010032C` (confirmed via `r407_get_module_info()`-style tooling to be `SYSMEM`'s own real entry point, `entry=0x001000A0`, module index 0 - the very first module the real boot list loads, chronologically before LOADCORE): full disassembly of `0x001000A0`-`0x00100114` shows a real, deliberate safety check - it reads a fixed heap-base symbol (`0x00100D00`, rounded from a linked constant `0x00100DD3`), compares it against `$a0` (clamped to a `0x007FFF00` cap, then AND-masked to a 256-byte boundary) to compute `top_bound`, and if `top_bound < heap_base+0x100`, concludes there is not enough memory and deliberately WRITES ZERO to its own "heap ready" gate at real RAM address `0x00100CC4` - otherwise it writes the real heap base and proceeds to build a working free-list. A dedicated write-watch on `0x00100CC4` confirmed exactly this live: two writes total across the whole boot, `0x00100D00` immediately followed by `0x00000000` at `pc=0x00100104` (the fail path), every single run.

**The actual bug, found and confirmed**: `$a0` at SYSMEM's real entry is `0x00100010` in this project's boot trace - and `source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`'s `iop_module_loader_boot()` explains exactly why: every module's entry point (SYSMEM included) is dispatched with `$a0 = g.boot_info_addr`, a small bump-allocated placeholder address, per the general "modules receive a pointer to a boot-info struct" convention this project established and validated back in Round 29 (task #151/#155/#158) for LOADCORE and later modules. But SYSMEM's own real disassembled entry code (traced fully this round, see above) never dereferences `$a0` as a pointer anywhere in this span - it uses it purely as a raw arithmetic byte quantity, compared and masked directly. This makes real chronological sense: SYSMEM is the memory manager itself, and it is the very first module to run - nothing could have allocated a boot-info struct for it to receive a pointer to yet. Real boot ROM code must instead pass SYSMEM's entry the raw, hardware-known top-of-memory value directly. Since this project's placeholder `g.boot_info_addr` (`0x00100010`) is numerically BELOW the heap-base+0x100 threshold (`0x00100E00`), SYSMEM's real, correct safety check has been concluding "not enough memory" and disabling its own heap on every single boot, which is the true, complete, verified root of the entire Round 402-409 chain (NULL pool handle -> NULL `list_insert` argument -> IOP stack leak -> `REBOOT` memory corruption).

**Fix implemented and tested** (scratch tree `/tmp/r409_clean`, never committed): special-cased `iop_module_loader_boot()`'s very first dispatch (matched by real module name, `strcmp(g.modlist[g.modlist_index], "SYSMEM") == 0`, not by position, to stay robust against any list-order assumptions) to pass `$a0 = 0x00200000` (the real, fixed 2MB IOP RAM size byte-form, matching this project's own already-established `BOOT_INFO_RAM_MB`/`IOP_RAM_SIZE_CONST` citation) instead of `g.boot_info_addr`. Every later module's dispatch (`advance_to_next_module()`) is untouched and continues passing `g.boot_info_addr` exactly as before. Host-native verification confirmed the fix works EXACTLY as predicted at the targeted layer: `MEM[0x00100CC4]` (the heap-ready gate) now correctly ends up `0x00100D00` (the real heap base) instead of `0x00000000`, at every checkpoint tested (200K and 2M cycles).

**However - live full-boot verification (200K/2M/500K-interval heartbeat runs) found a severe regression**: with the gate now correctly enabled, the IOP falls into what is effectively an infinite loop in the very-low address range (`pc` oscillating between `0x00000010` and `0x00000074`, advancing only ~20 bytes per 500,000-cycle slice) starting around the 1-2 million cycle mark, and EE progress simultaneously stalls, oscillating within a ~16-byte window around `0x8000B8A0`-`0x8000B8B0` rather than advancing normally. A run budgeted for 20,000,000 cycles never completed within the available time budget (repeatedly timed out), versus the current committed baseline's clean, fast run to its established `pc=0x8000CF9C` resting point. This is consistent with, and very likely IS, Round 402/403/408's already fully-characterized bogus indirect JALR call (`$v0=0x00000020`, at IOP `pc=0x001119A0`) becoming ACTIVE for the first time: that call site sits downstream of the exact `list_insert`/pool-allocation code path this round's fix finally allows to execute for real (instead of silently no-op'ing on a NULL pool handle as it always has before). Round 408 concluded the JALR corruption was "very likely a currently-inert cosmetic symptom" precisely because the pool handle was always NULL, short-circuiting that path before it ever ran with live data; this round's fix removes that short-circuit, and the previously-dormant bug now runs in what looks like a fast, repeating interrupt-driven loop that starves both cores' forward progress.

**Decision, per this session's established discipline**: reverted. The fix is real, disassembly-confirmed, and demonstrably corrects the exact mechanism this project has been tracing since Round 402 - but shipping it alone measurably regresses boot progress far worse than either of Round 408's two attempts did. No source changes committed this round; the fix lives only in the scratch tree `/tmp/r409_clean` (`source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`, `SYSMEM_ENTRY_TOP_OF_MEMORY`), confirmed via `git status --short` on the tracked repo showing a fully clean working tree.

**What remains open for Round 410**: this round's SYSMEM fix and Round 402/403/408's bogus-JALR bug are two separate, real bugs that must now be fixed TOGETHER - fixing only the first exposes the second's true severity for the first time; Round 408 already tried (and reverted) purely-interceptive fixes for the second in isolation. Round 410 should revisit the JALR corruption's real root cause (why `$v0` ends up `0x00000020` at `pc=0x001119A0` in the first place, not just how to intercept its symptom) now armed with a WORKING heap, and attempt a combined fix - verified, as always, against the non-regression baseline before shipping either half.

### Round 410 (task #136): re-applied the Round 409 SYSMEM fix in a scratch tree to trace the JALR corruption's real root cause - found the failure mode is earlier and different than Round 408 characterized; deeper root cause still open

Per the user's suggested debugging strategy (inspect the register state at the point of freeze, trace backward from there), re-applied Round 409's SYSMEM `$a0` fix in a fresh scratch tree (`/tmp/r410_build`, never committed) and added a live watch that fires the FIRST time IOP `pc` enters the `[0x0, 0x200)` range from above, capturing the preceding `pc`/`$ra`/`$v0`/`$a0`/`$sp`.

**Key correction to Round 409's hypothesis**: the corruption does NOT reach Round 402/403/408's previously-characterized JALR site (`pc=0x001119A0`, `$v0=0x00000020`) at all in this trace - that watch never fires. Instead, the IOP enters the near-zero address range much earlier (before 1.4M cycles) and well before THREADMAN's pool-creating init ever runs (`MEM[0x00113248]` stays `0x00000000` throughout every heartbeat checkpoint taken). This means Round 409's fix activates a DIFFERENT real code path than the one Round 408 traced - not the `list_insert`/pool-allocation chain, but something upstream of it that only starts running once SYSMEM's heap-ready gate is set.

**Full disassembly of the exact return site** (`prev_pc=0x00108DD4` immediately preceding the jump to `pc=0x00000000`, with `$ra=0x00000000` and `$v0=0xFFFFFF6A` at the moment of the jump): this is a completely ordinary, correct function epilogue (`lw $ra,28($sp); lw $s0,24($sp); jr $ra; addiu $sp,$sp,32` at `0x00108DC8`-`0x00108DD4`) returning from a real device/handler-table lookup function (`0x00108D14`-`0x00108DD4`) that searches a fixed 6-entry, 12-byte-stride table for an entry matching a caller-supplied ID, and - on a genuine "not found" outcome (real code, real control flow, not a decode error) - returns the specific, legitimate-looking error code `-150` (`0xFFFFFF6A`) via `ADDIU $v0,$zero,-150` at `0x00108D90`, exactly matching the observed `$v0`. This confirms the function itself is NOT the bug - it behaves correctly and returns a sensible "not found" error. The actual corruption is that `$ra` was ALREADY `0x00000000` when this function's own prologue saved it to the stack at entry (`SW $ra,28($sp)` at `0x00108D1C`) - meaning whatever called this lookup function had already lost its own valid return address before making that call. A direct-JAL static scan for callers of `0x00108D14` found zero hits, meaning it is reached via an indirect call (`JALR`) from somewhere not yet located.

**What this establishes**: the "IOP stack leak" mechanism Round 402/403 originally characterized is real and still present, but this round's evidence shows it strikes EARLIER and via a DIFFERENT call path than Round 408's specific `pc=0x001119A0` finding - Round 409's SYSMEM fix, by finally letting SYSMEM's real heap-dependent code run, exposes an entirely different manifestation of the same underlying class of bug (corrupted/zeroed `$ra` propagating through nested real calls) rather than the one previously traced. Chasing the ultimate origin (which indirect call first loses a valid `$ra`) needs a dedicated deeper trace with a fresh time budget - deferred to Round 411. The Round 409 fix remains reverted; no source changes shipped this round. All instrumentation and tracing this round was scratch-only (`/tmp/r410_build`, never committed), confirmed via `git status --short` on the tracked repo showing a fully clean working tree.

### Round 411 (task #137-148): found and fixed a genuine emulator bug (KSEG1 trampoline sign convention) that eliminates the near-zero-address memory corruption entirely - but a second, deeper wall (an always-empty LOADCORE registration-table walk) still holds EE at the same regressed resting point; both SYSMEM and trampoline fixes remain uncommitted pending a full resolution

**Root cause of the $ra corruption, found via live disassembly**: continuing directly from Round 410's finding (execution reaches `pc=0x00108D8C` via a real, deliberate `BGTZ $ra,0x00108D8C` branch at IOP `pc=0x00100D18`, inside SYSMEM's own real init code, disassembly-confirmed byte-for-byte: `1FE4201C` decodes exactly to `BGTZ $ra,0x00108D8C`). This is genuine, mature Sony code opportunistically reusing `$ra` as a plain signed data value mid-function (a real, legitimate MIPS idiom when a leaf sequence doesn't need `$ra` for its own return). The branch's condition (`$ra > 0`, i.e. "greater than zero" as a **signed** comparison) was being satisfied by this project's own synthetic module-dispatch trampoline placeholder, `g.trampoline_addr = bump_alloc(8)` in `source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`, which resolves to a small, RAM-based, POSITIVE address (`0x00100000`) - real hardware's equivalent boot-ROM return address would be KSEG1-mapped (uncached ROM mirror, `0xA0000000`-based), which is NEGATIVE as a signed 32-bit value and would never satisfy this branch's condition at all.

**Fix implemented and host-native-verified** (scratch tree `/tmp/r414_clean`, never committed): OR `0xA0000000` onto the trampoline address's stored/compared/register form only, immediately after allocation. This is safe because `iop_mem_ptr()` (and by extension `iop_mem_read32`/`iop_mem_write32`) already masks every address with `& 0x1FFFFFFF` before resolving physical memory - confirmed by direct code inspection - and `BRANCH_TO()`/`JR` propagate the raw, unmasked GPR value into `pc` without any masking of their own, so the self-jump instruction still writes to (and is found at) the exact same physical byte, `$ra`/`gpr[31]` now correctly holds a realistic, negative-as-signed placeholder, and the dispatcher's own `pc == g.trampoline_addr` return-detection check (which already compares against the same variable, never a hardcoded literal) continues to work unchanged.

**Live verification confirmed this eliminates the corruption entirely**: with the fix applied, repeated heartbeat checkpoints (200K-cycle intervals through 4,000,000 cycles) show the IOP staying consistently within a legitimate, bounded code range (`0x001011CC`-`0x00101294`) instead of wandering into near-zero invalid memory as it did in Round 410's trace. This is a real, disassembly-confirmed bug fix - not a symptomatic patch.

**However, a full 20,000,000-cycle run (10 x 2,000,000-cycle progress checkpoints) still ends at the same regressed EE resting point Round 408's reverted fixes also produced (`pc=0x80005E90`), not the established baseline (`pc=0x8000CF9C`)**. `MEM[0x00113248]` (THREADMAN's pool handle) stays `0x00000000` throughout - THREADMAN never runs at all. The reason: the IOP is stuck cycling through a bounded, 4-phase loop at `0x001011CC`-`0x00101294` (very likely LOADCORE's own real, multi-phase module-registration dispatch mechanism - each phase re-walks a small entry table via a masked-function-pointer `JALR` at `0x00101228`) that never has anything to actually call. A dedicated live watch (20 consecutive hits, `pc=0x001011EC`'s `BEQ $v0,$zero,...` empty-table check) confirmed the table pointer `$s2` (`0x001FFFB8`) is a per-call, dynamically-sized STACK `alloca()`-style buffer (confirmed via disassembly of its setup at `0x00100F90`-`0x00100FB8`: sized from a count read out of `fp+80`, shifted left 3 for an 8-byte stride, with its first entry explicitly zeroed right after allocation) - and it is empty on every single one of the 20 captured hits. Whatever earlier step is supposed to populate this per-call buffer with real registered entries either finds zero entries under this project's exact boot configuration, or itself has a gap not yet identified - a generic `memmove()`-style utility function (`0x00101EB0`) sits nearby in the call chain but is not itself the population logic.

**Decision, per this session's established discipline**: neither the SYSMEM `$a0` fix (Round 409) nor this round's KSEG1 trampoline fix has been committed. Both are real, individually-justified, disassembly-confirmed corrections - and together they successfully eliminate a genuine, confirmed memory-corruption bug - but the combined result still does not reach or exceed the established non-regression baseline, so per this project's "don't ship regressions" rule, they remain uncommitted, living only in scratch trees (`/tmp/r409_clean`, `/tmp/r410_build`, `/tmp/r414_clean`), pending resolution of this newly-found, deeper wall.

**What remains open for Round 412**: find what real code is supposed to populate the per-call registration-table buffer at `$s2` before the 4-phase walk runs, and why it's empty in this project's boot trace - very possibly connected to this project's own existing `build_real_registration_list()` mechanism (`source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`, referenced by name in that file's own Round-29-era comments) or a related, not-yet-modeled real hardware enumeration step. Once found and fixed, the SYSMEM `$a0` fix and the KSEG1 trampoline fix should be re-tested together with it and, if the combined result reaches or exceeds `pc=0x8000CF9C` at 20,000,000 cycles, all three should be committed together.

## Round 412 (task #148 continued, docs-only): identified the exact byte content of the empty 8-byte-stride list; determined it is a freshly-chained, not-yet-tagged node list rather than a populated-then-corrupted one - root cause of WHY it stays untagged still open, task #148 reframed and closed for this arc

Direct continuation of task #148 (find why LOADCORE's registration-table
walk at `0x001011EC`/`0x00101228` makes no forward progress with the
SYSMEM `$a0` fix + KSEG1 trampoline fix both applied). Rather than

directly, cross-referencing against docs/STATUS.md's own 36th-45th
findings (Round 29 continued) - which already investigated a
structurally identical "8-byte-stride list, walked backward, tag-
matched against `$s3`, gives up after 4 attempts" mechanism reached
from inside LOADCORE's own code, and connected it (43rd-45th findings)
to a real IOP syscall (0x10/0x08/0x14) implementation gap that was
subsequently found and fixed ("task #165 SOLVED").

**What the raw dump shows, byte-exact:** the region `0x00100D00`-
`0x00100DF4` is a genuine 8-byte-stride singly-linked list, freshly
chained: every "next-pointer" word (`0x00100D04`, `0x00100D0C`,
`0x00100D14`, ... stride 8) holds exactly `(its own address + 8)` -
i.e. each node points at the next one in a perfectly linear, never-
yet-relinked chain, the same shape `iop_heap.c`'s own `new_table()`
uses for its host-native free list (`t->list[i].next = &t->list[i+1]`)
- except this is genuine GUEST IOP RAM content, not that host-native
structure (confirmed `IOP_HEAP_BASE=0x00020000`, nowhere near this
`0x00100Dxx` region - ruled out as the source). The second word of
each node (offset+4) holds a real, non-zero, plausible-instruction-
shaped value in every slot inspected (e.g. `0x1FC6201C`, byte-
identical to the already-documented real `BGTZ $ra,0x00108D8C`
encoding from Round 411's own finding, appearing again here at its
real static address `0x00100D18` - a consistency check, not new
information, confirming this dump is reading real, correctly-mapped
BIOS-derived code/data, not garbage or a stale mapping).

**Assessment: this is a freshly-initialized-but-never-tagged list,
not a corrupted or partially-populated one.** Every node's "next"
pointer is exactly what a brand-new, untouched chain would look like;
nothing has begun overwriting it with real tagged entries yet. This
rules out one candidate hypothesis this round considered (a
population routine partially running then aborting, leaving a mixed
state) - the state is uniformly "never touched," consistent with
either (a) the routine that's supposed to write real tagged entries
into this list never being reached at all in this project's current
boot ordering with both fixes applied, or (b) it being reached but
immediately no-op'ing on some upstream zero/empty condition (matching
task #148's own earlier `$s0`/`$s2` aliasing observation - both
appeared to source from the identical stack address, i.e. the same
"nothing to insert yet" state, just observed from two different call
sites walking the same underlying list).

**Why Round 29's already-shipped syscall 0x10/0x08/0x14 fix (44th/
45th findings, "task #165 SOLVED") does not resolve this instance:**
that fix targeted a specific, already-reached, already-firing real
retry loop in the boot configuration of that round (SYSMEM heap
permanently disabled, per the bug the Round 409-411 arc fixed). The
current investigation reaches this same list-walk shape via a
DIFFERENT boot path - one where SYSMEM's heap is, for the first time,
genuinely enabled - and the list is not failing a tag-match after
real entries exist; it is being walked while still completely
unpopulated. These are the same STRUCTURAL shape (8-byte-stride,
tag-matched, bounded-retry list) but empirically distinct SCENARIOS,
and Round 29's fix - real and still correctly in place - was never
positioned to address a list that has no entries to begin with, only
one that has entries with the wrong tag.

**Honest conclusion for this arc.** Task #148's original framing ("the
walk makes no forward progress") is confirmed accurate, but the
specific mechanism is now understood one level deeper: an
uninitialized, never-populated list, not a broken walk or a corrupted
one. This is real, disassembly-confirmed progress on understanding
the blocker, but it does NOT, on its own, unblock the combined SYSMEM
`$a0` + KSEG1 trampoline fix's EE-progress regression (still measured
at `pc=0x80005E90` vs. the established `pc=0x8000CF9C` baseline - not
re-verified again this round since no code changed, per Round 411's
own most recent 20,000,000-cycle measurement). Both fixes remain
correct, individually justified, and uncommitted, exactly as Round 411
left them. Task #148 is closed for this specific investigative
technique (byte-level static dump); continuing it further needs live,
instruction-level tracing of WHAT (if anything) is ever supposed to
call the real population routine for this list under this project's
current module boot ordering, and whether that routine's own
prerequisites (very possibly a still-earlier real kernel-init step,
per the same "count=0 upstream" lead task #148 already flagged) are

## Round 413 (tasks #149/#151, docs-only): identified the real mechanism that should populate LOADCORE's internal registration table - RegisterLibraryEntries(), never modeled by this project, already flagged as a deferred architecture gap back in Round 59

Direct continuation of Round 412. Two quick, decisive checks resolved
both of Round 412's open sub-questions:

**Task #151 (is 0x00100D00 really LOADCORE's own table, or something
else - SYSMEM's self-hosted alloc table, or boot_info's externally-

`LOADCORE entry=0x00100CD0` - the list at `0x00100D00` sits only
0x30 bytes into LOADCORE's own module image, i.e. it is part of
LOADCORE's own `.data`/`.bss`, not SYSMEM's (ruled out in Round 412's
own speculative aside) and not the externally-supplied boot_info list
`build_real_registration_list()` builds (which is bump-allocated much
later, after all 29 modules' ELFs already occupy several hundred KB -
nowhere near `0x100D00`). This confirms the original Round 29/task
#148 attribution was correct all along: this is genuinely LOADCORE's
own internal table.

**Task #149 (what real code is supposed to populate it, and why
doesn't it):** cross-referenced against real, open-source PCSX2's own
`IopBios.cpp` (already fetched and cited in this project's own 
docs at an earlier round, task #whatever cited "no cdrom0: HLE
shortcut exists" finding) - which confirms real PCSX2 itself HLEs
`loadcore::RegisterLibraryEntries_HLE` as a first-class hook,
directly corroborating that `RegisterLibraryEntries()` is the real,
Sony-defined LOADCORE-exported kernel function every real IOP module
calls, from ITS OWN init code, to insert itself into LOADCORE's
internal table - not a single upfront bulk supplier. This project's
own history had already reached the same conclusion once before:
Round 59's 90th/91st findings (docs/STATUS.md, "P/I twin export-
shadowing bug") explicitly floated "the fuller 'trace real
RegisterLibraryEntries calls' architecture change" as the generically
correct fix for a related but distinct problem (export-table
visibility ordering) and deliberately deferred it, opting for a
narrower, lower-risk name-pattern fix instead, specifically because
the full change "needs full regression coverage across every already-
passing IOP module-loading test before being trusted."

**Why the table has stayed empty across every round since:** this
project's module dispatcher (`iop_module_loader.c`) runs each
module's real entry point exactly once via a synthetic trampoline,
and completely separately maintains its OWN host-side "who exports
what" table (`g.exports[]`, populated at ELF-parse time, well before
any module's real code executes) for import-resolution purposes. Real
`RegisterLibraryEntries()` calls - which would write into LOADCORE's
own guest-visible table at `0x100D00`, matching the exact freshly-
chained-but-never-tagged byte pattern Round 412 found - are never
intercepted, modeled, or synthesized anywhere in this call path. The
guest table is not broken or corrupted; it is simply never written to,
because the one real mechanism that writes to it does not exist in
this project yet.

**Honest scope, not implemented this round.** This is a real,
substantial architecture gap (touching every module's init-time
control flow, not a local patch), and per Round 59's own already-
established caution about this exact class of change, it is
deliberately NOT rushed into this round on top of an already-deep
investigation. It is a strong, well-evidenced candidate for the
actual real fix needed to let LOADCORE's real registration-walk
(task #151/#164/#165's already-fixed retry-loop machinery) do
something useful for the first time, and to let the combined SYSMEM
`$a0` + KSEG1 trampoline fix's EE-progress regression finally resolve
instead of dead-ending at the same empty table every time. Scoped as
Round 414's task: design and implement a minimal, targeted
`RegisterLibraryEntries()` interception (most likely modeled the same
way this project already handles other real IOP kernel calls it
doesn't fully interpret - via a recognized call-site/jump-table
pattern match, not full instruction-level reimplementation of
LOADCORE's real internals) scoped ONLY to populating this table for
modules that already run past their own entry point in this project's
boot trace, with full regression coverage before any commit.

## Round 414 (tasks #149-152 continued, docs-only, MAJOR CORRECTION): disassembled the real RegisterLibraryEntries() implementation directly - the 8-byte-stride list at 0x00100D00 is NOT what it writes to; it manages a completely different, separate linked list, and only LOADCORE itself ever calls it

Continuing directly from Round 413's identification of the real

each stub to a real target, `0x00101568`, in every case - confirmed
via temporary `fprintf` instrumentation on the resolution path), then
added a live execution watch on `pc==0x00101568` itself (not just
static resolution) across a real boot run.

**Result: `RegisterLibraryEntries` is executed exactly ONCE in the
entire boot trace - by LOADCORE itself, registering its own exports,
immediately after its own module entry begins** (`a0=0x00102830`
matches LOADCORE's own export-table pointer already seen in the
Round 412 dump at `0x00100E64`-`0x00100E6C`'s `jal 0x00101568`; the
call's return address `ra=0x00100E74` confirms this is exactly that

has no need to call it, being module 0), not EXCEPMAN, not any of the
other 19 modules whose stub is equally correctly resolved to the same
real target - is ever observed calling it, across the full run.

**Disassembled `0x00101568`-`0x00101640` directly (LOADCORE's real
RegisterLibraryEntries body) and found it manages an entirely
DIFFERENT structure than the one this investigation has been chasing
since Round 412.** Real, confirmed structure: validates the caller's
export-table pointer (`$a0`) against a real magic word
(`MEM[a0]==0x41C00000`, matching real ps2sdk's own `irx_export_table`
magic convention), then walks/inserts into a genuine doubly-linked
list whose HEAD is a fixed global at `0x00102940` (not `0x00100D00`),
calling three small helper subroutines (`0x00101B0C`, `0x00101B3C`,
`0x00101B54` - real per-entry comparison/insertion logic, not yet
individually decoded) to walk existing entries and splice the new one
in. This is real, working, genuinely-executed code (confirmed:
LOADCORE's own single call completes normally and returns - no crash,
no panic-loop hit).

**This means the entire investigative thread since Round 412 (the
"empty 8-byte-stride list," `is_registration_walk_panic_loop()`, the
4-phase retry loop at `0x001011CC`-`0x00101294`) has been chasing a
DIFFERENT, so-far-unidentified LOADCORE internal structure that is
NOT populated by `RegisterLibraryEntries()` - Round 412's own
speculative framing ("a freshly-chained, never-tagged node list...
very possibly connected to... `build_real_registration_list()`") is
corrected here: it is not connected to that mechanism at all. The
real, disassembly-confirmed library-registration list lives at global
`0x00102940`, uses full `_iop_library`-sized nodes (`prev`/`caller`/
`version`/`flags`/`name[8]`/`exports[]` per real `loadcore.h` -
much larger than 8 bytes, ruling out the 8-byte-stride shape entirely
as a match for this structure), and DOES get a real, live entry
written into it (LOADCORE's own). What the still-unidentified
`0x00100D00` list actually is remains open - it is reached by
different code (the `0x00100F90`-`0x00101294` region) that this
round's evidence now shows is unrelated to `RegisterLibraryEntries`.

**The real, narrower, well-evidenced open question going forward:**
why does no module other than LOADCORE ever reach its own
`RegisterLibraryEntries` call, when the stub is correctly resolved for
all of them? The well-established `trap_stubs_bypassed`/panic-loop
bypass mechanisms (task #148/#152/#157, `is_unconditional_trap_stub()`
and siblings) are the leading, already-precedented explanation - most
modules' real init code likely hits some other unmodeled real
syscall/trap BEFORE reaching their own registration call and gets
short-circuited there. This is a much more specific, tractable
question than the abandoned 8-byte-list thread, and directly explains
why LOADCORE's OWN internal library list (`0x00102940`) has exactly
