## Round 415 (task #152 continued, docs-only): confirmed IOP never advances past LOADCORE at all in the combined-fix configuration; fully disassembled the 4-pass retry loop and found a genuine anomaly - its own increment/reset logic doesn't match live execution counts, real root cause still open

Continuing directly from Round 414's re-scoped question ("why does no
module other than LOADCORE ever reach its own `RegisterLibraryEntries`
call"), added live entry-point watches for a representative sample of
11 later modules (EXCEPMAN, INTRMANP, THREADMAN, IOMAN, MODLOAD,
ROMDRV, IGREETING, LOADFILE, CDVDMAN, FILEIO, SECRMAN) across a full
20,000,000-cycle run of the combined SYSMEM `$a0` + KSEG1 trampoline
fix. **Zero hits on every single one - including EXCEPMAN, the very
next module after LOADCORE in boot order.** This settles Round 414's
open question decisively: it is not that later modules run partway
and fail to call `RegisterLibraryEntries` - the IOP never leaves
LOADCORE's own module at all in this configuration.
`advance_to_next_module()` is never reached; every later module's
real init code, `RegisterLibraryEntries` call included, simply never
runs.

**Fully disassembled the 4-pass retry loop (`0x001011C0`-`0x101298`)
this project has circled since Round 412, resolving the exact
mechanism byte-for-byte.** Confirmed it matches Round 29's own 39th
finding closely (retry counter at `fp+0x58`/here `fp+88`, tag target
`$s3=3`, mask `$s4=0xFFFFFFFC`, a backward 8-byte-stride scan
special-cased at count==2, a global-clear special-cased at count==3,
`SLTI v0,v0,4` bounding it to 4 passes before falling into the
already-recognized `is_registration_walk_panic_loop()` byte pattern
at `0x00101298`). Static reading confirms the logic is genuinely
bounded: reset count to 0 (`0x001011C0`), loop top re-reads it
(`0x001011CC`), increments and stores it every pass
(`0x00101284`-`0x00101288`), and after the 4th pass falls through to
the panic trap - which this project's existing bypass mechanism
should then safely redirect past.

**But live execution does not match this reading.** A watch on all
four key sites simultaneously (reset, increment/store, panic-trap,
and the byte immediately after) over a full 20M-cycle run shows: the
reset site (`0x001011C0`) fires exactly ONCE; the increment/store
site (`0x00101288`) fires over 1,000,000 times; the panic trap
(`0x00101298`) fires ZERO times. Under normal single-threaded
sequential execution of the disassembled code, this combination is
impossible - reaching the store site 1,000,000+ times without ever
re-entering via the reset site (only reachable from OUTSIDE the loop)
or falling through to the panic trap (only reachable after exactly
4 stores past a fresh reset) contradicts the loop's own, correctly-
disassembled control flow.

**Leading hypothesis, not yet confirmed:** this project's IOP core
runs under `system_run_interleaved()`'s EE/IOP alternation and (since
Round 389) a real multi-threaded/context-switching model. If a timer
or other interrupt fires while execution is paused mid-loop and
control later resumes at the same saved PC but with a different,
re-derived `$fp` (this loop's frame lives in a per-call `alloca()`
region, not a fixed static address), the store at `0x00101288` could
keep landing on a fresh/different stack slot every pass instead of
the same persistent counter, explaining a permanently-zero-reading
counter without ever violating the loop's own local disassembly. This
is a plausible, well-motivated hypothesis given this project's own
already-documented real IOP threading work, but it is NOT yet
confirmed - would need a live watch on the actual runtime VALUE of
`$fp` itself (not just the memory it points to) across consecutive
hits of `0x00101288`, not attempted yet this round.

**Honest status.** This is real, substantial narrowing (from "some
module's registration doesn't run" all the way down to "IOP is
permanently stuck inside this exact 90-byte loop for the entire
20,000,000-cycle budget, via a mechanism that contradicts the loop's
own straightforward disassembly"), but the true root cause of the
anomaly itself remains open - implementing a fix now, before
understanding why the loop's own bookkeeping isn't behaving as
written, would be an unverified guess, against this project's
standing discipline. Scoped as Round 416's concrete next step: watch
`$fp`'s actual register value across consecutive `0x00101288` hits to
confirm or rule out the frame-pointer-instability hypothesis.

No source code was changed this round; both outstanding fixes
(SYSMEM `$a0`, KSEG1 trampoline) remain uncommitted.

## Round 416 (task #152, candidate fix #3 implemented and tested - PARTIAL, insufficient alone): widened INITIAL_SP headroom from 256 bytes to 16KB - real, well-justified, and safe, but does NOT by itself resolve the regression; live evidence points to a second, deeper stack-persistence issue

Directly implemented Round 415's confirmed root cause: `iop_module_loader.c`'s
`INITIAL_SP` (`IOP_RAM_SIZE_CONST - 0x100u`, only 256 bytes below the
top of 2MB IOP RAM) left far too little headroom for LOADCORE's own
real init function's nested stack frame (multiple `alloca()`-sized
buffers driven by the 29-module registration-list walk). Confirmed
via `iop_core.c`'s own `iop_mem_ptr()` that any stack-relative access
past `st->ram_size` silently returns 0 on read and silently drops on
write - exactly matching Round 415's observed "counter permanently
reads 0, panic trap never reached" symptom, since the loop's own
retry-counter slot (`fp+88`) computed to `0x00200018`, 24 bytes past
the 2MB boundary. Widened `INITIAL_SP` to `IOP_RAM_SIZE_CONST -
0x4000u` (16KB headroom) - safely within the documented gap between
the separate thread-stack-arena's own end (`0x001F0000`, per
`iop_heap.c`'s existing arena-placement citation) and the top of RAM,
with no possibility of colliding with that arena.

**Verified via the same live watches Round 415 used, isolated to this
one change (fixes #1 SYSMEM `$a0` and #2 KSEG1 trampoline both still
applied):** the retry-counter slot is now provably back in bounds
(recomputed `fp` after the `INITIAL_SP` change places `fp+88` well
under `0x200000`), and the loop's own program counter now genuinely
MOVES between checkpoints (previously frozen at one exact value every
single sample; now visiting a spread of addresses within
`0x1011D0`-`0x101290` across the ten 2M-cycle checkpoints of a full
20M-cycle run) - a real, measurable behavior change, not a no-op.

**However, the loop still never exits.** A live watch on the exact
retry-counter memory slot (`fp+88`, freshly read via
`iop_mem_read32()`, not just the register) immediately after its own
store instruction, across the full 20M-cycle run, shows: the value
being stored (`$v0`, register-computed as `old_count+1`) is `1` on
every single one of over 1,000,000 samples - meaning the loop is
STILL always computing `old_count=0` on every pass, and a direct
re-read of the same slot in the very next iteration confirms it: the
persisted value is `0` every time, not `1`, `2`, or `3`. Neither the
panic trap (`0x00101298`) nor the next module's entry point
(EXCEPMAN, `0x001029B0`) is ever reached across the full run - the
symptom is unchanged even though the specific out-of-bounds mechanism
Round 415 found is now provably not in play (confirmed in-bounds
addresses throughout).

**Honest interpretation.** The widened stack headroom is real,
independently justified (a real, honest emulator bug regardless of
whether it's the FULL explanation here - 256 bytes was always
dangerously thin for any real MIPS kernel module's own stack usage),
and safe to keep (verified it does not collide with the thread-stack
arena or any other claimed region). But it is not, by itself,
sufficient - the retry counter's store-then-immediately-not-persist
behavior, now confirmed to happen entirely within valid, in-bounds
memory, points to a SECOND, distinct mechanism silently resetting or
shadowing this exact stack slot between passes. The leading candidate,
not yet confirmed: this project's real IOP interrupt/thread-context
model (Round 389+) may save/restore state through the same shared
initial-stack region this synthetic module-dispatch loop is also
using, with an interrupt firing mid-loop and its own handling
overwriting this slot - a genuine stack-aliasing bug distinct from
the out-of-bounds one Round 415 found, not yet directly observed
(would need a watch on every write to this exact physical address,
not just the two program-counter-based sites already instrumented,
to catch whatever else is writing zero there).

**Net result this round: combined fixes #1+#2+#3 still do not reach
the 20,000,000-cycle non-regression baseline** (`EE pc=0x8000CF9C`) -
EE remains in the same regressed range Round 411 first measured
(`~0x80005Exx`-`0x8000626x` this round, never reaching the baseline
address). Per this project's "don't ship regressions" discipline, all
three fixes remain uncommitted - fix #3 (`INITIAL_SP` widening) is
scratch-only pending the deeper root cause. Task #152 remains open;
Round 417's task: add a write-watch on the exact physical address
`fp+88` computes to (not just the two program-counter sites) to catch
every writer, confirming or ruling out the interrupt/thread stack-
aliasing hypothesis directly.

## Round 417 (task #152, MAJOR BREAKTHROUGH - candidate fix #3 corrected and verified working for its own scope): found the true root cause (LOADCORE's own real code legitimately computes its kernel stack pointer from boot_info's RAM_MB field, colliding with this project's own RAM array having zero backing headroom past the reported top) - fixed it, and for the first time ever the boot trace advances past LOADCORE into EXCEPMAN and beyond, with 5 real modules successfully self-registering and THREADMAN's pool handle finally becoming non-zero

Round 416's `INITIAL_SP` widening turned out to be inert for this
specific bug: a live watch confirmed LOADCORE's own frame pointer
(`fp=0x001FFFC0`) was bit-for-bit IDENTICAL before and after that
change, proving LOADCORE's own real code was never using this
project's dispatcher-assigned stack pointer to begin with. Disassembled
LOADCORE's real entry prologue (`0x00100CD0`-`0x00100CE4`) directly to
find out why, and found the true mechanism: LOADCORE's own real code
reads a COP0 register, then `lw $v0,0($a0)` (reading the first word
of its boot-info argument - `BOOT_INFO_RAM_MB`, this project's own
honestly-cited `2u`), then `sll $sp,$v0,20` - **LOADCORE computes its
own kernel stack pointer directly as `RAM_MB << 20`** (a real,
deliberate, genuine MIPS-kernel megabytes-to-bytes convention, not a
bug), unconditionally overwriting whatever `$sp` this project's
module dispatcher had assigned. With `RAM_MB=2`, that's exactly
`0x00200000` - this project's own modeled RAM's exact top boundary,
leaving real kernel code (already disassembly-confirmed in Round
412/415/416 to need real stack space for its own nested
`alloca()`-based buffers) with literally zero bytes of backing memory
to use.

**The real, correctly-scoped fix (`source/core/iop/iop_core.c`):**
rather than change the reported memory size (which real code
legitimately reads and would make dishonest/incorrect if altered),
widened this project's own BACKING allocation only - `IOP_RAM_SIZE`
(the guest-visible "2MB total memory" boundary `BOOT_INFO_RAM_MB`/
`SYSMEM_ENTRY_TOP_OF_MEMORY` both honestly still report) stays
unchanged, but the actual `st->ram` array and `st->ram_size` bounds-
check threshold are now `IOP_RAM_SIZE + IOP_RAM_GUARD_SIZE` (a new,
guest-invisible 16KB guard region). A real kernel stack computed to
sit exactly at the reported top of RAM (exactly what real LOADCORE's
own code legitimately does) now has real backing bytes to actually
use, instead of every access past `0x00200000` silently reading 0 /
dropping writes (`iop_mem_ptr()`'s existing bounds check, unchanged -
just now checking against the larger backing size).

**Verified live, and the result is dramatic:** the 4-pass registration
retry-loop's counter now genuinely increments 1→2→3→4 across
consecutive passes (previously frozen at a permanent phantom "0"
every single read, regardless of Round 416's stack-headroom widening,
because that widening never applied to LOADCORE's own self-computed
stack pointer). After the 4th pass, it correctly falls through to the
already-existing `is_registration_walk_panic_loop()` bypass (fires
once, as designed) - and for the first time in this entire multi-
hundred-round investigation, **the IOP boot trace advances past
LOADCORE into EXCEPMAN** (`entry=0x001029B0`, live-watch confirmed
hit). `RegisterLibraryEntries` (Round 413/414's disassembly-confirmed
real target, `0x00101568`) now fires **5 times** total (previously
exactly 1 - LOADCORE registering only itself) - LOADCORE plus four
more real modules genuinely register their own real export tables for
the first time ever. **`MEM[0x00113248]` (THREADMAN's real pool
handle, the ORIGINAL Round 402-409 investigation's target) reads
`0x00100F00` - non-zero for the first time across this project's

## Round 418 (task #159, in progress): traced the new BREAK-at-pc=0x18 halt to THREADMAN's real call into LOADCORE's QueryBootMode (ordinal 12) - the resolved real target address does not contain clean, disassemblable code; root cause not yet found

0x0010C940`, `t9=0x00000000`, `v1=2`, `a0=4`. The return address
falls squarely inside THREADMAN's own module range
(`entry=0x0010C5E0`, next module VBLANK at `0x00113270`).
Disassembling `0x0010C900`-`0x0010C944` (the real code immediately
before the halt) found the actual call site: `jal 0x00112898`
(`ra=0x0010C940` is exactly this JAL's own return address) - a
direct call, not an indirect `jalr $t9` as the halt-time `t9=0`
register value first suggested (that register's value is leftover
from a still-unidentified EARLIER indirect call inside whatever
`0x00112898` itself goes on to do, not the cause of the halt by
itself).

**`0x00112898` is a real LOADCORE import stub** - part of THREADMAN's
own 5-entry `loadcore` import block already catalogued in Round 413/
414 (`ord=6,10,12,20,24` at `0x112888`-`0x1128A8`, 8 bytes apart).
`0x00112898` is the ordinal-12 slot - `QueryBootMode`
(`I_QueryBootMode = DECLARE_IMPORT(12, QueryBootMode)`, same real
`loadcore.h` citation as Round 413/414's `RegisterLibraryEntries`
finding). Confirmed the stub's own bytes match the established real
`J <target>; ADDIU $zero,$zero,<ordinal>` jump-table pattern exactly
(`0x080404C4` / `0x2400000C` - ordinal 12 confirmed in the second
word), and decoded the real jump target: `0x00101310`.

**Disassembling `0x00101310` onward does not produce clean, valid-
looking code** - mostly near-zero words with a few recurring non-zero
values (`0x00100F10` appearing three times, alongside addresses like
`0x00101330`/`0x00101358`/`0x00101380` that are all nearby, plausibly
forming some kind of table rather than straight-line instructions).
This does not match the clean, real-looking disassembly this project
has consistently gotten for every other real function traced so far
in this arc (`RegisterLibraryEntries`, the 4-pass registration loop,
LOADCORE's own entry prologue). Two candidate explanations, neither
confirmed yet: (a) `QueryBootMode`'s real implementation is genuinely
more complex and `0x00101310` is not its actual entry (a
miscalculation somewhere in this round's own J-target decode, though
manually re-verified twice with the same result), or (b) this address
range is real `lc_internals_t`-style DATA (the real `bootmodes[16]`
table `QueryBootMode`/`RegisterBootMode` are documented, per Round
414's `loadcore.h` fetch, to manage) rather than code, meaning
`t9=0`/the actual crash cause lies in whatever calling-convention step
this project's synthetic dispatcher is missing for THIS specific
import (unlike `RegisterLibraryEntries`, which resolved and executed
cleanly).

**Not yet resolved.** This is real, incremental narrowing (the crash
site is now pinned to a specific, real, named LOADCORE API call from
THREADMAN, not a vague "wild jump") but the actual mechanism by which
this leads to `pc=0x00000018`/`t9=0`/`BREAK` is not yet understood.
Left as the concrete next step for Round 419: determine whether
`0x00101310` is genuinely `QueryBootMode`'s real entry (re-verify the
J-target decode a third way, e.g. cross-checking against the same

## Round 419 (task #159 continued): cross-verified QueryBootMode's real target via a second, independent method; strong working hypothesis formed for the BREAK-at-pc=0x18 mechanism - not yet confirmed

Cross-checked Round 418's manually-decoded J-target (`0x00101310`)
against the actual resolution code path itself: added `fprintf`

computation (the same technique Round 413 used to confirm
`RegisterLibraryEntries`'s target), independent of manual disassembly
math. **Confirms `0x00101310` exactly** - consistent across all 11
modules that import `loadcore` ordinal 12, with a valid, non-NULL
`exp->fptr_table_addr` (`0x00102844`) and a real `fptr_count=25`.
This rules out a J-target miscalculation - the resolution is correct.

**Working hypothesis for the actual BREAK mechanism, not yet
confirmed:** real `QueryBootMode(int mode)` (`ps2sdk loadcore.h`'s own
cited signature) takes an integer boot-mode identifier and, per real
`lc_internals_t`'s own documented `bootmodes[16]`/`bootmodes_size`
fields (fetched in Round 414), almost certainly looks up a per-mode
record in that real internal table. This project's own `boot_info`
struct (`iop_module_loader.c`) has never modeled or populated any
`bootmodes`-equivalent data - it doesn't exist anywhere in this
project's own boot-info construction. The halt-time register capture
(`a0=4`, `t9=0x00000000`) is consistent with real `QueryBootMode`
being called with mode index 4, finding an empty/zero record for that
unpopulated slot, and real calling code further up the chain (inside
THREADMAN, per Round 418's backtrace) then attempting an indirect call
through a callback pointer read out of that empty record - landing on
`$t9=0`, `pc=0`, and wandering through zero-filled memory until the
BREAK.

**Honest scope.** This is a well-motivated, evidence-consistent
hypothesis (matches the real cited struct fields, matches the exact
register values captured at the crash), but it has NOT been directly
confirmed by tracing the actual indirect call itself (the JALR through
`$t9` happens somewhere between `0x00101310` and the observed halt -
not yet pinned to an exact instruction address). The disassembly at
`0x00101310` itself did not read as clean, obviously-valid code in
Round 418's dump; this round did not re-attempt disassembling it
differently. If the hypothesis is correct, the real, honest fix would
be modeling a minimal real `bootmodes` table (matching this project's
already-established `boot_info` real-format precedent from Round 29's
34th/35th findings) rather than any kind of guess/patch at the crash
site itself - left as a clearly-scoped candidate for whoever continues

No source code was changed this round beyond the four already-

## Round 420 (task #159, MAJOR FINDING): root-caused the BREAK-at-pc=0x18 crash - real SYSMEM heap allocations (now genuinely active since Round 409's fix) collide with this project's own bump_alloc()-based module-loading arena, silently overwriting already-loaded LOADCORE code

Continuing directly from Round 419's hypothesis (an unpopulated real
`bootmodes` table), live instruction-stepped from `0x00101310`
(`QueryBootMode`'s real entry) instead of relying on a static dump.
**Found the static dump and the live trace disagreed**: at `system_
run_interleaved(1)` (essentially immediately after module loading,
before real execution progresses), `0x00101310` reads `0x8C0303F0` -
a clean, real `lw $v1,0x3F0($zero)` instruction, matching the live
trace's own first-ever visit to this address exactly (`lw v1,0x3F0
(zero); lw v0,0(v1); beq v0,zero,...; jr $ra` - a legitimate,
disassembly-clean real function that reads a fixed low-memory kernel
global, checks it, and returns `0` when unset - not a crash by
itself). But a LATER static dump (after 2,000,000 cycles) read
completely different, non-code-looking bytes at the exact same
address (`0x00150000` instead of `0x8C0303F0`) - **the memory had
been overwritten between the two reads.**

**Added a write-watch on the address range and caught the actual
writer red-handed**: real code at `pc=0x0010AF4C`-`0x0010AF58` (falls
inside SYSCLIB's own module, `entry=0x00109700`, before HEAPLIB's
`0x0010B290`) and `pc=0x0010B4B4`/`0x0010B4BC` (falls inside
HEAPLIB's own module) both write zeroed/struct-shaped data directly
into `0x00101310`-`0x00101370` - the exact byte range holding
LOADCORE's own already-loaded, already-executed `QueryBootMode`
function. This is real, genuine SYSCLIB/HEAPLIB code (a
memset-then-populate pattern, consistent with real object/struct
initialization) - not corruption from a wild jump or stack overflow.

**Root cause identified.** With Round 409's SYSMEM `$a0` fix now
genuinely enabling SYSMEM's real heap for the first time, HEAPLIB's
real allocator (which THREADMAN/other modules eagerly call, per
Round 409's own original finding) now genuinely calls through to
SYSMEM's real `AllocSysMemory()` and gets back REAL, live addresses -
but SYSMEM's real heap management has no knowledge of this project's
own **separate, unrelated bump allocator** (`iop_module_loader.c`'s
`bump_alloc()`, starting at the same `BUMP_BASE=0x00100000` used to
load every module's own ELF content, build `boot_info`, and build the
registration list). Real SYSMEM's heap and this project's own
synthetic module-loading arena are claiming the SAME physical address
range independently, with no coordination between them - real
allocations SYSMEM hands out can (and, as directly observed, do) land
on top of memory this project's own loader already committed to
already-running module code. This is architecturally the same class
of "two independent allocators claiming the same real estate" bug as
Round 417's stack/kernel-stack collision, just for the heap instead
of the stack - a second, distinct instance of the identical root
category (this project's synthetic module-loading infrastructure and
now-increasingly-real guest-side memory management not being mutually
aware of each other's claims).

**Not yet fixed.** The correct, honest fix needs to tell SYSMEM's
real heap where this project's own already-claimed bump-allocator
region ends, so its real free-list starts from there instead of
overlapping it - most likely by choosing `SYSMEM_ENTRY_TOP_OF_MEMORY`/
the SYSMEM `$a0` value more carefully (real hardware would report a
"low water mark" or comparable boundary; this project currently
passes the flat physical top of RAM with no floor), or by extending
`bump_alloc()`'s own tracked region to something SYSMEM's real
allocator is made aware of. This needs careful, disassembly-grounded
scoping (matching how Round 409's original `$a0` fix and Round 417's
stack-guard fix were each individually verified) before implementing,
consistent with this project's standing discipline. Left as Round
421's concrete task.

**Status:** all four existing candidate fixes remain uncommitted; this
finding identifies what is very likely the LAST blocker standing
between the current four-fix combination and genuine further boot
progress, but is not itself yet a verified fix.

## Round 421: SYSMEM heap sentinel gate implemented — but exposes a PRE-EXISTING, more serious EE-side regression from Round 417's own RAM-guard fix (docs-only, nothing shipped)

**Implemented (scratch-only, `/tmp/r414_clean`):** wired SYSMEM's real
heap-management exports (`AllocSysMemory`/`FreeSysMemory`/
`QueryMemSize`/`QueryMaxFreeMemSize`/`QueryTotalFreeMemSize` - real
ordinals 4/5/6/7/8, cited live from
`https://ps2dev.github.io/ps2sdk/sysmem_8h.html`) to this project's
own already-built, already-tested synthetic heap model (`iop_heap.c`,
Round 401) using the same "sentinel call-gate + intercept before
fetch" HLE mechanism already established for INTRMAN/EXCEPMAN (task
#109) and THREADMAN (Round 389). New files: `include/core/hw/
iop_hle_heap.h`, `source/hw/iop_hle_heap.c`; wired into
`link_imports_one()` (`iop_module_loader.c`) and `iop_step()`
(`iop_core.c`) at the same priority spot as the other HLE gates.
`iop_heap.c`'s own managed arena (`0x20000`-`0xF0000`) does not
overlap `BUMP_BASE=0x00100000`, so this directly resolves Round 420's
heap/bump_alloc collision with no new address-space bookkeeping.

**Result: the Round 420 BREAK-at-pc=0x18 crash is confirmed fixed.**
With fixes #1-#5 combined, the IOP no longer halts at all across a
20,000,000-cycle run (`iop_halted=0` throughout) - a genuine,
verified improvement over the four-fix combination's own BREAK crash.

**However, a full 20M-cycle run against the same baseline harness used
throughout this whole investigation (`driver414_progress.c`, 10 x
2,000,000-cycle checkpoints) shows the EE core landing at
`ee_pc=0x80005E90` at the 20M mark, vs. the established, freshly
re-verified baseline (fixes #1+#2 only, current committed HEAD
`f0e8c5a`) reaching `ee_pc=0x8000CF9C` at the exact same 20M mark
(re-run this round to confirm reproducibility - baseline still holds
exactly). This is a clear, measured regression by this project's own
established non-regression criterion.**

**Bisected the regression's origin** by building an isolated tree with
ONLY fix #3 (registration-list retry counter, Round 413) + fix #4
(Round 417's RAM backing-guard widening) - i.e. WITHOUT this round's
new heap sentinel gate at all. The exact same EE-side regression
(`ee_pc` bouncing in the `0x80005Exx`-`0x8000626C` range at every
2M-cycle checkpoint from 4M through 20M) is already fully present with
fix #4 alone. **This proves the EE regression was introduced by Round
417's RAM-guard fix itself, not by this round's heap sentinel work.**
Round 417 was previously verified only for its IOP-side effect
(advancing past LOADCORE, 5 modules self-registering, THREADMAN pool
handle becoming non-zero) - it was never checked against the 20M-cycle
EE-progress baseline specifically, and that check was overdue.

**Further diagnostic finding (more serious than initially apparent):**
dumped live EE RAM at `0x80005E00`-`0x80006300` after a full 20M-cycle
run (fix #3+#4 combination) and disassembled it with this project's
own MIPS decoder (`/tmp/mips_disasm.py`). The bytes at
`ee_pc=0x80005E58` decode as `UNK(op=0x19)` with raw word
`0x65746C61` - which, read as little-endian ASCII, spells "alte"
(part of a longer string, likely a diagnostic/panic message embedded
in BIOS/OSDSYS data). The EE core is not executing real code at this
address at all - **it has wandered off into a string/data region and
is "executing" ASCII text as if it were MIPS instructions**, with no
illegal-instruction exception raised (this project's own EE decoder
silently no-ops unrecognized opcodes rather than trapping - a
separate, pre-existing modeling gap, not itself Round 417's bug, but
what let this wild jump go unnoticed rather than halting cleanly).
This means Round 417's RAM-guard fix, despite being real, disassembly-
grounded, and directly responsible for the IOP's own furthest-ever
LOADCORE/EXCEPMAN progress, has a downstream side effect that causes
EE to jump to a garbage computed address - almost certainly because
IOP's new, different timing/register state changes some value EE
reads (a function pointer, a table entry, a SIF/shared-memory word)
that used to accidentally hold a safe value under the old two-fix
timing and now holds something else.

**Nothing shipped this round.** Per this project's standing "never
ship a measured regression" discipline: none of fixes #3/#4/#5 are
committed. All five remain scratch-only in `/tmp/r414_clean` (fixes
#1/#2 are the only ones on committed HEAD). This round's own new
heap-sentinel work (fix #5) is real, disassembly-grounded, and DOES
fix the BREAK-at-0x18 crash on its own terms - but it cannot ship
until the pre-existing EE wild-jump regression it was layered on top
of (introduced by fix #4, Round 417) is itself found and fixed, since
the combination as a whole currently regresses relative to the
committed baseline.

**Scoped for Round 422:** trace EE's own control flow starting from
where it diverges from the two-fix baseline's own path (both runs
share the same first ~2M cycles reaching `ee_pc=0x8000B8AC`
identically - the fix #4 RAM-guard change has zero EE-visible effect
until sometime after that point) forward to the first wild jump into
the `0x80005Exx`/string-data region, to find the specific jump-
register instruction and the specific memory location whose changed
value causes it. A live, in-flight instruction trace (not just
before/after static dumps, per this whole investigation's own
established "live vs static" methodology) is the natural next tool.

## Round 422: bisected the exact EE regression point - baseline's IOP does real CDVDMAN work around slice ~3,750,000 that fix #4's IOP never reaches, whether halted (BREAK) or looping at the interrupt-return trampoline (docs-only)

Built two isolated host-native trees - a clean copy of committed HEAD
(`f0e8c5a`, fixes #1+#2 only) and the fix #3+#4 combination without
Round 421's heap sentinel - and ran matched live traces to find
exactly where their EE-side behavior first diverges. Confirmed both
runs are bit-identical (same repeating `0x8000B8A0`-`0x8000B8B8` EE
idle-wait loop) all the way through slice 3,700,000. Between slice
3,700,000 and 3,800,000 the two runs diverge sharply:

- **Baseline (fixes #1+#2):** IOP is not halted; around slice
  ~3,750,000 it transitions from its resting state into the real,
  well-known CDVDMAN N-command dispatch alternation at
  `0x00118F0C`/`0x00118F90` (the exact resting-spin address pair
  identified back in Round 339). Correlated almost immediately (by
  slice 3,755,000) with EE jumping to `0x00200024`/`0x00200018` -
  OSDSYS's own loaded ELF entry point (the region identified in Round
  274) - real forward progress into the OS-side dispatcher, which is
  what eventually reaches `ee_pc=0x8000CF9C` by 20M.
- **Fix #3+#4 only (no heap sentinel):** IOP is ALREADY halted
  (`BREAK` at `pc=0x18`, Round 420's own already-documented crash) well
  before slice 3,700,000. Because IOP is frozen, it never reaches the
  CDVDMAN dispatch state the baseline reaches at ~3,750,000, so EE
  never receives whatever real signal that real IOP-side activity
  provides, and EE's own wait loop never exits toward
  `0x00200018` - it instead keeps spinning in the low kernel address
  range indefinitely, eventually reading further-out addresses that
  happen to contain ASCII string data (Round 421's finding) rather
  than real code.
- **Full fix #1-#5 (heap sentinel included):** re-ran the same
  bisection with the heap sentinel gate active. IOP no longer halts at
  `pc=0x18` (Round 421's fix genuinely works for that specific crash),
  but instead gets stuck cycling forever at `pc=0xE4`, which is
  `IOP_HLE_INTR_HANDLER_RETURN_TRAMPOLINE` (`include/core/hw/
  iop_hle_intr.h`) - i.e. the IOP is now stuck repeatedly entering and
  returning from a registered interrupt handler without making any
  further forward progress, never reaching CDVDMAN's dispatch either.
  **Same downstream symptom (EE never unblocks), different immediate
  cause** - this is not the same bug as the BREAK crash, it's a
  distinct interrupt-dispatch loop only reachable now that IOP
  survives past the point where it used to crash.

**Conclusion:** the EE regression is fully explained as a downstream
consequence of IOP never reaching its own real CDVDMAN dispatch state
under fix #4's changed boot timing - first because of the BREAK crash
(now fixed by Round 421's heap sentinel), and now because of a newly-
exposed interrupt-handler-return loop at `pc=0xE4`. This second loop
is very likely the same general category of bug as Round 340's
already-fixed "IRQ priority-starvation gap" - a new instance exposed
now that IOP reaches deeper boot state (EXCEPMAN/THREADMAN genuinely
active, per Round 417) where more interrupt handlers are registered
and can preempt each other more aggressively than the old, shallower
boot state ever allowed.

**Nothing shipped this round; all five fixes remain uncommitted.**
Round 423's task: disassemble the registered handler(s) reachable
through the `pc=0xE4` trampoline in the current five-fix combination
and find why control never escapes back to IOP's own main dispatch
loop toward the CDVDMAN N-command state, applying the same
"live-trace, not static-dump" methodology and the same category of
fix (likely another IRQ-priority/level-clearing gap) that resolved
Round 340's original instance of this bug class.

## Round 423 (MAJOR - first real source fixes shipped since Round 410): fixed the pc=0xE4 freeze - real root cause was this project's own interrupt-dispatch HLE clobbering the interrupted code's own $ra without restoring it - full five-fix combination now verified at or beyond the 20M-cycle baseline and SHIPPED

**Root cause (live-trace confirmed).** Added targeted instrumentation to
`iop_hle_intr_dispatch_interrupt()` and its own return trampoline and
traced the exact sequence live: dispatch#2 (irq=16) hands control to a
real registered handler with `$ra` clobbered to point at this
project's own `IOP_HLE_INTR_HANDLER_RETURN_TRAMPOLINE` (`pc=0xE4`) -
standard practice for this project's whole family of HLE call gates.
The handler finishes, `jr $ra` correctly lands back at the trampoline,
`in_dispatch` resets to 0, execution resumes at the real saved EPC -
all correct so far. But the code that was ORIGINALLY INTERRUPTED still
had its own real, legitimate `$ra` in the register file the instant
the interrupt was taken - and this project's dispatch mechanism had
silently overwritten it with the trampoline address to build its own
"return gate", without ever saving or restoring the original value.
The very next time that interrupted code does its own `jr $ra`
(returning to ITS real caller), it jumps straight back into the
trampoline instead - and since `in_dispatch` is already 0 by then, the
trampoline's own code had no `else` branch and silently left `st->pc`
completely unchanged, freezing forever at `pc=0xE4` with no further
forward motion (confirmed via `[R423tramp]` live trace: hit#1/#2 show
`in_dispatch=1` as expected, hit#3 onward show `in_dispatch=0`,
`st_ra=0xE4`, `st_pc=0xE4`, repeating roughly 19-20 million times -
essentially the entire remainder of every 20M-cycle run).

Real MIPS hardware interrupts never touch `$ra` at all - delivery is
purely EPC/Cause/Status-based, not a JAL-style call. This project's
own HLE dispatch mechanism's use of `$ra` as a synthetic "return gate"
is a deliberate, precedented convenience (matching every other HLE
call-gate in this codebase), but it was missing the one save/restore
step real hardware never needed in the first place.

**Fix (`source/hw/iop_hle_intr.c`):** added a `saved_ra` field to the
dispatch-globals struct; `iop_hle_intr_dispatch_interrupt()` now saves
`st->gpr[31]` before overwriting it; the return trampoline now
restores it (`st->gpr[31] = g.saved_ra;`) before resuming at the saved
EPC. Three lines of real logic change plus documentation - no other
behavior touched.

**Verification.** Bisection work (docs/STATUS.md Round 422) had
already isolated the freeze as blocking IOP from ever reaching its own
real CDVDMAN N-command dispatch state - the same state the committed
baseline (fixes #1+#2) reaches around slice ~3,750,000, correlating
with EE jumping to OSDSYS's own loaded ELF entry. With this fix
applied on top of the full five-fix combination (SYSMEM `$a0`, KSEG1
trampoline, `INITIAL_SP` widening, RAM backing-guard widening, SYSMEM
heap sentinel gate), a fresh 20M-cycle host-native run shows IOP never
halting and never freezing, and EE reaching `ee_pc=0x8000CFEC` at the
20M-cycle checkpoint - within 0x50 bytes of the committed baseline's
own `ee_pc=0x8000CF9C`, cycling through the same real OSDSYS
dispatcher address range the baseline itself cycles through
(`0x8000CCxx`-`0x8000Fxxx`), and reaching that same dispatcher region
by 4M cycles (baseline needs until ~4M-8M). This is a genuine match/
improvement over baseline, not a regression - full mandatory-workflow
verification:

- Rebuilt a clean copy of all six real changes (the two already-
  committed fixes plus `INITIAL_SP` widening, RAM backing-guard
  widening, the new SYSMEM heap sentinel gate files, and this round's
  `$ra` save/restore) directly into the tracked repo, stripped of
  every round's worth of scratch debug instrumentation accumulated in
  the investigation's own scratch trees.
- Ran the full existing host-native regression suite (every `tests/
  test_*.c` file, 88 total, using each test's own documented build
  recipe from `tests/README.md`): **88/88 pass**, zero build or
  runtime failures.
- Rebuilt for the real Wii target (devkitPPC + libogc, the project's
  actual cross-compilation toolchain): **clean build, zero warnings**,
  `pcsx2-wii-git.dol`/`.elf` produced successfully.

**Shipped.** All six changes committed together this round - the
first real source-code commit since Round 410. `include/core/hw/
iop_hle_heap.h` and `source/hw/iop_hle_heap.c` are new files; `source/
hw/iop_module_loader.c`, `source/core/iop/iop_core.c`, and `source/hw/
iop_hle_intr.c` are modified.

**What's next.** The IOP now runs indefinitely without halting or
freezing and reaches real OSDSYS dispatcher code - genuine, durable
forward progress past every wall this multi-hundred-round investigation
arc has hit. The EE side settles into cycling within the OSDSYS
dispatcher's own address range rather than monotonically advancing
further - consistent with this being the same real, repeating
dispatcher polling loop many earlier rounds (271, 313, 322-323)
already characterized, not a new blocker. Future rounds should
continue tracing what real condition (pad input, SIF2 payload, disc
read completion) OSDSYS's own dispatcher is still waiting on to break
out of that loop toward the splash screen itself.

## Round 424 (task #163, initial finding, docs-only): IOP has settled into executing the BOOT_INFO data struct itself at pc=BUMP_BASE (0x00100000), not real code - EE's own dispatcher cycling is real, but IOP's own resting state needs a closer look

Extended the checkpoint driver to 10M-cycle granularity across 40M+
cycles (host-native, Round 423's shipped six-fix combination). EE
continues cycling cleanly within the real OSDSYS dispatcher's own
address range (`0x8000CCxx`-`0x8000Fxxx`, plus a newly observed
`0x8000D010`) with no halts - consistent with Round 423's own
characterization of this as the same real, repeating dispatcher
polling loop earlier rounds (271, 313, 322-323) already identified.

IOP itself, however, is reproducibly parked at `iop_pc=0x00100000`
across every checkpoint from 10M through 40M cycles (never halted,
`iop_halted=0` throughout). A memory dump at that address shows NOT
clean code - a mix of a couple of real-but-degenerate instructions
(`ADD $at,$zero,$s0`, `SRL $zero,$zero,0` - a semantic no-op since it
targets `$zero`) interleaved with several genuinely undefined/reserved
SPECIAL-opcode words this project's own decoder has no mapping for.
Traced this address back to its real identity: `BUMP_BASE`
(`iop_module_loader.c`, `0x00100000`) is exactly where `boot_info_addr
= bump_alloc(BOOT_INFO_STRUCT_SIZE)` allocates the very first bytes
this project's own module loader ever hands out - i.e. **IOP's own PC
is sitting on top of the real BOOT_INFO data struct itself, not real
module code**. This project's IOP core already has an established,
documented "PC wandered below BUMP_BASE" guard (`iop_core.c` ~line
1068), but that guard only fires for `phys_pc < BUMP_BASE` - PC
sitting exactly AT `BUMP_BASE`, on real (if non-code) allocated data,
doesn't trip it.

**Not yet root-caused.** Two live open questions for the next pass:
whether this is a genuinely new, real bug (IOP wandered off its own
real code path via a bad jump and landed on BOOT_INFO, silently
"executing" a few of its words as harmless-by-coincidence
instructions and looping back via some real branch/jump embedded in
the data), or a project-side simplification already accounted for
elsewhere (e.g. an idle/park convention this project's own dispatcher
uses once IOP's real work for this phase is genuinely done, similar in
spirit to the already-documented CDVDMAN resting spin at
`0x00118F7C`-`0x00118F90` from Round 339, just at a different address
now that the boot sequence reaches further). A live instruction trace
(not just a static post-run dump) starting from the last known-good
IOP code address before this parking point is the natural next step,
following this whole investigation's own established "live over
static" methodology.

**Nothing shipped this round** - this is an investigatory finding

## Round 425 (task #164, SHIPPED): confirmed IOP boot genuinely completes - 29/29 real modules loaded, 28/29 run to completion for the first time ever - and fixed a real, previously-hidden correctness bug in the one-time idle transition

**Classified Round 424's finding.** Instrumented `iop_step()` with a
small ring buffer plus a first-arrival trap on `pc==0x00100000`, and
instrumented the module loader's own completion path directly. Live
trace confirmed: SYSMEM's real entry code runs its own genuine
24-instruction prologue starting at its real entry point (`0x1000A0`)
and returns cleanly via `jr $ra` - landing exactly on `g.trampoline_addr`
(`0x00100000`, the first byte the module-loading `bump_alloc()` ever
hands out), precisely as this project's own already-documented "call
gate" design intends (`iop_module_loader.c`'s trap-before-fetch check
at `pc==g.trampoline_addr`, mirroring every other HLE sentinel gate in
this codebase). **This is not a bug** - it's the real, working "module
entry finished, advance to the next module" mechanism, confirmed by a
direct completion-message capture: `29/29 real modules loaded, 28 run
to completion` at `instructions_executed=3,747,959` - full IOP module
boot completion, genuinely reached for the first time in this whole
multi-hundred-round investigation, thanks to Round 423's fix.

**Found a real, previously-hidden bug in what happens next.** Once
every module is exhausted, `advance_to_next_module()` returns false
and the loader transitions IOP into its already-documented `idle`
mode (Round 93/task #179) - but nothing ever moves `pc` away from
`g.trampoline_addr` afterward, so this same trap re-fires on *every
single subsequent IOP step* for the rest of the run (confirmed: the
completion message printed 2,082,370 times in one ~20M-cycle run,
not once). The one-time completion side effects were never gated
against re-entry, and one of them - `st->exception_pending = 0;`
(Round 93's own fix for a real leftover-exception-nesting artifact) -
was getting stomped back to 0 on every one of those re-fires. Per
`iop_core_step()`'s own idle-wake logic (`!pending_before &&
exception_pending`), a genuine hardware interrupt arriving while idle
needs a clean `0->1` transition on this exact flag to ever wake IOP
back up - this bug could silently eat that edge every time, making
real interrupts arriving during idle unable to ever resume IOP.

**Fix (`source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`):** added a single
`idle_transition_done` flag to the module-loader's own state struct,
gating the entire completion block (message, `mark_iop_boot_complete()`,
`idle=1`, the `Status.IEc`/`exception_pending` one-time corrections)
to run exactly once, matching the code's own already-stated intent.
Every later re-entry to the trap (which will keep happening - `pc`
has nowhere else to go once idle) is now a cheap, harmless no-op
early-return, exactly as originally intended.

**Verification (full mandatory workflow):**
- Host-native re-run: no regression - EE reaches `ee_pc=0x8000CC9C`
  at the 20M-cycle checkpoint, cycling through the same real OSDSYS
  dispatcher address range as both the committed baseline
  (`0x8000CF9C`) and Round 423's own verification run
  (`0x8000CFEC`); IOP still never halts or freezes.
- Full host-native regression suite: **88/88 pass**, zero build or
  runtime failures.
- Wii-target rebuild (devkitPPC/libogc): **clean, zero warnings**,
  `pcsx2-wii-git.dol`/`.elf` produced successfully.

**Shipped.** `source/hw/iop_module_loader.c` modified (new
`idle_transition_done` field + the one-time gate). This closes out
Round 424/425's investigation: the BUMP_BASE parking behavior itself
was always correct by design; the real bug was the unguarded re-
execution of its one-time completion logic, now fixed.

## Round 426 (self-discovered follow-up fix, SHIPPED)

Live wake-tracing found that Round 425's own fix, while correctly
stopping the `exception_pending` stomping, was too broad: gating the
*entire* module-completion block (including `st->idle = 1;`) behind a
single one-shot `idle_transition_done` flag meant that after the
*first* real hardware interrupt woke IOP from idle and its handler
RFE'd back to the parked trampoline address, `st->idle` never got set
back to 1. `iop_core_step()`'s idle branch (the only place that still
calls `iop_check_hw_interrupt()` while idle) was therefore permanently
skipped from that point on - IOP was stuck "not idle, but also not
doing real work", spinning through the now-harmless no-op trap every
single step for the rest of the run, unable to ever service a second
real interrupt.

A 10,000,000-instruction host-native trace with a wake-event counter
confirmed exactly one wake (`pc=0x00117CB4`, `instructions_executed=
3747960` - the real SIF0 DMA-completion handler at
`intr_handler_addr[42]`, per Round 174's own citation) both before and
after this round's fix, proving the defect was real but that it is not
(yet) what's gating further progress - see Round 427 below.

Fix (source/hw/iop_module_loader.c, `iop_module_loader_try_handle()`):
split the gate so re-parking into idle (`st->idle = 1;`) is a real,
repeatable action on every one of these re-entries, while the one-time
completion bookkeeping (message, `mark_iop_boot_complete()`,
Status.IEc-force, `exception_pending` clear) still runs exactly once,
guarded by falling through only when `idle_transition_done` was false.

Verification:
- 20M-cycle EE-progress checkpoint: `ee_pc=0x8000CC9C` at slice
  20,000,000 - identical to the Round 425 baseline, confirming no
  regression.
- Host-native regression suite: 88/88 PASS, no new failures.
- Wii target (devkitPPC/libogc) rebuild: clean, zero warnings.

Committed. This is a genuine correctness fix (the module-loader's
completion trap now behaves correctly across repeated wake/re-idle
cycles instead of only the very first one), but by itself it does not
yet unblock further EE/OSDSYS progress - the wake count is unchanged
because the real limiter lies elsewhere (see Round 427).

## Round 427 (queued): why does IOP only ever wake once?

`iop_check_vblank()` (source/core/iop/iop_core.c, ~line 609) is called
unconditionally every IOP step, even while idle, and does raise
`IOP_INTC_IRQ_VBLANK_START`/`_END` via `iop_intc_raise()` roughly every
615,186 instructions (`IOP_CYCLES_PER_FRAME_NTSC`/`_DURATION`).
Despite that, `iop_check_hw_interrupt()`'s `(intc->istat & intc->imask)`
gate only ever asserted Cause.IP2 once in the observed 10M-instruction
window, for the SIF0 DMA line - never for VBLANK. This strongly
suggests IOP_INTC's IMASK bit 0 (VBLANK) is never unmasked by any
module's real code at this point in the boot trace, so the interrupt
is raised into `istat` but never actually delivered. Next round should
trace whether any module ever writes IMASK bit 0, and if not, whether
that's a genuine emulation gap (real OSDSYS driver should unmask
VBLANK earlier) or expected/correct behavior for this exact boot
stage.

## Round 427 (SHIPPED): fixed the real reason IOP only ever woke once

Followed up on Round 426's own queued question ("why does IOP only
ever wake once?"). Live-traced `EnableIntr()` calls and confirmed
VBLANK (irq=0) IS unmasked early (`instructions_executed=45658`),
ruling out the initial IMASK-never-written hypothesis. The real cause
was simpler and more fundamental: `IOP_HLE_INTR_HANDLER_RETURN_
TRAMPOLINE` in source/hw/iop_hle_intr.c - the return path used every
time a real, module-registered interrupt handler finishes and RFEs
back - never cleared `st->exception_pending`, unlike every other
"async event fully handled" site in this codebase (the default-vector
stub in iop_core.c, and iop_module_loader.c's own idle-transition/
panic-bypass completion paths, which all explicitly follow a
documented three-part "done" convention: idle=1, IEc=1,
exception_pending=0). Once the first real interrupt (SIF0 DMA,
irq=42) dispatched through this trampoline, `exception_pending`
latched at 1 forever, which silently defeated `iop_core_step()`'s
idle-wake edge detector (`!pending_before && exception_pending`) -
`pending_before` could never be false again, so no second real
interrupt could ever register as a fresh wake event, regardless of
Round 426's own (still-necessary, still-correct) idle-regate fix.

Fix: add the missing `st->exception_pending = 0;` to that trampoline.

Live verification: a 10,000,000-instruction wake-event-counting trace
went from exactly 1 wake to 2,082,370 wakes after the fix - confirming
the diagnosis directly. Almost all of the new wakes are the SAME
already-known, already-documented VBLANK gap from Round 298/299/340
(no module has registered a real handler for irq=0 at this point in
the boot trace, so every VBLANK the CPU takes falls through to the
generic unhandled-interrupt default vector, which restores Status/
IEc but - correctly, per real level-triggered hardware semantics -
never acks intc->istat bit 0, so the same pending VBLANK keeps
re-triggering as soon as interrupts are re-enabled). This is expected,
physically-plausible behavior for an unresolved level-triggered
interrupt line, not a new bug - it reflects a genuine, real,
already-documented gap (no VBLANK ISR registered yet at this boot
stage), now finally OBSERVABLE for the first time instead of being
masked by the exception_pending latch bug.

Verification: 20M-cycle EE-progress checkpoint identical to the Round
426 baseline at every single 2M-instruction checkpoint (`ee_pc=
0x8000CC9C` @ 20M) - the interrupt-storm side effect does not disturb
EE-side timing/progress. 88/88 host-native regression tests pass,
clean zero-warning Wii (devkitPPC/libogc) rebuild.

Next: whether real OSDSYS/IOP code is SUPPOSED to register a VBLANK
handler this early, or whether this boot stage genuinely predates
that registration on real hardware too, is still open - see the new
Round 428 task queued to investigate.

## Round 429 (task #171, synthesis + fresh disassembly, docs-only): the real, precise, still-current architectural gap blocking the splash screen - re-confirmed via fresh live disassembly and cross-referenced against the full Round 271-338 investigation arc

Directly answering the user's "check what is missing for the splash screen." Disassembled a fresh live memory dump of the current resting loop (`0x8000CC00`-`0x8000D080`, captured post-Round-427) using this project's existing `mips_disasm.py` scratch decoder - confirmed byte-for-byte this is the SAME real per-frame kernel dispatcher (`0x8000CF88`+, SMFLAG debounce-read at `0x8000CC68`, device-table maintenance at `0x8000CC00`) that Rounds 265-271 already exhaustively characterized over 150 rounds ago, and Round 277 already established is OSDSYS's own genuine, correctly-functioning per-frame idle-loop code, not a bug in itself.

**Reconstructed the full arc's current, still-standing conclusion** (Rounds 271-340, cross-referenced against this session's own Round 425-428 IOP-side work):

1. OSDSYS's real ELF genuinely loads and executes (Round 273). Two real emulation bugs in this project's own code were found and fixed along the way: a `SetupThread` stack-pointer integer-overflow crash (Round 274, `stack_base=-1` sentinel mishandled) and an unimplemented `CD_SERVER_NCMD` SIF RPC causing a permanent semaphore park (Round 276), plus a real MCSERV protocol bug (Round 278). All three fixes are still present and active in the current tree (verified this round).
2. With those fixed, OSDSYS reaches real PADMAN/MCSERV/SPU2 RPC activity, creates a genuine second thread (Round 282) meant to install a VBLANK handler and/or signal a semaphore the main thread polls - but that thread's entry point is never dispatched, because this project's IOP/EE thread model supports exactly one schedulable execution context at a time (Round 330), not real concurrent scheduling.
3. **The precise, load-bearing root cause** (Rounds 335-338, re-confirmed by this session's Round 428 zero-`dispatch_ncmd()`-calls finding at 50M cycles): `ee_core.c`'s `SIF_SID_CDVD_NCMD` RPC handler answers every real CD-ROM command request with a hardcoded fake "success" reply instead of routing it to the real, already-loaded, already-initialized IOP-side `CDVDMAN` module. `CDVDMAN`'s real init genuinely runs (confirmed: real `RegisterIntrHandler(2, 0x00120d60)` call captured, Round 338), and this project's own `iop_cdvd.c` hardware-register-level dispatch layer (`dispatch_ncmd()`/`iso_read_sector()`) is fully built and already covered by tests (Round 206) - but nothing ever calls it in the real boot path, because this project's IOP model has no mechanism to re-invoke an already-initialized module's RPC-service code after its one-time init returns (Round 337).
4. Real hardware, by contrast, issues one genuine, front-loaded `ReadCd` command very early in boot (live-hardware-confirmed, Round 326/333) - this is very likely how real OSDSYS reads `SYSTEM.CNF`/its boot descriptor and proceeds toward either the disc-browser splash screen or game auto-boot, permanently bypassing the idle dispatcher this project's own trace instead spins in forever.

**This session's Round 425-428 work is real, correctly-scoped, and necessary - but addresses a different layer than this gap.** It fixed genuine IOP-CPU-level correctness bugs (module boot completion, idle/wake cycling, an `exception_pending` latch bug) that were real and worth fixing, but none of them touch the actual architectural bridge missing between the SIF RPC layer and real module re-entry - confirmed directly this round by re-running the exact same `dispatch_ncmd()` call-count check post-Round-427 and getting the same zero result Round 335 got 150+ rounds and roughly 2.6 billion fewer/more instructions ago.

**Honest bottom line on "what is missing for the splash screen"**: a real IOP RPC-request-delivery/re-entry mechanism - something that can deliver an incoming `SIF_SID_CDVD_NCMD` (or the `SIF_SID_CDVD_SCMD`/other CDVD-RPC family) request to `CDVDMAN`'s already-loaded, already-initialized real code and let it genuinely run again (not just once at init), extract real command parameters from the RPC payload, and let the reply be constructed from the real resulting hardware state (`iop_cdvd.c`'s already-correct register model) instead of a hardcoded placeholder. This is a real, scoped, non-trivial architectural feature - not a one-line fix - and it has been the single most concrete, most-evidenced next step on record since Round 337, still unattempted as of this round.

No fix shipped this round (synthesis + re-verification only). `git diff --stat` confirms only docs/STATUS.md changed.

## Round 430 (task #172, real fix): root-caused and fixed the Round 351/352 NULL-pointer TLB fault - a missing real `FIO_F_LSEEK` implementation, not a missing newline in real BIOS content

Directly continuing the user's own instruction ("disassemble those two and see if there is a solution") on the most concretely-evidenced open thread: the call chain `0x00213D18 -> 0x00213AA0 -> 0x002134A8` feeding a `strchr()`-style call (`0x00218368`) that Round 352 found genuinely returns NULL (no `0x0A` byte found), causing a real `sb $zero,0($s2)` NULL-pointer TLB-store-miss that routes execution into the OSDSYS dispatcher loop.

**Disassembly of the two remaining functions** (`/tmp/mips_disasm.py` applied to live memory dumps): `0x00213AC8` (inside the `0x00213AA0` function) is a real init routine that polls a device-status function (`0x00213300`, called with `$a1=0x80000001`) until it stops returning 0, then writes `1` to global `0x0028AA3C` (a "subsystem initialized" flag). `0x002134A8` issues a real `SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL` via the generic RPC dispatcher `0x00212AA8`. `0x0046E800` is a pointer target used by a guard function (`0x00213BC0`) that reads the `0x0028AA3C` flag.

**Live RPC trace** (scratch `R430_TRACE`/`EE_FILEIO_DEBUG` instrumentation, never committed) captured the real chain end-to-end: `0x00213AC8`'s init issues a real `SIF_SID_FILEIO` OPEN -> LSEEK -> LSEEK -> READ -> CLOSE sequence for `rom0:OSOPEN`. Verified via a standalone ROMDIR scanner that this specific BIOS's ROMDIR genuinely contains an `OSOPEN` entry (19 bytes) - ruling out "file not found" as the direct cause.

**Root cause, found by tracing the real bytes through each step.** The real `romdir_lookup()` function (already in `ee_core.c`, already used successfully by `LOADFILE`'s own `rom0:OSDSYS` resolution) correctly finds `rom0:OSOPEN`'s real content when called directly: `"100\nMOPEN\n00500000\n"` - three real newline bytes present, ruling out "missing newline in the real ROM content" as the cause (this fully retires the leading hypothesis Round 351/352 left open). Watching the real EE register/memory state at every live call to the `strchr()`-equivalent function found the actual failure: the buffer it receives (`a0=0x01FEFC80`, a real stack address, not the RPC recvbuf) is populated with **zero real bytes** - `FIO_F_READ`'s own real byte-copy loop never runs because the real caller's request `read_size` was `0`.

Tracing why `read_size` was `0` found the true root cause: real OSDSYS callers use the classic "`lseek(fd,0,SEEK_END)` to discover the real file size, `lseek(fd,0,SEEK_SET)` to rewind, then `read(fd,buf,<that size>)`" idiom (exactly the live-captured OPEN/LSEEK/LSEEK/READ/CLOSE sequence). Before this round, `SIF_SID_FILEIO`'s `FIO_F_LSEEK` (`rpc_number==4`) fell into the generic catch-all handler, which always wrote a neutral `0` regardless of real `whence`/`offset` - so the real caller's own `SEEK_END` request always answered `0`, and its subsequent `fioRead()` request size (computed from that real `SEEK_END` result) collapsed to `0` bytes. The destination buffer was therefore never populated with the real ROM content, and `strchr()`-scanning that untouched stack memory for `0x0A` genuinely, correctly finds nothing - this is the full, concrete explanation for Round 351/352's fault, fixable and NOT a missing-newline edge case in the real BIOS data.

**Fix** (`source/core/ee/ee_core.c`, new `SIF_SID_FILEIO && rpc_number==4` branch before the generic catch-all): implements real `fioLseek(fd,offset,whence)` semantics - reads the real `{fd,offset,whence}` sendbuf payload via the same DMA-table-indirection pattern `FIO_F_READ`/`FIO_F_OPEN` already use, computes the new file position for `SEEK_SET`/`SEEK_CUR`/`SEEK_END` (clamped to `[0, rom_size]`, matching this project's existing "no fabricated bytes past real EOF" convention), updates the real `fdrec->cursor`, and returns the real resulting position - exactly the value a real caller's `SEEK_END` request needs to size its subsequent `read()` correctly.

**Verification, live-traced end-to-end.** With the fix, the same `strchr()` call site now receives real, correctly-populated content across 20 consecutive real calls: `"100\nMOPEN\n00500000\n"` (OSOPEN), `"100\nMCLOCK\n00600000\n"` (OSCLOCK), `"100\nMBROWS\n007a0000\n"` (OSBROWS), `"100\nFONTM\n01d00000\n"` (OSFONTM), `"100\nFONTS\n01f00000\n"` (OSFONTS) - each a real 3-line descriptor (format tag / overlay-module name / hex load address) pointing to a larger real ROMDIR-resident module (e.g. `MOPEN`, confirmed present in the ROMDIR at 194401 bytes). The Round 351/352 NULL-pointer fault no longer occurs anywhere in this sequence. **Real forward progress**: full 20M-cycle re-trace shows the EE no longer parks statically at the old baseline `ee_pc=0x8000CC9C` for the entire run - it now genuinely executes OSDSYS's own loaded ELF code (`0x00200000`+ range, matching Round 274's own citation of where OSDSYS's ELF loads) partway through the run, before settling into a new, stable, tight resting loop (`ee_pc` oscillating `0x000820D0-0x000820E8`, a 24-byte/~6-instruction span) for the remainder of the 20M-cycle budget. This is the resource-loading sequence (OSOPEN/OSCLOCK/OSBROWS/OSFONTM/OSFONTS - real icon/font assets the splash-screen UI needs) completing successfully and the boot proceeding to whatever real condition gates the next step - not yet the splash screen itself, but a genuine, evidenced advance past a wall that has stood since Round 351.

**Sandbox-reset recovery note** (process transparency, not a finding): this round's compute sandbox was reset mid-investigation (a recurring, previously-documented environmental limitation - `/tmp` is ephemeral). The working git clone and all in-progress scratch instrumentation were lost before the fix could be committed. Recovered by: (1) confirming the `outputs/pcsx2-wii/` mirror folder's working-tree files were still current at the full Round 429 state (its own local `.git` history had drifted stale from a much earlier point in the project and was never the authoritative record - real progress lives in this session's own reasoning plus whatever the user has pushed to GitHub), (2) committing that current state as an explicit recovery checkpoint, (3) reconstructing the real BIOS/disc test fixtures from the user's own originally-uploaded files (`PS2_BIOS (1).zip`'s `ps2-0100j-20000117.bin` - confirmed byte-identical via the same `ROMVER` string cross-check used throughout this investigation; `Tekken Tag Tournament (Europe) (Demo).bin` as the disc image), and (4) re-applying and re-verifying this round's fix from this transcript's own preserved reasoning - the re-verification reproduced byte-for-byte identical results to the pre-reset run, confirming nothing was lost or altered in the recovery.

## Round 431 (task #179-182, investigation, docs-only): precisely characterized the new resting wall Round 430's fix exposed - a real "wait-then-consume" SIF_SMFLAG primitive called twice for the same one-shot bit

Directly continuing past Round 430's fix (per the user's "next to the splash screen"). Disassembled the new stable resting loop (`0x000820D0-0x000820E8`) the EE now reaches after the OSOPEN/OSCLOCK/OSBROWS/OSFONTM/OSFONTS resource-load sequence completes.

**The loop itself**: `lw $v0,0($v1)` (v1=`0x1000F230`=`SIF_SMFLAG`) `; and $v0,$v0,$a0 ; beq $v0,$zero,<loop>` - a standard poll for `($a0 & SMFLAG) != 0`. Live register dump at the point the EE is permanently stuck confirms `$a0=0x00040000` - `SIF_STAT_BOOTEND` ("IOP boot completed", same real, ps2sdk-cited bit this project's `mark_iop_boot_complete()` already sets - see Round 172/431's own citation of `sifdma.h`'s `SIF_STAT_BOOTEND=0x40000`).

**Full disassembly of the loop's containing function (`0x000820C0-0x000820F8`) reveals its real purpose**: a generic "wait for one caller-specified SMFLAG bit, then consume it" primitive - `jr $ra` / `sw $v1,0($v0)` in the branch-delay slot immediately writes the SAME bit value back to `SIF_SMFLAG`, which (per this project's own already-correct, PCSX2-sourced write-1-to-clear semantics for that register) clears the exact bit it just waited on. This is a real, standard one-shot event-wait-and-acknowledge idiom - not a bug in itself.

**The actual mechanism causing the new wall, live-traced end-to-end**: this function is called *twice* for the *same* bit (`BOOTEND`) in this boot trace. First call (`instr=30000891`): `SIF_SMFLAG` already holds `0x00070000` (`SIFINIT|CMDINIT|BOOTEND`, correctly set by this project's own `mark_iop_boot_complete()` earlier in the run - confirmed via a full write-history trace of `SIF_SMFLAG`), so the wait is satisfied instantly, the function clears `BOOTEND` (`smflag` becomes `0x00030000`) as its own real acknowledgment, and returns. Execution proceeds through OSDSYS's own further init code (including the real OSOPEN/OSCLOCK/OSBROWS/OSFONTM/OSFONTS resource-load sequence Round 430's fix unblocked, and a real one-time GS/display-related init routine at `0x00083B88`+, guarded by a static-init flag at global `0x00089530`). ~29 million real instructions later (`instr=58944431`), execution calls the *same* wait-and-consume function *again*, requesting the *same* `BOOTEND` bit - but nothing in this project's model re-sets that bit after the first call's own real consumption, so this second wait never resolves. The EE has been spinning in this exact loop, forever, for the remainder of every 20M-cycle trace since Round 430's fix landed.

**Why no fix was implemented this round.** `SIF_STAT_BOOTEND` is documented (ps2sdk `sifdma.h`) as a one-shot "IOP has finished its own boot-time module loading" signal - real hardware's IOP has no obvious reason to re-assert it a second time outside the already-modeled `_LoadExecPS2`-reset scenario (which this is not - no game load has been requested yet). The real, correct fix therefore is NOT "just set the bit again unconditionally" - that would be exactly the kind of unevidenced guess this project's own Round 279/280 history proves can actively harm progress (a speculative IOP-interrupt injection with no real trigger evidence routed straight into a real BIOS panic handler). The honest open question this round leaves unresolved: what real IOP-side event or module-completion is OSDSYS's second wait actually waiting for - is it truly the exact same `BOOTEND` bit semantically reused for a second, different real purpose (in which case some other real IOP action this project doesn't yet model should be setting it), or is this project's own control flow reaching this second wait call earlier/differently than real hardware would (in which case the bug is elsewhere, not in the SMFLAG model at all)? Answering this with real evidence (rather than guessing) is next round's task - likely requires either finding real ps2sdk/BIOS documentation of a second real BOOTEND-style handshake, or forward-disassembling the intervening `0x00084218`+ init code far enough to identify what specific real completion this second wait is gating.

**Verification**: docs-only round, no source changes - `git diff --stat` (pre-commit) confirmed only `docs/STATUS.md`/`docs/ROADMAP.md` touched. All instrumentation lives in scratch copies (`/tmp/r431/`, `/tmp/driver431_*.c`), never committed, pushed, or rsynced. No BIOS ROM bytes or disc image data touched the tracked repo or outputs mirror at any point.

## Round 432 (investigation, docs-only): user-provided real SIF/RPC documentation cross-referenced against `eesync.c`/`loadcore.h` - the "recurring dynamic-module-load" hypothesis is now evidence-against, not evidence-for; the `_LoadExecPS2` re-signal path is ruled out by timing; the second BOOTEND wait's real trigger remains unconfirmed

Directly continuing Round 431 using new evidence: the user supplied detailed real SIF-register/SIF-RPC documentation this round (SIF_MSCOM/SIF_SMCOM/SIF_MSFLG/SIF_SMFLG bit meanings, SIF DMA fifo mechanics, SIF RPC BIND/CALL/END protocol). It confirms `0x40000` ("IOP has finished booting") is real, is "sent by EESYNC", and confirms the write-1-to-clear wait/consume idiom Round 431 already found is standard, correct real protocol - not a bug in itself. This directly named the real IOP module responsible for the bit Round 431 traced, so this round re-opened the investigation to find and read that module's real source.

**Found and read `eesync.c` and `loadcore.h`** (`[RO]man` 2002-2003 archive, already present in the user's uploads, already partially cited by this project since Round 395). Key real facts extracted:

`eesync.c`'s `start()` does NOT call `sifman_call24_setBD000030(0x40000)` (the real function that writes the BOOTEND bit) directly. It only registers a callback: `loadcore_call20_registerFunc(SyncEE, 2, NULL)`. `SyncEE` itself (the function that actually sends the bit) only runs when LOADCORE later invokes that registered callback. This looked, at first, like real evidence for a "BOOTEND re-fires whenever LOADCORE completes loading a later module" hypothesis - the leading theory going into this round.

**Initial reading of `loadcore.h`'s cross-reference comment (`registerFunc` annotated `20(28)`, i.e. "called by module 28 only") looked like it argued against a recurring-hook theory - checking the fuller archive proved that reading wrong, and it's corrected here rather than left standing.** The single extracted `loadcore.h` only shows EESYNC (module 28) using `registerFunc`. But the project's own uploaded `modules03.zip`-`modules08.zip` archives (not yet fully extracted to the flat uploads folder) also contain `modules.iop/threadman.c`, which genuinely calls `loadcore_call20_registerFunc` TWICE - `registerFunc(&lc20_2, 2, 0)` and `registerFunc(&lc20_3, 3, 0)` - inside THREADMAN's own `thbase_start()`. THREADMAN is module 12 (`[iopboot] 12`), not module 28, and registers the SAME type value (2) EESYNC later registers. `loadcore.h`'s inline cross-reference comment was simply never updated across any of the 7 archive revisions checked (Aug 2002 - Feb 2003, 766-1281 bytes) to include THREADMAN's later call - real, human documentation drift in the source archive itself, not a project-side error, but real evidence that the comment is NOT an exhaustive/authoritative caller list and cannot be used to argue "EESYNC is the only real caller of registerFunc." That specific negative-evidence claim in this round's own earlier draft was wrong and is retracted here.

**Read `lc20_2`'s real content** (THREADMAN's own type-2 callback): it prints the real, well-known IOP boot banner - `"IOP Realtime Kernel Ver.0.9.1\r\nCopyright 1999 (C) Sony Computer Entertainment Inc."` - a message widely documented as appearing EARLY in real PS2 boot logs, immediately after Thread Manager initializes, not at the very end of the full 29-module static list. This is real corroborating evidence that `registerFunc`'s callbacks fire promptly, at or near the point of registration - not deferred to some later, separate broadcast event far downstream. Applied to EESYNC (module 28, the real last static module): its own `SyncEE` callback firing "promptly at registration" and firing "once, when the static list finishes" are the same real moment, since EESYNC is last - fully consistent with this project's existing `mark_iop_boot_complete()` model, and giving no reason to expect EESYNC's specific callback to fire a second time absent a genuine full module-list re-load (i.e. a real IOP reboot, which is the already-modeled and already-ruled-out-by-timing `_LoadExecPS2` path - see below). Two real modules using `registerFunc` strengthens the case that "type 2" is a genuine, reusable LOADCORE mechanism (not a one-off EESYNC hack), but does not, on the evidence gathered so far, show that EESYNC's OWN specific callback content re-fires more than once per boot.

**Re-examined the previously-ruled-in `_LoadExecPS2` re-signal path (`g_ee_loadexecps2_seen`, Round 251/task #411) as a candidate explanation for the second wait - ruled it out by timing.** That path only fires after `_LoadExecPS2` (EE syscall 6), which real OSDSYS only invokes when the user has actually selected a game/app to launch. Round 431's own live trace places the second BOOTEND wait immediately after the OSOPEN/OSCLOCK/OSBROWS/OSFONTM/OSFONTS resource-load sequence and the `0x00083B88` one-time GS/display init routine - both real, very-early boot-time initialization, well before any user selection or ELF-launch decision could plausibly have occurred. No `_LoadExecPS2`-syscall or IOP-reset-MMIO pattern appears anywhere in the captured instruction trace between the two waits (`instr=30000891` to `instr=58944431`). This rules out the one re-signal mechanism this project already has as the explanation for what's currently observed.

**Confirmed no real `loadcore.c` implementation exists anywhere in the user's uploaded archives** - checked all 7 revisions of `modules*.zip` (`modules.zip` through `modules08.zip`, plus `modules2.zip`), every one contains only `include/loadcore.h` (the header), never a `.c` body. `loadcore_call20_registerFunc`'s actual dispatch/invocation logic is real, but not present in any material this project has access to.

**Net state, honestly**: the real documentation the user provided confirms this project's SIF_SMFLAG model (bit meanings, write-1-to-clear semantics, EESYNC as BOOTEND's real sender) is correct. Finding THREADMAN's real second use of `registerFunc` (type 2, printing the real "IOP Realtime Kernel" banner) strengthens the case that this is a genuine, reusable LOADCORE mechanism rather than an EESYNC-specific one-off - but the banner's own well-documented EARLY real boot-log timing (right after Thread Manager inits, not deferred) is evidence FOR "callbacks fire promptly at/near registration," which for EESYNC (the real last static module) still lands on the same single moment this project's `mark_iop_boot_complete()` already models. Nothing found this round shows EESYNC's own specific callback content re-firing a second time absent a genuine full module-list reload. Per this project's own Round 279/280 precedent, no speculative fix (e.g. unconditionally re-firing BOOTEND on the second wait) was implemented this round - that remains exactly the kind of unevidenced guess previously shown to actively route into failure states rather than progress. The concrete, narrowed-down open question for next round: with no real `loadcore.c` available, the remaining paths are (a) find whether ps2sdk's own modern loadcore reimplementation (already partially cited Round 375) documents an equivalent callback-invocation mechanism with clearer timing semantics, or (b) forward-disassemble far enough past `0x00084218`/`0x00083B88` (the GS/display init routine Round 431 left unfinished) to identify what real, different condition the second wait call site might actually be checking - i.e. re-examine whether this is genuinely the same semantic BOOTEND check reused, or whether this project's own disassembly/tracing has mis-identified the second call site's real purpose.
