## Round 463 (tasks #333, #337-338): the entire five-round mystery resolved - real kernel mechanism confirmed 100% correct end-to-end, but hands back to OSDSYS's own resource loader instead of the target game (major finding, still no safe fix)

Direct continuation of Round 462, now armed with the real `ps2sdk
ExecPS2.c` source the user shared (three URLs: `struct_t_c_b.html`,
`_exec_p_s2_8c_source.html`, and a tangential PS2-homebrew blog post).
Cross-referencing every previously-disassembled address against this
authoritative source confirmed near-perfect matches for every function
traced since Round 459: `0x800125EC` (ThreadID global), `0x80004970`
(CancelWakeupThread), `0x80004288` (ChangeThreadPriority), `0x80017400`
(TCB base), and the real TCB struct layout (identical to Round 380's
earlier citation).

Extended the instrumented trace with 10 landmark breakpoints drawn
directly from the real `SoftPeripheralEEReset()`/`ExecPS2Patch()`
pseudocode. A first run confirmed InitSemaphores, InitPgifHandler2,
InitializeGS, SetGSCrt, InitializeINTC (9x), InitializeTIMER, ResetEE,
and InitializeFPU all fire in exactly the documented order - but the
run ended with PC parked at `0x8000B8B4`, one instruction inside a
loop just before `InitializeScratchPad`'s own entry point, with 8.8M
instructions spent motionless.

Disassembly of `0x8000B878-0x8000B8C8` revealed this isn't a hang -
it's a **second, generic quadword-fill loop** whose bounds come from
a helper call to `0x80000C40` (a simple getter reading global
`0x80013C10`). Direct register instrumentation confirmed the real
numbers: start=`0x00082000`, end=`0x02000000` - a genuine ~33MB
memory clear from just past the kernel-reserved area to the top of
physical EE RAM (which is exactly 32MB), needing ~2,067,456 quadword
iterations. This is real, correct, textbook PS2 kernel hygiene -
clearing stale memory before handing off to untrusted game code -
just inherently slow to execute in an interpreter. Not a bug.

Extending the trace budget from 16.5M to 26M slices let this loop run
to completion (`instr=137614390`), and everything that had been
missing for five rounds fired immediately afterward, in order:

1. **InitializeScratchPad** landmark hit (`instr=137615588`) -
   confirming SoftPeripheralEEReset()'s full real sequence is now
   100% accounted for.
2. **`p_ExecPS2` landmark hit** (`instr=137696432`) - the real kernel
   genuinely takes the REUSE_EXECPS2 branch and calls the real
   fixed-address kernel function, exactly as the ps2sdk source
   describes.
3. **TCB slot 3's `entry` field (the calling thread - confirmed by
   Round 462) is finally written** - multiple times, settling on
   `0x00210e78` after several intermediate writes to `0x00210d68`.
   This is the exact write this project has been hunting since Round
   461.

**The catch**: `0x00210e78`, like every other TCB.entry value written
this round (`0x00200008`, `0x0020c260`, `0x00203d78`, `0x00204308`,
`0x00205dc0`, `0x00214a70`), sits inside OSDSYS's own resident code
range (`0x00200000-0x00220000`), not the target game's real load
address. And the FIO_F_OPEN calls that follow are all OSDSYS's own
internal resources - `rom0:OSBROWS`, `mc0:/mc1:.../OSBROWS`,
`rom0:OSFONTM/OSFONTS`, `rom0:MOPEN/MCLOCK/MBROWS/FONTM/FONTS` - not
Tekken Tag Tournament's own files.

**Conclusion**: the real kernel's `_LoadExecPS2`/`ExecPS2Patch`
mechanism is now confirmed **100% correct, call-for-call, end-to-end**
against the authoritative ps2sdk source - every sub-call fires in the
right order, `p_ExecPS2` really is reached, and the calling thread's
TCB really is repurposed. The mechanism itself is not broken. What's
missing is upstream of it: this project's synthetic trampoline (Round
457) calls `_LoadExecPS2` with a dummy filename string and `argc=0`,
and the real kernel's response to that specific input is to fall back
into OSDSYS's own resource-reload path - not evidence that real
argument passing is broken, but evidence that **the trampoline's
synthetic call arguments don't carry whatever real information (likely
the actual SYSTEM.CNF-derived BOOT2 path, or a correctly-populated
argv) the real kernel needs to target the game instead of OSDSYS's own
menu flow.**

No source fix implemented (same honest classification as Rounds
459-462 - this is real, correct BIOS code, now confirmed complete).
This closes the "is the exception-dispatch mechanism itself broken"
question for good - it isn't. The next concrete step is upstream:
verify what filename/argv this project's Round 457 trampoline actually
passes, and whether constructing a real SYSTEM.CNF-derived BOOT2-style
call (instead of a synthetic placeholder) changes the outcome. See
docs/ROADMAP.md for full detail.

## Round 464 (tasks #343-344, #347-348, #351): filename-argument loss pinpointed to before the first sub-call - no safe fix yet, organic boot re-verified unchanged (honest negative result)

Direct continuation of Round 463, attempting to act on its leading
hypothesis: that the trampoline's synthetic `argc=0`/`argv=NULL` call
was why `p_ExecPS2` ends up targeting OSDSYS's own code instead of the
game. Disassembled `p_ExecPS2` itself (`0x800057E8-0x800058E4`) for the
first time and found it's much simpler than expected: it saves its own
`$a0` (filename), `$a1` (argc), `$a2` (argv) into callee-saved
registers, optionally copies `argc` argv strings into a real ArgsBuffer
(skipped when `argc<=0`, confirming Round 462's dead ArgsBuffer
observation), then **writes its own `$a0` (filename pointer) directly
into `TCB[currentThreadID].entry`** - real ELF-loading/entry-point
resolution is not done here; the filename pointer itself becomes the
new "entry", presumably interpreted later at thread-scheduling time.

Instrumented `p_ExecPS2`'s entry directly and captured the real
arguments it received: `a0=0x00200008` (OSDSYS's own ELF entry
address, not our trampoline's string buffer at `0x01FE0000`),
`a1=0`, `a2=1`. The string at `0x00200008` isn't text - it's OSDSYS's
own code. This confirms Round 463's TCB.entry writes (`0x00210d68`/
`0x00210e78`) trace back to this substituted filename, not a separate
issue - and explains the repeated `FIO_F_OPEN` pattern for OSDSYS's own
OSBROWS/OSFONTM/MOPEN/etc. resources both before AND after `p_ExecPS2`
fires: it's OSDSYS's own startup sequence running twice, not the game.

To find where the substitution happens, added `$a0` snapshots at every
real sub-call already instrumented (`CancelWakeupThread`,
`ChangeThreadPriority`, the `TerminateThread`/`DeleteThread` loop,
`InitSemaphores`, `InitPgifHandler2`, `InitializeGS`, `InitializeFPU`,
`InitializeScratchPad`). Result: **our trampoline's filename pointer is
already gone by the very first sub-call** (`CancelWakeupThread`, where
`$a0=3`, the thread ID) - `$a0` is legitimately reused as a scratch/
argument register by every one of these real subroutines for their own
purposes throughout the whole chain, exactly as MIPS calling convention
allows for a caller-saved register. This is not a preservation bug in
any of the callees - it means the real top-level dispatcher (the
function that calls `CancelWakeupThread` first, immediately after the
exception vector) must itself save the filename into its own
callee-saved register before making any of these calls, and by the
time it finally invokes `p_ExecPS2` at the end, that saved value is
already `0x00200008` - not our string.

**This function - the actual top-level `_LoadExecPS2`/`ExecPS2Patch`-
equivalent dispatcher that receives the syscall and orchestrates the
whole sequence - has never been disassembled in this project's own
investigation.** Everything traced since Round 459 has been its
*callees*. Finding out whether it substitutes the filename due to a
real, evidenced validation failure (most likely: our synthetic
trampoline never performs whatever pre-flight file-open/validate step
a real OSDSYS caller would do before reaching this syscall) or due to
a genuine emulation gap requires disassembling that function directly
- not yet done, and not a small task given its address is still
unknown.

**No safe fix implemented.** This is not a case of "we found the bug
but didn't get to it" - the actual root cause is still one level
removed from anything this investigation has directly observed.
Implementing a fix without disassembling that dispatcher first would
be exactly the kind of unevidenced guess this project's discipline
(task #180) rules out.

Re-verified the organic (non-trampoline) boot path is unchanged: a
fresh 35M-slice run shows the same real BIOS intro-animation content
(0 triangles, 375 sprites, 4888 lines - matching Round 452's already-
documented stable state) and all GS display registers still zero.
Cross-checked against the live PCSX2 reference session (still
connected, real Tekken Tag Tournament Demo paused mid-game-code at
`pc=0x003993b8` since Round 458): its GS registers are *also* entirely
zero at this exact paused point, meaning even accurate, real hardware
emulation hasn't configured a display path yet this early in real game
code either - reassuring context, not a new finding.

**No new visual milestone this round.** The current best rendered
frame remains the Round 450 intro-animation capture (640x448,

## Round 465 (tasks #353-354): major structural discovery - real p_ExecPS2 caller found, two leading hypotheses both disproven as dead code, true branch point still open

Direct continuation of Round 464's exact next step: locate the real
top-level `_LoadExecPS2` dispatcher function. Found it via the fastest
possible method - capturing `$ra` (return address) at
`CancelWakeupThread`'s entry, which pointed straight at `0x80005664`,
inside a real function starting at `0x800055A0`.

Disassembled `0x800055A0`'s full body (~360 instructions) and confirmed
it: saves the filename argument into `$s6`, calls the real `eestrcpy`
helper twice (building a combined string in the real ArgsBuffer -
finally resolving Round 459's 5-round-old "EELOAD" mystery: the buffer
starts with a 7-byte `"EELOAD\0"` prefix from a fixed kernel string,
with our filename appended right after it, confirmed byte-for-byte via
direct instrumentation), then proceeds through the real
`CancelWakeupThread`/`ChangeThreadPriority`/`TerminateThread`-loop/
`InitSemaphores`/`InitPgifHandler2` sequence already traced in Rounds
461-463.

Two major surprises this round, both found by tracing *actual executed
PCs* rather than trusting linear disassembly order:

1. **The hypothesized ROM-residency validation block
   (`0x80005670-0x800056CC`, containing calls to `0x8000ABC0`/
   `0x8000AC58` that looked like a real ROMDIR scan + name-check) is
   never executed on this path.** A full window-trace of every PC
   visited between `ChangeThreadPriority`'s call and the
   `TerminateThread` loop's start shows execution actually flows
   through several small helper functions (real O(1) priority-queue
   bucket helpers at `0x80005938`/`0x80005978`/`0x80005AE8`/
   `0x80005B08`, presumably internal to `ChangeThreadPriority`'s own
   real implementation) directly into the `TerminateThread` loop -
   completely bypassing the ROMSCAN block. This round's leading
   hypothesis from the write-up is disproven by direct evidence.

2. **`p_ExecPS2` is not called from within `0x800055A0`'s own body at
   all.** Tracing the exact PC window immediately before `p_ExecPS2`
   fires (`instr≈137696432`) shows it's actually called from
   `0x80002F88` - a completely different, much lower kernel address,
   positioned immediately after a real COP0-register get/set syscall
   dispatch table (`0x80002E80-0x80002F74`, handling individual
   `mfc0`/`mtc0` syscalls for registers 14/16/23/24/25/28/29/30). Right
   before `p_ExecPS2`, this code calls `0x80003680` - disassembled and
   confirmed to be a **full register-context-save routine** (saves all
   GPRs, `$gp`/`$fp`/`$sp`, and all FPRs into a fixed per-thread save
   area) - with zero instructions between that call and `p_ExecPS2`.
   This means `p_ExecPS2`'s `$a0` argument is simply whatever the live
   `$a0` register organically holds at that exact point - and per
   Round 464's own `$a0`-snapshot trace, that's the tail end of a long
   chain of legitimate scratch-register reuse (thread IDs, loop
   counters, semaphore pointers, GS/FPU/ScratchPad control values),
   not our filename.

A third finding narrows things further: `0x800055A0`'s own tail
(`0x8000578C-0x800057B4`) contains what looks like the *real* final
step of the documented `SoftPeripheralEEReset()`/`ExecPS2Patch()`
sequence - two genuine I/D-cache-flush routines (confirmed via
disassembly: `cache` instruction loops, matching the real source's
"flush caches" step) followed by an EPC write (`mtc0 $s2,$14` with
`$s2=0x00082000`, the exact same address as Round 463's 33MB RAM-clear
loop's start) and an `ERET`. But Round 461 already proved ERET never
executes in this trace and EPC is only ever written once, to our
trampoline's own dead-loop address - meaning **this tail sequence,
which looks like the "textbook correct" ending, is also dead code on
our execution path.**

**Conclusion**: `0x800055A0` receives our filename correctly and does
real, legitimate setup work, but execution never reaches either of its
two "obviously important" tail blocks (ROM validation, cache-flush+
ERET). Something diverts control flow elsewhere between
`InitPgifHandler2`'s call (`0x80005744`) and wherever it ultimately
rejoins the `0x80002F80`/`p_ExecPS2` path - a transition this round
didn't find. This is a real structural discovery (the function
boundary and caller relationship was completely misunderstood before
this round), not a dead end - it's a much more precisely scoped next
step. See docs/ROADMAP.md for the full disassembly and the concrete
Round 466 plan.

No source fix implemented this round - the actual branch point that
would explain the divergence is still unlocated, and guessing at it
would violate this project's standing discipline against unevidenced
fixes. Organic boot path unchanged (no new run needed this round;
Round 464's re-verification still holds since no source changed).

## Round 466 (tasks #361 revised, #362-365): corrected entry-address trampoline built and run - real game crt0 executes for the first time ever, reaches a new, more precisely located dead end

User shared three reference URLs this round and asked to continue
toward the splash screen. The first (`ps2sdk`'s `ExecPS2.c` full
source, already partially cited in earlier rounds but this time
fetched and read in FULL) produced the round's key architectural
correction: `ExecPS2Patch(EntryPoint, gp, argc, argv)` - the real
function underlying both `_ExecPS2` (syscall 7) and, after real
file-loading, `_LoadExecPS2` (syscall 6) - takes an **already-resolved
jumpable entry-point address** as its first argument, not a filename.
Every trampoline test since Round 457 used syscall 6 with `$a0` set to
a raw filename-string pointer, based on the real, correct
`_LoadExecPS2(filename, argc, argv)` signature - but this project's
BIOS ROM model has no real IOP-side LOADFILE-RPC file-reading service
backing that syscall, so the filename could never actually be resolved
to an entry point by resident ROM code. This retroactively explains
every `$a0` loss/substitution documented in Rounds 457-465: the test
methodology itself, not any single function's logic, was miscalibrated.

This project's own `ee_core.c` already contains independent, real
confirmation: its `sysnum==7` handler comment (written back in the
Round 195/196 era) cites **byte-exact real organic-boot evidence** for
`_ExecPS2`'s calling convention - `$a0=0x00200008` (OSDSYS's own real
`e_entry`, matching a `sif_loadfile_elf_load()` ELF-header read that
same round), `$a1=0` (gp), `$a2=1` (argc), `$a3`=an argv-style
pointer. This is exactly the signature the fetched `ExecPS2.c` source
describes, and confirms syscall **7**, not 6, is the right dispatch
mechanism to use once the ELF has already been loaded by other means.

**What was built and run this round** (scratch only - see below for
why no tracked source changed):

1. Extracted the real game ELF (`SCED_500.41;1`) from the disc image
   using this project's own, previously-built, tested infrastructure -
   `iso_loader.c`'s `iso_open()`/`iso_find_in_root()`/`iso_read_sector()`
   (Round 139/170), which correctly auto-detected the disc's real raw
   Mode-2-Form-1 sector format (2352-byte stride, 24-byte data offset) -
   an earlier hand-rolled plain-2048-byte-sector extraction attempt
   this round produced garbage bytes and was discarded once this was
   understood. Verified the extracted file is a genuine ELF32/MIPS
   ET_EXEC image with real `e_entry=0x003572a0` and three PT_LOAD
   segments spanning `[0x00100000,0x01fcdaf0)`.
2. Used this project's own, pre-existing, tested ELF loader
   (`ee_elf_loader.c`, Round 171) to load all three PT_LOAD segments
   into EE RAM host-side, before ever touching the CPU state - i.e.
   this driver performs the file-read + ELF-parse + memory-load work
   that a real IOP-side LOADFILE RPC would normally do, so the BIOS
   syscall itself doesn't need to.
3. Rebuilt the Round 457 trampoline with the corrected calling
   convention: `$a0=0x003572a0` (the real, resolved entry address,
   not a filename pointer), `$a1=0` (gp), `$a2=1` (argc), `$a3`=a
   pointer to a one-entry argv array (matching the real organic-boot
   precedent exactly), `$v1=7` (`_ExecPS2`, not 6), then `syscall`.

**Result - real, substantial, evidenced forward progress:**

For the first time in this project's history, **real PS2 game code
actually executes past the initial hijack point.** Fine-grained
single-instruction tracing confirms the EE core, immediately after our
syscall fires, executes a genuine ps2sdk crt0 BSS-clear loop at
`0x003572B0-0x003572C8` - decoded instruction-by-instruction: `$v0`
(`_fbss=0x005f6700`) and `$v1` (`_end=0x01fcdaf0`, exactly matching
our own loader's reported `load_end`) are compared via `sltu`, and a
real EE-specific `SQ $zero,0($v0)` (128-bit store-quadword-of-zero)
clears 16 bytes per iteration, advancing `$v0` by `0x10` each pass -
textbook-correct real ps2sdk crt0 behavior, clearing the game's real
~27MB BSS region one quadword at a time (roughly 1.7M iterations,
which is why the loop dominates the first ~1.48M emulated slices after
install).

After the BSS-clear loop genuinely completes (`$v0` reaches `$v1`),
crt0 continues into real code at `0x003572D4-0x00357324`, which issues
a real syscall - and single-instruction tracing shows the EE
transitions into genuine BIOS ROM code (`0x8000021C` through
`0x800016F4`, including a captured real `STATUS`-register write at
`0x800003C8`) that is exactly consistent with the real **SetupThread**
syscall (EE syscall 60) crt0 is documented to call for a real stack
pointer, per `ee_elf_loader.h`'s own citation of real crt0 behavior.

**The new, more precisely located dead end**: after this real
SetupThread-style dispatch completes (traced through a real
JALR/ERET/EPC-write sequence at `0x80002848-0x80002878`, captured live
by this project's existing Round 461 ERET/EPC instrumentation), the
thread-resume jump lands at `0x00203BE0` - inside the *other* game
PT_LOAD segment (`PT_LOAD1`, `0x00200000-0x00340000`), which is a
pure-BSS segment our own `ee_elf_load()` correctly zero-fills (verified
by direct source read - the zero-fill loop unconditionally covers
`[p_filesz,p_memsz)` for every segment, including `p_filesz==0` ones,
so there is no loader bug here). Landing there means the CPU executes
an extended run of literal zero words, which decode as `SLL
$zero,$zero,0` (NOP) - confirmed by the per-slice PC advancing by
exactly `0x20` bytes (8 instructions) per emulated slice, matching this
project's known 8:1 EE:IOP interleave ratio exactly, with GPRs
completely static across many single-step traces (real NOPs touch no
registers). Extending the run to 40,000,000 slices shows the EE
eventually resumes real code again near `0x00340000` (PT_LOAD2's base)
and, through further genuine BIOS exception activity (more real
ERET/EPC-write/STATUS-write cycles, all captured live), ultimately
resettles into the *same* long-standing OSDSYS dispatcher resting loop
this project has observed since deep in its history
(`0x8000CF90`/`0x8000CFD8`/`0x8000F864`-class addresses) - not a crash,
but also not new visible progress. GS state is unchanged from every
prior round (`pmode=0x66`, `dispfb1=0`, `display1=0`), and GIF draw
counts are byte-identical to the pre-install organic-boot steady state
(343 sprites, 4888 lines, 333 points, 0 triangles) - confirming no new
rendering occurred during this excursion.

**Open question for a future round**: why does the real thread-resume
jump (immediately after the real SetupThread-style dispatch) land at
`0x00203BE0` instead of continuing crt0 execution back in the game's
own code region (`~0x003572xx` onward)? The real `ExecPS2Patch` source
(quoted in full in `docs/ROADMAP.md`) only ever writes `tcb->entry`/
`tcb->gpReg`/`tcb->argc`/`tcb->argstring` for the repurposed TCB - it
never touches `tcb->stack`/`tcb->stackSize`/`tcb->stack_res`, which
real hardware (and this trace) correctly leaves pointing at the
*original* calling thread's (OSDSYS's) own stack - that part is
expected, matches real ps2sdk semantics, and is not the bug. The
`0x00203BE0` jump target itself is the open question: is it read from
a TCB field this project's `p_ExecPS2`/dispatch modeling doesn't set
correctly, or is it genuinely a stale/leftover value from OSDSYS's own
original thread context that real hardware would also produce here
(in which case the actual real-hardware divergence point is even
further upstream)? Needs a targeted disassembly of
`0x80002840-0x80002878` (the JALR/ERET site) in a future round - not
guessed at here, per this project's standing discipline against
unevidenced fixes.

**Why no tracked source changed this round**: `ee_core.c` was not
modified - the architectural correction (syscall 7 vs 6, entry-address
vs filename) applies entirely to the *scratch test trampoline*
(`/tmp/driver_r466.c`, never committed), not to any BIOS-emulation
logic in tracked source. The real syscall 6/7 dispatch (raising a real
exception and letting resident BIOS ROM code handle everything) was
already correctly implemented in Rounds 195/196/251 and needed no
change. `ee_elf_loader.c`/`iso_loader.c` (both pre-existing, both used
read-only this round) also needed no change - both behaved exactly as
documented. This is therefore a docs-only investigation round: host-
native regression suite and Wii cross-build are correctly skipped (no
source changed), matching the precedent set by Rounds 463-465.

This round is real, significant, evidenced forward progress - the
first time this project has ever gotten real PS2 game code to execute
meaningfully past a hijack point, including a fully genuine BSS-clear
and a fully genuine BIOS syscall dispatch - even though it does not
yet reach a splash screen or any new visible GS output. See
`docs/ROADMAP.md` for the full instruction-level trace excerpts and
the concrete Round 467 plan.

## Round 467 (tasks #366-370): fully decoded the ERET-glue chain - 0x00081FE0 is a fixed, generic kernel thread-start trampoline; the real per-call entry point travels through $v1, not $a0

Continued directly from Round 466's open question: why does the
post-SetupThread thread-resume jump land at `0x00203BE0` (zero-filled
BSS) instead of continuing the game's real crt0? Disassembled the
real BIOS glue at `0x80002840-0x80002878` (the JALR/EPC-write/ERET
site captured live by Round 461's instrumentation) directly from a
Round 466 checkpoint's EE RAM contents, using this project's own
Round 350 MIPS decoder.

**The glue function itself** (`0x80002840`) is a small, generic,
real primitive:
```
lui  $k0,0x8001; sw $ra,...($k0)   ; save $ra to a fixed slot
lui  $k0,0x8001; sw $sp,...($k0)   ; save $sp to a fixed slot
mtc0 $a0,$14                        ; EPC = $a0 (jump target)
sync
daddu $v1,$a1,$zero                 ; v1 = a1  (args shift down by one)
daddu $a0,$a2,$zero                 ; a0 = a2
daddu $a1,$a3,$zero                 ; a1 = a3
daddu $a2,$t0,$zero                 ; a2 = t0
mfc0 $k0,$12; ori $k0,$k0,0x12; mtc0 $k0,$12; sync   ; STATUS bits
eret
```
This is a generic "jump to `$a0` via `eret`, shifting `$a1..$t0` down
into `$a0..$a2` for the callee" mechanism - not something specific to
our game's boot at all.

**The caller** (`0x80001630`, reached via `0x800016F4-0x80001704`)
walks a real kernel table at base `0x80015C60` (computed via
`mult $s3,$v0` where `$s3` is a "slot/priority" argument passed into
`0x80001630`), reading four fields from the indexed entry: `+8`
(becomes the glue's `$a1` -> ultimately `$v1`), `+12` (loaded directly
into `$gp`), `+16` (becomes `$a3` -> ultimately `$a2`), and `+20`
(checked `==2`, a type/kind discriminator gating this whole dispatch
path). Crucially, `$a0` passed to the glue is **not** read from this
table at all - it's read from a separate fixed global at `0x800124E4`.

**The key discovery**: instrumented every write to `0x800124E4`
across a full fresh-boot run (initially found zero hits due to a
scratch-instrumentation brace-nesting bug - fixed, not a tracked-
source issue - then confirmed real writes once corrected). Exactly
**one** write occurs in the entire run, at `instr≈29,931,092` (deep in
the pre-trampoline organic-boot phase, tens of millions of
instructions before our own syscall-7 ever fires) - a tiny real
kernel setter function (`0x80001578: lui $at,0x8001; sw $a0,...;
jr $ra`) called from real one-time kernel-init code at `0x80001060-
0x800010B8`, with the value passed as a **literal hardcoded constant**
(`lui $a0,0x0008; ori $a0,$a0,0x1FE0` -> `$a0=0x00081FE0`) - not
anything computed from thread/TCB state. This means `0x800124E4`
holds the same fixed value for the entire run regardless of which
thread or syscall is active - it is a genuine, static real-kernel
"default dispatch target" constant, not something our trampoline
could have corrupted.

**Disassembled `0x00081FE0` itself** (the EPC/`$a0` target) and found
it is exactly the real, generic **thread-start trampoline** every PS2
kernel thread launch goes through:
```
0x80081FE0: lui   $sp, 0x0008
0x80081FE4: jalr  $ra, $v1        ; call through $v1 - the REAL entry point
0x80081FE8: addiu $sp, $sp, 8128  ; (delay slot) sp = 0x00081FC0
0x80081FEC: addiu $v1, $zero, -5
0x80081FF0: syscall                ; cleanup syscall if the thread body returns
```

**This resolves the actual mechanism precisely**: the real per-call
entry point is not `$a0` (the constant `0x81FE0` we chased in Round
466 - that's just the generic trampoline's own address) but **`$v1`**,
which the `0x80002840` glue sets from the *caller's* `$a1`, which in
turn is `table[0x80015C60 + s3*stride].field+8` - a genuine, real
per-slot kernel table entry, not `TCB.entry` (a different structure,
different base address, different field offset - `TCB.entry` is at
offset `0x0C`/12 within the 76-byte `p_TCBs` array at `0x80017400`,
already tracked since Round 461; this new table is a completely
separate 20+-byte-stride structure at a different base). In our
traced run, that field evaluated to `0x00203BE0` - the actual, precise
value this project needs to trace the real writer of, not a vague
"wrong jump" as characterized in Round 466.

**Reframing of Round 466's finding**: the `0x00203BE0` jump was never
really about `$a0`/EPC being wrong - `0x00081FE0` is working exactly
as real hardware intends (a shared, generic thread-launch trampoline).
The actual, now precisely-located open question is narrower and more
tractable: what real kernel table lives at `0x80015C60`, what does
slot `s3` mean, and why does that specific slot's `field+8` hold
`0x00203BE0` instead of a value that would continue our game's real
crt0 execution. Live PCSX2 (still connected, `Tekken Tag Tournament
[Demo]`, paused at `pc=0x003993b8`, `cycles=2,501,038,456` - unchanged
from prior rounds) was checked but no new breakpoint was set this
round; a live-hardware comparison of this specific table is a strong
Round 468 candidate once the table's real identity is narrowed further
offline.

No tracked source changed this round - all disassembly was done
offline against a Round 466 checkpoint's EE RAM contents, and the one
scratch-instrumentation bug found (a watch print accidentally nested
inside an unrelated `if` block, meaning two Round 462 debug prints -
`R462-THREADSTATUS-WRITE`/`R462-THREADID-WRITE` - have been
unreachable dead code since they were added) exists only in scratch
`ee_core_r46*.c` copies, never in tracked `ee_core.c` (confirmed via
direct grep - those print statements don't exist in tracked source at
all). Docs-only round: regression suite and Wii rebuild correctly
skipped.

## Round 468 (tasks #376-382): ROOT CAUSE FOUND - the 0x00203BE0 dead end is a stale OSDSYS VBLANK-interrupt-handler registration, orphaned by our trampoline's ELF load, not an emulator bug

Continued directly from Round 467's precisely-scoped question (what
writes `table[0x80015C60+slot].field+8`, and what does `slot`
represent). Fully closes out the Round 466-468 investigation arc with
a complete, evidenced causal chain.

**`s3` (the table "slot" argument) = 3, and 3 is the real EE INTC
interrupt cause number for VBLANK-END.** Disassembled the real
generic EE interrupt dispatcher (`0x800003E0-0x80000434`, reached via
this project's own already-established Cause-register/MMI leading-
zero-count decode): it computes a cause number, acknowledges it in
real hardware (`sw` to `0xB000F000`, the KSEG1-uncached mirror of real
`INTC_STAT=0x1000F000` - confirmed against this project's own
`ee_intc.h` citation of real PCSX2's `HwWrite.cpp`/`Hw.cpp`), looks up
a real per-cause handler-chain-head table at `0x80012400`
(`table[cause*4]`), and calls it via `jalr`. For our trace, cause=3,
matching `ee_intc.h`'s own documented real cause ordering ("GS, SBUS,
VBLANK start/end, VIF0/1, VU0/1, IPU, Timers 0-3, SFIFO, VU0
watchdog") - cause 3 is VBLANK-END. **`0x80001630` (the function this
project chased since Round 466) is simply this project's own
correctly-modeled real EE kernel's registered-handler-chain dispatcher
for VBLANK-END - it has nothing to do with `_ExecPS2`/`SetupThread`
at all; it was already running as ordinary, periodic background kernel
activity, and just happened to be interleaved with our own syscall-7
sequence in the trace.**

**Found the real writer of the handler's `field+8` (function pointer)
via a value-based memory watch** (watching for any 32-bit write of
exactly `0x00203BE0`, anywhere in EE RAM, across a full fresh-boot
run): exactly one write, at `instr≈76,490,796` - deep in the
pre-trampoline organic-boot phase (our syscall-7 doesn't fire until
~120M instructions in), called from `pc=0x8000191c`. Disassembling
that site (`0x800018C0-0x800019B4`) identifies it precisely as the
**real `AddIntcHandler()`-class kernel primitive**: it allocates a
small fixed-size struct (via a pool allocator at `0x800015A0`), then
fills `struct+8 = handler_function_pointer` (from the caller's real
`$a1` argument), `struct+12 = caller's own $gp` (exactly matching the
dispatcher's own `lw $v0,12($s0); daddu $gp,$v0` restore seen in
Round 467 - the real kernel correctly preserves the *registering*
code's `$gp`, not the interrupted thread's, for later dispatch),
`struct+16` and `struct+20` (a "next"/link value and the `type==2`
tag the dispatcher gates on). **This is OSDSYS's own, real, entirely
legitimate `AddIntcHandler(VBLANK_END, 0x00203BE0, ...)` call**,
happening as part of its normal early startup - and `0x00203BE0` was
a completely valid OSDSYS code address at the time (within OSDSYS's
own loaded ELF range, `0x200000-0x480000`, per Round 274's finding).

**The actual root cause**: Round 466's corrected trampoline calls
`ee_elf_load()` to load the new game's PT_LOAD segments - including a
full zero-fill of `PT_LOAD1` (`0x200000-0x340000`, confirmed correct
per Round 466's direct source read), which is exactly the memory range
containing OSDSYS's real, still-registered VBLANK handler code. The
trampoline never calls anything equivalent to real `RemoveIntcHandler`
to un-register that handler first. The very next real VBLANK-END
interrupt - an entirely ordinary, periodic, unrelated hardware event -
fires exactly as real hardware would, and the real kernel's real
dispatch mechanism (also fully decoded this round) faithfully calls
the still-registered handler, which is now zeroed memory - producing
the NOP-slide and eventual fall-back-to-OSDSYS-resting-loop documented
in Round 466.

**Confirmed this is not a gap in this project's own real syscall 6/7
modeling**: instrumented every write to `INTC_MASK` (`0x1000F010`)
across the full run and found **zero** - only repeated `INTC_STAT`
acknowledgements (`0x1000F000`, write-1-to-clear, bits for VBLANK-
start/end) ever occur. `INTC_MASK` is never touched anywhere in this
trace, meaning whatever enable state OSDSYS itself set for VBLANK
persists completely unchanged through our own syscall-7 dispatch. A
live PCSX2 check this round (still connected, `Tekken Tag Tournament
[Demo]`, `pc=0x003993b8`) read real `INTC_MASK=0x00000000` (all
sources masked) at that already-well-into-the-game pause point -
consistent with real games disabling interrupts themselves once
running, not with `_ExecPS2`/`InitializeINTC` clearing the mask as
part of the boot transition itself (real `ExecPS2Patch`'s
`p_InitializeINTC(0xdffd)` call, quoted in Round 466/467, would need
to write `INTC_MASK` with a value whose XORed bits actually include
VBLANK's to change its state, and OSDSYS's original enable state may
survive that specific mask value unchanged - consistent with what
this project's own trace shows).

**Conclusion**: the whole Round 466-468 "dead end" is a real,
well-understood limitation of the *test trampoline methodology*
itself, not a bug in `ee_core.c`'s actual, already-correct real
syscall 6/7 exception-raising behavior. The trampoline hijacks the
currently-running thread's PC directly, bypassing OSDSYS's own real
"user selected a game, clean up, call `_LoadExecPS2`" code path
entirely - a path that on real hardware (or in a fuller OSDSYS
emulation) would very plausibly include the game's own real interrupt-
handler cleanup before ever reaching `_ExecPS2`. No tracked source
changed this round - `ee_core.c`'s real syscall dispatch, `ee_intc.c`'s
real INTC_STAT/MASK semantics, and `ee_elf_loader.c`'s zero-fill
behavior are all confirmed correct and unchanged.

**Path forward for a future round**: either (a) have the scratch test
trampoline explicitly clear/disable INTC_MASK's VBLANK bits before
firing syscall 7 (simulating what real OSDSYS's own pre-boot cleanup
would do), to see if the game's crt0 then proceeds further
uninterrupted, or (b) accept this as a known test-methodology
limitation and treat Round 466's "real crt0 executes, correct BSS-
clear, correct SetupThread dispatch" as the actual milestone, with
the VBLANK collision understood as an artifact of the synthetic test
rather than a genuine boot blocker.

Docs-only round: no tracked source changed, regression suite and Wii
rebuild correctly skipped.

## Round 469 (tasks #386-391): VBLANK-END masking test confirms Round 468's root cause - real game code now runs measurably further before a different, later blocker is hit

Direct experimental test of Round 468's diagnosis: extended the
scratch test trampoline (`/tmp/driver_r469.c`) to directly clear bit 3
(VBLANK-END) in the emulated `INTC_MASK` register
(`ee_intc_get_state()->mask &= ~(1u<<3)`) immediately before firing
the corrected syscall-7 trampoline, simulating what real OSDSYS's own
pre-boot interrupt-handler cleanup would very plausibly do (a step
this raw PC-hijack test methodology otherwise skips entirely, per
Round 468's conclusion).

**Confirmed: this measurably changes the outcome.** With the same
BIOS/disc/checkpoint fixtures, `INTC_MASK` before/after the mask
write was `0x0000100a -> 0x00001002` (bit 3 cleared, confirmed).
Fine-grained tracing through the identical BSS-clear-loop-exit and
SetupThread-style dispatch sequence (byte-identical up through
`fine_offset=1482074`, matching Round 466/467's trace exactly) shows
that this time, execution does **not** jump to `0x00203BE0` at all -
instead it continues in real game code at `0x00401E60-0x00401EA8`
(within `PT_LOAD2`'s real code range, `0x340000-0x1FCDAF0`), running
what looks like a further real initialization loop (walking addresses
from `~0x01fc8780` downward in 4-byte-ish steps - plausibly another
real data-structure or heap-initialization pass) for tens of thousands
of additional real instructions beyond where Round 466's baseline run
first derailed.

**This is real, confirmed, additional forward progress**, and directly
validates Round 468's root-cause diagnosis (the stale OSDSYS VBLANK-
END handler was in fact the proximate cause of the earlier, immediate
`0x00203BE0` jump - removing it lets real crt0 continue).

**However, by the full 40,000,000-slice budget, this run's final
resting point (`pc=0x8000CF98`, `GS: pmode=0x66 dispfb1=0x0
display1=0x0`, GIF counts unchanged at 343/4888/333/0 triangles) is
statistically indistinguishable from Round 466's un-masked baseline
(`pc=0x8000F864`, same GS/GIF state)** - both eventually settle back
into the same long-standing OSDSYS resting-loop address family. This
means VBLANK-END was not the *only* blocker: something else, further
along in the game's real execution, still eventually redirects
control back to the same place - either another stale interrupt-
handler collision (a strong candidate, given OSDSYS very plausibly
registered handlers for multiple interrupt causes, not just VBLANK-
END, during its own early real startup) or a different, unrelated
real blocker entirely.

This round does not claim a splash screen or resolve the full boot -

## Round 471 (docs-only, direct continuation of Round 470 per user's "continue until something changes or is fixable"): CLOSES the Round 335-471 CDDASTREAM/dispatch_ncmd() investigation arc - the organic boot's steady-state loop is now fully explained end-to-end as a real, correctly-modeled idle heartbeat, not a bug; the actual blocker is a missing real stimulus (further real pad/disc-menu input), not an emulation gap

**Part 1: found the real outer dispatcher entry (`0x0021477C`) and confirmed it, too, is called indirectly (no static `JAL`).** Backward-scanned for `sd $ra,N($sp)` / `addiu $sp,$sp,-N` prologue patterns from `0x002149C4` and found the true function boundary at `0x0021477C` (`addiu $sp,$sp,-240`, a large 13-callee-saved-register-plus-`$ra` prologue). A static `JAL`-word scan across the full `0x00080000-0x00500000` OSDSYS range found zero direct callers - like `0x002134A8`'s own outer callers before Round 385/386 clarified them, this is reached indirectly.

**Part 2: live-instrumented `pc==0x0021477C` entry (scratch `ee_core_r471.c`, one `fprintf` guarded by a new `g_r471_trace_on` flag, never touching tracked source) and re-ran the clean Round 470 organic-boot driver.** Captured 94 real entries across a 40,000,000-slice run. The first ~34 entries (instr 30.97M-31.0M, a single dense burst) come from many distinct real call sites in the `0x002001D0-0x00200A3C` range with varying `$a1` "command" values (`0x5001`, `0x5006`, `0x500C`, `0x5007`, `0x501A`, etc.) - consistent with a real OSDSYS init-time sequence of distinct disc-browser/menu setup calls, plausibly the on-screen icon/menu-list construction Round 360's own citation already flagged as a real, completing init sequence.

**After that initial burst, the trace settles into ONE single repeating real call site for the entire remaining ~285,000,000 instructions surveyed**: caller `ra=0x00214a0c` region (same function block, not shown as varying), constant `a1=0x0000500D`, and a **monotonically increasing `a3`** (`0x60c -> 0x662 -> 0x6b8 -> ...` up to `0xfca` by the end of this run, incrementing by a fixed `0x56` (86 decimal) roughly every 4.9M instructions - i.e., once per driver "leg"). This is very likely the same real per-tick counter that drives Round 452's own already-documented sprite-count growth (`343 -> 514` sprites across chained legs) - the animation's frame/tick heartbeat.

**Part 3: disassembled `0x0021477C`'s body to find where `a1=0x500D` actually routes, and confirmed it reaches the CDDASTREAM dispatch.** The function is a real, large command dispatcher on `$a1`: an initial `slt`-gated block handles a high `0x80XX`-family of commands (skipped entirely for our `0x500D`, since `0x80FF < 0x500D` is false), then two specific literal-value cases (`0x6240`, `0x7600`), then two masked-family cases (`a1 & 0xF000 == 0x6000` and `== 0x7000`, both of which call `0x002134A8` with real N-command-shaped arguments) - and finally a **default fallthrough** (reached when `a1`'s masked value matches none of the above, exactly our `0x500D` case, since `0x500D & 0xF000 = 0x5000` matches no explicit branch) that ALSO calls `0x002134A8`, with `$a2 = $s0` = the outer function's own unchanged `$a0` argument, which every one of this round's captures shows is the constant `1`.

Per Round 385's already-decoded gating logic (`0x002134A8` reads flag bits 0/1 out of its `$a2` argument to choose "immediate issue" vs "deferred"), `$a2=1` sets bit 0 - the **immediate-issue path**, which calls `0x00212AA8` with the fixed tag `$a0=0x8000000A` (`SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL`/`CD_NCMD_CDDASTREAM`, Round 365/385's own citation) - **the exact same call site this project's entire Round 335-470 investigation has been examining from the other end** (`0x00213600`/`0x002135B4`, Round 385's corrected labeling).

**This closes the investigation with a complete, end-to-end, honestly-verified explanation.** The organic boot's steady state is: OSDSYS's real disc-browser/intro-animation code runs a per-tick default command (`0x500D`) that, via a large real command dispatcher (`0x0021477C`) and its shared CD-command-issue primitive (`0x002134A8`), re-issues the real `CD_NCMD_CDDASTREAM` "is the audio stream subsystem alive" probe once per animation tick, forever - a real, legitimate heartbeat behavior, not a stuck retry or a missing-completion-signal bug (Rounds 347/386-388 already independently confirmed every layer of this chain - the RPC dispatch, the semaphore lifecycle, the reply convention - is correctly modeled and matches real hardware protocol). **The reason the boot never progresses past this state is not an emulation bug in this chain at all: it is that this project's boot fixture never supplies whatever further real stimulus (additional real pad-button sequences beyond Round 270-272's single-press test, or a fuller real CDVDFSV disc-type/session-negotiation exchange this project does not model) real OSDSYS's own disc-browser logic is actually waiting on before it would escalate from "showing intro animation, probing audio" to "building a menu/proceeding".** This is architecturally the same class of finding as Round 388's own assessment ("six call-frames deep... without finding a genuine bug or a point where this project's own implementation observably diverges from what real hardware does") - now extended one more level up the call stack and brought to a definitive, rather than provisional, close.

**No source fix implemented, and none is warranted here** - every function in this now-fully-traced chain (`0x0021477C`, `0x002134A8`, `0x00212AA8`, `0x00212968`, `0x00210F40`/`0x00210F50`/`0x00210F80`, `dispatch_ncmd()`'s deliberate CDDASTREAM exclusion per Round 347's own citation) is confirmed correct and matches real hardware/protocol behavior at every layer this project can verify against real, cited sources. The remaining gap is a missing real STIMULUS (input/disc-protocol richness this project's test fixture doesn't yet provide), not a bug in the emulator's own logic.

**Left as the concrete next step, if this thread is picked up again**: the one testable, evidenced-but-unexplored lever is real pad input richness - Round 270-272 tested only a single one-shot button press years (in project-round terms) before this chain was understood this deeply; worth revisiting with a real, repeated/held button-press sequence (or a real multi-button combo, if OSDSYS's real disc-browser expects one) now that the exact command dispatcher (`0x0021477C`) and its full family of real command IDs (`0x5001`,`0x5006`,`0x500C`,`0x5007`,`0x501A`,`0x500D`, plus the `0x6XXX`/`0x7XXX`/`0x80XX` families) are known, since a real button-press event's IOP-side effect would enter this exact same dispatcher via a different, not-yet-observed `a1` command value.

## Round 472 (docs-only, direct continuation of Round 471's own stated next step): tested the one remaining lever - real pad input richness - and got a clean negative result, ruling it out as the missing stimulus

Round 471 closed the CDDASTREAM/dispatch_ncmd() mechanism investigation but left one concrete, testable lever open: whether richer real pad input (beyond the standing CROSS-only repeated press/release toggle, Round 312's own convention) could unstick OSDSYS's disc-browser past its `a1=0x500D` idle-heartbeat steady state.

**Test**: built `driver_r472.c` (copy of Round 471's clean organic driver) with the existing 2,000,000-slice repeated press/release toggle (Round 312's convention) extended to press/release `IOP_PAD_BTN_START` together with `IOP_PAD_BTN_CROSS` (real PS2 pads' actual "confirm/enter" button, more semantically plausible than CROSS alone for advancing a disc-browser splash screen), instead of CROSS alone. **Result: byte-for-byte identical to Round 471's CROSS-only run.** Same final `pc=0x0050172C`, same `ee_total_instr=319998310`, same GS state (`pmode=0x66`, circuit 1 zero), same GIF draw counts (`sprites=384, lines=4888, points=333, triangles=0`), same 94 total dispatcher entries, same full `a1` command-value set observed (`0x5001/0x5006/0x5007/0x5009/0x500A/0x500C/0x500D/0x5012/0x5013/0x5014/0x501A/0x5100/0x5201/0x8600/0xE621` plus the low-value housekeeping ones `0x1/0x2/0x1031`) - adding a second, more semantically appropriate button to the existing repeated-press/release convention changed nothing observable anywhere in the traced chain.

**This is a clean, honest negative result that further narrows (not just re-confirms) the standing wall**: real pad input - at least CROSS and START, held or repeatedly toggled - is conclusively not what OSDSYS's disc-browser is waiting on to escalate past its intro/CDDASTREAM-probe steady state. Combined with Round 471's finding that every layer of the CDDASTREAM dispatch chain matches real hardware protocol, the most likely remaining explanation is that OSDSYS's real escalation condition depends on a fuller real CDVDFSV disc-type/session-negotiation exchange this project does not model (a substantial new feature, not a quick fix) - or, less likely, a pad button/combination outside this test's two candidates, or an unrelated real timer/event this investigation has not yet identified.

Further progress toward a splash screen/menu would require either modeling substantially more of the real CDVDFSV disc-negotiation protocol (a new feature, scoped work, not a bug fix) or a fundamentally different investigative lead not yet identified.

## Round 473: implemented real CD_NCMD_CDDASTREAM sub-command (CdvdStCmd_t) payload parsing in tracked source, per the user's explicit "implement the cdvdfsv... audio" request - found and fixed a real bug in this project's OWN instrumentation, recovered a coherent, valid payload, and confirmed the audio-pipeline gap is real but not the current boot blocker

**Context.** Following Round 472's close (organic-boot investigation fully characterized, pad input ruled out as the missing stimulus, real gap identified as "a fuller real CDVDFSV disc-negotiation protocol, new feature work"), the user gave an explicit, direct instruction: "implement the cdvdfsv and i think i know the issue it might be something with audio which is not implemented." This redirected the round from pure investigation to implementation, with the user's own hypothesis that missing audio/CDDA-streaming support is the real gap.

**Part 1 (task #401): fetched the real ps2sdk `ee/rpc/cdvd/src/ncmd.c` source.** Confirms `sceCdCddaStream()`'s real 5-word wire payload (`lbn, nsectors*sector_size, buf, cmd, mode`), the real `CdvdStCmd_t` sub-command enum (`START=1, READ, STOP, SEEK, INIT, STAT, PAUSE, RESUME, SEEKF`), and that `CD_NCMD_CDDASTREAM` is normally an application/game-level audio-streaming API - plausible for OSDSYS's own disc-browser if it plays background music, matching the user's hypothesis.

**Part 2 (task #402, self-correcting): live-instrumented the real CDDASTREAM payload and found a bug in this round's OWN scratch tooling, not the emulator.** A first-pass payload-dump hook (`ee_core_r473.c`, gated on `rpc_number==10`) read `w0..w4` directly from the 16-byte-stride SIF DMA transfer-table entry at `dmat_ptr+(i-1)*16`, producing incoherent values (`cmd=0x00000000`, invalid - `CdvdStCmd_t` starts at 1; `buf=0x00000014`, far too small to be a real pointer). Cross-checking against this file's own already-established convention elsewhere (`read_payload_src`/`open_payload_base`, used identically for the FILEIO branches) revealed the real bug: that 16-byte descriptor is `{src, dest, size, attr}` - word 0 is a POINTER to the real payload, not the payload itself. The original hook was reading raw descriptor fields, not dereferencing them.

**Fixed the dereference and re-ran the same 40,000,000-slice organic-boot trace.** Recovered a fully coherent, valid real payload: `psrc=0x00445630 lbn=0x00000000 nsectors=0x00000000 buf=0x0046ba80 cmd=0x00000005 mode=0x00000000`. `cmd=5` = real `CDVD_ST_CMD_INIT` - OSDSYS's one real CDDASTREAM call this round observed is a stream-subsystem INIT, not a data-streaming START, with a real, plausible EE RAM buffer pointer (not garbage). Cross-verified with a second, independent, broader instrumentation pass (`[R473-ALL-RPC]`, logging every real `SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL` packet unconditionally) that found exactly one `sid=0x80000595`/`rpc_number=10` packet in the entire 40M-slice run (out of 200 total real RPC packets of all kinds) - confirming Round 471's "94 outer-dispatcher visits" figure counts internal dispatcher re-entries, not new RPC transmissions: only the very first `a1=0x500D` visit actually issues a fresh SIF RPC; the ~93 subsequent visits are satisfied locally (already-cited real `ee_try_cdvd_ncmd_real_dispatch`/`g_ee_cdvd_ncmd_reentry.valid` single-outstanding-RPC guard prevents re-issue while one is in flight, and this one was answered immediately by the existing Round 276 placeholder reply).

**Part 3 (task #403): implemented the corrected, real protocol-shaped parsing in TRACKED source** (`source/core/ee/ee_core.c`, `SIF_SID_CDVD_NCMD` branch). Added real dereferencing logic (matching the file's own established `read_payload_src` idiom) that correctly extracts the real `CdvdStCmd_t` sub-command from `rpc_number==10` calls into two new globals (`g_ee_cddastream_last_cmd`, `g_ee_cddastream_last_cmd_valid`) for future-round observability. The actual reply behavior is UNCHANGED (still the existing real leading-result-int placeholder, `0`=success) - since only `cmd=INIT` is evidenced in this project's own traces and the existing placeholder already satisfies it correctly (Round 276's real fix), this is honest infrastructure for handling other sub-commands (`START`/`STAT`/etc.) once/if a future round observes them live, not a claim of full CDDASTREAM coverage or a fabricated behavior change.

**Audio-pipeline audit (task #402, per the user's own hypothesis): confirmed real, but not evidenced as the current blocker.** `source/hw/iop_spu2.c` and `source/hw/iop_spu_legacy.c` are both bare MMIO register stores (read/write pass-through only) with zero real audio pipeline: no voice-key-on-triggered playback, no ADPCM/DMA decode, no core IRQ/status modeling, no connection whatsoever to CDDASTREAM buffer contents. This is a real, genuine gap matching the user's hypothesis. However, it is NOT evidenced to be what's blocking the current boot resting point: the one real CDDASTREAM call OSDSYS issues is `cmd=INIT`, already correctly replied to (success), and OSDSYS's own dispatcher does not re-issue further RPC traffic waiting on audio progress (confirmed via the `[R473-ALL-RPC]` full-packet trace above) - it simply proceeds to its normal per-tick idle/animation loop, matching Round 471/472's already-established "correct heartbeat, no bug" characterization. Building a real SPU2/CDDA audio pipeline would be substantial, legitimate new feature work, but implementing it this round would not be evidenced to fix a specific observed blocker - consistent with this project's standing no-guessing discipline, it is documented as a real, scoped-but-not-undertaken gap rather than given a fabricated implementation.

## Round 474: implemented real CD_SCMD_GETDISKTYPE reply-shape fix (CDVDFSV protocol depth, direct continuation of Round 473's "implement the cdvdfsv" work) - a genuine, evidenced S-command protocol-completeness bug found and fixed, confirmed not yet reachable on the current boot path

**Context.** Continuing directly from Round 473's own stated remaining gap ("fuller CDVDFSV disc-negotiation protocol modeling"), following the user's terse "remaining gap" instruction to keep pushing on that thread.

**Part 1 (task #406): fetched the real ps2sdk `ee/rpc/cdvd/src/scmd.c`, `ee/rpc/cdvd/include/libcdvd.h`, and `common/include/libcdvd-common.h` sources.** Confirms `#define CD_SERVER_SCMD 0x80000593` and the full real `CD_SCMD_CMDS` enum (35 entries: `READCLOCK=1` through `SETTHREADPRI=35`, including `GETDISKTYPE=3`). Critically, `sceCdGetDiskType()`'s real body is a single-reply-word read: `result = *(int *)UNCACHED_SEG(sCmdRecvBuff); return result;` - no separate status/value split, unlike most other real S-commands. `libcdvd-common.h` provides the full real `SCECdvdMediaType` enum: `SCECdNODISC=0x00, SCECdDETCT=0x01 ("detecting disc type")` through `SCECdDETCTDVDD=0x04, SCECdUNKNOWN, SCECdPSCD=0x10, SCECdPSCDDA, SCECdPS2CD=0x12 ("PS2 CD, no CDDA tracks"), SCECdPS2CDDA, SCECdPS2DVD=0x14`, plus `SCECdDVDVR/SCECdCDDA/SCECdDVDV/SCECdIllegalMedia` at the high end.

**Part 2 (task #407): audited this project's real `SIF_SID_CDVD_SCMD` dispatch coverage in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c`.** Found a specific branch for `rpc_number==0x18` (`CD_SCMD_FORBID_DVDP`, Round 302's finding), then a generalized catch-all for every other `rpc_number` (Round 302, corrected in Round 303) that writes a hardcoded leading result word of `1`. Round 303's own citation established `1` as the correct generic "success" sentinel for that command family (real callers like `OPEN_CONFIG`/`READ_CONFIG`/`CLOSE_CONFIG` were observed retrying until the leading word went nonzero). **This round found that sentinel is wrong specifically for `GETDISKTYPE`**: per the real enum above, `1` literally decodes as `SCECdDETCT` ("still detecting, try again") - if a real caller ever invoked `sceCdGetDiskType()` against this project's existing catch-all, it would read "still detecting" forever, since the value never changes on retry.

## Round 475: implemented real SIF_SID_CDVD_DISKREADY (sceCdDiskReady) dispatch - a completely separate, previously-undiscovered CDVD RPC service this project had ZERO coverage for, per the user's "finish the gap" instruction

**Context.** Direct continuation of Round 474's own stated remaining gap ("fuller CDVDFSV disc-negotiation protocol modeling"), following the user's explicit "finish the gap" instruction.

**Part 1 (task #411): fetched the real ps2sdk `ee/rpc/cdvd/src/libcdvd.c` source.** This revealed that `sceCdDiskReady()` - a real, commonly-used PS2 SDK function that checks whether a disc is ready/present - binds to `CD_SERVER_DISKREADY = 0x8000059A`, its OWN dedicated RPC service (`clientDiskReady`, a separate `SifRpcClientData_t` from `clientInit`/`clientNCmd`/`clientSCmd`) - a THIRD, wholly independent CDVD RPC service this project had never identified or modeled at all, distinct from `SIF_SID_CDVD_NCMD` (0x80000595) and `SIF_SID_CDVD_SCMD` (0x80000593) which this project already handles.

**Part 2 (task #412): audited this project's dispatch coverage and confirmed a total gap.** Grepping `source/core/ee/ee_core.c` and `include/core/hw/sif.h` for `0x8000059A`/`DISKREADY` found zero references to this sid anywhere - not even inside `SIF_SID_CDVD_SCMD`'s own generic catch-all, since `DISKREADY` is a genuinely separate real sid, not a sub-command of the S-command family. Traced the generic `SIF_CMD_RPC_BIND` handler (`source/hw/sif.c`) and confirmed it is sid-agnostic (any bind succeeds via a synthetic REND reply, regardless of which service is being bound), so a real `sceCdDiskReady()` caller's *bind* would complete fine - but the subsequent `SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL` dispatch chain in `ee_core.c` is a plain `if`/`else-if` ladder with no final catch-all `else`, so a call to an unrecognized sid like `0x8000059A` would simply fall through completely un-replied, parking the calling thread forever - the same class of real bug this project has fixed multiple times before (Round 278 MCSERV, Round 302/303 CDVD_SCMD, Round 346 FILEIO).

**Part 3 (task #413): live-instrumented full RPC bind/call traffic** (scratch `ee_core_r475probe.c`, two `fprintf` hooks logging every real `bind_sid` and `call_sid` observed) and re-ran the standard 40,000,000-slice organic-boot survey. As a valuable side-effect, this survey also confirmed every OTHER real CALL sid observed in the entire run (`FILEIO`, `IOPHEAP`, `LOADFILE`, `PAD`, `MCSERV`, `CDVD_INIT`, `CDVD_SCMD`, `CDVD_NCMD`, `SPU2DRV`) matches an already-handled branch - there is no OTHER silently-unhandled sid currently being called and dropped.

**Part 4 (task #414): implemented the real, evidenced fix in tracked source.** Fetched the real return-value semantics: `sceCdDiskReady()`'s own source (`ee/rpc/cdvd/src/libcdvd.c`) reads its single 4-byte reply word directly as the ready-state value (`return *(s32 *)UNCACHED_SEG(sCmdRecvBuff);` - no separate status/value split, the same shape as `GETDISKTYPE`), with `rpc_number` always fixed at 0. Added `SIF_SID_CDVD_DISKREADY` (`0x8000059Au`) to `include/core/hw/sif.h` with full citation, and a new specific branch in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c`'s `SIF_CMD_RPC_CALL` dispatch (`call_sid == SIF_SID_CDVD_DISKREADY && rpc_number == 0u`) that writes the real `SCECdComplete` (2) constant - chosen because this project's own disc loader (`core/iso_loader.c`) always has a valid CD image mounted synchronously with no real async spin-up/tray-state modeling, so the only defensible real value is the terminal "drive ready, disc present" state, matching this project's own established convention (Round 474's immediate `SCECdPS2CD` reply) of answering "already done" for functions not modeled as multi-step async processes.

**Verification (task #415).** Host-native: `gcc -O2 -Wall` on both changed files compiles clean. ## Round 476 (docs-only, per user-provided links): researched OSDMenu (pcm720) and FreeMcBoot-Installer (israpps) as a potential alternative strategy to the stalled real-OSDSYS-escalation investigation

**Context.** The user shared two links (github.com/pcm720/OSDMenu, github.com/israpps/FreeMcBoot-Installer) without further comment, immediately after Round 475 closed with an open question about whether to keep chasing the real-OSDSYS escalation blocker or try a different angle.

**What these projects are (from their own READMEs).** OSDMenu is "patches for OSDSYS and HDD OSD (Browser 2.0) based on Free McBoot 1.8" - an open-source, standalone ELF (`osdmenu.elf`) that REPLACES the real Sony OSDSYS browser entirely, rather than trying to make the real one work. Its own README states "All OSD initialization code is removed" - i.e. it deliberately does NOT perform the real CDVDFSV disc-negotiation/hardware-init sequence this project has spent Rounds 335-475 trying to characterize; it's a self-contained homebrew file browser/launcher with its own simpler logic for detecting and launching CD/DVD games, memory-card content, HDD content, etc. FreeMcBoot (FMCB), which OSDMenu is based on, is "a homebrew bootloader and launcher for PS2" with the same fundamental approach.

**How real PS2 hardware boots this instead of Sony's real OSDSYS.** Per OSDMenu's own README ("OSDMenu as the System Update" section, using a tool called KELFBinder), the real mechanism is installing the patched ELF as a "system update" - a real, Sony-documented mechanism where the EE kernel's own real boot chain (EELOAD) checks the memory card for a system-update KELF (`osd???.elf`/`osdmain.elf`) BEFORE falling back to loading the real OSDSYS from BIOS ROM. This is not a hack unique to these projects - it's real, intended Sony functionality (used historically for actual system software updates), which FMCB/OSDMenu repurpose to substitute their own browser.

**Cross-referenced against this project's own prior findings - a critical blocker for this approach.** Round 456 (task #276) already investigated this project's real McServ/memory-card protocol implementation and found/implemented that this project's MCSERV emulation currently replies `-ENODEV` ("no such device") to all real `mc0:`/`mc1:` device-open attempts - i.e., this project currently models "no memory card is present at all," not "a memory card is present but empty." This is a deliberate, evidenced, real fix (matching the real errno a console with no inserted memory card would return), but it also means the real EELOAD system-update check this OSDMenu/FMCB approach depends on would find nothing and always fall through to the real ROM OSDSYS - exactly the path this project has been stuck on.

**Assessment: this is a real, viable, and likely more tractable alternative strategy, but it is a substantial new feature, not a quick fix.** To pursue it, this project would need genuinely new work, not yet attempted in this project's history: (1) real memory-card CONTENT modeling (currently only a "device absent" errno exists - actually emulating MCSERV's real read/write/directory-listing protocol against a real or synthetic memory-card image is unbuilt), (2) a real or synthetic memory-card image containing an OSDMenu-equivalent ELF at the correct real path, and (3) verifying/implementing the real EE kernel's own system-update-check logic (not yet disassembled or confirmed in this project's own trace - a research task, not an assumption). This is comparable in scope to some of this project's largest past feature builds (e.g. Round 389+'s real IOP threading implementation), not a narrow protocol fix like Rounds 474-475.

**Why this could be more tractable than continuing the current thread.** The core appeal: OSDMenu/FMCB are real, actively-maintained, open-source, well-documented C code (not a closed proprietary Sony binary requiring blind reverse-engineering) that are specifically designed to be simple and to work reliably - sidestepping the entire "why doesn't real OSDSYS's disc-browser escalate past its idle heartbeat" question (Rounds 335-475, still unresolved after ~140 rounds) by replacing the problematic code entirely rather than continuing to reverse-engineer around it.

**No source change this round - pure research/strategy assessment, per the user's bare-link message.** Docs-only round: `git status`/`git diff --stat` confirm only `docs/STATUS.md`/`docs/ROADMAP.md` changed. Regression suite and Wii rebuild correctly skipped.

**Decision needed from the user before any implementation work begins**: whether to commit to this new strategic direction (real memory-card content modeling + OSDMenu-as-system-update boot path), given its substantial scope relative to the narrow, evidence-driven protocol fixes this project has been doing recently.

## Round 477 (docs-only, continuation of Round 476): refined the OSDMenu strategy assessment - the primary install path is far more tractable than Round 476 estimated, and reuses this project's own already-built ELF-trampoline infrastructure

**Context.** Following the user's "do both in parallel" decision on Round 476's strategy question, this round researched the concrete real mechanics of running OSDMenu, to scope actual next implementation steps.

**Part 1: confirmed the real PS2 "system update" mechanism exists and is real** (via Woon Yung's PS2 System Update Paths documentation and general PS2 architecture references): EELOAD checks the memory card/HDD for an updated OSDSYS binary (`osdXXX.elf` version-specific, or `osdmain.elf` on newer consoles, in region-specific directories) before falling back to the ROM-resident `rom0:OSDSYS`. This is real, Sony-intended functionality (originally for real system software updates like the DVD player/HDD driver updates), and it is what OSDMenu's "as the System Update" install option (using KELFBinder) exploits.

**Part 2 (major revision to Round 476's assessment): fetched OSDMenu's own `patcher/README.md` and `utils/loader/README.md` directly, and found the PRIMARY, default OSDMenu usage does NOT require implementing this system-update mechanism at all.** Per the main README's own "Usage" section, the default installation is simply: copy `osdmenu.elf` to `mc?:/BOOT/` and launch it as a normal ELF (manually, or via a bootloader) - i.e., `osdmenu.elf` is a self-contained program that reads/patches an OSDSYS resource in memory and runs its own logic, not something that depends on Sony's memory-card auto-update detection. The "as System Update" install method Round 476 focused on is explicitly one of several alternate installation options, not the primary mechanism, and was the wrong thing to scope against.

**Part 3: found OSDMenu's real disc-launch mechanism reuses infrastructure this project has ALREADY built and validated.** Per `utils/loader/README.md`, OSDMenu's embedded loader (used for both regular app launches and its "eGSM" disc-launch path) loads a target ELF specified by `argv[0]`, and for CD/DVD game launches specifically routes through `rom0:PS2LOGO` (patched to skip the logo and fix region/master-disc detection) followed by the standard real `SYSTEM.CNF`-driven game-ELF load - the exact same real boot chain stock retail OSDSYS itself uses for normal game launches, NOT a new or exotic mechanism. This project already has: (a) working `rom0:` ROMDIR-based file access (Round 346), (b) a validated real ELF-load/entry-dispatch mechanism with confirmed real game crt0 execution (Round 457-469's `_LoadExecPS2` trampoline arc), and (c) working ISO9660 disc-image access (Round 367). The "embedded Neutrino GSM (eGSM)" is a video-mode-forcing wrapper around this already-real, already-partially-modeled path, not a separate protocol.

**Part 4: found OSDMenu's memory-card CONFIG dependency (the actual blocker Round 476 flagged) is optional, not required.** Per the patcher README: "The OSDMenu configuration file can be embedded into the patcher at compile time for memory card-independent setups and faster boot times" - a build mode exists that needs zero real memory-card access at all. This directly neutralizes Round 476's main scope concern (this project's MCSERV currently reports "-ENODEV, no card present" for all real memory-card access, per Round 456) for a first attempt: a memory-card-independent OSDMenu build would not be blocked by that at all.

**Revised assessment: this path is substantially more tractable than Round 476 estimated, and is a natural extension of already-completed work (Round 457-469's trampoline/ELF-load infrastructure) rather than a large new feature (real memory-card content modeling can be deferred).** The concrete next steps are: (1) obtain a real `osdmenu.elf` binary - either build from source (requires setting up a ps2sdk EE-side toolchain, a new environment dependency this project hasn't needed before, since all prior work has been either host-native scratch drivers or the existing devkitPPC/Wii cross-build) or fetch a pre-built release binary from OSDMenu's GitHub releases, and (2) adapt this project's existing trampoline harness (currently pointed at the mounted Tekken Tag Tournament Demo's own game ELF) to instead load and execute `osdmenu.elf`, observing how far its own real, simpler, open-source init code progresses compared to the real BIOS OSDSYS's stuck disc-browser heartbeat.

## Round 478: real open-source OSDMenu code executes for the first time via the existing trampoline; found and fixed a genuine, total EE-core emulation gap (the entire standard MIPS trap-instruction family) that it hit

**Context.** The user uploaded `osdmenu-v1.3.0.zip`, a pre-built OSDMenu release package (pcm720/OSDMenu v1.3.0), directly answering Round 477's question about whether to build from source or use a prebuilt release. Extracted `osdmenu.elf` (271,844 bytes, real MIPS-I ET_EXEC, entry=0x01D0001C).

**Part 1: adapted the existing Round 457-469 `_ExecPS2` trampoline to load `osdmenu.elf` instead of the game ELF.** Reused this project's own real `ee_elf_load()` (Round 171) to parse OSDMenu's program headers and copy its LOAD segment into emulated EE RAM (`[0x01cc3280, 0x01d05c60)`), reused the corrected syscall-7 `_ExecPS2` trampoline (Round 466) and the VBLANK-END INTC_MASK pre-clear (Round 469) that together simulate OSDSYS's real pre-boot interrupt-handler cleanup, and hijacked the running thread's pc to OSDMenu's real entry point after 15M slices of organic boot.

**Part 2 (landmark result): real, unmodified, open-source OSDMenu code executed for the first time in this project's history**, independent of the long-stuck real-BIOS-OSDSYS disc-browser investigation (Rounds 335-475). Confirmed genuine execution (not a trampoline artifact) by the EE pc advancing from the real entry point (`0x01D0001C`) forward to `0x01D02008` before halting.

**Part 3: root-caused the halt to a genuine, total EE-core emulation gap - not an OSDMenu-specific issue.** Parsed the raw ELF bytes at the failing address directly (Python struct-unpack against the program-header-mapped file offset, no guessing): this project's own halt()-reporting convention prints `this_pc+4`, so the actual failing instruction is at `0x01D02004`, word `0x006001F4`. Decoded: opcode=SPECIAL(0), rs=3($v1), rt=0($zero), sa=7, funct=0x34. This is `teq $v1, $zero, 7` - the standard GCC-generated MIPS divide-by-zero guard, immediately following a real `divu $v0, $v1` at `0x01D02000`. `TEQ` (Trap if Equal, SPECIAL funct 0x34, real MIPS II/III/EE-standard instruction, ExcCode 13 "Tr" per the MIPS32/64 Architecture Reference Manual's ExcCode table) had zero implementation in this project's `ee_core.c` - confirmed by grep that `case 0x10`-`0x13` (MFHI/MTHI/MFLO/MTLO) and the DIVU used just before it were already implemented, but `case 0x30`-`0x36` (the entire TGE/TGEU/TLT/TLTU/TEQ/TNE trap family) fell straight through to the unconditional `default: halt("unimplemented SPECIAL funct")`. This is a real, standard-ISA, universally-documented instruction family, not a guess or an OSDMenu-specific quirk - any compiled MIPS code doing integer division with runtime zero-checks (a default GCC codegen behavior) would hit the same wall.

**Part 4: implemented the fix.** Added `EE_EXC_CODE_TR` (`13u << 2`, matching this file's existing `EE_EXC_CODE_BP`/`EE_EXC_CODE_SYS` real-ExcCode convention) and all six real trap-family funct cases (`0x30` TGE, `0x31` TGEU, `0x32` TLT, `0x33` TLTU, `0x34` TEQ, `0x36` TNE - `0x35`/`0x37` are reserved/unassigned in the real ISA and correctly left unimplemented) in `source/core/ee/ee_core.c`'s SPECIAL-funct switch, between the existing `DSUBU` (`0x2F`) and `DSLL` (`0x38`) cases. Semantics: raise a real Trap exception via the existing `ee_raise_exception()` (same mechanism already used for the `BREAK` case just above) when the comparison holds; otherwise no-op and continue, per the real MIPS ISA specification. This exactly mirrors this file's own established BREAK-case precedent (call `ee_raise_exception()`, fall through to the switch's normal `break`, do NOT `return 1` - raising an exception redirects pc, it does not halt the core).

**Part 5: verified the fix.** Host-native syntax check clean. Rebuilt the OSDMenu boot-survey driver against the fixed tree and re-ran the identical 40M-slice budget from a fresh checkpoint: **zero halts across the entire run** (previously halted after ~1,580 instructions of OSDMenu's own code). The EE pc progressed far beyond the previous `0x01D02008` wall, through `0x00200000`-`0x00518000`-range addresses, and settled into a real interrupt-driven idle loop (`0x8000CC94`/`0x8000CD3C`/`0x8000CE08`/`0x8000CCC4`, cycling every slice-cap chunk) - the same category of steady-state resting behavior this project's organic OSDSYS boot has reached in many prior rounds, reached this time via real OSDMenu code instead.

**Part 6: full regression + Wii build.** Rebuilt all 38 source objects and reran the full host-native test suite: **128/128 PASS**, zero build or run failures. Wii cross-build (`devkitPPC`/`libogc`, after fixing a session-local `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` gap for `libmpfr.so.4` that was blocking `cc1`) compiled clean; `pcsx2-wii-git.elf`/`pcsx2-wii-git.dol` both produced successfully with no new warnings.

**No-regression basis for the organic (non-OSDMenu) BIOS boot path**: this fix is purely additive - six new `case` labels in an existing `switch` statement, touching no previously-implemented case's logic. Every prior organic-boot survey in this project's history (Rounds 470-477, each running tens of millions of slices) never once reported a `"SPECIAL funct"` halt, meaning the real OSDSYS/BIOS code on that path never exercises the TEQ/TNE/TGE/TGEU/TLT/TLTU family within the depth this project has explored - so the fix cannot regress that path, only extend coverage. Confirmed by the 128/128 regression suite.

**Classification.** A genuine, evidenced, narrow, standard-MIPS-ISA opcode-emulation fix - the same class of fix as Round 400 (BC1FL/BC1TL) and Round 446 (VADDq), not a guess or a speculative addition. Also the most significant milestone in the OSDMenu-as-alternative-strategy thread opened by Rounds 476-477: real, open-source, third-party PS2 software now runs measurably further via this project's own EE-core emulation than the real BIOS OSDSYS ever has on the disc-browser path, and the specific blocker it hit was a genuine, fixable emulator gap rather than an intractable protocol-negotiation mystery.

**Next steps for whoever continues this thread**: characterize OSDMenu's new resting state in more depth (disassemble the `0x8000CCxx`-range idle loop, check GS/framebuffer state for any OSDMenu-drawn UI, determine whether it is waiting on a real interrupt/RPC/pad-input stimulus this project can supply), and continue the parallel real-OSDSYS-escalation investigation per the user's "do both in parallel" decision.

## Round 480 (direct continuation of Round 479's proposed next step): disassembled the caller at ra=0x00214a0c - found the 0x0021477C/0x00214778 cluster is a status-text formatter, not a disc-command dispatcher; the "a1=0x500D heartbeat" call site is elsewhere

Nothing in the previously-decoded body (Round 471) actually issues any CDVD RPC, SIF call, or IOP-facing syscall - it only ever touches the `$gp`-relative global struct at `0x0046F100` and calls further internal helpers (`0x00210D40`, `0x00210D60`, `0x00213700`, `0x00213A10`, `0x002136A0`) that were never confirmed to reach any disc-I/O boundary. **Correction to this project's own multi-round working assumption**: this `0x00214778` cluster is very likely OSDSYS's on-screen status-text renderer (the thing that draws whatever line of text the disc browser displays), not the disc-command dispatch/escalation gate the investigation has been chasing since Round 471.

Either the `a1=0x500D` heartbeat originates from a *different* call site to the same `0x00214778` function (there may be several - the preceding block at `0x00214880-0x00214924` alone contains at least one other indirect dispatch through a jump table, see Finding 4), or the original Round 471 attribution was itself imprecise and never re-verified until now.

None of the branches here read any CDVD, SIF, or IOP-facing register or memory location - every comparison and side effect stays within this function's own `$gp`-relative globals and stack.

Rounds 471-479 spent significant effort on the `0x0021477C`/`0x00214a0c` thread on the working assumption that it was the disc-command escalation gate; this round's actual disassembly (the first time this specific code has been decoded rather than inferred from indirect behavior) shows it is very likely a status-text formatter instead, and the specific `ra` this project tracked as "the a1=0x500D heartbeat site" is a fixed, non-branching, single-value call that cannot be that site. This closes off this specific thread as a dead end for the escalation-gate search, while producing a corrected, disassembly-verified understanding of what this code cluster actually does (useful in its own right - e.g. it may be the mechanism that renders the disc-browser's own idle-state text such as "PlayStation" or "No Disc").

## Round 481 (direct continuation of Round 480's proposed next step): live-instrumented every real call to the status-formatter (0x00214778) with a caller/argument census - found the true a1=0x500D heartbeat producer/consumer mechanism and its real gating condition

**Context.** Round 480's disassembly showed the `ra=0x00214a0c` call site (tracked as "the a1=0x500D heartbeat caller" since Round 471) is actually a fixed, non-branching, single-value (`a1=0xE621`) wrapper - contradicting the old attribution.
