- Left analog: W/A/S/D
- Circle (○決定/Confirm): **`l`**
- Cross (✕戻る/Back): **`k`**
- Triangle (△本体設定/△詳細設定): **`i`**

This matches PCSX2's standard "IJKL diamond" default keyboard scheme (I=Triangle/top, J=Square/left, K=Cross/bottom, L=Circle/right - mirrors the physical DualShock button diamond).

**Real OSDSYS menu flow, now mapped end-to-end for the first time in this project's history (Screens A -> B -> C -> D):**
- **Screen A** (top-level resting/carousel screen): black viewport, faint icon at the left edge; the animated background cycles through multiple distinct scenes over time (a static-orb scene and a rotating-crystal-cubes scene were both observed at this same screen on different visits, plus a third white-cube/red-line scene - confirming Screen A's idle animation is a longer multi-scene loop, not a single static clip). Prompts: `○決定` / `△本体設定`.
- **Screen A --Circle--> Screen B**: real "PS2" logo card (the disc-browser root). Prompts: `✕戻る` / `○決定`.
- **Screen B --Circle--> Screen C**: real **"MEMORY CARD"** screen, showing genuine live capacity text `空き容量 7,989キロバイト` (free space 7,989 KB). Prompts: `✕戻る` / `○決定` / `△詳細設定`.
- **Screen C --Triangle--> Screen D**: real memory-card **Detailed Settings** view - a card-icon graphic plus five real property labels: `場所` (Location), `種類` (Type), `サイズ` (Size), `更新日時` (Update date/time), `操作条件` (Operating conditions). Prompt: `✕戻る` only.
- **Screen D --Cross--> Screen C --Cross--> Screen B --Cross--> Screen A**: Cross reliably backs out one level at a time, confirmed repeatedly.

No disc/CD icon was found anywhere in the Screen A carousel - consistent with the user's own expectation (no ISO mounted in this PCSX2 instance) and not evidence of a gap.

**Render-gap investigation (raised by the user's "if we are inside the bios we should see where is the issue" prompt).** A dark-grey rectangle covering roughly the right 64% of the viewport has been visible since the Controller Settings dialog in the prior window, and was still present across every OSDSYS screen this round. Diagnosed properly this round instead of just working around it:
- Zoomed into the region at full resolution: confirmed flat, uniform color with no hidden/obscured text underneath.
- Toggled real PCSX2 fullscreen mode (View > Fullscreen / Alt+Enter): the rectangle scaled proportionally with the video content rather than staying a fixed screen-pixel mask - ties it to the actual rendered output geometry, not a compositor overlay artifact.
- **Switched the real renderer from Direct3D 12 to Vulkan** (Settings > Graphics > Graphics API) and re-observed the same OSDSYS screens: **the rectangle was pixel-identical in position/size under Vulkan as under D3D12.** Reverted back to Direct3D 12 afterward to match the established baseline.

**Conclusion.** Because the gap is renderer-independent (identical under two completely different graphics backends), it is almost certainly **not a driver/rendering bug** - if it were D3D12-specific, Vulkan would very likely render differently. The far more consistent explanation is that real OSDSYS content genuinely only occupies the left portion of the window at this aspect-ratio/scaling setting (`Aspect Ratio: Auto Standard (4:3 Interlace)` in Graphics settings), and the panel graphics (PS2 logo, MEMORY CARD card, Detailed Settings card) are narrow by design, with the remainder of the window left as an unfilled background fill color rather than being centered or stretched. This also retroactively explains why earlier sessions' "MEMORY CARD" and "PS2" text looked cut off at the same x-boundary in every screenshot - real label text was reaching the edge of that same narrow content area, not being clipped by a rendering fault.

**Also confirmed while investigating alternatives to the disc-browser path:** real PCSX2's `System` menu has a native **"Start File..."** option - PCSX2's built-in "boot an ELF directly" feature (equivalent to what FreeMCBoot does on real hardware via memory card). This bypasses BIOS/disc navigation entirely and would be the natural next step if the user wants to test homebrew/ELF loading instead of continuing to push on the OSDSYS disc-browser thread; it requires an `.elf` file to be supplied (none uploaded yet this round).

**Session-loss note carried over from the prior window:** an earlier accidental session close (during the interrupted portion of this excursion) was recovered cleanly by re-running System > Start BIOS - no save-state was needed, the JP BIOS reboots deterministically in ~5-6 seconds.

**Classification.** Investigative/GUI-exploration round - no tracked source changed. Regression suite and Wii rebuild correctly skipped.

**Leak check.** No BIOS/disc files or checkpoints were written to `/tmp/pcsx2-wii-git` or the outputs mirror this round (this was a live-GUI-only excursion, no scratch driver files created). Filename-pattern scan, `.ckpt` scan, and `git ls-files` grep all clean (below).

**Next.** Task #447 (JP-path OSDSYS decision) remains the standing next step on the primary investigative thread - this round's real menu map is useful ground truth for it but doesn't resolve it by itself. ## Round 507: custom ps2sdk diagnostic ELF - full real BIOS ROMVER, host: path, rom0: readdir behavior, CDVD status

**Context:** user asked how far a custom diagnostic ELF could go toward reading real ground truth from the emulator/BIOS, proposing it as an alternative/extension to the uLaunchELF Debug Info approach used in Round 506 (which was limited by the render-gap truncation). **Diagnostic ELF** (`tools/round507-diag-elf/diag.c`, committed this round): uses ps2sdk's `debug.h` on-screen console (`scr_printf`/`init_scr`) rather than host: log files, so results are readable via screenshots without needing host filesystem access from this sandbox. Uses POSIX `open`/`read`/`opendir`/`readdir` (not the legacy `fio*`/`fileXio*` API, which this ps2sdk version's newlib port blocks at compile time via `io_common.h`'s `#error`). Paces each info screen with `sleep()` so it can be read one section at a time. Built cleanly, stripped to 178KB, copied to the outputs folder and loaded into real PCSX2 via System > Start File... (confirmed window title changes to the ELF's own name, confirming real boot).

**Real ground truth obtained (JP BIOS, ps2-0100J, live PCSX2):**
- `rom0:ROMVER == "0100JC20000117"` (len=16) - the full, uncut BIOS version string, resolving Round 506's partial `"0100JC200..."` capture (which was truncated by the render-gap bug, not a data limitation).
- `argv[0] == "host:C:\Users\box\pcsx2wii-round507-diag.elf"` - confirms real `host:` filesystem passthrough resolves to the actual Windows path the ELF was launched from.
- `opendir("rom0:")` + `readdir()` returns 0 entries, despite `open("rom0:ROMVER", O_RDONLY)` succeeding moments earlier. Real behavioral finding: this ps2sdk/PCSX2 combination's `rom0:` device supports direct named-file open but not directory enumeration via the POSIX dirent API. Relevant scope note for this project's own `rom0:` FILEIO wiring (Round 346) - a `rom0:` directory listing should not be expected to work even on real hardware/reference PCSX2, so it's not a gap specific to our own emulator.
- `opendir("mc1:/")` fails ("opendir failed") - consistent with Round 456's finding of no memory card present in slot 2. (`mc0:/`'s result was not captured across several attempts - the on-screen pacing made that specific screen's real-time window too short to reliably catch via manual screenshot timing; not considered a blocking gap since mc1's null result already corroborates Round 456.)
- `sceCdGetDiskType() = 0 (0x0)`, `sceCdStatus() = 10 (0xa)` - real "no disc mounted" CDVD status from live PCSX2 in this session (no ISO loaded).

**Answering the user's actual question ("how far would a diagnostic ELF go"):** as far as any real PS2 homebrew ELF can go via legitimate BIOS/kernel syscalls when run under the reference PCSX2 - full ROMDIR-adjacent data (named opens), real host-path resolution, real CDVD/memory-card status, real thread/semaphore introspection if pursued further. It cannot reach outside the PS2's own address space into PCSX2's C++ internals (that needs Pine/the debugger interface, a different mechanism, already used extensively in earlier rounds). Run under this project's own from-scratch emulator core instead of real PCSX2, the same ELF would be bounded by our own syscall/device coverage - which makes it a reusable coverage-probe tool for future rounds (run once against real PCSX2 for ground truth, run again against our own core, diff the two outputs) rather than a one-off.

## Round 508: minimal bootable test disc (SYSTEM.CNF + ELF ISO) - real BIOS disc-browser boot attempt

**Context:** following Round 507's diagnostic ELF, the user proposed going further: wrap the ELF in a proper bootable disc image (`SYSTEM.CNF` + `BOOT2`) so the real BIOS disc-browser would organically detect and launch it as a genuine disc boot, rather than using PCSX2's dev-only `System > Start File...` ELF shortcut. Explicit user sign-off: "Yes, build it and test in real PCSX2 first." This is a direct, real-hardware test aimed squarely at task #447 (accept disc-browser idle as correct BIOS behavior, or pivot to the syscall-7 trampoline path).

**Built:** a minimal ISO9660 (interchange level 1) disc image via `pycdlib`, containing:
- `SYSTEM.CNF` at the root: `BOOT2 = cdrom0:\BOOT.ELF;1` / `VER = 1.00` / `VMODE = NTSC` (the standard real PS2 boot descriptor format).
- `BOOT.ELF`: a reused copy of the Round 507 diagnostic ELF (our own original code, no Sony IP).

Source (`tools/round508-testdisc/SYSTEM.CNF`, `build_iso.py`, `README.md`) is committed. The built `.iso` itself (and the `BOOT.ELF` binary copy used to build it) are **not** committed or rsynced - kept in the outputs root only, matching the Round 507 pattern, as an extra precaution even though neither contains any real Sony IP.

**Real-hardware result (live PCSX2, JP BIOS scph10000 / ROMVER 0100JC20000117):**
1. Mounted via `System > Start File...`. PCSX2's window title changed to `BOOT.ELF [?]`, confirming the BIOS/PCSX2 parsed `SYSTEM.CNF`'s `BOOT2` line and resolved our ELF as the disc's boot target.
2. From OSDSYS's real root menu (ブラウザ / システム設定 - "Browser" / "System Settings", not previously documented at this precision), entering ブラウザ shows a 3-item carousel cycled via D-pad Left/Right: `MEMORY CARD / 1`, `MEMORY CARD / 2`, `PlayStation2 ディスク`.
3. Our disc is specifically, correctly type-detected as **`PlayStation2 ディスク`** ("PlayStation 2 Disc") - a genuine disc-type-specific label, not a generic placeholder. This confirms our minimal SYSTEM.CNF + ISO9660 structure is sufficient for real BIOS-level disc-type identification/enumeration.
4. Pressing 決定 (Circle) on the `PlayStation2 ディスク` card does **not** launch/boot it. The browser silently wraps back to `MEMORY CARD / 1` (the carousel's first entry) - no loading screen, no error message, no black-screen transition, no BOOT2 dispatch observed. Reproduced twice (fresh approach to the disc card each time), identical result both times.
5. As a side finding, maximizing/resizing the PCSX2 window revealed the actual PS2 framebuffer render area is a fixed 640x448 (confirmed via the status bar: "Direct3D 12  640x448  FPS: 60  VPS: 60") embedded inside a wider window frame - this is consistent with Round 506's revised conclusion (PCSX2-Qt video-widget layout bug, not narrow BIOS content) and explains why the "blue disc" icon the user saw on their real screen was only partially visible in earlier narrower-window screenshots (it sits right at/past the ~525px layout boundary).

This is a direct, real-hardware reproduction of the user's live observation: *"the disc shows up in the ps2 menu but it wont load."*

**Interpretation / reconciling with task #447:** the real BIOS's disc-enumeration/type-detection path and its actual BOOT2-dispatch path are evidently two separate mechanisms - our minimal disc satisfies the first (genuine, specific disc-type recognition) but not the second (no launch). This is a meaningful negative result: even a hand-authored, syntactically-plausible `SYSTEM.CNF` + ELF disc, mounted in the *real, reference* PCSX2 with a *real* BIOS, does not organically boot through OSDSYS's disc-browser. That raises the bar for what "the disc-browser idle is correct BIOS behavior and just needs a valid disc" would require - it's evidently not sufficient to have a structurally valid SYSTEM.CNF and a working ELF; there's additional real BIOS-side validation (exact format expectations, ELF header checks, or ISO structure details) not yet identified. Root cause was not isolated at the code level this round; that would need Pine/debugger CDVD register tracing or IOP-side BIOS disassembly, which is a substantially bigger investment than this round's GUI-based test. Given this project's syscall-7 trampoline path already reliably gets real game code executing (Rounds 457-469), and given that even real Sony hardware doesn't organically launch a minimal homebrew disc without deeper BIOS-format knowledge we don't yet have, this result leans the task #447 decision toward continuing with the trampoline path as the practical way forward, rather than further chasing organic disc-browser escalation in our own emulator - though it does not conclusively close the door on the organic path, since the exact real-BIOS validation gap remains unidentified and could in principle be closed with further investigation (e.g. Pine-assisted tracing of a real commercial disc's boot for comparison).

**Classification:** live-hardware investigative round; no tracked emulator source (`ee_core.c` etc.) changed, so host-native regression suite and Wii cross-build were correctly skipped.

**Leak check:** outputs mirror scanned (filename patterns + `.ckpt` + `git ls-files` grep) - all clean, zero matches. Neither the built `.iso` nor the `BOOT.ELF` binary copy (both our own original content, no Sony IP) were committed or rsynced to the tracked mirror, kept in the outputs root only per the established precaution.

**Next:** task #447 can now be revisited with this round's real-hardware evidence in hand. ## Round 509: does this project's OWN emulator core boot uLaunchELF's real BOOT.ELF?

**Context:** the user uploaded uLaunchELF v4.43a's real `BOOT.ELF` (497,108 bytes, real ELF32/MIPS ET_EXEC, `e_entry=0x01D0001C`, confirmed via `readelf -h`) and asked whether this project's OWN emulator (not real PCSX2, which Round 505-508 used) can launch it - a direct, substantial third-party homebrew test of the syscall-7 `_ExecPS2` trampoline mechanism already evidenced against real game code (Rounds 457-469, re-run Round 502) and `osdmenu.elf` (Round 478).

**Method:** reused the exact trampoline recipe: organic BIOS warm-up (40M slices) to reach OSDSYS's steady idle state, `ee_elf_load()` the uploaded `BOOT.ELF` directly (no disc/ISO involved, matching Round 478's approach), mask VBLANK-END in `INTC_MASK` (Round 469's evidenced fix), install a real `SYSCALL` instruction in EE scratchpad with `$v1=7` (`_ExecPS2`), `$a0=`entry, then run 80M more slices in 10 sampled 8M-slice chunks (finer sampling than prior rounds, to catch any transient progress a single big run might miss). Driver committed as `tools/round509-ulaunchelf-test/driver.c` + `README.md` (the `BOOT.ELF` binary itself is not committed - third-party GPL homebrew, kept out of the tracked repo pending a separate licensing decision, same precautionary pattern as Round 507/508's binary artifacts).

**Result:**
1. `ee_elf_load()` parses the real PT_LOAD segments cleanly: `load_start=0x01C8C290 load_end=0x01D05C60`, matching the real ELF header's `entry=0x01D0001C` exactly.
2. The trampoline dispatches correctly - the syscall exception fires, landing at the real EE exception vector `0x80000180`, identical to every prior real-game trampoline test.
3. Execution continues crash-free for 640,000,000 instructions (10x 8M-slice chunks, EE never halts).
4. But the sampled EE PC across all 10 chunks stays entirely within the same well-documented shared kernel per-frame idle-dispatch loop this project has characterized extensively since Rounds 265-271 and re-confirmed as recently as Round 469/502 (`0x8000CC8C`-`0x8000F868`, including the landmark `0x8000CF88`/`0x8000D008`/`0x8000D010` addresses from that existing writeup) - not any uLaunchELF-specific address.
5. GS state (`PMODE=0x66 DISPFB2=0x1400 DISPLAY2=0x1BF9FF0183227C`) is byte-identical immediately after warm-up (before the ELF was even loaded) and at every one of the 10 sampled post-trampoline chunks. This is OSDSYS's own inherited splash-screen display state (matching Round 321's GS-circuit-2 finding) - no evidence uLaunchELF's own code wrote a single GS register during the entire run.

**Interpretation:** this is the third independent confirmation (after Tekken's game ELF and `osdmenu.elf`) of the same real, previously-documented finding: the syscall-7 trampoline correctly loads and dispatches into any real PS2 ELF's entry point, but whatever real kernel call the target's own early crt0/init code makes ends up parked in the same shared, real kernel per-frame idle-wait dispatcher already root-caused in Rounds 265-271 as genuinely waiting on a pad-input/disc-insert/SBUS stimulus this project's test harness has never delivered *during* a post-trampoline run (only once, before warm-up). This is not a uLaunchELF-specific bug, not a new gap, and not evidence against `ee_elf_load()` or the trampoline mechanism - both behaved correctly against a real, substantial (497KB) third-party ELF.

**Direct answer to the user's question:** yes, in the sense that the emulator core correctly parses, loads, and begins real execution of uLaunchELF's actual code (no crash, no malformed-ELF rejection, correct entry dispatch, sustained 640M-instruction run). Not yet, in the sense that it doesn't reach uLaunchELF's own visible UI/menu - for the same reason no trampoline-loaded ELF has reached its own UI in this project yet: the shared kernel idle-wait loop needs a real stimulus that hasn't been tried mid-run (a pad-button-press event delivered *during* the post-trampoline run, not just once before warm-up).

**Classification:** no tracked emulator source (`ee_core.c`, `ee_elf_loader.c`, etc.) was changed - both behaved correctly against a real, substantial third-party ELF, so there was nothing to fix. Regression suite and Wii cross-build correctly skipped.

**Leak check:** outputs mirror scanned (filename patterns + `.ckpt` + `git ls-files` grep) - all clean. The uploaded `BOOT.ELF` (third-party GPL homebrew, not Sony IP but also not our own code) was not committed or rsynced to the tracked mirror.

## Round 511: real SIF2 (IOP DMA channel 2) inbound transfer engine - correct fix, but insufficient alone

**Context:** per the user's explicit instruction ("do first 2 and after that 1" - implement the SIF DMA inbound payload-copy path, then persistent IOP threading), this round implements the first of the two remaining candidate fixes for task #447's real blocker (the OSDSYS `0x8000F768` per-frame wait loop's `DMAC_STAT` bit 0x80/SIF2-completion condition, established Rounds 265-271, re-confirmed Round 267: "SIF2's DPCR enable bit is set... but `dma_channel_kick()` is never called for it").

**Real source grounding:** the user's own previously-uploaded, real 2002-era IOP SIFMAN reimplementation source (`dmacman.h`, `sifman.c`) settles the exact real semantics. `dmacman.h`: `#define DMAch_GPU 2 // SIF2 both directions` - IOP DMA channel 2 (PS1-legacy "GPU" base `0x1F8010A0`) is real hardware's dual-purpose SIF2 channel on PS2, exactly matching this project's own existing (previously plain-latch) channel-2 mapping in `iop_dma.c`. `sifman.c`'s real kicker, `sceSifSetSIF2DMA()`: sets MADR (masked to `0xFFFFFF`), BCR_size/BCR_count (low/high halfwords - the same BS*BA convention this project's existing SIF0 transfer function already used, independently confirmed matching, not assumed), then CHCR with `DMAf_TR` (`0x01000000`, the same STR/start bit SIF0 already gates on) OR'd with `DMAf_DR` (`0x00000001`) when-and-only-when the caller requests `SIF_TO_EE` - i.e. DR=1 is the real, cited signal for the IOP-RAM-to-EE-RAM direction this project's existing `dma_channel_receive_quadwords()` inbound-write primitive (Round 198) already implements.

**Implementation:** `source/hw/iop_dma.c`: new `iop_dma_sif2_try_transfer()`, a direct sibling of the existing `iop_dma_sif0_try_transfer()` (Round 199), wired into `iop_dma_mmio_write32()`'s CHCR write path for channel 2, triggered only when both `DMAf_TR` and `DMAf_DR` are set (the real, cited IOP-RAM-to-EE-RAM direction). The reverse direction (TR set, DR clear) is intentionally left as a plain register latch - honest unmodeled scope, matching Round 199's own SIF1 caveat, not fabricated. Also added `iop_dma_get_sif2_transfer_count()`, a hit-counter diagnostic following this project's established convention.

**Empirical result:** built `tools/round511-sif2-dma/driver.c`, an organic-BIOS-boot survey (no disc, no trampoline). Across two independent runs totaling ~145,000,000 instructions, `iop_dma_get_sif2_transfer_count()` stayed at 0 throughout, and `DMAC_STAT` bit 0x80 was never set - `DMAC_STAT`'s enable bits (`0x00a00000`) confirm both SIF0 and SIF2 are enabled (matching Round 267), but no CHCR write with both `DMAf_TR` and `DMAf_DR` ever occurred in this trace window. The EE's PC in this organic (no-disc) boot mode rests in a `0x00501xxx`-`0x00518xxx` region, distinct from the previously-documented `0x8000Cxxx` shared kernel loop family (mostly reached via disc-mounted or trampoline paths in prior rounds) - not further characterized this round.

**Interpretation:** the fix is correct and real-source-grounded, but **alone it is not sufficient** to unblock OSDSYS's SIF2 wait condition - no guest code path in the currently-modeled boot trace ever issues the real `sceSifSetSIF2DMA(SIF_TO_EE)` kick in the first place. This was the honestly-anticipated outcome, not a surprise, and directly motivates Round 512: the code that would call `sceSifSetSIF2DMA()` most plausibly lives inside a loaded IOP module's own ongoing service logic, which this project's IOP core currently never reaches because it halts once it finishes running the fixed set of modules discovered at boot (task #92's documented simplification) instead of staying alive as an event-driven scheduler.

**Classification:** real, additive, citation-grounded fix - kept in tracked source regardless of the negative result (closes a genuine, evidenced DMA-model gap, matching real hardware behavior for the direction it's needed, and is a building block Round 512's IOP-threading work will need).

**Verification:** host-native regression - `tests/test_dma_sif2.c` (EE-side, unaffected by this IOP-side change, still 0 failures), `tests/test_iop_dma.c` (0 failures, linked with `iop_intc.c`+`dma.c` per its own self-contained-test convention), `tests/test_dma_inbound.c` and `tests/test_dma_reply_delivered.c` (both 0 failures) - all four tests that reference the touched symbols pass clean. Full standalone compile of the entire tracked `source/` tree (excluding the Wii-only `main.c`/`ppc_dynarec.c`/`gs_wii_output.c`) succeeds. Wii cross-build: reused this session's freshly-set-up devkitPPC r32 + libogc 1.8.18 toolchain (see Round 510's entry for the setup details) - every changed/tracked file, including `source/hw/iop_dma.c`, compiles clean under the real `powerpc-eabi-gcc` cross-compiler (full link still blocked only by the pre-existing, unrelated `libfat`/`fat.h` gap noted in Round 510).

**Leak check:** outputs mirror scanned (filename patterns including `.elf`, `.ckpt` scan, `git ls-files` grep) - all clean. No BIOS/disc/binary data added; `tools/round511-sif2-dma/` contains only our own diagnostic driver source and documentation.

## Round 512: IOP thread-scheduler survey - corrects Round 511's "IOP halts, needs threading built" framing

**Context:** per the user's instruction to tackle persistent IOP threading after the SIF2 DMA fix, this round began by investigating `source/hw/iop_hle_thread.c` before writing any new code - and found a full, real, priority-based preemptive THREADMAN scheduler (real `CreateThread`/`StartThread`/`WaitSema`/`SignalSema`/`SleepThread`/`WakeupThread`/EventFlags/Alarm, ps2sdk-cited ordinals and struct layouts) already implemented in an earlier investigative arc (task #116/117, "Round 389+"), and that `iop_module_loader.c`'s "task #179" fix already changed post-module-exhaustion behavior from a hard `halted` state to a genuinely interrupt-responsive `idle` (not halted) state. **Round 511's framing - "the IOP halts... instead of staying alive as an event-driven scheduler" - is corrected here as stale/inaccurate relative to the current tracked source.**

**Method:** built `tools/round512-iop-thread-survey/driver.c`, an organic-boot survey using the existing (not new) `iop_hle_thread_get_thread_count()`/`get_sema_count()`/`get_evf_count()`/`get_alarm_count()`/`get_status()` diagnostic getters.

**Result (20,000,000-instruction organic boot, re-confirmed stable through 60,000,000 in the companion Round 511 driver):**
- 6 real threads, 3 real semaphores, 2 real event flags created from actual interpreted module init code - the scheduler is genuinely exercised, not dormant.
- Thread 1 = **RUN**, threads 2/3 = **DORMANT**, threads 4/5/6 = **READY** (created and schedulable, but never dispatched).
- IOP PC oscillates between `0x00100000` (module-loader trampoline/idle-park) and `0x80000080` (real general exception vector) repeatedly - consistent with thread 1 fielding real periodic hardware interrupts and returning, without ever calling a THREADMAN primitive that would trigger `reschedule()`.

**Interpretation:** `reschedule()` is correctly wired to every real THREADMAN primitive that could change readiness - not itself a bug. The observed starvation (3 live threads permanently READY while thread 1 permanently RUNs) has two possible explanations this round's evidence doesn't yet distinguish: (1) genuinely correct, real starvation-by-design if thread 1's priority number is ≤ threads 4-6's (real hardware would behave identically - a non-yielding higher-or-equal-priority thread legitimately monopolizes the CPU), in which case the real question becomes what should cause thread 1 to yield; or (2) a genuine dispatch gap if thread 1's priority is actually lower urgency than 4-6's and something fails to trigger `reschedule()` at the right point. Identifying thread 1's real module identity and each thread's actual priority number is the concrete next step - not yet done this round.

**Classification:** diagnostic/investigative round - no tracked emulator source changed (only new scratch driver code added under `tools/`). Host-native regression suite and Wii cross-build correctly skipped, matching this project's own established convention for docs-only rounds.

## Round 513: thread-1 identity + priority survey - classifies the Round 512 starvation as a genuine dispatch/integration gap

**Context:** direct continuation of Round 512's open question, per the user's explicit "yes" to keep going. Added two small diagnostic getters (no behavior change): `iop_hle_thread_get_priority(thid)` (`include/core/hw/iop_hle_thread.h`, `source/hw/iop_hle_thread.c`) and `iop_module_loader_get_module_count/get_module_name/get_module_entry` (`include/core/hw/iop_module_loader.h`, `source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`), exposing the already-tracked internal module list/entry-point table for PC-to-module correlation.

**Result (`tools/round513-thread-priority/driver.c`, 20,000,000-instruction organic boot):** thread 1 = RUN, priority=64; thread 2 = DORMANT, priority=8; thread 3 = DORMANT, priority=10; thread 4 = READY, priority=80; thread 5 = READY, priority=96; thread 6 = READY, priority=96. Live IOP pc=0x00100000 - below every one of the 29 real IOPBTCONF modules' entry points (0x001000a0-0x00145b40), confirming thread 1 is not executing any real Sony module code.

**Thread 1's real identity:** 0x00100000 is exactly `BUMP_BASE` and specifically `g.trampoline_addr` (`source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`) - this project's own synthetic "module returned" landing pad, installed as `$ra` for every module's `_start()` call, not real PS2 code. Once all 29 modules have run to completion (`g.idle_transition_done`, task #179/Round 425-426), every re-entry to this address sets `g_iop.idle = 1` and skips real fetch/decode/execute; pc only leaves 0x00100000 to service a real hardware interrupt at 0x80000080 before RFE-ing straight back. This is Round 512's observed oscillation, now fully explained as the real, correct idle/wake-on-interrupt cycle - not module code. "Thread 1" in THREADMAN's bookkeeping is the scheduler's own "IMPLICIT ROOT THREAD" bridge for this idle context, and its priority (64) is confirmed, by its own source comment, to be an explicitly-uncited placeholder default.

**Classification: genuine dispatch/integration gap, not correct real starvation-by-design.** Threads 4/5/6 are real, module-created worker threads with real assigned priorities. `g_iop.idle` (CPU-core level, `source/core/iop/iop_core.c`) and THREADMAN's TCB status (`source/hw/iop_hle_thread.c`, Round 389+) are two mechanisms from different rounds that were never integrated: `iop_hle_thread_tick()` runs unconditionally every step (including while idle) but nothing transitions thread 1's TCB status away from RUN when the CPU goes idle, and `reschedule()` only fires from specific THREADMAN-primitive trigger events - "CPU went idle" isn't one of them. So thread 1 permanently outranks threads 4/5/6 by priority even after it has genuinely stopped doing real work. A safe fix needs a real design decision (what TCB state the implicit root thread should enter on idle, and whether interrupt-handler execution during idle still logically belongs to it) that this round did not rush - deferred to a follow-up round.

**Classification (process):** real, additive source change (two diagnostic getters only, zero behavior change to existing logic) - full mandatory workflow applies.

## Round 518: real wait-target audit corrects Round 515 - threads 4-8 block on SleepThread, not WaitSema (task #447)

Added `iop_hle_thread_get_wait_type()`/`get_wait_id()` getters (exposing each TCB's `wait_type`/`wait_id` fields) and extended the survey driver to print them per-thread. Result: **all of threads 4-8 show `wait_type=1` (`IOP_TSW_SLEEP`), not `IOP_TSW_SEMA`** - this corrects Round 515's characterization ("shared SIF RPC/semaphore primitive"), which was inferred from the shared PC alone without actually checking the wait-primitive type.

Disassembled the real blocking sites using the project's MIPS decoder (`mips_disasm.py`): threads 5/6/7/8 are all parked at pc=0x0011ad58, which is the return address of `jal 0x0011AF14` inside a small dispatcher loop at 0x0011ad20-0x0011ad5c (SIFCMD's range). The loop's shape (walk a linked list via 0x0011AB3C; if non-null, call handler 0x0011ABA4 and loop; if null/empty, call 0x0011AF14 then return) is a textbook real "process queue, sleep when empty" RPC-server pattern - matching ps2sdk's own sceSifStartRpcThread-class dispatch loop design. Thread 4 (CDVDFSV's own thread, not the shared SIFCMD one) is parked at a structurally identical call site (0x0013a364, return address of `jal 0x0013E8FC` after the same "call helper twice, then wait" shape) in CDVDFSV's own code range.

Checked whether anything in this project's current source ever calls the real WakeupThread mechanism (`IOP_HLE_THREAD_WAKEUPTHREAD`, already implemented and dispatchable via the trap-ordinal table) on these thread IDs - it doesn't, anywhere in the current boot trace. This is **not evidence of an emulation bug**: SleepThread-based RPC/queue-dispatcher threads are *supposed* to sit idle exactly like this until a real event enqueues work and calls WakeupThread on them (in real hardware, typically the SIF DMA-complete interrupt handler enqueuing an arrived RPC packet). Since `dispatch_ncmd()` is still 0 and `iop_dma_get_sif2_transfer_count()` is still 0 (no real disc command or SIF2 payload has occurred yet in this organic-boot trace), nothing has genuinely happened that *should* wake these threads. Their idleness is consistent with, not contradictory to, the current boot depth.

**Conclusion for task #447:** this rules out "these specific threads are stuck due to a scheduler/wakeup bug" as an explanation - they are correctly modeled and correctly idle. The real blocker remains further upstream: what should cause OSDSYS to issue the first real SifCallRpc/SifSendCmd or CD-ROM command that would enqueue work for these dispatcher threads in the first place. This is the same open question Round 515 already deferred to (task #447 decision: continue the organic-boot path) - this round narrows the search space (rules out a dispatch-thread-level bug) without resolving the deeper upstream question.

**Verification:** full 129-test regression suite (129/129 PASS) and Wii cross-build health check (37/37, 0 WIIFAIL) re-run against the new getters/driver instrumentation - clean.

## Round 519: Round 514 was a severe regression, not forward progress - root-caused and fixed (task #485)

While pursuing task #485 (find what should trigger OSDSYS's first real RPC/CD command, the upstream question Round 515/518 kept deferring to), a from-scratch ground-truth check was run before starting new investigation: the real SIF RPC dispatch counters `g_r303_rpc_pending_sets`/`g_r303_rpc_delivered_count` (globals in `ee_core.c`, incremented by the real RPC bind/delivery path) against the current tree. Result: **0 real RPC calls of any kind**, with the EE resting at `pc=0x000820E0` (the BOOTEND poll loop, the same early resting point last seen at Round 431) - not the long-established deep steady state at `pc=0x0050172C` (~320M real EE instructions, 228 real RPC calls) that every round since Round 513 had been implicitly building on.

This is a severe, silent regression that the existing 129-test regression suite could not detect, because that suite tests subsystems in isolation and does not exercise full-boot integration depth. Bisected via isolated git clones (`/tmp/round519_pre514` at commit 6108774/Round 513, `/tmp/round519_514` at commit 1add1b0/Round 514) running the identical host-native boot survey: Round 513's tree shows `rpc_pending_sets=228 rpc_delivered=228 ee_pc=0x0050172C`; Round 514's tree shows `rpc_pending_sets=0 rpc_delivered=0 ee_pc=0x000820E0`. The regression was introduced by commit 1add1b0 (Round 514) itself, not by anything in Rounds 515-518.

**Root cause:** Round 514 added `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread(iop_state_t *st)` and wired an unconditional call to it into all 4 idle-bypass call sites inside `iop_module_loader_try_handle()` (the pre-existing trap/trampoline idle mechanism from the task #179 era). Those 4 sites fire *repeatedly* on every re-entry to the idle trampoline in the steady-state idle loop - not once. The original function body had no guard against this: it forced whatever thread happened to be `g.current_thread_id` at that moment into `IOP_THS_DORMANT` on every single re-entry, silently corrupting the scheduler and starving all subsequent real IOP activity, including the real SIF RPC dispatch machinery. Round 514/515/518's own STATUS.md entries characterized the resulting "new thread activity" (CDVDFSV/FILEIO worker threads becoming visible) as genuine forward progress - it was real thread creation, but it came at the cost of silently breaking a much deeper, already-working part of the boot path that nothing was checking.

**First fix attempt (disproved):** added a guard restricting retirement to `current_thread_id==1`, `status==RUN`, firing only once via a static flag - the minimal, most conservative version of "correctly do what Round 514 intended, just once." Rebuilt and re-ran the RPC-counter check: still `rpc_pending_sets=0`. This disproves the "repeated/wrong-thread retirement" hypothesis as the sole cause - even a single, correctly-scoped one-time retirement of thread 1 is incompatible with this project's real boot-progress dependency on thread 1 remaining `RUN`.

**Working fix:** fully disabled (commented out) all 4 call sites in `iop_module_loader.c`, leaving `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()` defined but unused (its body left in its guarded form in `iop_hle_thread.c`, with a header comment explaining this incident, rather than reverted - since the function is provably unsafe to call anywhere in the current idle-bypass path, not just in its original unguarded form). Rebuilt and re-ran: restores the exact pre-Round-514 baseline bit-for-bit (`rpc_pending_sets=228 rpc_delivered=228`, `ee_pc=0x0050172C`, `iop_pc=0x00100000`).

**Verification:** full 129-test regression suite re-run against the fix - 129/129 PASS (56 direct-link, 73 via the established selective-object-exclusion fallback), 0 BUILDFAIL, 0 TESTFAIL. Wii cross-build health check - 37/37 files clean, 0 WIIFAIL.

**Task #485 status:** the round's actual contribution was discovering and fixing this regression, not answering the original question. With the fix applied, the project is back to its pre-Round-514 state: 228 real RPC calls happen and OSDSYS reaches its deep steady state, but still settles into the disc-browser idle loop without ever issuing a first real CD-ROM/NCMD command - this is simply the same open task #447 question from Rounds 470-502, now correctly restored rather than newly resolved.

**Historical-record note:** Round 514's "verify fix + re-survey thread dispatch" entry and Round 515/518's characterizations of the new thread activity as forward progress should be read alongside this entry - the new thread visibility was real, but it was purchased at the cost of a much larger, undetected regression. This project's own Round 425/426 precedent (a broad fix later found too broad and corrected) applies again here; per that precedent this correction is recorded plainly rather than silently folded into the original entries.

**Lesson for pacing:** this regression went undetected for 4 rounds (514-518) under the user's "fast, less verification per step" authorization for this batch, specifically because the regression suite alone was insufficient - it took a from-scratch ground-truth check (the RPC counters) to surface it, not the standing verification battery. Flagging this to the user is warranted once this fix is delivered.

## Round 520: CPU/RAM/CDVD gap audit - hypothesis not supported, the real gap is narrower (task #486)

Per the user's explicit request to slow down (full verification per change from now on, no more batching) and to re-check whether CPU emulation, RAM/DMA handling, or CDVD handling have a genuine missing-integration gap explaining the disc-browser wall, this round did a careful read-only audit of all three subsystems. No source was changed this round.

**EE CPU (`ee_core.c`, 9198 lines):** the instruction interpreter is extensive - full MIPS III integer core, ~67 of ~90 MMI SIMD opcodes, LQ/SQ 128-bit load/store, COP0 with a real 48-entry TLB, COP1 FPU core arithmetic, a documented subset of COP2/VU0. Every genuinely unimplemented opcode halts cleanly with a labeled message rather than silently misbehaving. The current 320M+ instruction organic boot trace never hits any of these halts - meaning nothing the real boot code path actually executes is missing at the CPU level. Documented, real gaps exist (7 MMI ops needing SA-register infra, full VU0 macro-mode arithmetic, FPU exception-cause flags, BC1FL/BC1TL likely branches) but none are on the currently-reached path.

**IOP CPU (`iop_core.c`):** already covered by Round 516's ps2sdk iop/ tree audit (task #440, closed with no gap found) plus this round's spot-check - no new findings.

**RAM/DMA (`dma.c` + `iop_dma.c`):** all 10 real EE DMA channel register windows (VIF0/VIF1/GIF/IPU_FROM/IPU_TO/SIF0/SIF1/SIF2/SPR_FROM/SPR_TO) and all 12 real IOP DMA channels (MDEC in/out/GPU/CDROM/SPU/OTC/SPU2/DEV9/SIF0/SIF1/SIO2 in/out) are register-mapped. GIF/VIF0/VIF1 have working sinks that actually draw to the real framebuffer; SIF0/SIF2 have a working real RPC reply/receive path (228 real RPC calls completed pre-regression, confirmed again this round after the Round 519 fix). One genuine, real gap found: **the IPU (Image Processing Unit, real hardware's MPEG2/DVD macroblock decoder) has no hardware model anywhere in this codebase** - IPU_FROM/IPU_TO DMA channels exist as register windows but have no processing logic behind them, and IPU's own MMIO register range (0x10002000-0x10002080) isn't mapped at all. This is already honestly documented in `ee_core.c`'s own comments (search "INIT_IPU"). It is very unlikely to be the cause of the current wall specifically - Round 450-452's framebuffer dump showed the BIOS intro using GS triangle-fill / vector graphics (the well-known PS2 BIOS spinning-cube-style logo), not video playback, and IPU is normally only needed for actual FMV/game-video decode, which is well beyond the current wall - but it is a real, currently-unaddressed gap worth having on record for later (e.g. once past OSDSYS into an actual game).

**CDVD (`iop_cdvd.c`):** the N-command (NOP/NOPSYNC/STANDBY/STOP/PAUSE/SEEK/READCD/READDVD/GETTOC) and S-command register protocols are both implemented against cited real hardware/ps2tek semantics. Importantly, **`dispatch_ncmd()`'s READCD/READDVD handler is fully functional** - if OSDSYS ever wrote that command to the real NCMD register, this code would genuinely read real sector data from the mounted disc image (via the already-real ISO9660 parser, `iso_loader.c`) and deliver it through IOP DMA channel 3 with the correct IRQ2 raise, exactly matching cited real hardware behavior. This was traced through in full this round to confirm it, not just assumed from old comments.

**Conclusion:** the user's hypothesis (a broad missing integration in CPU, RAM, or CDVD handling) is not supported by the evidence - all three subsystems are unusually complete for a project at this stage, and the one real, confirmed gap found (IPU) sits well past the current wall, not in front of it. The actual blocker remains exactly what task #447 has been circling for ~50 rounds: not "can this emulator read a disc" (it demonstrably can, end-to-end, if asked), but "what specific condition in OSDSYS's own real code should cause it to ask." This is a much narrower problem than a missing subsystem, which is honestly both good news (the hard infrastructure work is done) and the frustrating part (the remaining gap is a single needle, not a haystack).

**Classification:** docs-only round, no tracked source changed. Regression suite and Wii rebuild correctly skipped. Per the user's new pacing instruction, all subsequent rounds return to full verification (build + regression suite) after every single source change, no batching.

## Round 521: real IPU hardware protocol research (task #487) - begins the video-decoder arc

Per the user's explicit request to build a real video decoder (IPU) that also runs on Wii, this round gathers citable real-hardware documentation before writing any code, following this project's own established research-before-implementation discipline (e.g. Round 259/261's CDVD register work, Round 445's SetGsCrt research).

**Register map** (ps2tek, IOP/EE memory map page, directly cited):
```
10002000h  8h   IPU_CMD  (DATA:32, BUSY:32 - top bit 0x80000000)
10002010h  4h   IPU_CTRL
10002020h  4h   IPU_BP   (bit pointer control)
10002030h  8h   TOP / TOPBUSY (top of bitstream)
10007000h 10h   Out FIFO (read)
10007010h 10h   In FIFO (write)
```
DMA channels: IPU_FROM = channel 3 (0x1000B0xx), IPU_TO = channel 4 (0x1000B4xx) - these already match this project's existing `DMA_CHANNEL_FROMIPU`/`DMA_CHANNEL_TOIPU` constants in `dma.c` (Round 199-era), which were register-mapped but never had processing logic behind them (the Round 520 gap).

**IPU_CTRL bitfield** (ported from PCSX2's `pcsx2/IPU/IPU.h` `tIPU_CTRL`, GPL-3.0, matching this project's own established citation practice for `ee_core.c`): `IFC:4` (input FIFO count) / `OFC:4` (output FIFO count) / `CBP:6` (coded block pattern) / `ECD:1` / `SCD:1` (start-code-detected) / `IDP:2` / `AS:1` (alternate scan) / `IVF:1` (intra VLC format) / `QST:1` / `MP1:1` (MPEG1 bitstream flag) / `PCT:3` (picture type) / `RST:1` (reset) / `BUSY:1`. Real writable-bits mask is `0x47f30000` (the rest are read-only/status bits set by the IPU itself) - directly cited from PCSX2's own `tIPU_CTRL::write()`.

**Command set** (`enum SCE_IPU`, cmd field is the top 4 bits of the 32-bit IPU_CMD word, `OPTION` is the low 28 bits): `BCLR=0` (clear input FIFO), `IDEC=1` (I-picture macroblock decode), `BDEC=2` (B/P-picture macroblock decode), `VDEC=3` (generic VLC-table decode, used for header parsing), `FDEC=4` (fixed-length 32-bit read, used to bootstrap the very first header read before any table is loaded), `SETIQ=5` (load quantization matrix), `SETVQ=6` (load VLC table), `CSC=7` (YCbCr-to-RGB colorspace conversion + optional macroblock-to-raster repack), `PACK=8` (pixel format packing, e.g. 16bpp), `SETTH=9` (set skip-block threshold). IDEC/BDEC/CSC each have their own real sub-field layouts (e.g. IDEC: `FB:6, QSC:5, DTD:1, SGN:1, DTE:1, OFM:1`; BDEC: `FB:6, QSC:5, DT:1, DCR:1, MBI:1`; CSC: `MBC:11, DTE:1, OFM:1`) - captured from PCSX2's own `tIPU_CMD_IDEC`/`tIPU_CMD_BDEC`/`tIPU_CMD_CSC` unions.

**FIFO/bitstream model:** real hardware (and PCSX2's model of it) uses two 8-quadword FIFOs (in/out) plus a small internal 2-QWC "IPU_BP" staging buffer that tracks a bit-level read position (`BP`, 0-256 bits) into the input stream, refilling one QWC at a time from the input FIFO as bits are consumed (`Advance()`/`FillBuffer()` in PCSX2's `tIPU_BP`). The IPU_TO DMA channel (IOP... actually EE-side channel 4) pushes quadwords into the input FIFO; IPU_FROM (channel 3) pulls decoded/packed quadwords out of the output FIFO. A real, documented quirk worth keeping: if data arrives via DMA before any command is issued, IPU_CMD's DATA field transparently reflects the first 32 bits of the raw bitstream - some real games depend on this to peek at a header before issuing their first FDEC.

**Scope decision for the next round:** matching this project's own established incremental pattern (e.g. Round 206 built CDVD's register protocol completely before `dispatch_ncmd()` had any real command logic, several rounds before READCD actually worked), Round 522 will build the register interface, FIFO plumbing, and DMA wiring first, with the decode commands (IDEC/BDEC/VDEC/FDEC/CSC/PACK) initially accepted-and-acknowledged but not yet performing real MPEG2 macroblock decode - that real decode logic (VLC tables, IDCT, motion compensation) is its own, later, evidence-driven arc once something in the real boot/game trace actually exercises the IPU and there's a concrete real bitstream to test against, rather than writing a decoder speculatively with nothing to verify it against.

**Classification:** docs-only round - no tracked source changed. Regression suite and Wii rebuild correctly skipped.

## Round 522: real IPU register/FIFO skeleton implemented (task #487)

Built on Round 521's research: added `source/hw/ipu.c` + `include/core/hw/ipu.h`, a real register interface for IPU_CMD (DATA/BUSY), IPU_CTRL (real bitfield, real `0x47f30000` writable-bits mask, real RST behavior), IPU_BP, and TOP/TOPBUSY at their real addresses (0x10002000-0x10002038). Wired into `ee_core.c`'s existing MMIO dispatch chain (`ee_mem_read32`/`write32`, alongside DMA/SIF/MCH/INTC/timers/SIO) and into the DMA_CHANNEL_TOIPU sink (`dma_set_sink()`, registered in both `ee_core_init()` and the checkpoint-safe `ee_core_rebind_dma_sinks()` - this project's own Round 449 lesson about stale function pointers surviving checkpoint restore applies here too, so the second registration point was not skipped).

BCLR (cmd 0) really clears the input FIFO and resets BP, matching the real cited semantics. All other commands (IDEC/BDEC/VDEC/FDEC/SETIQ/SETVQ/CSC/PACK/SETTH) are accepted and correctly acknowledge at the register level (ECD/SCD cleared per real spec, BUSY set-then-cleared) but do not yet perform real MPEG2 decode - exactly the scope Round 521 decided on, matching this project's own CDVD-register-before-dispatch_ncmd() precedent. The input FIFO real fill-level bookkeeping (IFC, 0-8 QWC) is live and fed by real DMA_CHANNEL_TOIPU traffic; consumed bytes are currently discarded since there's no decoder to hand them to yet, honestly documented rather than silently faked. The output FIFO/OFC and DMA_CHANNEL_FROMIPU's real delivery path are intentionally not wired up this round, since nothing yet produces real output data.

**Verification:** wrote and ran a scratch sanity harness (`/tmp/ipu_sanity.c`, not part of the tracked test suite - covers FIFO-fill/overflow-clamp, BCLR-clears-FIFO, command-ack/BUSY-clears, CTRL-write-mask, RST-full-reset, plain TOP/BP register R/W, and unmapped-address pass-through) - all checks pass. Full 129-test regression suite re-run against the new tree: 129/129 PASS (56 direct-link, 73 via the established selective-object-exclusion fallback), 0 BUILDFAIL, 0 TESTFAIL. Wii cross-build health check: 38/38 files clean (37 previous + the new ipu.c), 0 WIIFAIL - confirms this compiles clean with devkitPPC, i.e. genuinely runs on real Wii per the user's explicit requirement, not just host-native. Re-ran the standard organic-boot survey (real BIOS + real Tekken Tag Tournament Demo disc, 40M slices) against the new tree: `ee_pc=0x0050172C`, `rpc_pending_sets=228`, `rpc_delivered=228` - bit-for-bit identical to the pre-Round-522 baseline, confirming the new IPU wiring introduces zero regression to the real boot path (expected, since nothing in the current boot trace touches IPU registers yet - task #447's wall is unrelated to and unaffected by this arc, exactly as Round 520 concluded).

**Next round:** the register/FIFO skeleton is real and tested but still does no actual video decoding. The next step in this arc is either (a) finding a concrete real bitstream this project can actually exercise the IPU against (e.g. once task #447 is eventually resolved and real game/BIOS code reaches a point that issues real IDEC/BDEC/CSC commands), or (b) building a synthetic/scratch test harness with a hand-constructed minimal MPEG2 macroblock to start on real VLC/IDCT decode logic against a known-correct reference, independent of the boot-trace wall. Undecided which until the user weighs in.

## Round 524: implement real SPU2/SPU-legacy KON/ENDX/CTRL register semantics (task #490)

Researched real SPU register-level semantics via psx-spx (https://psx-spx.consoledev.net/soundprocessingunitspu/), which documents the PS1 SPU register model that PS2's SPU2 core extends (same real hardware lineage this project's own Round 185 citation already relies on). Confirmed, citable facts: KON (Key On) and KOFF (Key Off) are real write-only trigger registers - "should be treated as write-only (although, reading returns the most recently 32bit value...)". ENDX (voice loop-end status) is real hardware-owned/read-only - "writing is possible in so far that the written value can be read-back for a short moment, however, thereafter the hardware is overwriting that value" - and critically: "The bits get CLEARED when setting the corresponding KEY ON bits." SPUCNT (here named CTRL)/SPUSTAT (here named STATUS/STATX) real relationship: "Current SPU Mode (same as SPUCNT.Bit5-0... applied a bit delayed)".

**Scope decision**, matching the IPU precedent (Round 522: real register/FIFO skeleton, real MPEG2 decode explicitly deferred): implemented the real, hardware-cited register-level side effects that do NOT require an audio synthesis/envelope engine, and explicitly deferred everything that does.

Implemented in `source/hw/iop_spu2.c` (PS2-native, both cores) and `source/hw/iop_spu_legacy.c` (PS1-compat block): (1) writing a KON bit unconditionally clears the matching ENDX bit for that voice - real, cited, hardware-mandated behavior, needs no synthesis engine. (2) CTRL bits 5-0 (transfer-mode/enable bits) are mirrored into STATUS/STATX bits 5-0 on write - real cited behavior, applied immediately rather than "a bit delayed" since this project has no cycle-accurate timing model (an explicit, documented simplification of a real behavior, not a fabrication). KOFF remains a real write-only trigger (latched, readback returns last value) with no further effect, since its only real consequence - driving an ADSR envelope from Sustain into Release - requires the envelope engine this project does not have. ENDX auto-set-on-real-loop-end is explicitly NOT fabricated, for the same reason.

`include/core/hw/iop_spu_legacy.h` gained five new named, cited register offsets (`SPU_LEGACY_KON/KOFF/ENDX/CTRL/STATUS`) needed to implement the above - `iop_spu2.h` already had the equivalent names from Round 185. For SPU2's per-core KON0/KON1 vs ENDX0/ENDX1 split (voices 0-15 / 16-23), and for SPU-legacy's single 32-bit-wide KON/KOFF/ENDX fields (bits 0-23, one per voice), the write-side-effect logic is applied at 16-bit-half granularity so a 32-bit write correctly drives both halves exactly as two real 16-bit writes would.

**New, concrete finding this round:** disassembled the exact resting PC of thread 1 (the current/RUN thread, priority 64) for the first time - `0x0011c324`, which is `addu $v0, $zero, $zero` (setting the return value to 0), immediately followed by `lw $ra, 40($sp)` / `jr $ra` at `0x0011c328-0x0011c330`. This is the literal tail end of REBOOT's own module `_start`/init function (`0x0011c270`, matching the module table's REBOOT entry point exactly) - thread 1 is captured two instructions from legitimately returning 0 (success) from REBOOT's init. Threads 4/5/6 (CDVDFSV/FILEIO real worker threads, entries `0x0013a2b4`/`0x00141924`/`0x00141b90`) are all `READY` (not `WAIT`) at both 40M and 60M slices - runnable, correctly created, but never actually given the CPU.

**Source cross-check:** `iop_module_loader_try_handle()` (`source/hw/iop_module_loader.c`) sets `st->idle = 1` once "module boot sequence complete" is detected (all 29 real modules loaded/registered - confirmed via `module_count=29` in this round's survey, matching the real IOPBTCONF list). This is itself correct, cited real behavior (task #238's own citation: "real IOP hardware never halts", it idles) - so the IOP genuinely, correctly enters its real post-module-load idle/wait-for-interrupt state. The gap is not that the IOP idles; it's that nothing in the current trace ever performs a genuine THREADMAN scheduler dispatch that would switch the CPU away from the idle trampoline (`BUMP_BASE`, `0x00100000`) into actually running one of the `READY` threads' real code for good. This is the exact same gap Round 512-514/519 already identified and is the site of this project's worst-ever regression (Round 514's overly-broad `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()` fix, reverted in Round 519) - this round adds the precise instruction-level ground truth (thread 1 sits at REBOOT's own natural return point, not stuck in an infinite loop) that was missing before.

The next concrete step is to pull real ps2sdk `threadman`-equivalent source (or disassemble IOP kernel code at the real scheduler-dispatch call site inside/around the trap-stub/panic-loop bypass mechanism) to find the exact real condition that should trigger a context switch when the current thread's init function legitimately returns, before touching `iop_module_loader.c`/`iop_hle_thread.c` again.

## Round 527 (continued): real ps2sdk THREADMAN source confirmed unavailable; READY-vs-WAIT discrepancy reconciled as depth, not a new bug (task #447)

Per the user's request, fetched 6 real ps2sdk pages to look for the IOP-side THREADMAN scheduler internals needed to design a safe fix for the gap identified above:

- `ee/kernel/src/thread.c` (EE-side): shows the real `iWakeupThread`/`iRotateThreadReadyQueue`/`iSuspendThread` wrapper pattern - when called on the *currently running* thread from privileged/interrupt context, real code doesn't dispatch inline; it queues a request and signals a semaphore consumed by a dedicated low-priority "top" (Thread Operations Proxy) helper thread, which then performs the actual `WakeupThread`/`RotateThreadReadyQueue`/`SuspendThread` call safely outside interrupt context. Real, citable, but EE-side kernel HLE convention, not directly the IOP mechanism this project needs.
- `ee/kernel/src/delaythread.c`: a clean, minimal real example of the general "blocked thread woken by a later real event" pattern this project needs to replicate correctly on the IOP side - `DelayThread()` creates a semaphore, arms a timer alarm, `WaitSema`s; the timer's real completion callback (`DelayThreadWakeup_callback`, which runs in interrupt/alarm-handler context) does `iSignalSema()` then `ExitHandler()`. Confirms the general real shape (interrupt/alarm handler signals a primitive, blocked thread's `WaitSema` naturally returns) already assumed correct for CDVDFSV/FILEIO's SleepThread-based dispatcher threads.
- `ee/kernel/src/libosd_full.c`: real `InitOsd()` mechanism for patching OSD-related syscalls (0x5A/0x5B, `SetOsdConfigParam`/`GetOsdConfigParam` families) by copying an embedded `osdsrc` blob to EE RAM and patching the syscall table - a real, citable mechanism, but for third-party/homebrew OSD-syscall compatibility layers, not the retail BIOS's own OSDSYS module load path. Interesting but tangential to the current disc-browser wall; noted for the record, not acted on.

**READY-vs-WAIT discrepancy reconciled:** this round's fresh 40M/60M-slice survey showed threads 4/5/6 as `READY` (not yet run) with no threads 7/8 present, differing from Round 518's documented snapshot (threads 4-8, all `WAIT`/`IOP_TSW_SLEEP`, with 7/8 spawned by CDVDFSV). Cross-checking Round 518's own text confirms this is not a contradiction: Round 518's snapshot was simply taken at a later point in the same real, slow progression this round's 40M-vs-60M comparison already demonstrated - threads 4/5/6 start `READY` (freshly created, not yet run), then genuinely execute once, spawn 7/8, and settle into real `SleepThread` waits. No new bug; consistent with the existing timeline, just a different, earlier sample point.

**Net assessment:** real IOP THREADMAN scheduler internals remain unavailable via any source citation (confirmed, not just assumed, this round) - further progress on the dispatch-handoff gap must come from this project's own disassembly of the real BIOS/IOP ROM's actual scheduler code (the same methodology already used successfully for LOADCORE, SYSMEM, and the SIFCMD dispatch loop), not from ps2sdk source. The next concrete step remains tracing REBOOT's real caller (the return address saved at `40($sp)` in its stack frame, live only in thread 1's saved TCB register context, not statically knowable) to find what real code is supposed to run immediately after REBOOT's module-init legitimately returns - this requires either a live register-context getter for a sleeping/current thread's saved $ra (not currently exposed by `iop_hle_thread.h`) or single-stepping the interpreter across that exact `jr $ra` boundary.

## Round 528: real ps2sdk THREADMAN source review + true idle-trigger PC located (task #447)

**Correction to Round 527 (continued)'s STATUS entry.** That entry concluded "real IOP THREADMAN scheduler internals remain unavailable via any source citation" based on fetching the `iop/system/threadman/src` Doxygen directory-listing page and finding no "Files" table. That conclusion was wrong - the listing page's file table is populated by client-side JavaScript that the raw-HTML fetch tool used that round did not execute, so the page appeared empty when it is not. The user's next message supplied 7 direct URLs into that exact same directory: `thbase.c`, `thcommon.c`, `thevent.c`, `thfpool.c`, `thmsgbx.c`, `thsemap.c`, and the IRX-imports header. These are real, citable, from-scratch reimplementations of Sony's own IOP kernel scheduler (not thin syscall-trap wrappers to an opaque ROM kernel as the corrected understanding might otherwise suggest) - `iop/system/threadman/src/thcommon.c`'s `schedule_next()` contains an actual real priority-bitmap dispatcher (128 priority levels, `readyq_highest()`/`ntz()` bitmap scan, preemption only if the candidate thread's priority number is strictly lower/more-urgent than the current thread's), and `thbase.c`'s `thread_init_and_start()` (called from `StartThread`/`StartThreadArgs`) presets every newly-started real thread's `$ra` to `ExitThread`'s address before first dispatch - the real "thread returns from its own entry function" trampoline mechanism. `thsemap.c`/`thevent.c` implement real waiter-list/bitmask state machines for `WaitSema`/`SignalSema`/`SetEventFlag` (with `i`-prefixed interrupt-context variants deferring the actual context switch to the next `new_context_cb()` invocation), not simplified stand-ins.

**Cross-referenced against this project's own `source/hw/iop_hle_thread.c`.** Three things fell out of this comparison:

1. `ensure_root_thread()` creates thread 1 as a SYNTHETIC bridge construct (arbitrary, uncited priority 64) representing "whatever this project's sequential module loader was already running" - fundamentally different from a real `CreateThread()`-created thread, since it never goes through `thread_init_and_start()` and therefore has no `$ra=ExitThread` trampoline preset. This means the working hypothesis carried over from Round 527 - "thread 1's `jr $ra` return from REBOOT should transfer into a real `ExitThread`-equivalent" - was wrong; an ordinary module-init subroutine return is not a thread-exit event for this synthetic thread.

2. This project's own `pick_next_ready()` (priority-bitmap-style selection, ties broken by ready-sequence/FIFO) and `reschedule()` (save/restore context swap, called from ~18 real syscall-trap handlers throughout the file) already closely mirror the real `schedule_next()`/`readyq_highest()` algorithm just reviewed - the dispatch mechanism itself is not the gap.

3. `iop_hle_thread_get_pc(thid)` reads the TCB's *stored* `pc` snapshot field, updated only by an explicit `save_context()` call during a real context-switch-away event - not the live CPU `iop_state_t->pc`. For a thread that has never been switched away (thread 1, priority 64, more urgent than threads 4/5/6's 80/96), this getter can report a stale position.

**True idle-trigger PC located (empirically, this round).** Built a scratch-only instrumented copy of `iop_module_loader.c` (`/tmp/round528_instr_loader.c`, not part of the tracked tree) adding a one-shot diagnostic print at each of the 5 `st->idle = 1;` sites inside `iop_module_loader_try_handle()`, then linked it into a fresh boot-survey driver against the existing precompiled regression-suite objects and ran a 40M-slice organic boot (real BIOS + real Tekken Tag Tournament Demo disc). Result:

- Site 5 - the **genuine, one-time "all modules ran to completion" path** (task #92/#179's documented normal completion, *not* any panic-loop or trap-stub emergency bypass) - fires exactly once, with `run_to_completion=28` already recorded and `reg_walk_bypassed=1` (one earlier registration-walk-panic-loop bypass assisted advancing past one module along the way, not a permanent halt). This event is the 29th and final module (EESYNC) completing its own real init code and falling through to the shared trampoline address `g.trampoline_addr = 0x00100000`.
- Site 4 - the intentional, already-documented (Round 425/426) re-park block - then fires on every subsequent re-entry: 12,080,553 times across the remaining ~34M slices of the 40M-slice run, each time harmlessly re-asserting `st->idle = 1` exactly as its own header comment describes.
- Sites 1/2/3 (the panic-loop, trap-stub, and registration-walk emergency-bypass completion paths) never fired at all this run.

**This directly answers the open question from Round 527: is `0x0011c324` (REBOOT's ordinary function return, disassembled that round) the true idle-trigger site?** No. The true, final trigger site is `g.trampoline_addr = 0x00100000`, reached only after literally all 29 real BIOS/IOP modules (SYSMEM through EESYNC, the full real IOPBTCONF order) have run their own real init code to completion - including CDVDFSV (entry `0x0013a1b0`) and FILEIO (entry `0x00140c20`), the two modules whose worker threads were the subject of Round 518's investigation. The "premature idle-bypass truncating real necessary work" hypothesis that motivated this round's investigation is **disproven**: nothing is being cut short here.

**The stale-TCB-snapshot hypothesis is now fully explained, not just suspected.** `0x0011c324` is REBOOT's real syscall-return address: REBOOT's own init code (module 21 of 29) issues a real recognized syscall (syscall #6, via the `jal 0x0011c574` at `0x0011c31c` disassembled in Round 527) - a real MIPS `jal` sets the return address to `jal_addr + 8` (delay-slot convention), i.e. exactly `0x0011c324`. That syscall's handler in `iop_hle_thread.c` legitimately calls `reschedule()`, which calls `save_context()` and correctly captures thread 1's TCB `pc` snapshot at that address. Because thread 1 remained the highest-priority ready thread throughout (as established above), it was never subsequently context-switched away, so no later `save_context()` call ever refreshed the snapshot - even though `iop_module_loader.c`'s own front-loading trampoline mechanism (`advance_to_next_module()`) directly manipulates the live CPU `pc`, bypassing `iop_hle_thread.c`'s save/load-context path entirely, and carried real execution forward through 7 more modules (LOADFILE, CDVDMAN, CDVDFSV, SIFINIT, FILEIO, SECRMAN, EESYNC) after REBOOT. The module-loading front-loader and the IOP thread-scheduler's context-tracking are two distinct, only loosely-coupled subsystems operating on the same `iop_state_t` - this is by design, not a bug, and the TCB `pc` field is diagnostic bookkeeping for thread 1, not a control input used anywhere in dispatch. A secondary implication: REBOOT was the *last* of modules 21-28 to issue any recognized syscall that touches `iop_hle_thread.c`'s real dispatch path during this boot - modules 22-28 either issue no such syscalls during their own init, or take a different dispatch path (e.g. the trap-stub bypass) that doesn't touch the TCB.

**The `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()` "already tried, did not work" history (rediscovered this round while reading `iop_hle_thread.c` in full) remains unresolved and was deliberately not re-attempted.** That guarded, one-time, correctly-scoped experiment (Round 519, disabled) retired thread 1 and still saw RPC delivery stay at 0 - directly falsifying the assumption that RPC delivery is purely interrupt/DMA-driven and independent of thread 1's scheduling state, despite no explicit code coupling between `current_thread_id` and any RPC/interrupt-dispatch logic being found via grep (outside `iop_hle_thread.c` itself). This round's findings narrow *where* the dispatch-handoff gap is not (it is not premature module-loader truncation, and it is not a stale-PC display bug), but do not yet explain *why* thread-1 retirement breaks RPC delivery - per the code's own explicit warning and this project's "go slow" pacing rule, no new fix was attempted at this site.

**Classification:** docs-only round - the only new file is the scratch, untracked `/tmp/round528_instr_loader.c` diagnostic copy; no tracked source changed. Regression suite and Wii rebuild correctly skipped.

## Round 529: real ps2sdk IOPDEBUG review + thread-1 retirement re-tested with new evidence (task #447)

Per the user's 2 new URLs, reviewed real ps2sdk `iop/debug/iopdebug/src/iop_debug.c` (the real `IOP_RegFrame`/`iop_dbg_install()`/`iop_exception_dispatcher()` mechanism, a genuine third-party/homebrew debug-exception-handler library built on the real `RegisterDefaultExceptionHandler()`/`RegisterPriorityExceptionHandler()` EXCEPMAN API). Confirmed this is off the retail OSDSYS boot path (IOPDEBUG is not among this project's real 29-module IOPBTCONF list) - same category as Round 527's `libosd_full.c` finding - but its "install a real exception handler, capture the true live register frame" pattern directly informed this round's methodology: rather than trust `iop_hle_thread_get_pc()`'s TCB snapshot (shown stale in Round 528), this round instrumented and directly read live `iop_state_t` fields.

**Re-tested `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()` with new evidence, per the code's own explicit requirement before ever touching this site again.** Built two scratch-only diagnostic drivers (`/tmp/round529_retire_diag.c`, calling the already-compiled-but-unused `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()` at the exact moment of genuine module-loader completion; `/tmp/round529_control_diag.c`, identical but skipping the retire call) and ran both to 40M slices with periodic fine-grained snapshots (`iop->pc`, `iop->idle`, `iop->halted`, `current_thread_id`, per-thread status/PC, RPC counters) every 200,000 slices early on and every 5,000,000 slices later. Neither driver modifies tracked source - `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()` is a real, already-linked, exported symbol.

Result, directly contradicting the historical Round 519 "rpc_pending_sets stayed 0" framing under the **current** codebase:

- **RPC delivery is identical between the retired and non-retired runs at every single checkpoint** (2 -> 107 -> 112 -> 117 -> 131 -> 148 -> 164 -> 180 -> 196 -> 212 -> 228, same values at the same slice depths in both runs, reaching 228 by slice 40M in both - matching the long-established baseline exactly). This is decisive: it proves SIF RPC delivery in this codebase is entirely independent of which IOP "thread" is current, and independent of whether the IOP CPU is executing any instructions at all (see next finding).
- Retiring thread 1 does cause thread 4 (a real CDVDFSV worker thread, previously perpetually `READY`-but-never-scheduled per Round 512/513/518) to actually become `RUN` and execute real code for the first time - briefly. Within 200,000 slices of being scheduled, thread 4's code reaches a real IOP BIOS `EXIT`/`_EXIT` syscall (the A0-table call handled in `source/hw/iop_hle_bios.c`, the *only* code site anywhere in this project that sets `st->halted = 1`). From that point on `iop->halted` reads 1 for the rest of the run (confirmed directly via the `iop_state_t.halted` field, not inferred).
- Cross-checked `iop_core_step()` (`source/core/iop/iop_core.c`): the very first line is `if (g_iop.halted) return 1;` - once halted, the IOP core does not tick timers, does not check interrupts, does not do anything at all, ever again. This is a strictly worse terminal state than the current code's deliberate `idle` (interrupt-responsive, timers still tick per `iop_core_step()`'s own header comment) - retirement trades a real, working, interrupt-responsive idle state for a real, permanent, total CPU stop, for zero RPC benefit.
- EE-side progress is completely unaffected either way (`ee_pc=0x0050172C` at 40M slices in both runs, matching the long-established baseline) - so this round's retirement experiment, unlike Round 519's original (unguarded, wrong-thread) version, causes no EE-side regression either. It's a clean, harmless-but-useless result, not a repeat of the historical incident's severity.

**A methodology note, not a code finding:** an earlier attempt this round to disassemble thread 4's real code (to see the exact `EXIT` call site) used a scratch RAM-dump tool that read `iop_state_t.ram` with an incorrect offset/assumption - verified broken by cross-checking against REBOOT's own well-established real entry point (`0x0011c270`, real disassembled code per Round 527/528), which the same broken tool also showed as all-zero. The "thread 4's code is all NOPs" observation from that broken dump has been discarded; it is a tooling artifact, not a real finding. All conclusions in this entry rest on the proper getter-function-based instrumentation (`iop_hle_thread_get_*()`, direct `iop_state_t` field reads via `iop_core_get_state()`), which is unaffected by this bug.

**Conclusion on `iop_hle_thread_retire_root_thread()`:** this round supplies the new evidence the code's own guard comment explicitly required, but the verdict is unchanged - do not wire it back up. The specific symptom described in Round 519 ("rpc_pending_sets stayed 0") does not reproduce under the current codebase, so whatever exact interaction caused that historical result has evidently changed since (likely as a side effect of the Round 520-528 subsystem audits/fixes) - but the underlying reason retirement is not useful is now precisely understood rather than mysterious: it hands the CPU to a real worker thread that immediately exits, permanently halting the IOP for no compensating gain, since RPC delivery was never gated by thread-scheduling state in the first place. `iop_hle_thread.c`'s own header comment above this function should be read alongside this entry, not replaced by it.
